statement: The mission, vision, and goals of the cluster support the safety and quality of care, treatment, and services.
elements: Cluster governance describes, in writing, its mission, vision, and goals that support the safety and quality of care, treatment, and services.
Cluster governance develops a written plan to communicate the mission, vision, and goals to health care organization staff and the population(s) the organization serves.
The cluster mission, vision, and goals guide the actions of health care organization leaders.

statement: The structure and authority of cluster governance are described in bylaws, policies and procedures, or similar documents.
elements: The structure and authority of cluster governance are described in a written document, bylaws, policies and procedures, and/or similar document(s).
The document(s) identifies members of cluster governance and describes when and how the authority of governance can be delegated.
The cluster evaluates governance annually and documents the results.

statement: The operational responsibilities and accountabilities of cluster governance are described in a written document(s).
elements: Cluster governance approves the cluster’s strategic plans, operational plans, policies, and procedures, and approves, periodically reviews, and makes public the cluster’s mission statement.
Cluster governance approves the cluster’s capital and operating budget(s) and allocates other resources required to meet each organization’s mission.
Cluster governance approves the cluster’s participation in health care professional education and research and in the oversight of the quality of such programs.
Cluster governance appoints and annually evaluates each health care organization’s executive leader, and the evaluation is documented.
Cluster governance appoints and annually evaluates each executive leader at the cluster level, and the evaluation is documented.

statement: Cluster governance oversees the cluster’s program for quality improvement and patient safety and regularly receives and acts on reports of the quality improvement and patient safety program.
elements: Cluster governance annually approves the cluster-wide program for quality improvement and patient safety.
Cluster governance receives and acts on reports of the quality improvement and patient safety program at least quarterly, including reports of adverse and sentinel events.
Minutes reflect actions taken and any follow-up on those actions.

statement: Cluster governance establishes a strategic plan that involves all health care organizations in the cluster.
elements: Cluster governance partners with leaders of health care organizations in defining cluster-wide strategies.

Cluster governance aligns strategies that include the following items: • Aligning existing cluster-wide policies and procedures to promote consistently high-quality care delivery throughout the enterprise, at all times, on reducing harm (See also GLS.4.) • Assisting health care organizations with advancing knowledge, skills, and competence of staff by recommending methods that will improve quality and patient safety processes (See also HRC.1.) • Encouraging and recommending proactive quality improvement and patient safety methods that will increase accountability, trust, and knowledge while reducing the impact of fear and blame

statement: Cluster governance provides the foundation for effective alignment and performance of systems that affect the safety and quality of the delivery of care, treatment, and services.
elements: Cluster governance sets expectations for using data and information to identify and respond to internal and external changes in the environment.
Cluster-wide planning of care, treatment, and services is systematic and involves designated individuals and information sources.
Cluster governance establishes a communication process on the variety of care, treatment, and services available from each health care organization.
Cluster governance has a systematic approach to operational changes and performance improvement.
Cluster governance oversees the provision of a sufficient number and mix of individuals appropriate to the scope and complexity of the services offered.

statement: Cluster governance aligns programs and services to support the patient-centered delivery of integrated care, treatment, and services.
elements: Cluster governance identifies programs and services that may be aligned to promote consistent and uniform practice.
Cluster-wide programs incorporate the needs of patient populations and clinical care partners throughout the cluster.
Changes to cluster-wide programs consider potential risks to patient populations and incorporate mitigation strategies.
Cluster governance establishes policies and procedures for each identified cluster-wide program and service.

statement: Cluster governance plans, develops, and implements a cluster-wide quality improvement and patient safety program within its performance improvement activities.
elements: Cluster governance identifies five high-priority patient safety initiatives at cluster level that affect individual organizations.
Patient safety initiatives focus on high-volume, high-risk, or problem-prone processes as key performance indicators (KPIs) for performance improvement activities.
The five KPIs identified by cluster governance are communicated to all health care organizations in the cluster.
Cluster governance reprioritizes performance improvement activities in response to changes in the internal or external environment.

statement: Cluster governance develops and implements an evidence-based process to allocate appropriate resources (human and technical), understanding the quality and safety implications of resource allocation decisions for each individual organization.
elements: Cluster governance uses data and information on the quality and safety implications of medical equipment choices.
Cluster governance uses data and information on the quality and safety implications of staffing choices and cluster-wide staffing assignments.
Cluster governance uses the recommendations of professional organizations and other authoritative sources in making resource decisions.
Cluster governance provides direction, support, and oversight of health information technology resources.
Cluster governance provides direction, support, and oversight of the emergency and disaster management program(s).
Cluster governance monitors the results of its decisions and uses the data to evaluate and improve the quality of its resource purchasing and allocation decisions.

statement: Cluster governance identifies and uses data on supply chain safety to protect patients and staff from unstable, contaminated, defective, and counterfeit supplies.
elements: Cluster governance outlines the steps in the supply chains for supplies defined as at most risk.
Cluster governance identifies any significant risk points in the steps of the supply chains.
Cluster governance makes resource decisions based on its understanding of the risk points in supply chains.
The cluster has a process for tracing supplies found to be unstable, contaminated, defective, or counterfeit to their source.
The cluster notifies the manufacturer and/or distributor when unstable, contaminated, defective, or counterfeit supplies are identified.
Cluster governance notifies health care organizations when unstable, contaminated, defective, or counterfeit supplies are identified. Communication and Patient Care Coordination

statement: Cluster governance develops and implements a process to ensure effective communication and coordination throughout the cluster.
elements: Cluster governance coordinates with leadership from each health care organization on the type of care, treatment, and services as follows: • Provide the type of care and services that are consistent with the mission and needs of the patient population(s) served by the organization. • Communicate with key stakeholders in its community to facilitate access to care and information about its patient care services (for example, ongoing communication with key community stakeholder groups; direct communication to individuals or through public media, agencies in the community, or third parties). • Communication includes information on the hours of operations and services provided. • Provide data and communicate information related to safety and quality of its services to stakeholders, which include nursing staff, nonclinical and management staff, patients, families,

statement: Cluster governance develops and implements a process to coordinate, review, select, and monitor clinical and nonclinical contracts at the cluster level.
elements: Cluster governance works with health care organization leadership to ensure that the services provided through contractual agreements meet patient and management needs.
Cluster governance describes, in writing, the nature and scope of services provided through contractual agreements.

Cluster governance involves health care organization department/service leaders in reviewing and selecting all clinical and nonclinical contracts and identifies individuals who are accountable for monitoring those contracts.
Cluster governance establishes a process to inspect compliance with contracted services as needed.
When contracts are renegotiated or terminated, cluster governance has a plan to ensure continuity of patient services throughout the cluster.

statement: Cluster governance ensures that contracts and other arrangements are included in individual organizations’ quality improvement and patient safety programs.
elements: All contracts stipulate the quality data to be reported to cluster governance, the reporting frequency and mechanism, and how the health care organization will respond when quality requirements or expectations are not met.
Quality data reported under contracts are integrated into the cluster’s quality improvement and patient safety program.

The relevant clinical and managerial leaders from health care organizations participate with the quality improvement and patient safety program in analyzing quality and safety information from outside contracts.

statement: Cluster governance establishes a framework for ethical management that promotes a culture of ethical practices and decision-making to ensure that patient care, treatment, and services are provided within business, financial, ethical, and legal norms and protect patients and their rights.
elements: Cluster governance establishes a framework for ethical management that promotes a culture of ethical practices and decision-making to ensure the protection of patients and their rights.
The ethical framework ensures that patient care is provided within business, financial, ethical, and legal norms.
Cluster governance ensures nondiscrimination in employment practices and provision of patient care in the context of the country’s cultural and regulatory norms.
Cluster governance examines national and international ethical norms for incorporation when developing the framework for ethical conduct.

statement: The cluster’s framework for ethical management addresses operational and business issues, including marketing, admissions, transfer, discharge, and disclosure of ownership, and any business and professional conflicts that may not be in patients’ best interests.
elements: Cluster governance discloses its ownership and any conflicts of interest.
Cluster governance accurately portrays its services to patients.
The cluster accurately bills for services and ensures that financial incentives and payment arrangements do not compromise patient care.

statement: The cluster’s framework for ethical management addresses ethical issues and decision-making in clinical care.
elements: The cluster’s framework for ethical management establishes a mechanism by which health care practitioners and other staff may raise ethical concerns without fear of retribution.
The cluster organizational structure(s) and processes support oversight of professional ethical issues.
Support for identifying and addressing ethical concerns is readily available and includes ethics resources and training for health care practitioners and other staff.
Cluster governance requires health care organizations to effectively resolve ethical conflicts that arise in a timely way.

statement: Cluster governance supports and coordinates the culture of safety program across all its health care organizations.
elements: Cluster governance provides a coordinated system to manage adverse event reporting, including sentinel event reporting as defined in the National Sentinel Event policy, and the process should embed the principle of just culture.
The process for supporting the cluster-wide safety culture includes allocating any resources necessary to respond to adverse/sentinel events.
The process for supporting the cluster-wide safety culture includes disseminating lessons learned from the review of adverse/sentinel events across the cluster.
Cluster governance uses measures to evaluate and monitor the safety culture across the cluster and identifies and implements improvements.

group: Coordinated Response to Global Communicable Diseases
statement: Cluster governance develops, implements, and evaluates an emergency preparedness program to respond to the presentation of global communicable diseases.
elements: Cluster governance develops and implements an emergency preparedness program to respond to the presentation of global communicable diseases.

The emergency preparedness program addresses the following: • Identification of the signs and symptoms of communicable diseases • Communication of the presence or potential presence of communicable disease across the cluster • Coordination of the response to the presentation of communicable disease across the cluster

The coordination process developed by governance addresses the following: • The allocation of patients depending on clinical needs and isolation requirements • The allocation of resources—including staff, physical space (such as available rooms), and

statement: The cluster program establishes program-specific performance improvement (PI) priorities.
elements: The program’s leadership uses patient and family feedback to identify at least three priorities for cluster-level PI.
The program’s leadership sets priorities for PI activities, including consideration of data related to close calls (“near misses”), hazardous conditions, and adverse safety events.
The program’s PI priorities and activities focus on patient outcomes.

The program’s leadership reprioritizes PI improvement activities in response to changes across the continuum of care. For example, these changes could include infection prevention and control surveillance activities or variance in performance measurement results.

statement: The program’s leadership conducts performance improvement (PI) activities that span the continuum of care.
elements: The ongoing PI activities occur programwide.
Program PI activities in the cluster focus on improving the quality, safety, patient-centeredness, and clinical integration of care, treatment, and services.

The program collects data on chronic disease management outcomes from each of the cluster’s health care organizations as required by the Saudi Model of Care, including adherence rates, follow-up visits, and health outcomes such as HbA1c levels, blood pressure control, and reduction in hospitalizations.

The program collects data on patients’ experiences, including the following, from each of the cluster’s health care organizations: • Patient access within established time frames • Patient experience and satisfaction with care, treatment, and services • Patient satisfaction with communication across the program, including education • Patient perception of comprehensiveness of care, treatment, and services • Patient perception of how well their care was coordinated across the program • Patient perception of the continuity of care, treatment, and services

The program collects and analyzes data on measures related to integration of care, to extract PI opportunities. Examples of measures being collected by health care entities for other purposes that can contribute to understanding effectiveness of clinical care integration include the following: • Wait times for scheduling ambulatory care appointments • Ambulatory appointment no-shows • Hospital readmissions • Hospital lengths of stay • Emergency department and urgent care utilization • Home care initial assessment visit timing, frequency of visits, referrals to the emergency

statement: The program evaluates the effectiveness of its processes that support clinical integration and coordinated care.
elements: The program evaluates how well it supports the continuity of care, including partnering with the patient to deliver care that meets the patient’s needs.
The program evaluates new or modified services or processes to determine if expected results have been achieved.
The program evaluates the care, treatment, and services received by patients who are referred to nonprogram providers.

statement: The cluster develops and implements a quality improvement and patient safety program to manage data generated by health care organizations and at the cluster level.
elements: The cluster develops and implements a quality improvement and patient safety program to manage risk assessment data throughout the cluster and data generated at the cluster level.
An individual(s) experienced in improvement methods and processes guides the cluster quality improvement and patient safety program.

The individual(s) with oversight for the quality improvement and patient safety program selects and supports qualified staff for the program and supports staff with quality improvement and patient safety responsibilities throughout the cluster.

The cluster develops, implements, and maintains systemwide quality programs in the following areas: • Quality improvement and patient safety • Medication management • Prevention and control of infections • Facility management and safety of the environment • Management of information

The cluster quality improvement and patient safety program includes the following elements: • The collation of data from each health care organization program mentioned above • The prioritization of risks • Processes to support each organization to mitigate the identified risks • Processes for managing the data requirements at the cluster level • A standardized approach for conducting quality improvement initiatives across the enterprise
The cluster has a process to collect data on any interventions implemented at the cluster level and monitor outcomes to evaluate the effectiveness of the interventions.

statement: The cluster quality improvement and patient safety program includes a process for aggregating, analyzing, and communicating data.
elements: The cluster quality improvement and patient safety program implements a process for data aggregation, analysis, and communication.
The program uses these data to measure, analyze, and validate performance in the following ways: • Services within individual health care organizations (at a more detailed level, according to the

statement: Cluster quality improvement and patient safety program staff support the measure selection process at the cluster level and coordinate and integrate measurement activities at the cluster level.
elements: The cluster quality improvement and patient safety program supports the selection of measures, including five key performance indicators (KPIs) at the cluster level.
The cluster quality improvement and patient safety program coordinates and integrates measurement activities throughout the cluster.
The cluster quality improvement and patient safety program supports the monitoring of the five KPIs at the cluster level.
The cluster quality improvement and patient safety program aggregates and analyzes International Patient Safety Goals (IPSGs) data from each health care organization.

The cluster quality improvement and patient safety program has a process to collect data on any interventions implemented at the cluster level and monitors outcomes to evaluate the effectiveness of the interventions.

statement: Cluster leadership builds a culture and environment that uses data, evidence-based practices, and current scientific knowledge to promote continuous learning and high reliability.
elements: Cluster leadership builds a culture and environment that promotes continuous learning and high reliability.1

Cluster leadership creates the framework to work toward the goal of becoming a high reliability organization, defined as the following: • Leadership committed to the goal of zero harm • An organizational safety culture where all staff can speak up about things that would negatively

statement: The cluster develops and implements a process to manage the flow and exchange of information throughout the cluster.
elements: The cluster develops and implements a process to manage the flow and exchange of information throughout the cluster.
The cluster determines which information management systems are uniform throughout the cluster.
The information management process addresses the following: • Coordination of information flow from each health care organization throughout the cluster as

group: Management of Policies, Procedures, and Protocols
statement: Documents, including policies, procedures, and protocols, are managed in a consistent and uniform manner across the cluster.
elements: There is a written guidance document that defines the requirements for developing and maintaining policies, procedures, protocols, and programs, including at least key elements: • Review and approval of all documents by an authorized person before issue • The process and frequency for periodic review and reapproval of documents • The controls for ensuring that only current, relevant versions of documents are available • Clear identification of changes in or updates to a document • Maintenance of document identity and legibility • Identification of where the document applies (for example, at one specific health care

group: Management of Policies, Procedures, and Protocols
statement: The cluster coordinates and standardizes policies, procedures, protocols, and clinical practice guidelines as appropriate to the services provided.
elements: The cluster determines, in writing, which policies, procedures, and/or protocols are uniform across all health care organizations.
The cluster assesses at least annually the clinical and operational departments and services provided by the health care organizations of the cluster.
There is a process to ensure that staff have read, are familiar with, and implement policies, procedures, and protocols that are standardized throughout the cluster.

group: Management of Policies, Procedures, and Protocols
statement: The cluster uses standardized diagnosis and procedure codes and ensures uniform use of approved symbols and abbreviations across the cluster.
elements: The cluster uses standardized diagnosis codes and procedure codes such as ICD10 coding (International Classification of Diseases, 10th revision).
The cluster implements uniform use of approved symbols and identifies those not to be used.
If the cluster allows abbreviations, the cluster implements uniform use of approved abbreviations, and each abbreviation has only one meaning.
If the cluster allows abbreviations, the cluster develops and/or adopts a do-not-use list of abbreviations.
Abbreviations are not used on informed consent and patient rights documents, discharge instructions, and discharge summaries.

statement: The cluster develops a staffing strategy that identifies the needs of individual health care organizations and its effect on cluster-wide operations.
elements: The cluster develops a written, systemwide strategy for staffing in a manner that complies with local laws and regulations.
The cluster coordinates with health care organizations to define in the strategy the adequate number, types, and desired qualifications of staff using a recognized staffing method.
The strategy addresses the assignment, reassignment, and rotation of staff throughout the cluster.
The effectiveness of the cluster staffing strategy is monitored and updated when necessary.

statement: Each staff member’s role and responsibilities are defined in a current job description.
elements: Each staff member not permitted to practice independently has a job description.

The following individuals have a job description appropriate to their activities and responsibilities or have been privileged to work in the organizations. Job descriptions are also needed for the following health care practitioners, who may or may not be licensed to practice independently: • The individual serves in primarily a managerial role, such as a department manager, or in dual clinical and managerial roles, with the managerial responsibilities identified in a job description. • The individual has some clinical responsibilities for which they have not been authorized to practice independently, such as an independent practitioner learning a new role or new skill. • The individual is in an educational program and under supervision, and the academic program identifies, for each stage or level of training, what can be done independently and what must be completed under supervision; the program description can serve as the job description in such cases. • The individual is permitted to temporarily provide services in the health care organizations, for example, a nurse from a temporary staffing agency.
Job descriptions are current according to cluster and health care organization policy.

statement: There is documented personnel information for each staff member of the cluster.
elements: Personnel files for each staff member are standardized, maintained, current, and kept confidential according to cluster and health care organization policy.
Personnel files contain the staff member’s qualifications and work history.
Personnel files contain the staff member’s job description when applicable.
Personnel files contain a record of orientation to the cluster and the health care organization, the staff member’s specific role, and in-service education attended by the staff member.
Personnel files contain the results of performance reviews.
Personnel files contain required health information.

statement: Leaders develop and implement a cluster-wide process for recruiting, evaluating, and appointing staff that meets the needs of all health care organizations.
elements: Cluster leaders establish and implement a cluster-wide process to recruit staff.
Cluster leaders establish and implement a cluster-wide process to evaluate the qualifications of new staff.
Cluster leaders establish and implement a cluster-wide process to appoint individuals to the staff.
Cluster leaders establish and implement a cluster-wide process that is uniform across the cluster for similar types of staff.

group: Standardized Staff Orientation and Safety Requirements
statement: All clinical and nonclinical staff members are oriented to the cluster, the health care organization, the department or unit to which they are assigned, and their specific job responsibilities upon appointment to the staff.
elements: The cluster provides uniform and standardized staff orientation to new clinical and nonclinical staff.
Standardized staff orientation includes the following: • Cluster governance structure and its relation to the specific health care organizations to which

group: Standardized Staff Orientation and Safety Requirements
statement: The cluster provides a staff health and safety program that addresses staff physical and mental health and safe working conditions.
elements: The cluster provides a staff health and safety program that is responsive to urgent and nonurgent staff needs through direct treatment and referral.
The staff health and safety program addresses the following: • Initial employment health screening • Measures to control harmful occupational exposures, such as exposure to toxic drugs and

group: Standardized Staff Orientation and Safety Requirements
statement: The cluster identifies staff at risk for exposure to and possible transmission of vaccine-preventable diseases and implements a cluster-wide staff vaccination and immunization program.
elements: The cluster coordinates with health care organizations to identify epidemiologically significant infectious disease, as well as staff at high risk for exposure to and transmission of infections.
The cluster develops and implements a cluster-wide staff vaccination and immunization program consistent with local laws and regulations.
The cluster evaluates the risks associated with unvaccinated staff and identifies strategies for reducing the patients’ risk of exposure to infectious diseases from unvaccinated staff.

The cluster coordinates with the health care organization’s infection prevention and control program and provides cluster-wide support for evaluation, counseling, and follow-up of staff exposed to infectious diseases.

statement: Cluster leadership ensures that licensed health care professionals and licensed independent health care practitioners not employed by the cluster have the right credentials and are competent and/or privileged for the services provided to the cluster’s patients.
elements: The cluster coordinates with health care organization leadership to determine those services that will be provided by licensed independent practitioners outside the cluster.

All diagnostic, consultative, and treatment services provided by licensed independent practitioners outside the cluster are credentialed and privileged based on the scope of services that they will be assigned to in each site.
Licensed independent practitioners who provide patient care services in the cluster but are not employees or members of the clinical staff are credentialed, privileged, and evaluated.
Any support staff accompanying independent practitioners and providing care, treatment, and services in the cluster are compliant with requirements for primary source verification.
The quality of care, treatment, and services provided by independent practitioners outside the cluster is monitored as part of the cluster-wide quality improvement and patient safety program.

When the cluster uses staff contracts for licensed health care professional staff, the cluster ensures that a credentials review comparable to the health care organization’s review process is conducted.
When the cluster uses staff contracts for licensed health care professional staff, the cluster ensures that the licensed employees’ practice licenses are renewed in a timely manner.

statement: The program is organized to provide integrated care.
elements: The health care organizations in the cluster and clinical care sites that have organized into an integrated care program are identified in writing.

The program plans and organizes structures, processes, and resources to provide integrated care that supports continuity and coordination of care, including at least the following: • Emergency services and inpatient admission • Primary care services • Diagnostic services and treatment services • Surgical and nonsurgical treatment services • Outpatient care programs • Other organizations and other care settings
The program engages patients and families to guide the development and refinement of its structures, processes, and resources to support the delivery of integrated care.
The program evaluates available resources, identifies additional resources needed, and then obtains the needed resources to achieve the delivery of patient-centered, integrated care.
The program’s health care organizations identify and agree on strategies, priorities, and timelines for achieving clinically integrated, patient-centered care, treatment, and services.

statement: Individuals responsible for program leadership are identified, and the roles and responsibilities of program leadership are defined.
elements: The program identifies individuals responsible for the integrated care program, including representatives from all participating health care organizations.
The program leaders delineate responsibility for planning and managing activities that are key to achieving and sustaining integration and coordination across health care organizations.

statement: The program defines its mission, vision, and goals.
elements: The program describes in writing its mission, vision, and goals for clinical integration.
The mission, vision, and goals of the program guide the provision of comprehensive, patient-centered care, treatment, and services.
The program adopts a culture of safety that spans the continuum of care.
The program defines specific clinical and operational performance goals.

statement: The program’s services and processes are designed to support the delivery of integrated care, treatment, and services that are population based and patient centered.
elements: The program’s design of new or modified services or processes incorporates the needs of its patient population and health care organizations.
The program identifies health care priorities for its patient population.
The program identifies health care disparities in its patient population.
The results of performance improvement activities influence the program’s design of new or modified services or processes.
The program’s design of new or modified services or processes considers potential risks to its patient population and incorporates mitigation strategies.
The program’s design of new or modified services or processes incorporates evidence-based information in the decision-making process.
The program uses the identified health care priorities and health care disparities to inform the design of new or modified services.
The program tests and analyzes its design of new or modified services or processes to determine the impact on clinical care partners, patients, and families.

statement: Program communication processes facilitate the delivery of integrated care, treatment, and services that are safe, high quality, and patient centered.
elements: Program leaders provide for the resources needed to support timely communication of accurate patient health information among its health care organizations.
The program requires and facilitates clinical decision support tools, care plans, or guidelines to guide decision-making as applicable to its health care organizations.

The program requires and facilitates use of health information technology for the patient’s medical record(s) by health care organizations to do the following: • Support the continuity of care, with medical record(s) or transfer summary with details of the reason for admission, significant findings, diagnosis, procedures, medications, other treatments, and the patient’s condition at transfer. • Document and track the patient’s care, treatment, and services. • Share the patient’s goals for care, treatment, and services. • Share data about the patient’s health literacy needs. • Share and synchronize the patient’s plan for care. • Support safe medication management. • Support disease management. • Support preventive care. • Exchange information between clinical care sites. • Support performance improvement activities.
Program leaders monitor and evaluate the effectiveness of communication processes.

statement: The cluster organizations involve the patient and their family, when appropriate, in care and treatment planning and decisions.
elements: The cluster organizations establish guidelines and performance expectations related to involvement of the patient and their family, when appropriate, in care, treatment, and services, whenever possible. These guidelines and performance expectations include at least the following: • Respecting patient rights to make decisions about their care and treatment • Identifying patient health literacy needs and providing education that meets their needs • Encouraging patients to establish an ongoing relationship with a primary care clinician when

statement: The cluster organizations provide care, treatment, and services in a manner that facilitates clinically integrated care.
elements: The cluster incorporates the principles of chronic disease management models into the design and plan for clinically integrated care.

The cluster organizations use clinical practice guidelines to design or improve processes that evaluate and treat specific diagnoses, conditions, or symptoms aligned with the Saudi Model of Care and Integrated Pathways. The list should include but it is not limited to the following: • ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction (STEMI) • Stroke Pathway • Master Major Trauma • Master Breast Cancer Screening • Master Colorectal Cancer Screening • Type II Diabetes Mellitus • Obesity • Master Palliative Care • Hypertension • Dyslipidemia Intensive Care Coordination Plan (ICCP)
The cluster requires clinical care services to use an interdisciplinary approach in providing patient care, treatment, and services.

The cluster organizations identify the need for and composition of each patient’s interdisciplinary team. The team must include a physician, nurse, and professionals relevant to the Integrated Care Pathways.
The cluster organizations establish interdisciplinary team membership to provide comprehensive, coordinated care throughout the patient’s course of care, treatment, and services.
The cluster requires cluster organizations to form interdisciplinary teams that include representatives from different cluster organizations in order to meet a patient’s needs.

statement: The cluster facilitates transition-of-care activities that promote patient safety and quality of care.
elements: The cluster organizations define and implement risk-screening criteria for identifying patients in need of increased support to manage chronic, unstable illnesses.

The cluster organizations develop a process to manage transitions of care and provide or facilitate patient access (in person or by telehealth) to the following, as needed: • Admission to a hospital • Case management services or care coordination assistance • Primary care services • Appointments with cluster organizations following hospital admission • Preventive services that are age- and gender-specific • Behavioral health care services • Oral health services • Substance use treatment services • Urgent or emergent care services • Home care services, including home health, home infusion, durable medical equipment, and

statement: Patients admitted to the hospital or who seek outpatient services are screened to identify if their health care needs match the hospital’s mission, scope of care, and resources.
elements: The hospital has a written policy that defines the screening methods and tests required before accepting patients for care.

The policy is implemented, and the screening results determine if patients are accepted or admitted to the hospital, dependent on patient needs matching the hospital’s mission, scope of care, and available resources.
The hospital has a policy and procedure for elective admissions and patients admitted for a day procedure.
Screening of patients in the emergency department is performed during triage or before admission to inpatient areas.
The hospital has a policy and procedure for admitting emergency patients.

The hospital has a written policy aligned with the Integrated Cluster Care Model for receiving patients referred from the cluster’s primary care centers, hospitals, home care organizations, and long-term care organizations.
Patients outside the hospital’s mission, scope of care, or available resources are assessed and stabilized within the capacity of the hospital prior to transfer.

The hospital transfers, refers, or assists the patient or family in identifying and/or obtaining appropriate sources of care if their needs do not match the hospital’s mission, scope of care, or available resources.
Patients are admitted to the service or unit that meets their most urgent needs.
Assessments and treatments completed prior to transfer are documented in a record maintained by the transferring hospital. (See also ACC.03.00, ME 4)
There is a process to provide the results of diagnostic tests to those responsible for determining if the patient is to be admitted, transferred, or referred.
In the outpatient settings, there is a written policy and procedure describing the screening prior to registration.
The hospital has a policy and procedure for registering outpatients.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: Patients with emergent, urgent, or immediate needs are given priority for assessment and treatment.
elements: The hospital selects and uses an evidence-based triage process, appropriate to its patient population, to identify and prioritize patients with emergent, urgent, and immediate needs.
Patients with urgent or emergent needs are given priority for assessment and appropriate, timely care.
Re-triage is performed when appropriate (for example, change of medical condition, long wait time).
The hospital has identified which specific screenings or diagnostic tests must be completed prior to admitting or registering patients.
The triage process includes early recognition of communicable diseases.
Staff are trained to use the triage process, including early recognition of communicable diseases.
The hospital has a process for holding and managing patients under observation in the emergency department and when clinically indicated.
The hospital has a process for managing patients requiring admission when no bed is available.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The hospital considers the clinical needs of patients and informs patients when there are unusual delays for diagnostic and/or treatment services.
elements: Patients are informed when there will be a delay in care and/or treatment.
Patients are informed of the reasons for the delay and provided with information on available alternatives consistent with their clinical needs.
The information on unusual delays and reasons for the delay are documented in the patient’s medical record.
Hospital leaders address all variations contributing to waits, delays, and cancellations that impact smooth and timely flow of patients through hospital departments.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The hospital has a process for managing the flow of patients throughout the hospital, including admission and registration of patients, as applicable to the patient care setting.
elements: The hospital leaders implement strategies to maximize the efficiency of the flow of patients by implementing patient flow processes, including the following: • Availability of appropriate beds • Sufficient number of medical staff at all times with no significant variation during holidays and

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: At admission, the patient and family receive education and orientation to the patient care area, information on the proposed care and any expected costs for care, and the expected outcomes of care.
elements: The patient and family receive education and orientation to the patient care area.
The patient and family receive information on the proposed care, treatment, and services, including expected outcomes.
The patient and family receive information on any expected costs related to the proposed care, treatment, and services.
Patients and families are informed as to the scope of a general consent, if used by the hospital. (See also PCC.03.00, ME 3)
The hospital defines, in writing, how a general consent is documented in the patient’s medical record, if used by the hospital. (See also PCC.03.00, ME 1)
All patients receive information about the likelihood of students and trainees participating in care processes.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The hospital establishes criteria for admission to and discharge from units or departments providing specialized services.
elements: The hospital has established written admission criteria, based on prioritization, diagnostic, and/or objective parameters, for specialized units or departments, including the following: • Identification of their specific patient populations based on age, weight, and diagnosis-related

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The hospital provides continuous patient care services and coordination among health care providers.
elements: Hospital leaders implement processes that support the continuity and coordination of care across all care settings. (See also ACC.02.02, ME 4; ACC.05.00, ME 1; GLD.06.00, ME 4)
The hospital has a policy and procedure for transferring patients between hospital units.

Information about the patient’s care and response to treatment is shared between medical, nursing, and other care providers (for example, patient rounds, multidisciplinary teams, case management for patients requiring complex care).
Information about patient care and progress is exchanged during change-of-shift reporting (handovers), between shifts, and during transfers and referrals between health care providers.
The most responsible physician assesses the need for transfer and matches the condition of the patient with admission criteria of the unit.
Verbal or written agreement from the receiving unit is documented in the patient’s medical record, including the name of the receiving physician.
The most responsible physician assesses the transfer requirements, both staff and equipment.
The physician and the nurse at the receiving unit assess the patient at arrival to ensure safe and smooth handover.
The patient’s medical record is available to those practitioners who are authorized to have access and need it for the care of the patient. (See also MOI.01.01, ME 4)
The patient’s medical record is up to date with the patient’s latest information.
The patient’s medical record or a summary of patient care information is transferred with the patient to another service or unit in the hospital. (See also ACC.01.00, ME 5)

The written transfer summary of the patient’s medical record contains, at a minimum, the following: • Medical and nursing assessment findings • The reason for admission • Significant findings and test results • Diagnosis • Procedures performed • Medications administered during hospitalization, including last time of administration and

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: There is a qualified individual responsible for the patient’s care.
elements: A qualified individual responsible for coordinating the patient’s care is available through all phases of inpatient care and identified in the patient’s medical record.
The hospital has a policy and procedure for transferring patient responsibility from one physician to another.
The transfer of care and coordination is documented in the patient record.
The process identifies how transferred responsibility is assumed, and the participation or coverage is documented.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The hospital develops and implements a discharge planning and referral process based on the patient’s readiness for discharge.
elements: The patient’s discharge and/or referral is consistent with relevant criteria, indications, or guidelines.
Discharge planning begins with the initial assessment by proposing an estimated date and includes care, treatment, equipment, and services that meet the continuing needs of the patient.
Staff are aware of the discharge planning process, particularly for common cases with predictable outcomes.
Patients not directly referred or transferred are provided with the name and location of a site(s) for continuing care.

Patients not directly referred or transferred are provided instructions, in writing, on when to return to the hospital for continued care, treatment, and service, and when and how to obtain urgent care.
Patients, family as appropriate, and staff involved in the patient’s care participate in discharge planning.
Discharge planning and instructions are documented in the patient’s medical record and provided to the patient in writing.

The hospital has a written process which is aligned with the integrated care model whereby patients are referred to the primary care center for follow-up care or transferred to another health care setting within the cluster to ensure continuum of care (for example, home care or long-term care organization).

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The hospital’s discharge process includes patient and family education related to the patient’s ongoing need for continuing care, treatment, and services.
elements: Patients and families are provided with a complete written list of medications to be taken at home and are educated on their safe use, including the following: • Potential side effects • Potential interactions between medications • Potential interactions between medications and foods
Patients and families are educated about proper diet and nutrition.
Patients and families are educated about pain management. (See also COP.07.00, ME 3)
Patients and families are educated about safe and effective use of medical equipment and rehabilitation activities and services.

Patient and family education is documented in the patient’s medical record and includes the following: • What information and education were provided • How the information and education was delivered (for example, in writing, verbally, by

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The complete discharge summary is prepared for all patients and included in the patient’s medical record.
elements: A qualified individual prepares the discharge summary.

The discharge summary contains at least the following: • Reason for admission, diagnoses, and comorbidities • Significant physical and other findings • Diagnostic and therapeutic procedures performed • Medications at time of discharge, including date/time of last dose given while hospitalized • All medications to be taken at home • Therapeutic equipment at time of discharge • The patient’s condition at the time of discharge • Follow-up instructions, appointments, and information
A copy of the discharge summary is provided to the health care provider responsible for the patient’s continuing or follow-up care.
The patient or caregiver is provided with a copy of the discharge summary.
A copy of the completed discharge summary is included in the patient’s medical record at the time of discharge.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: Emergency care is documented.
elements: The medical records of all emergency patients include arrival and departure times.
The medical records of patients discharged from the emergency department include conclusions following completion of treatment.
The medical records of patients discharged from the emergency department include the patient’s condition at discharge.
The medical records of patients discharged from the emergency department include any follow-up care instructions.
The hospital ensures the continuity of care after discharge or referral.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: Medical records contain patient profiles.
elements: All patient medical records contain a patient profile or similar overview.
The hospital identifies necessary information to be included in the profiles.
The patient profile is easy to access and review and is consistent within care areas.
The process is evaluated to ensure that the implementation is consistent with the policy and provides clinicians with an accurate overview of the patient.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The hospital has a process for managing patients who leave against medical advice.
elements: The hospital has a written process for managing patients who leave against medical advice, including the following: • Inpatients who leave with and without informing hospital staff • Patients who have absconded • Patients receiving complex treatment who do not complete or do not return for treatment (“no

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The hospital has a process to transfer patients to other health care organizations based on the patient’s status and the hospital’s ability to meet those needs.
elements: The hospital develops a written transfer process, including criteria based on patients’ needs for continuing care, and ensures that the receiving organization meets the needs of the patient to be transferred. (See also ACC.02.02, ME 4; ACC.03.00, ME 1; GLD.06.00, ME 4)
The transfer process addresses how and when responsibility for continuing care is moved to another provider.
There is a written acceptance for transfer of responsibility for the patient’s care by the receiving provider/organization.
The hospital communicates with all potential receiving organizations, and necessary arrangements are made whenever applicable.
The transfer process identifies who is responsible for monitoring the patient during transfer and the staff qualifications required for the type of patient being transferred.
The most responsible physician ensures that all patient’s health needs during transportation are met, and the transfer occurs at the most suitable time.
The transfer process identifies the medications, supplies, and medical equipment required during transport.
The transfer process addresses a follow-up mechanism that provides information about the patient’s condition upon arrival to the receiving organization.
The transfer process addresses the situations in which transfer is not possible.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The receiving organization is given a written summary of the patient’s clinical condition and the interventions provided by the hospital, and the process is documented in the patient’s medical record.
elements: A written clinical summary is transferred with the patient and includes at least the following: • Patient’s condition or status • Procedures and other interventions provided • Patient’s continuing needs and reason for transfer

The transfer documentation includes at least the following: • Name of the service provider and the name of the individual agreeing to receive the patient • Reason(s) for the transfer • Changes in the patient’s condition or status • Other documentation required by hospital policy

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The hospital’s transportation services comply with relevant laws and regulations and meet requirements for high-quality, safe transport.
elements: The process for discharging or transferring patients includes an assessment of patient transportation needs, which is done by the most responsible physician.
Transportation services, including contracted services, and transport vehicles owned by the hospital meet relevant laws and regulations and the hospital’s requirements for quality and safe transport.
The emergency department has appropriate channels of communication with Red Crescent services upon receiving or transferring patients.
The emergency department director or emergency department nursing manager supervises the ambulance services.
The ambulances have adequate equipment and supplies to be ready to transfer patients 24 hours a day, 7 days a week.
Equipment and supplies are based on trauma/resuscitation area preparation to transfer critically ill patients.
A documented daily check is conducted on both medical and mechanical functions of the ambulances.
Ambulance equipment is regularly maintained and documented.
All vehicles used for transportation, contracted or hospital owned, comply with the hospital’s infection prevention and control program.
All vehicles used for transportation, contracted or hospital owned, have appropriate medical equipment, supplies, and medications to meet the needs of the patient being transported.
The transportation provided or arranged is appropriate to the needs and condition of the patient.
The hospital has a process to monitor the quality and safety of transportation provided or arranged by the hospital, including a complaint process.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: All patients have their health care needs identified through an assessment process that has been defined by the hospital.
elements: Hospital policy defines, in writing, the assessment process and minimum content of assessments for inpatients, including critical care, for each clinical discipline that performs assessments. (See also AOP.01.01, ME 2)
Hospital policy defines, in writing, the assessment process and minimum content of assessments for outpatients for each clinical discipline that performs assessments. (See also AOP.01.01, ME 2)

Hospital policy defines, in writing, the assessment process and its scope and content for all categories of patients (adults, geriatrics, pediatrics, pregnant women, trauma patients and others), and its scope and content for all disciplines (physicians, nurses, physiotherapists, social service, and others).
Only qualified individuals permitted by licensure, applicable laws and regulations, experience, or certification perform the assessments. (See also AOP.01.01, ME 3)

The hospital identifies the information to be documented for the assessments, with an aim to identify the general patient’s medical and nursing needs and a provisional diagnosis so that it can initiate care and treatment.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: Each patient’s initial assessment includes a health history and an evaluation of the patient’s physical, psychological, spiritual/cultural, social, and economic needs.
elements: All patients have an initial assessment that is consistent with the requirements defined in hospital policy.

The assessment includes the following: • Physical examination • Health history • Main complaint • Details of present illness • Systems review • History including previous admissions and surgeries • Family history • Pain (screening followed by assessment if required) • Risk for fall (screening followed by assessment if required) • Physical status and functionality (screening followed by assessment if required) • Diagnostic test(s) as indicated by the patient’s condition • Need for additional or specialized assessment as indicated by the patient’s condition • Need for discharge planning as indicated by the patient’s condition • Provisional diagnosis • Medication history, prior drug reactions, and known allergies • Initial psychological and social assessment as indicated by the patient’s condition identified in the initial screening of patient. A qualified social worker conducts the psychosocial assessment, guided by a policy and procedure that identifies factors facilitating or impeding health care progress, including emotional, social, and psychological factors; home situation; financial considerations; noncompliance with treatment; and physical or mental disabilities. Psychosocial assessment is completed within 24 hours of referral. • Initial economic assessment, when indicated by the patient’s needs • Initial spiritual and cultural assessment, when indicated by the patient’s needs (See also AOP.01.00, MEs 1 and 2)

The hospital outlines requirements about the most responsible physician being responsible for the initial assessment and the timeliness of the assessment, including the following: • What parts of the initial assessment each discipline is responsible for completing, including that

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The hospital has a process for accepting initial assessments from outside sources.
elements: Initial medical assessments accepted are less than or equal to 30 days old.
The hospital implements a policy that defines the time frame for completing the medical, nursing, and other assessments required for different care settings and services.

For initial assessments less than or equal to 30 days old, the assessment is reviewed and validated; any changes in the patient’s condition since the assessment or “no change” are documented in the patient’s medical record at the time of admission or registration.
Assessments completed within 30 days prior to admission, or an outpatient visit can be used with a documented update of any significant changes.

If the initial assessment is greater than 30 days old at the time of admission or registration, the medical history is updated, and the initial assessment is repeated in accordance with the hospital’s initial assessment policy.
Assessments completed more than 30 days prior to admission, or an outpatient visit must be repeated.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: Patients are screened for nutritional, functional, and other special needs and are further assessed when indicated by the screening.
elements: Hospital policy defines, in writing, the evidence-based screening tools developed by qualified individuals (including dietitians) used to identify patients who require further nutritional assessment, and the tools are implemented consistently throughout the hospital. Qualified hospital staff (for example, registered nurses) conduct the nutritional screening to determine the patient’s need for comprehensive nutritional assessment by a licensed dietitian.

Patients whose initial screening indicates a nutritional risk or problem, or during the course of treatment are prescribed a therapeutic diet, receive a nutritional assessment. Such patients are referred to a licensed dietitian who completes the nutritional assessment within 24 hours of referral.

Nutritional assessment, as defined in the policy, includes but is not limited to the following: • Height and weight chart for children • Body mass index (BMI) for adults • Eating habits • Food allergies • Need for therapeutic diet • Physical difficulties with eating and drinking and the need for any assistive devices

A qualified dietitian does the following: • Develops a nutritional plan of care • Highlights food-drug interactions to clinical staff • Makes recommendations related to patient dietary needs • Monitors that the patient has nil per os (NPO) or nothing by mouth • Educates other health staff, patients, and families • Ensures documentation in medical record for the nutritional activities

Hospital policy defines, in writing, the screening tools, developed by qualified individuals (including therapists), used to identify patients who require further functional assessment, and the tools are implemented consistently throughout the hospital.

Patients whose screening indicates a functional risk or problem receive a functional assessment, described in a policy or procedure, by a qualified therapist who completes the assessment within 24 hours of referral.
When the need for additional specialized assessments is identified, patients are referred within the hospital or outside the hospital.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: All patients are screened for pain and assessed when pain is present.
elements: All inpatients are screened for pain, and the screening is documented.
Outpatients whose condition, diagnosis, or situation may indicate that they are at risk for pain are screened for pain.

When pain is identified by the screening, a comprehensive pain assessment is performed and documented as defined in a policy. (See also COP.07.00, ME 1) The assessment process clearly defines the following: • Requirements for a comprehensive pain assessment and management • Role of staff in pain assessment • Items included in pain assessment (intensity, type, duration, frequency, location, and progress) • Pain relieving measures, including medications and their dosage, frequency, and route
Patients in pain receive pain assessment and management according to the policy, and this is documented in the patient’s medical record.
Patients are reassessed for pain following any pain management interventions.
Hospital policy defines, in writing, the frequency of pain reassessment and role of staff in the process of reassessment.
If needed, the patient is referred or transferred to a care setting that has the capabilities and resources to treat the patient’s pain.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: All patients are reassessed at intervals based on their condition and treatment.
elements: Hospital policy defines, in writing, how often patients are reassessed by various members of the health care team and other circumstances when a reassessment is required, including the following: • Defined intervals by various members of the care team, including physicians, nurses, and other

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The hospital develops and implements a process to reduce the risk of falls, and patient harm resulting from falls.
elements: The hospital screens all inpatients for fall risk and uses evidence-based screening tools appropriate for the patient population.
The hospital screens all outpatients whose condition, diagnosis, situation, or location may put them at risk for falls and uses screening tools appropriate for the patients being served.

The hospital implements a process for the assessment and, when applicable, reassessment of patients who may become at risk for falls due to a change in condition or are already at risk for falls based on the documented assessment.

Evidence-based interventions to reduce fall risk are implemented for those identified patients, situations, and locations within the hospital assessed to be at risk, and the interventions are documented.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: Laboratory services are available to meet patient needs, and all laboratory services meet applicable local and national standards, laws, and regulations.
elements: Laboratory services, including outside sources of laboratory services, have a clearly defined scope of services and meet applicable local and national standards, laws, and regulations.
Laboratory services meet the needs of the patients and other services the hospital provides, including a process to access laboratory services after hours and for emergency needs.
Basic laboratory services (hematology, blood bank, biochemistry) are available 24 hours a day, 7 days a week.
Experts in specialized diagnostic areas are contacted when needed. (See also GLD.05.00, ME 1)

The laboratory has a defined organization chart that displays key positions, including the laboratory director, section heads and supervisors, quality management officer, facility and safety officer, and, as applicable, infection control officer, point-of-care testing coordinator, and training and education coordinator.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: A qualified individual(s) is responsible for managing the clinical laboratory service or pathology service, and all laboratory staff are qualified to perform the tests and interpret the results.
elements: The clinical laboratory, and other laboratory services throughout the hospital, are under the direction and oversight of one or more qualified individuals, according to the complexity of the laboratory scope of services: • The laboratory director of a high-complexity laboratory (laboratories of tertiary care hospitals/ referral facilities or laboratories providing anatomical pathology and/or transfusion medicine services) is a licensed/registered anatomical or clinical pathology consultant (board certified or equivalent). • The laboratory director of a moderate- or low-complexity laboratory (laboratories with no anatomical pathology and transfusion medicine services) is a licensed/registered clinical scientist or laboratory specialist. (See also GLD.06.00, ME 1)

Responsibilities of the qualified laboratory leader include the following: • Developing, implementing, and maintaining policies and procedures • Administrative oversight of laboratory services • Maintaining any necessary quality control programs • Developing and implementing a staffing program • Recommending outside sources of laboratory services • Monitoring and reviewing all laboratory services
All laboratory staff have the required qualifications, training, and experience to perform and interpret tests.
A laboratory staffing program is implemented so staff can perform tests promptly and provide staffing during all hours of operation and during emergencies.

The laboratory implements an orientation, training, and competency assessment program that ensures the following: • Satisfactory completion of training program for all laboratory personnel in their assigned areas • Training on new equipment or method • Competency assessment of all laboratory personnel before working independently and annually

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The hospital has defined requirements for the oversight and supervision of the point-of-care testing program.
elements: The person responsible for managing the laboratory services, or a qualified designee, provides oversight and supervision of the point-of-care testing (POCT) program as POCT coordinator. The assignment of responsibility of oversight and supervision of the POCT program is defined in hospital policy.
Staff performing POCT have the required qualifications and training and are competent to perform POCT.
The POCT program includes a defined process for reporting abnormal test results, including reporting critical results. (See also IPSG.02.00, ME 1)
The POCT program includes requirements for quality control performance, documentation, and maintenance of POCT devices.
The POCT program includes the process of acquiring POCT devices/methods.
The POCT program is monitored, evaluated, and included in quality improvement activities.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: Laboratory results are reported within time frames defined by hospital policy, including defined turnaround times (TATs) for routine and STAT tests.
elements: The hospital has a written policy that establishes the expected report time for routine and STAT test results. Expected report times are established in agreement with relevant clinical departments.
The hospital monitors whether STAT tests are reported within the expected time frame.
The hospital monitors whether routine laboratory results are reported within the expected time frame.
When laboratory results are not reported within the expected time frame, the hospital takes corrective action.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: All laboratory testing equipment is regularly inspected, maintained, and calibrated, and appropriate records are maintained for these activities.
elements: The laboratory manages laboratory equipment with a written process for how equipment is selected, acquired, and installed.
There is an inventory of all laboratory equipment. (See also FMS.07.00, ME 2)
Laboratory equipment is inspected and tested when new and according to manufacturers’ guidelines; the inspections are documented.
Laboratory equipment is calibrated and maintained according to manufacturers’ guidelines, and the calibration and maintenance are documented.

The laboratory implements policies and procedures describing the validation of critical laboratory equipment for its intended use, including the following: • Installation qualification • Operational qualification • Detailed functional validation study with predefined acceptance criteria • Critical laboratory equipment is not used before completing the validation studies
The hospital monitors and acts on laboratory equipment hazard notices, recalls, reportable incidents, problems, and failures. (See also FMS.07.01, ME 1)

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: Essential reagents and supplies are available, and all reagents are evaluated to ensure accuracy and precision of results.
elements: Essential reagents and supplies are identified and available, and there is a process to address when essential reagents are not available. (See also FMS.05.00, ME 2)

The laboratory implements policies and procedures for documenting the receipt, inspection, and testing (as applicable) of incoming critical materials, supplies, and reagents and for inventory management and tracking the use of critical materials, supplies, and reagents to ensure the following: • Materials are used within their expiration dates. • New reagents lot numbers are tested against old lots or suitable reference materials before use. • Kit components are used within the kit lot number. • Lot number use is traceable to patient/blood donors or inclusive dates of use.

All reagents are stored and dispensed according to manufacturers’ instructions under controlled conditions or in an appropriate storage device. Storage conditions are continuously monitored using an appropriate temperature monitoring and recording system. If monitoring systems fail, the storage temperature is monitored and recorded every 8 hours using a standardized thermometric device.
The laboratory establishes and follows the hospital’s written policy for the evaluation of all reagents to ensure accuracy and precision of results.
All reagents undergo quality control testing as required by the manufacturer.

Records for reagents include the following information: • Identity of the reagent • Content • Concentration/titer • Date of receipt or preparation • Lot number • Expiration date • Date put into use • Storage requirements (See also FMS.05.00, ME 2)

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: Procedures for collecting, identifying, handling, safely transporting, and disposing of specimens are established and implemented.
elements: Procedures are established and implemented for the ordering of tests.
The laboratory develops a services/specimen collection manual that includes available tests and services on and off site (reference laboratory) and their turnaround times.

Procedures are established and implemented for the collection and identification of specimens, including the following: • Specimen containers labeled immediately after sample collection at the patient’s side • Two patient identifiers (patient’s full name and medical record number) • Date and time of sample collection • Identification of the person collecting the specimen

Procedures are established and implemented for the transport, storage, and preservation of specimens, including packing instructions (use of biohazard leak-proof containers), personnel training (including safety and proper packaging), and specimen tracking system.

Procedures are established and implemented for the receipt and tracking of specimens to ensure the performance and documentation of the following: • Date and time of specimen reception • Check for proper packaging • Check for quality and quantity of specimen • Check for adequacy of specimen labeling • Check for request completion • Check for label/request discrepancies • Any suboptimal specimen is clearly highlighted in the reported results • Final decision (accept/reject)
Procedures are established and implemented to maintain the identity of laboratory specimens during receipt, processing, examination, and archiving.

Procedures are established and implemented for specimen disposal that comply with national and international laboratory safety standards as well as the hospital safety and infection control plan to ensure disposal using prick-proof containers and leak-proof bags.
The procedures are followed when contracted laboratory services are used.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: Established norms and ranges are used to interpret and to report clinical laboratory results.
elements: The laboratory establishes reference ranges for each test performed.
The range is included in the medical record at the time test results are reported.
Ranges are provided when tests are performed by contracted laboratory services.
Ranges are appropriate to the hospital’s geography and patient demographics.
The laboratory reviews and updates ranges as needed.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The hospital has implemented comprehensive systems and processes for quality control of test methods and proficiency testing sufficient for the extent and complexity of the laboratory scope of services.
elements: The hospital establishes and implements a written quality control program for the clinical laboratory in conformity with the manufacturer’s instructions, including assignment of performance and review responsibility (control specimens are handled and tested in the same manner and by the same laboratory personnel testing patient samples); number and frequency of running controls; tolerance limits of controls results; and corrective action in the event of unacceptable results.
The program includes the validation of test methods for accuracy, precision, and reportable range.
The program includes the daily surveillance and documentation of test results.
The program includes rapid correction and documentation of deficiencies.
The laboratory participates in a proficiency testing program or an alternative for all laboratory tests when external quality assessments are not available.

The laboratory establishes processes for the receipt, processing, and reporting of proficiency testing results and samples, which covers the following: • Samples are tested by the same personnel handling patient/donor samples. • Sample are tested by the same method used for testing patient/donor samples. • Samples are not referred to other laboratory for testing. • Results are not shared with other laboratories.
The laboratory’s proficiency testing results meet satisfactory performance criteria in accordance with laws and regulations.

Laboratory management reviews and approves proficiency testing records, and whenever appropriate, they investigate unacceptable performance and take, implement, and monitor appropriate corrective actions.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The hospital ensures the quality of services provided by contracted laboratories.
elements: There is a clearly defined and implemented process describing the laboratory’s role in selecting and evaluating providers of contracted laboratory services, including selection criteria (including accreditation status) for the provider of contracted laboratory services, inclusive list of send-out tests, and detailed procedures for transporting specimens and reporting results.
The hospital maintains a copy of the license and the certificate or letter of accreditation or certification, from a recognized authority, for all contracted laboratories used by the hospital.
The hospital maintains documentation that any contracted laboratory used by the hospital participates in a proficiency testing program.
The hospital determines the frequency and type of performance expectation data from contracted laboratories. (See also GLD.05.00, MEs 4 and 5)
The individual responsible for the laboratory or a designee reviews the performance data from contracted laboratories and acts based on the results. (See also GLD.05.00, MEs 4 and 5)
