An annual report of the data from contracted laboratories is provided to the leaders responsible for the management and renewal of contracts.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: A qualified individual(s) is responsible for blood bank and/or transfusion services and ensures that services adhere to laws and regulations and recognized standards of practice.
elements: A qualified individual(s) is responsible for blood bank and/or transfusion services. (See also GLD.06.00, ME 1)

The blood bank, in collaboration with the blood utilization committee, has implemented and documented processes for the following: • Blood donor selection • Blood screening for disease • Blood collection • Blood storage • Compatibility testing • Blood distribution

The laboratory implements criteria for accepting blood donors to minimize the risk of harm to them. The criteria include the following: • Whole blood is not collected from a donor weighing less than 50 kilograms or under 17 years of age. • Whole blood is not collected from a donor more frequently than once every 8 weeks and not from donors who donated apheresis product less than 48 hours ago. • The blood pressure and pulse rate of a prospective donor are within normal ranges: diastolic blood pressure less than 100 mm Hg, systolic blood pressure less than 180 mm Hg, and pulse rate between 50 to 100 beats per minute. • The hemoglobin level of the prospective donor should be greater than 12.5 g/dL or a hematocrit of more than 38%. • The prospective donor has no history of heart or lung disease. • Female donors are not pregnant or have not been pregnant within the last six weeks. • The prospective donor’s history is evaluated and the donor examined by a qualified person before whole blood collection.

The policies and procedures minimize the risk of harm to blood recipients by preventing donations by individuals who have any of the following: • Evidence of disease transmissible by blood transfusion • Conditions thought to compromise the suitability of the blood or blood component • Body temperature exceeding 37.5°C • History of liver diseases, cancer, or bleeding tendency • History of laboratory or clinical evidence for viral hepatitis, HIV, and HTLV • History of laboratory or clinical evidence for malaria within the last three years • History of syphilis treatment or unconfirmed test result for syphilis within the past 12 months • Prospective donor has been excluded per the current recommendations for preventing HIV

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: Clinical guidelines and procedures are implemented for the handling, use, and administration of blood and blood products.
elements: The hospital identifies who is permitted to administer blood and blood products in accordance with laws and regulations.
Individuals permitted to administer blood and blood products must have the education, knowledge, and clinical expertise to do so safely.
The hospital provides and documents training of practices associated with administering blood and blood products.
Clinical guidelines and procedures are uniformly implemented for the handling and administration of blood and blood products.

Clinical guidelines and procedures address the processes for the following: • Patient consent for administration, obtained by a physician, describing the transfusion process, identifying risks and benefits of transfusion, identifying alternatives including the consequences of refusing the treatment, giving opportunity to ask questions, and giving the right to accept or

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: Radiology and diagnostic imaging services are available to meet patient needs, and all services meet applicable local and national standards, laws, and regulations.
elements: Radiology and diagnostic imaging services meet applicable professional standards and local and national laws and regulations, including for radiation therapy (if included in the scope of service).

Radiology and diagnostic imaging services are available to meet the needs related to the hospital’s patient population, scope of services, and emergency needs, including after normal hours. There is 24-hour coverage by a radiologist and a diagnostic imaging technologist.
The hospital maintains a list of experts in specialized diagnostic areas and ensures that the list is accessible to staff who need it.

Outside sources are selected based on recommendations of the individual responsible for radiology and diagnostic imaging services and have an acceptable record of timely performance and compliance with applicable laws and regulations.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: A qualified individual(s) is responsible for managing the radiology and diagnostic imaging services, and individuals with proper qualifications and experience perform diagnostic imaging studies, interpret the results, and report the results.
elements: Radiology and diagnostic imaging services are under the direction of one or more qualified individuals who is a radiologist qualified by education, training, and experience. (See also GLD.06.00, ME 1)

Responsibilities of the individual managing radiology and diagnostic imaging services include the following: • Developing, implementing, and maintaining policies and procedures • Overseeing administrative tasks • Overseeing quality control • Developing and implementing a staffing program • Recommending outside sources of radiology and diagnostic imaging services • Monitoring and reviewing all radiology and diagnostic imaging services

The radiology department has policies and procedures to address all important radiological investigations and procedures, including the following: • X-rays • Ultrasonography • Computed tomography • Magnetic resonance imaging • Angiogram • Interventional radiological procedures • Fluoroscopy • Contrast agent reactions • Nuclear medicine imaging • Molecular imaging (positron emission tomography [PET] scanning) • Bedside and critical care radiography • Radiopharmaceuticals calibration and quality control • Portable radiological machines • Mammography

Staff with proper qualifications and experience perform diagnostic and imaging studies. Adequate staffing includes the following: • Technical director • Medical physicists • Radiation safety officer and supervisor (for radiotherapy nuclear medicine and diagnostics) • Quality officer • Picture archiving and communications system (PACS) administrator, when applicable
Staff with proper qualifications and experience interpret study results and verify and report the results within the time frame defined by hospital policy.
There is an adequate number of staff, who are trained and qualified in their respective fields, to meet patient needs and the hospital’s scope of services.
Radiology and diagnostic imaging supervisory staff have proper qualifications and experience for the role.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: A documented radiation and/or diagnostic imaging safety program for patients, staff, and visitors is implemented and complies with applicable professional standards, laws, and regulations.
elements: A radiation and/or diagnostic imaging safety program for patients, staff, and visitors is implemented as evidenced by the daily practice and is compliant with applicable professional standards, laws, and regulations. The safety program covers the following: • Periodically inspecting, maintaining, and calibrating all equipment • Managing radioactive materials used for therapeutic and diagnostic purposes, particularly

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: Radiology and diagnostic imaging study results are available in a timely way as defined by hospital policy.
elements: The hospital has a written policy that establishes the expected report time for diagnostic imaging results.

The hospital monitors whether urgent or emergent radiology and diagnostic imaging results are reported within the expected time frame, which should not exceed 24 hours. For emergency cases, the expected reporting time should be immediate.
The hospital monitors whether routine radiology and diagnostic imaging results are reported within the expected time frame, which should not exceed 48 hours.
When radiology and diagnostic imaging results are not reported within the expected time frame, the hospital takes corrective action.

The radiology department defines and implements the format and content of radiology reports (paper or electronic). Essential elements of the report include the following: • Identification of the patient • Type of procedure • Identification of the ordering physician • Reporting date and time • Identification of the reporting radiologist

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: All equipment used to conduct radiology and diagnostic imaging studies is regularly inspected, maintained, and calibrated, and appropriate records are maintained for these activities to ensure safety.
elements: The hospital develops and implements a written program to manage radiology and diagnostic imaging equipment, including how radiology equipment is selected and acquired.
There is a documented inventory of all radiology and diagnostic imaging equipment. (See also FMS.07.00, ME 2)
Radiology and diagnostic imaging equipment is inspected and tested when new and according to age, use, and each manufacturer’s recommendations; the inspections are documented.
Radiology and diagnostic imaging equipment is calibrated and maintained according to each manufacturer’s recommendations, and the calibration and maintenance is documented.

The hospital has a system in place for monitoring and acting on radiology and diagnostic imaging equipment hazard notices, recalls, reportable incidents, problems, and failures. (See also FMS.07.01, ME 1)

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The hospital has implemented quality control and safety procedures for radiology and diagnostic imaging services.
elements: The hospital establishes and implements a written quality control program for the radiology and diagnostic imaging services.
Quality control includes validating test methods for accuracy and precision.

The radiology department ensures the following tests are conducted at least annually: • Automatic exposure control (AEC) test • Kilovoltage Peak (KvP) reproducibility and repeatability • Half value layer test • Alignment of collimator and x-ray field • Mean glandular dose test (for mammography)
Quality records are maintained for radiation therapy services, including the following: • Periodic inspection, maintenance, and calibration of the linear accelerator and other radiation

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The hospital ensures the quality of services provided by all outside contracted sources of radiology and diagnostic imaging services.
elements: The hospital maintains a copy of the license from a recognized authority for all contracted radiology and diagnostic imaging services used by the hospital.

The hospital maintains a copy of the certificate or letter of accreditation or certification from a recognized authority for all contracted radiology and diagnostic imaging services used by the hospital.
The hospital determines the frequency and type of quality data from contracted radiology and diagnostic imaging services. (See also GLD.05.00, MEs 4 and 5)

The individual responsible for the radiology and diagnostic imaging services or a designee reviews the performance measure data from contracted radiology and diagnostic imaging services and takes action based on the results. (See also GLD.05.00, MEs 4 and 5)
An annual report of the data from contracted radiology and diagnostic imaging services is provided to those who make decisions about management and renewal of contracts.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: When applicable, the hospital establishes and implements a nuclear medicine safety program that complies with applicable professional standards, laws, and regulations.
elements: A qualified individual(s) is responsible for overseeing nuclear medicine services, and relevant staff members are properly trained, qualified, and certified to perform their respective roles in nuclear medicine safety and procedures.
The hospital implements radiation safety protocols, including the use of appropriate shielding, personal protective equipment (PPE), and monitoring devices for both patients and staff.

Radiation doses administered to patients are optimized for diagnostic and therapeutic purposes, and the procedure includes monitoring and minimizing radiation exposure while obtaining the necessary diagnostic information or therapeutic effect.
The procurement, storage, handling, and disposal of radiopharmaceuticals complies with laws, regulations, professional standards, and manufacturers’ guidelines.
Patients and family are informed about the procedures and safety precautions.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The hospital provides sedation and anesthesia services to meet patient needs, and in accordance with professional practice standards and laws and regulations.
elements: The hospital provides sedation and anesthesia services that meet the needs of the patients the hospital serves.
The hospital provides sedation and anesthesia services that comply with laws and regulations.
The hospital provides sedation and anesthesia services that comply with professional practice standards for care.
All policies and procedures of the anesthesia department are collaboratively developed and approved by the head of anesthesia in collaboration with relevant disciplines.

An individual(s) qualified by education, training, experience, and license assumes professional responsibility for the anesthesia services provided regardless of the location at the hospital, and these responsibilities include the following: • Developing, implementing, and maintaining policies and procedures • Providing administrative oversight • Maintaining any necessary quality improvement programs • Monitoring and reviewing all sedation and anesthesia services throughout the hospital • Reinforcing the implementation of the infection control guidelines inside the operating and

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The administration of procedural sedation is standardized throughout the hospital.
elements: The hospital has established a written policy and standardized processes for procedural sedation throughout the hospital, and the areas where moderate and deep sedation/analgesia are performed have adequate equipment and supplies that include at a minimum: • Wall suction or suction machine • Oxygen source • Pulse oximetry • Automated blood pressure monitor or means of taking blood pressure • ECG monitor • Crash cart with defibrillator, medications, IV access, and intubation equipment that is

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: Practitioners responsible for procedural sedation and staff responsible for monitoring patients receiving procedural sedation are qualified.
elements: Health care practitioners responsible for providing procedural sedation have competency-based privileges granted after showing evidence of competence in at least the following: • Techniques and various modes of sedation • Pharmacology of sedation drugs and the use of reversal agents • Monitoring requirements • Response to complications • Airway assessment (See also SQE.01.03, ME 1)

The individual responsible for patient monitoring during procedural sedation is competent in at least the following: • Monitoring requirements from the active administration phase during the procedure through the

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: Procedural sedation is administered and monitored according to professional practice guidelines and documented in the patient’s medical record.
elements: A presedation assessment is performed and documented by a qualified physician.

The scope and content of the presedation assessment includes at least the following criteria when evaluating risk and appropriateness of procedural sedation for the patient: • History and physical examination • History of medication allergy and adverse experience with sedation and analgesia, as well as with

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The risks, benefits, and alternatives related to procedural sedation are discussed with the patient, their family, or those who make decisions for the patient.
elements: The patient, family, and/or decision-makers are educated on the risks, benefits, and alternatives of procedural sedation. (See also PCC.03.00, ME 2)
The patient, family, and/or decision-makers are educated about postprocedural sedation recovery and pain management. (See also PCC.04.00, ME 1)
A qualified individual provides and documents the education.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: A qualified individual conducts a preanesthesia assessment and preinduction assessment.
elements: A preanesthesia assessment is performed and dated less than 30 days prior to the scheduled surgery/ procedures and includes at least the following elements when evaluating risk and appropriateness of anesthesia for the patient: • Medical history including anesthesia, drug, and allergy history • Identification of airway problems and limited intra-vascular access that may influence the type of

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: Each patient’s anesthesia plan of care is discussed with the patient and/or those who make decisions for the patient and documented in the patient’s medical record.
elements: A qualified individual plans and documents anesthesia care in the patient’s medical record, including the following: • Age, sex, weight, height, and preoperative vital signs • The anesthetic agent • The dosage, time, and route of administration of all medications and anesthetic agents used • The techniques used to administer the anesthesia • If blood is used, the amount of blood, rationale for administration, and the time given • Investigations carried out (for example, blood glucose, blood gases) • Unusual events or complications • The patient’s status at the end of the procedure • Intravenous fluids given • The anesthesiologist and anesthesia assistant(s)
Qualified anesthesiologist is present inside the operating room throughout the operation.

Anesthesia consultant administers and supervises anesthesia for major/specialized operations or high- risk patients, including the following: • Pediatric operations • Cardiopulmonary operations • Neurosurgery operations • Transplant operations • Anesthesia staff are certified in advanced life support as appropriate to the patient’s age
The patient, family, and/or decision-makers are educated on the risks, benefits, and alternatives of anesthesia (See also PCC.04.00, ME 1), including a documentation of patient informed consent.

When applicable, the patient, family, and/or decision-makers are educated, prior to the procedure being performed, about the options available for postoperative pain management; this education is documented.
The anesthesia agent, dose (when applicable), and anesthetic technique are documented in the patient’s anesthesia record.
The anesthesiologist, or other qualified individual allowed to administer anesthesia, and the anesthesia assistants are identified in the patient’s anesthesia record.
Anesthesia care is administered and monitored according to professional practice guidelines and as defined in hospital policy.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: Each patient’s physiological status during anesthesia and surgery is monitored according to professional practice guidelines and documented in the patient’s medical record.
elements: The frequency and type of monitoring during anesthesia and surgery are based on the patient’s preanesthesia status, the anesthesia used, and the surgical procedure performed.
Monitoring of the patient’s physiological status is consistent with professional practice guidelines.
The results of monitoring are documented in the patient’s medical record. (See also COP.01.00, ME 5)

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: Each patient’s postanesthesia status is monitored, and the patient is discharged from the recovery area by a qualified individual or by using established criteria.
elements: Patients transported to the recovery room shall be accompanied by a qualified member of the anesthesia care team.
The patient shall be continually evaluated and treated during the transport with monitoring and support appropriate to the patient’s condition.
Patients are monitored during the postanesthesia recovery period according to professional practice guidelines and as defined in hospital policy and documented in the patient record.
Upon arrival to the recovery room, the patient is properly handed over and reevaluated.
The patient’s status and time of arrival to the recovery room are documented.
Qualified anesthesiologist is in charge of the recovery room at all times.
Qualified staff members provide postanesthesia care in the recovery room.
A policy defines the monitoring requirements for patients during postanesthesia phase.
There is a recovery from anesthesia record for documentation of monitoring findings and services provided in the recovery room.

Patients are discharged from the postanesthesia unit or recovery monitoring is discontinued in accordance with one of the following alternatives: • Patient is discharged or recovery monitoring is discontinued by a fully qualified anesthesiologist or other individual authorized by the individual(s) responsible for managing the anesthesia services. • Patient is discharged or recovery monitoring is discontinued by a nurse or similarly qualified individual in accordance with postanesthesia criteria developed by hospital leadership, and the

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: Each patient’s surgical care is planned based on the results of the preoperative assessment and documented in the patient’s medical record.
elements: A preoperative assessment is performed and documented by a qualified provider before surgery.

The preoperative assessment includes the following: • History, physical exam, and test results (laboratory and radiology) • Preoperative diagnosis • Planned procedure • Medical needs • Psychological needs • Social needs • Economic needs • Discharge needs
Surgical care for each patient is planned based on the preoperative assessment information.
A preoperative diagnosis and the planned surgical procedure are documented in the patient’s medical record prior to the procedure.
In emergency situations where a complete medical assessment cannot be documented, a brief note is written by the most responsible physician.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The risks, benefits, and alternatives are discussed with the patient and their family or those who make decisions for the patient.
elements: The patient, family, and/or decision-makers are educated on the following elements related to the planned surgical procedure: • Name of test, procedure, or treatment covered by the informed consent • Name of responsible practitioner(s) performing the procedures(s) • Risks and benefits of the planned procedure • The likelihood of success, potential complications, the recovery process, and possible results of

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: Information about the surgical procedure (operative report) is documented in the patient’s medical record to facilitate continuing care.
elements: Surgical reports, templates, or operative progress notes include at least the following elements: • Preoperative diagnosis and planned procedure • Postoperative diagnosis • Name of operative surgeon and assistants • Procedures performed and description of each procedure finding • Perioperative complications (presence or absence) • Tubes and/or drains placed intraoperatively • Surgical specimens sent for examination • Amount of blood loss and amount of transfused blood • Date, time, and signature of responsible physician
The hospital identifies information that may routinely be recorded in other specific areas of the medical record.
The surgical report, template, or operative progress note is available immediately after surgery before the patient is transferred to the next level of care.
The surgical operative report is signed/authenticated by the surgeon performing the procedure.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: Patient care after surgery is planned and documented.
elements: All postsurgical care, treatment, and services meet the patient’s immediate postsurgical needs.

The continuing postsurgical plan(s) is documented in the patient’s medical record before discharge from recovery within 24 hours by the responsible surgeon or verified by a co-signature from the responsible surgeon on the documented plan entered by the surgeon’s delegate.

The continuing postsurgical plan of care includes care, treatment, and services based on the patient’s assessed needs, as follows: • Postoperative monitoring parameters and frequency • Wound care • Care of drains and catheters • Special patient positioning requirements • Nutritional instructions • When to start mobilization • Special referrals (for example, physical therapy, respiratory therapy) • A new order for all required medications • Any other postoperative care needed, including required follow-up.

When indicated by a change in the patient’s needs, the postsurgical plan of care is updated or revised based on the reassessment of the patient by the health care practitioners. (See also COP.01.01, ME 3)

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: Surgical care that includes the implanting of a medical device is planned with special consideration for how standard processes must be modified.
elements: The hospital’s surgical services identify the types of implantable medical devices that are included within its scope of services.

Written policies and practices include, at least, the following: • Selection of devices based on current science and research • Verification that implants are present in the operating theatre • Verification of the qualifications and training of any outside technical staff required during the implant procedure (for example, the manufacturer’s representative who may be required to

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: There is a uniform process for prescribing and completing treatment orders.
elements: The hospital implements a written uniform process for prescribing patient orders that includes the following: • Information required in the order • Identification of orders that may be received verbally, via telephone, and via text (See also

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: An individualized plan of care is developed and documented for each patient.
elements: The care for each patient is planned by the responsible practitioner, nurse, and other members of the health care team within 24 hours of admission as an inpatient, and the care planning process involves the patient and family.
The plan of care is individualized based on the patient’s initial assessment data and identified needs and is documented in the patient’s medical record.
The plan of care contains the measurable goals/desired outcomes toward discharge.
The plan of care is updated or revised based on any changes in the patient’s condition and documented in the patient’s medical record. (See also AOP.01.05, ME 1; ASC.04.03, ME 4)
The results or conclusions of any patient care team meetings or other collaborative discussions are documented in the patient’s medical record.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The provision of high-risk services is guided by professional practice guidelines, laws, and regulations.
elements: Hospital leaders identify, in writing, the high-risk services, including at least the following when provided by the hospital: • Emergency services • Life support, including ventilators and extracorporeal membrane oxygenation • Infectious disease services • Dialysis • Restraints • Chemotherapy • Critical care services • Neonates and infants • Frail elderly

Hospital leaders establish and implement written policies, procedures, and/or principles of care for high-risk services provided by the hospital, including infection control, safety, security, and ethical guidelines.
Staff are trained to use the written tools for high-risk services.
Hospital leaders identify additional risks that may affect high-risk services and implement measures to reduce and/or prevent these risks.
Hospital-acquired conditions are tracked and included in the hospital’s quality improvement program.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The hospital implements policies and procedures for safety of clinical alarm systems.
elements: Hospital leaders implement a written management program for alarm signals that pose a risk to patient safety.
The program identifies the most important alarm signals to be managed based on the risk to patient safety.

Hospital leaders develop and implement strategies for managing alarms that include the following: • Clinically appropriate settings for alarm signals • Situations in which alarm signals can be disabled • Circumstances under which alarm parameters must be reviewed and/or changed (for example, with significant changes in patient condition, when patients are transferred to different levels of

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
group: Recognition of Changes to Patient Condition
statement: Clinical staff are trained to recognize and respond to changes in a patient’s condition.
elements: The hospital has a systematic process to recognize and respond to changes or deterioration of patient condition, and the team provides coverage 24 hours a day, 7 days a week.
The hospital implements documented, age-specific, early-warning criteria describing early signs of a change or deterioration in a patient’s condition.
The hospital has a process for staff to seek additional assistance when they have concerns about a patient’s condition.
The hospital regularly evaluates the activities and outcomes of the rapid response teams.
The hospital informs the patient and family how to seek assistance when they have concerns about a patient’s condition.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: Resuscitation services are available throughout the hospital.
elements: Resuscitation services are available and provided to all patients 24 hours a day, every day, throughout all areas of the hospital.

The hospital has a policy and procedure for cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) across all hospital areas that includes the following: • A simple number to dial (such as 999) or other mechanism to call when summoning help for a

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
group: Management of Patients at Risk of Suicide or Self-Harm
statement: The hospital has a process to identify and protect patients at risk for suicide and self-harm.
elements: The hospital conducts an environmental risk assessment that identifies features in the physical environment that could be used to attempt suicide or self-harm; the hospital takes necessary action to minimize the risk(s). (See also FMS.03.00, ME 1; FMS.04.00, ME 2)
Using a validated screening tool, the hospital screens all patients for suicidal ideation who are being evaluated or treated for behavioral conditions as their primary reason for care.

The hospital uses an evidence-based process to conduct a suicide assessment of patients who have screened positive for suicidal ideation. The assessment directly asks about suicidal ideation, plan, intent, suicidal or self-harm behaviors, risk factors, and protective factors.
Suicide screenings and assessments are documented in the patient’s medical record or in accordance with laws and regulations when applicable.

The hospital follows written policies and procedures addressing the care of patients identified as at risk for suicide. At a minimum, the policies should include the following: • Training and competence assessment of staff who care for patients at risk for suicide • Guidelines for reassessment of patients who are at risk for suicide and self-harm • Monitoring patients who are at high risk for suicide and self-harm
The hospital follows written policies and procedures for counseling and follow-up care at discharge for patients identified as at risk for suicide and self-harm.

The hospital monitors implementation and effectiveness of policies and procedures for screening, assessment, and management of patients at risk for suicide and self-harm, and takes action as needed to improve compliance.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: Food, nutrition products, and nutrition therapy are available to patients.
elements: A variety of food choices or nutrition, consistent with the patient’s condition, care, and needs, is regularly available.

The hospital has a clinical dietitian who is responsible for the following: • Developing a nutritional plan of care • Highlighting food-drug interactions to clinical staff • Making recommendations related to patient dietary needs • Nil per os (NPO) monitoring • Educating other health care staff, patients, and families • Dietary manual development, review, approval, and update process by the medical staff,

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: Pain is managed effectively.
elements: Patients are informed about the likelihood of pain and options for pain management when pain is an expected result of planned treatments, procedures, or examinations. (See also AOP.01.04, ME 3)
Patients in pain receive care according to pain management guidelines and in alignment with the patient’s goals for pain management.
The hospital has processes to communicate with and to educate patients and families about pain. (See also ACC.01.04, ME 3)
The hospital educates clinical staff about pain assessment and management.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The hospital has a process to provide end-of-life care that addresses the needs of the patient and family and optimizes the patient’s comfort and dignity.
elements: The hospital has a process to assess and manage the needs of patients receiving end-of-life care.
Staff are educated and trained about assessing and managing needs of patients and their families at the end of life.
The hospital provides patient care and support services that accommodate the patient and their family with consideration of their personal, spiritual/religious, and cultural preferences.
End-of-life care addresses the symptoms, conditions, and health care needs of the dying patient as indicated by their assessment, including pain and comfort needs.
The patient and family are involved in end-of-life care decisions.
The hospital provides support to the patient’s family, caregivers, and staff members caring for the dying patient.
When required, the hospital provides referral and transfer services to another facility that can provide palliative care (for example, bed or resources availability).
When applicable, the hospital provides or arranges for nursing home care (for example, inability to refer, patient/family wish).

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
group: Drug Administration (FDA) as a tissue or a medical device
statement: The hospital informs patients and families about how to donate organs and other tissues.
elements: The hospital complies with existing laws and regulations on organ and tissue donation, procurement, and transplantation.
The hospital supports patient and family choices to donate organs and other tissues.
The hospital provides information to patients and families on the donation process.
The hospital provides information to the patient and family on the way organ procurement is organized.
The hospital ensures that adequate controls are in place to prevent patients from feeling pressured to donate.
If the hospital performs organ transplants, it collaborates and coordinates with the Saudi Center for Organ Transplantation (SCOT).

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
group: Drug Administration (FDA) as a tissue or a medical device
statement: The hospital provides oversight for the process of organ and tissue procurement.
elements: The hospital develops a written organ and tissue donation and procurement process that is consistent with the region’s laws and regulations and its religious and cultural values.
The hospital identifies consent requirements for organ and tissue donation and procurement and develops a consent process consistent with those requirements.
Staff are trained on the issues and concerns related to organ donation and tissue procurement and the availability of transplants.
The hospital cooperates with relevant hospitals and agencies in the community to respect and to implement choices to donate.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
group: Drug Administration (FDA) as a tissue or a medical device
statement: The hospital’s leaders provide resources to support the organ, tissue, and/or cell transplant program.
elements: Staff education and training are specific to the types of organs, tissues, and/or cell transplants provided by the hospital.
The hospital’s leaders allocate resources for the transplant program.
Information management systems are used to support the quality of the transplant program.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
group: Drug Administration (FDA) as a tissue or a medical device
statement: The hospital identifies a qualified transplant program leader(s) and includes an interdisciplinary team that consists of clinical staff with expertise in the relevant transplant programs.
elements: The transplant program has an infrastructure, including systems and written policies and procedures, capable of supporting all aspects of the program.
A qualified individual(s) oversees and manages the transplant program.
The individual(s) fulfills the program’s oversight responsibilities as defined by the transplant program.
The transplant program documents the composition of each transplant team(s).
The transplant program documents the team members’ responsibilities.

Based on the services provided by the transplant team, the team includes individuals experienced in medicine, nursing, nutrition, pharmacology, infection prevention and control, social services, psychological services, rehabilitative services, and transplant coordination.
The transplant program evaluates team members for qualifications, training, and experience at the time each is being considered for the transplant team.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
group: Drug Administration (FDA) as a tissue or a medical device
statement: There is a designated coordination mechanism for all transplant activities.
elements: The individual responsible for the coordination of the live donor’s and transplant recipient’s care is identified and available through all phases of transplant care.
The hospital ensures that continuity of care for transplant patients (candidates and recipients) is facilitated through the pre-transplant, transplant, and discharge phases of transplantation.
Continuity of care is facilitated for living donors during the evaluation, donation, and discharge phases of donation.
The coordination of all transplant activities is communicated to all staff involved in the transplant program activities.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
group: Drug Administration (FDA) as a tissue or a medical device
statement: The hospital complies with organ, tissue, and cell transplant responsibilities.
elements: The hospital performing solid organ, tissue, and/or cell transplants complies with all rules set by the local, regional, or national procurement and transplantation network.
The hospital performing solid organ transplants shares all data related to transplant processes required by the local, regional, or national procurement and transplantation network.
The hospital develops and maintains standardized written procedures for the acquisition, receipt, storage, and issuance of organs, tissues, and/or cells.

The hospital verifies at the time of receipt of the organ that package integrity is met, and transport temperature range was controlled and acceptable for the organ(s), tissues, and/or cells. This verification is documented.
The hospital follows the tissue suppliers’ or manufacturers’ written directions for transporting, handling, storing, and using tissue.
The hospital follows a process to track transplanted tissues.
Refrigerators, freezers, nitrogen tanks, and other storage equipment used to store organs, tissues, and cells at a controlled temperature have functional alarms and an emergency backup plan.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
group: Drug Administration (FDA) as a tissue or a medical device
statement: The transplant program obtains informed consent specific to organ, tissue, and/or cell transplant from the transplant recipient candidate.
elements: The transplant program follows the hospital’s written policy when obtaining informed consent from solid organ, tissue, and/or cell transplant candidates. (See also PCC.03.00, MEs 1 and 2)

The transplant program informs the prospective transplant candidate of organ donor risk factors that could affect the success of the graft or the candidate’s health as a recipient, including but not limited to the following: • Donor’s history, as appropriate to the laws and regulations of the country/region • Condition of the organ(s) used • Age of the organ(s) • Potential risk of contracting infectious disease(s) if disease(s) cannot be detected in an infected

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
group: Drug Administration (FDA) as a tissue or a medical device
statement: The transplant program has documented protocols, clinical practice guidelines, or procedures for organ recovery and organ receipt to ensure the compatibility, safety, efficacy, and quality of human cells, tissues, and organs for transplantation.
elements: The transplant team follows written organ recovery protocols, clinical practice guidelines, or procedures, which include reviewing the essential donor data and recipient data to ensure compatibility before organ, tissue, or cell recovery takes place.
The transplant surgeon is responsible for confirming, in writing, the medical suitability of donor organs, tissues, and cells for transplantation into the recipient.

When an organ or tissue arrives at the transplant center, the transplanting surgeon and at least one other health care practitioner at the transplant center verify and document that the donor’s blood type and other essential data are compatible with the recipient prior to transplantation.

The transplant surgeon is responsible for confirming that donor evaluation and donor testing for infectious diseases and malignancy have been completed, and are documented in the medical record, before organ, tissue, or cell recovery and transplantation occur.

When an organ arrives at the transplant center, the transplanting surgeon and at least one other health care practitioner at the transplant center verify and document that evaluation and testing of the donor organ shows no evidence of disease, and the condition of the organ is suitable for transplant.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
group: Drug Administration (FDA) as a tissue or a medical device
statement: Clinical practice guidelines and clinical criteria guide the selection and care of organ, tissue, and cell transplant patients.
elements: The transplant program has documented cell-, tissue-, and/or organ-specific clinical practice guidelines for the pre-transplant, transplant, and discharge phases of transplantation.

Each transplant patient is under the care of a multidisciplinary patient care team coordinated by the patient’s primary transplant physician throughout the pre-transplant, transplant, and discharge phases of transplantation.
Transplant recipient candidates are evaluated for the suitability of other medical and surgical therapies that may yield short- and long-term survival rates comparable to transplantation.

Transplant recipient candidates receive a psychological evaluation by a psychiatrist, psychologist, social worker, or other qualified health care professional with experience in transplantation to determine the decision-making capacity of the patient and screen for any preexisting psychiatric illness.
The transplant program updates clinical information in the transplant donor’s and/or recipient’s medical record on an ongoing basis.
The transplant program documents organ compatibility confirmation in the living donor’s medical record. Transplant Programs Using Living Donor Organs

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
group: Drug Administration (FDA) as a tissue or a medical device
statement: Transplant programs that perform living donor transplantation adhere to local and regional laws and regulations and protect the rights of prospective or actual living donors.
elements: Transplant programs that perform living donor transplantation adhere to local and regional laws and regulations.
The living organ donor has the right to make a decision about donation in a setting free of coercion and pressure.
An individual with knowledge of living organ donation, transplantation, medical ethics, and informed consent is identified and appointed as an advocate for the living donor.
The individual appointed as the living donor advocate is not involved in routine transplantation activities.
The individual appointed as the living donor advocate informs, supports, and respects the living donor in a culturally appropriate manner during decision-making.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
group: Drug Administration (FDA) as a tissue or a medical device
statement: Transplant programs performing living donor transplants obtain informed consent specific to organ donation from the prospective living donor.
elements: Informed consent for living donation is obtained by trained staff and is in a language the prospective living donor can understand. (See also PCC.03.00, MEs 1 and 2)
The transplant program informs the prospective living donor of potential complications, risks (including psychological risks), and future health problems associated with living organ donation.
The transplant program informs the prospective living donor of alternative treatments for the transplant candidate.
The transplant program informs the prospective living donor of the donor’s right to opt out of donation at any time during the donation process.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
group: Drug Administration (FDA) as a tissue or a medical device
statement: Transplant programs that perform living donor transplants use clinical and psychological selection criteria to determine the suitability of potential living donors.
elements: The transplant program documents defined organ-specific living donor selection criteria.
The transplant program’s living donor selection criteria are consistent with laws and regulations and the principles of medical ethics. (See also GLD.07.00, ME 1)
The results of a medical evaluation related to the living donor’s own physical health are included in the determination of suitability for donation.
The results of medical tests identifying infectious diseases or malignancies are included in the determination of suitability for donation.

The results of a psychological evaluation conducted by a psychiatrist, psychologist, or social worker with experience in transplantation are documented in the living donor’s medical record and included in the determination of suitability for donation.
The transplant program documents organ compatibility confirmation in the living donor’s medical record.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
group: Drug Administration (FDA) as a tissue or a medical device
statement: Individualized patient care plans guide the care of living donors.
elements: Transplant programs performing living donor transplants are guided by documented living donor guidelines for care in the evaluation, donation, and discharge phases of donation.

Transplant programs performing living donor transplants provide interdisciplinary care by a team coordinated by a physician to each donor throughout the donor evaluation, donation, and discharge phases of donation.
The living donor candidate receives ongoing psychological support following donation.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The hospital implements a process to improve accuracy of patient identification.
elements: The hospital uses at least two patient identifiers, that do not include the use of the patient’s room number or location in the hospital, to identify the patient and to label elements associated with the patient’s care and treatment plan. (See also MMU.04.01, ME 4; MMU.05.03, ME 4; MOI.03.00, ME 1)
The hospital identifies patients with at least two identifiers before performing diagnostic procedures, providing treatments, and performing other procedures. (See also MMU.04.01, ME 4)
Patients are actively involved in the process of patient identification.
The hospital ensures the correct identification of patients in special circumstances, such as the comatose patient or newborn who is not immediately named.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The hospital implements a process for reporting critical results of diagnostic tests.
elements: The hospital defines, in writing, critical test results that may represent urgent or emergent life- threatening values for diagnostic tests. (See also AOP.03.02, ME 3)

The hospital develops a formal reporting process that identifies how critical results of diagnostic tests are reported/communicated to health care practitioners and the expected time frame for reporting the critical results as soon as they are received and not to exceed 30 minutes.

The hospital’s policy on critical results of diagnostic tests includes the following: • Identification of results that should be reported as critical • Identification of the notified party • Identification of the means of communicating critical results • Description of the sequence of conveying the result and read-back

The hospital identifies what critical result information is documented in the medical record, including the following: • Date and time of notification • Patient identification • Test results • Documentation of read-back • Identification of the notifying person • Identification of the notified person
The hospital monitors compliance with the defined time frames for reporting and acting on critical results, and documents actions taken when time frames are not met.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The hospital implements a standardized process for handover communication.
elements: The hospital implements a standardized procedure to communicate critical information between health care practitioners during handovers of patient care.

Patient care information is appropriately documented in a clearly understandable form (for example, Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation [SBAR]) to all care providers within and between care settings (for example, at shift changes, between different patient care units during a patient transfer).

The hospital uses standardized forms, tools, or methods that support a consistent and complete handover process that includes the opportunity for all staff involved to clarify information and ask questions.

Information about the patient’s care and response to treatment is shared between medical, nursing, and other care providers (for example, patient rounds, multidisciplinary teams, case management for patients requiring complex care).
The patient’s medical record is available to the authorized care providers to facilitate the exchange of information.
Information about patient care and progress is exchanged during change-of-shift reporting (handover), between shifts, and during transfers and referrals between health care providers.
The hospital collects, analyzes, tracks, and trends data for patient safety events related to handovers.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
group: Goal 3: Improve the Safety of Medications
statement: The hospital implements a process to improve the safety of high-alert medications.
elements: The hospital identifies, in writing, its list of high-alert medications.

The hospital identifies an annually updated list of high-alert medications and hazardous pharmaceutical chemicals based on its own data and national and international recognized organizations (for example, Institute of Safe Medication Practice, World Health Organization). The list contains, but is not limited to, the following: • Controlled and narcotics medications • Neuromuscular blockers • Chemotherapeutic agents • Concentrated electrolytes (for example hypertonic sodium chloride, concentrated potassium

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
group: Goal 3: Improve the Safety of Medications
statement: The hospital implements a process to improve the safety of look-alike/sound-alike (LASA) medications.
elements: The hospital identifies, in writing, its list of LASA medications. (See also MMU.02.00, ME 1; MMU.07.01, ME 2)
The hospital implements a written policy and procedure for handling and managing LASA medications that is comprehensive and uniform throughout the hospital. (See also MMU.07.01, ME 2)
The hospital reviews and revises annually its list of LASA drug names, which include LASA medication name pairs that the hospital stores, dispenses, and administers.

The hospital takes actions to prevent errors involving LASA medications, including the following, as applicable: • Providing education on LASA medications to health care professionals at orientation and as part

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
group: Goal 3: Improve the Safety of Medications
statement: The hospital implements a process to manage the safe use of concentrated electrolytes.
elements: Only qualified and trained individuals have access to concentrated electrolytes, and they are labeled with appropriate warnings and segregated from other medications throughout the storage and dispensing process. (See also MMU.04.00, ME 1; MMU.04.01, MEs 4 and 5; MMU.05.00, ME 1; MMU.05.03, ME 4)

The hospital stores vials of concentrated electrolytes outside the pharmacy only for emergency situations or specific purposes, and these are clearly identified in hospital policy. (See also MMU.03.00, MEs 1 and 2)

The hospital defines in writing the list of concentrated electrolytes by using evidence-based information and following the Joint Commission International (JCI) definition: Concentrated electrolytes are vials of concentrated forms of electrolytes that require dilution or other preparation before intravenous (IV) administration.
The hospital performs initial and ongoing proactive risk assessments at least annually for all areas where concentrated electrolytes are stored.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The hospital implements a process for the preoperative verification and surgical/invasive procedure site marking.
elements: The hospital implements a preoperative verification process using a checklist or other mechanism to document verification of the following: • Informed consent appropriate to the procedure • Correct patient, correct procedure, and correct site • All required documents, blood products, medical equipment, and implantable medical devices

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The hospital implements a process for the time-out that is performed immediately prior to the start of the surgical/invasive procedure and the sign-out that is conducted after the procedure.
elements: The full team actively participates in a time-out process, which includes the following elements in the area in which the surgical/invasive procedure will be performed, immediately before starting the procedure, and this is documented: • Correct patient identity • Correct procedure to be done • Correct surgical/invasive procedure site

Before the patient leaves the area in which the surgical/invasive procedure was performed, a sign-out process is conducted, which includes at least the following: • Name of the surgical/invasive procedure that was recorded/written • Completion of instrument, sponge, and needle counts, as applicable • Labeling of specimens • Any equipment problems to be addressed, as applicable
When surgical/invasive procedures are performed, including medical and dental procedures done in settings other than the operating theatre, the hospital uses uniform processes to ensure safe surgery.
When two or more separate procedures are being performed on the same patient by different surgeons, the team must perform another time-out before each new procedure is initiated.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The hospital implements evidence-based hand-hygiene guidelines to reduce the risk of health care–associated infections.
elements: The hospital adopts current evidence-based hand-hygiene guidelines. (See also PCI.07.01, MEs 2, 5, and 6)
The hospital implements an evidence-based hand hygiene program throughout the hospital. (See also PCI.07.01, MEs 2, 5, and 6)
The hospital collects and analyzes data for compliance with handwashing and hand disinfection.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The hospital manages its medication management processes.
elements: A qualified individual, who is a senior medical or pharmaceutical care staff member, oversees the medication management interdisciplinary team, called the pharmacy and therapeutics committee, established to develop the policies and processes for medication management in the hospital. (See also GLD.06.00, ME 1; HRP.02.01, ME 2)

The medication management interdisciplinary team (medical, nursing and management staff) develops written policies and a plan for a uniform medication management system that complies with applicable laws and regulations and includes the following processes, as applicable: • Planning • Selection and procurement • Storage • Prescribing and ordering • Preparing, dispensing, and distribution • Administration • Monitoring the effects of medication • Medication error and adverse event reporting • Evaluation • Formal processes for managing medication shortages and substitutions, including policies and procedures for properly communicating medication shortages and outages to prescribers and all health care professionals involved in medication management and other health care professionals

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The hospital implements a program for the prudent use of antimicrobials based on the principle of antimicrobial stewardship.
elements: The hospital implements a written program for antimicrobial stewardship that is based on scientific evidence, accepted clinical practice guidelines, and local laws and regulations and, at a minimum, includes the following: • Documentation indicating that the scope of the antimicrobial stewardship program includes the

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The hospital has a medication recall system process.
elements: The hospital implements a written policy for receiving and acting on notifications of recalled medications, including medications compounded within the hospital in which products that have been recalled have been used.
The policy includes identifying, retrieving, and returning, or safely and properly destroying, medications recalled by the manufacturer, supplier, or regulatory agency.
The hospital isolates recalled medications from the rest of the medication stock to prevent accidental use or distribution and clearly labels them as “recalled.”
The hospital notifies patients who received recalled medication and provides them with appropriate guidance.
The hospital has a process to inform health care providers about the recall and advise them on alternative treatments, if necessary.

The process includes documenting all actions taken related to the medication recall, including details such as the recall notice, affected lot numbers, actions taken, communications sent, and any responses received.
The process includes maintaining on file all drug recall memoranda from the Saudi Food and Drug Authority, manufacturers, and/or other relevant legal bodies.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The hospital has a process for handling expired medications.
elements: The hospital establishes and implements a written process for the following: • Identifying, retrieving, and returning opened and unopened, expired medications and outdated

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The hospital implements a process for the selection and procurement of medications.
elements: The interdisciplinary team collaborates with hospital leaders to develop criteria for determining how decisions are made for which medications are available for dispensing or administering. (See also IPSG.03.00, ME 1; IPSG.03.01, ME 1) Furthermore, there is a policy and procedure for selecting, approving, and procuring non-formulary medications within an acceptable time frame, including the following: • A readily available, patient-specific, non-formulary drug request form • Proper handling of non-formulary drug requisition within an acceptable time frame • Regular review of non-formulary drug requests by the pharmacy and therapeutics committee or an equivalent multidisciplinary body.

The list of medications (that is, the hospital formulary) by both brand name and generic name and properly classified using therapeutic classification, stocked in the hospital or readily available from contracted services, is reviewed annually.
The list of medications is accessible to all those involved in medication management.
The hospital formulary includes short drug monographs that illustrate the generic drug name, strength, and dosage form(s), indication(s), adverse drug reactions, and prescribing information.
The hospital formulary provides guidance on antibiotic use (both prophylactic and therapeutic uses).
The hospital formulary provides a list of approved prescribing abbreviations.
The hospital formulary provides a list of prohibited prescribing abbreviations.
The hospital formulary provides appendixes on important policies, therapeutic guidelines, drug safety in pregnancy and lactation, and dose adjustment in organ failure.

The process used to develop and monitor the list (unless determined by regulation or an authority outside the hospital) is developed by the interdisciplinary team in collaboration with hospital leaders.
There is a process for procuring medications during the following: • At night or when the pharmacy is closed (a pharmacist should be on call when the pharmacy is

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: Medications are properly and safely stored.
elements: Medications are stored under conditions suitable for product stability, including medications stored on individual patient care units and ambulances, as applicable. (See also IPSG.03.02, ME 2)
Medications in the patient care areas should be stored separately and labelled properly.
There is a policy and procedure on proper storage and control of medications, nutrition products, and free medical samples (from the point of receipt until the point of administration).

There is a policy and procedure to control the access of pharmaceutical care and nonpharmaceutical care staff to stores, pharmacies, and patient care areas, including after hours and in case of emergency (for example, fire, flood).
There are measures in place to secure medication storage areas, including limited access, proper locking procedures, and door key handling.
Only authorized individuals have access to stored medications.
No medications are stored directly on floor (a minimum of 10 centimeters is left to manage spills).
Medications are not stacked so high to block sprinklers or come in contact with overhead lights or pipes.
Medications are stored according to manufacturer’s recommendations (temperature, light, humidity, sanitation).
There is an appropriate storage area for regular medications with controlled temperature (between 18 and 25 degrees centigrade), 24 hours a day, 7 days a week.
The room air temperature is checked and documented at least once daily on the temperature log sheet.
Temperature records are kept for at least three years.
All antiseptics, disinfectants, and medications for external use are stored separately from enteral and injectable medications.
The “first expiry/first out” (FEFO) principle is followed.
Medication quality issues are reported to the Saudi Food and Drug Administration, as required.
There is a policy and procedure on proper storage and control of refrigerated and frozen medications from the point of receipt until the point of administration.
There are medication refrigerators and freezers for storing refrigerated and frozen medications, biologicals, and vaccines.
All medication refrigerators and freezers are equipped with appropriate thermometers or equivalent device for temperature recording.
Refrigerator temperature is checked and documented at least once daily on the temperature log sheet.
Refrigerator temperature is kept between 2 and 8°C.
Freezer temperature is kept between -10 and -25°C.
All vaccine refrigerators are connected to an emergency power source, and electric outlets are marked accordingly.
Vaccine refrigerator temperature is continuously recorded around the clock, or an equivalent process is in place to monitor temperature around the clock.
Temperature records are kept for at least three years.

There is a clear and defined mechanism to deal with an electric power outage or out-of-range temperature of the medication refrigerators and freezers to ensure the integrity of the affected medication before its reuse.
Food, drinks, biological samples, and culture media are not allowed inside any medication refrigerator or freezer.

The hospital stores all medications, including biologicals and controlled (scheduled) medications, in a secured area to prevent diversion, and locked, as applicable, in accordance with laws and regulations. These medications are accurately accounted for according to applicable laws and regulations. (See also IPSG.03.02, ME 2; FMS.05.00, ME 2)

The hospital stores narcotics and psychotropic and other controlled medications in accordance with relevant laws and regulations in a secured area to prevent diversion, and locked, as applicable, in accordance with laws and regulations (behind steel doors with double locks).

The following medications are accurately accounted for according to applicable laws and regulations: (See also IPSG.03.02, ME 2; FMS.05.00, ME 2) • Limited floor stock supply of controlled and narcotics medications to meet patient needs • Proper drug count, endorsement, and accountability • Documentation of empty containers of narcotics and proper disposal of unused portions

There is a written process for managing medications or products requiring special handling, such as hazardous medications, radioactive medications, and investigational medications. (See also MMU.06.00, ME 6)
The hospital has a list of hazardous medications and pharmaceutical chemicals in areas where they are stored or used.
Hazardous medications and pharmaceutical chemicals are stored separately on low shelves and in the original labeled containers.
Flammables and volatile substances are stored in appropriate safety cabinets in well-ventilated areas.
Spill kits and personal protective equipment are readily available.

For staff involved in handling chemicals and hazardous medications (such as chemotherapeutic agents) and who are attempting to conceive, are pregnant, or are breastfeeding, a structured process is in place to review potential exposure risks and offer alternative work assignment.
Material safety data sheets (MSDS) for all available hazardous medications and pharmaceutical chemicals are available and accessible to staff.
Eye wash station and emergency water shower are available where hazardous medications and pharmaceutical chemicals are located.
The hospital staff are well educated on the proper storage and handling of hazardous medications and pharmaceutical chemicals and spill management.
Medications and chemicals used to prepare medications are accurately labeled with contents, expiration dates, and applicable warnings.
All medication storage areas, including medication storage areas on patient care units and ambulances (as applicable), are periodically inspected to ensure that medications are stored properly.

Medications are protected from loss or theft throughout the hospital. Inspection includes, but is not limited to, availability, stock level, expiration date, and storage conditions. (See also FMS.04.00, ME 2)

The hospital should have in place a safe and secure system for managing medications in the patient care areas that includes the following: • Defining floor stock quantities to the limited quantities per the needs of each unit • Anesthesia reversal agents available in operating rooms and areas where moderate or deep

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: Emergency medications are available, uniformly stored, monitored, and secure when stored out of the pharmacy.
elements: Emergency medications are immediately available in the patient care areas or are readily accessible within the hospital to meet emergency needs and based on the current Saudi Heart Association recommendations.

The hospital establishes and implements a consistent and uniform written process for how emergency medications are stored; maintained; replaced when used, damaged, or out of date; and protected from loss or theft. (See also FMS.04.00, ME 2)
There is an inspection program per shift by nursing staff and per month by pharmaceutical care staff.

Access to emergency medications shall not require a specific individual or keys to unlock the emergency cart; emergency medications are protected from loss or theft using safety plastic seals, and those plastic seals are stored in a secured location and under the supervision of nursing or pharmaceutical staff.

The hospital uses a risk-based approach to identify and implement strategies to improve the efficiency and accuracy of medication administration during emergency resuscitation. This approach at a minimum includes the following: • Review of internal data from previous emergency situations to assess the availability of

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The hospital identifies those qualified individuals permitted to prescribe or to order medications.
elements: Only those permitted by the hospital and by relevant licensure, laws, and regulations prescribe or order medications. (See also COP.01.00, ME 1; IPSG.03.02, ME 1)
Individuals permitted to prescribe and to order medications are known to the pharmaceutical service or others who dispense medications.
The hospital has a multidisciplinary policy and procedure for identifying those individuals permitted to prescribe or order controlled and narcotic medications and their prescribing privileges.
Only individuals permitted by the hospital and relevant laws and regulations prescribe or order controlled and narcotic medications.
Individuals permitted to prescribe or order controlled and narcotic medications are known to pharmaceutical care staff and nursing staff who dispense medications.

The hospital implements its policy on prescribing privileges such as those for controlled and narcotic substances, chemotherapy agents, and high-alert, radioactive, investigational, and other specialty medications.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The hospital identifies safe prescribing, ordering, and transcribing practices and defines the elements of a complete order or prescription.
elements: The hospital establishes, implements, and trains staff on a written process for the safe prescribing, ordering, and transcribing of medications in the hospital.
A diagnosis, condition, or indication for use exists for each medication ordered.
All orders and prescriptions contain the following elements: • Name of the drug • Dose • Frequency • Route of administration (See also IPSG.03.02, ME 1)

Additional elements of complete medication orders or prescriptions include, at a minimum, the following as appropriate to the order: • Data necessary to accurately identify the patient • When generic or brand names are acceptable or required • Specific guidelines for the use of as-needed (PRN) orders • Weight-based orders • Rates of administration for intravenous infusions • Special orders such as titrating, tapering, or range orders • Titration orders include the medication name, medication route, initial rate of infusion (dose/ unit of time), incremental units to which the rate or dose can be increased or decreased, how often the rate or dose can be changed, the maximum rate or dose of infusion, and the objective

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The hospital has a medication reconciliation process.
elements: The hospital identifies, in writing, the information needed to reconcile current and newly ordered medications.

The patient’s medical record contains a list of current medications taken prior to admission or registration as an outpatient, and this information is made available to the patient’s health care practitioners and the pharmacy as needed. (See also ACC.03.00, ME 5)
Medication reconciliation includes comparing the initial medication orders with the list of medications taken prior to admission, according to the hospital’s established process.
A medication review is conducted when there are changes to the patient’s level of care, unit, or health care practitioner service, including the discharge planning process for medication management.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: Medications are prepared and dispensed in a safe and clean environment.
elements: Medication preparation and dispensing adhere to laws, regulations, and professional standards of practice. (See also IPSG.03.02, ME 1)
Medications are prepared and dispensed in clean, uncluttered, safe, and functionally separate areas with appropriate medical equipment and supplies. (See also PCI.04.00, MEs 1 and 2)

Staff preparing/compounding sterile products/medications are trained and competent in the principles of medication preparation and aseptic techniques and are provided resources to support the medication preparation process. (Refer to Appendixes 1, 2, 3, and 4 at the end of MMU chapter.)
During preparation, staff visually inspect the medication for particulates, discoloration, or other loss of integrity.
Guidelines for use of single-use and multidose vials are identified and implemented in the medication processes.

Guidelines for use of multidose vials are identified and implemented in the medication processes, including the following: vaccines, oral liquids, and other multidose medications (for example, eye, ear, and nasal drops; creams; ointments; nebulization solutions).
All open multidose medications are labeled with open date, expiration date, initials, and time.
There should be a mechanism to ensure that there are no expired open or unlabeled open multidose containers available in patient care areas.
Medications stored, prepared, and dispensed from areas outside the pharmacy (for example, patient care units) comply with the same cleanliness measures required in the pharmacy.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The hospital’s process for radiopharmaceuticals is in accordance with laws, regulations, and guidelines.
elements: The hospital has a written process to prepare and dispense radiopharmaceuticals in accordance with laws and regulations and clinical practice guidelines.

Radiopharmaceuticals are prepared by, or under the supervision of, an appropriately trained and qualified individual (for example, a nuclear technologist, registered pharmacist, doctor of medicine or osteopathy, chemist, biologist, or qualified nurse).
Sterile radiopharmaceutical facilities are designed and controlled to minimize airborne contamination and provide an appropriately lighted and comfortable working environment.
Radiopharmaceuticals are transported and stored in accordance with laws and regulations and guidelines to maintain their stability and radioactivity until they are administered.

Radiopharmaceuticals are packaged in appropriate containers and labeled to provide the following essential information: • Name of the radiopharmaceutical • Dosage • Expiration date • Radiation warning symbol(s)

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: Medication prescriptions or orders are reviewed for appropriateness.
elements: The hospital defines, in writing, the patient-specific information required for an effective review process, and the source or availability of this information is available at all times when the pharmacy is open or closed.

Each prescription or order is reviewed for appropriateness in a manner, identified by the hospital, that ensures a full appropriateness review prior to dispensing and administration, except in an emergency or when the ordering physician is present for ordering, administering, and monitoring of the patient, in accordance with laws and regulations. (See also MMU.06.00, ME 2)

The process to conduct an appropriateness review for an order or prescription prior to dispensing is performed by a trained pharmacist and includes evaluation of the following: • Appropriateness of the drug, dose, frequency, and route of administration • Therapeutic duplication • Real or potential allergies or sensitivities • Real or potential interactions between the medication and other medications or food • Variation from hospital criteria for use • Patient’s weight and other physiological information • Current or potential impact as indicated by laboratory values • Other contraindications

Individuals permitted to conduct appropriateness reviews meet the following criteria: • Are assessed competent to do so by a qualified individual(s) • Are permitted to do so by privileges or job descriptions • Are provided resources to support the review process
