When the designated licensed professional (pharmacist) is not available to perform the full appropriateness review, a trained individual conducts and documents a review of the following critical elements for the first dose, prior to the full appropriateness review that must be conducted within 24 hours: • Allergies • Lethal drug-drug interactions • Weight-based dosing • Potential organ toxicity

Clinical decision support programs used in conjunction with a designated licensed professional or trained individual for the full appropriateness review, as well as other computer programs and print reference materials used to cross-check the critical elements of an appropriateness review, are current and updated.
After the medication order has been reviewed, concerns, issues, or questions are clarified with the individual prescriber and documented before dispensing according to hospital policy.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: A system is used to safely dispense medications in the right dose to the right patient at the right time.
elements: The hospital dispenses medications and maintains records in accordance with laws and regulations, licensure, and professional standards of practice.
Medications are dispensed in the most ready-to-administer form available, such as repackaged unit doses, to minimize the likelihood of errors during distribution or administration.

The system supports accurate and timely dispensing and documentation of dispensing practices that meet patient needs, and it should not exceed 24 hours for inpatient care, except for oral or topical preparations
For high-alert medications, an independent double-check process should be implemented.

The hospital has a written policy for medication labeling practices that at a minimum includes the following: • Information on medication labels • Medications not immediately administered • Preparing individualized medications for multiple patients (See also IPSG.01.00, ME 1) • When a patient medication(s) is prepared by someone other than the person administering the

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The pharmaceutical care department has a system for provision of outpatient education and counseling.
elements: The pharmaceutical care department has a system for providing outpatient education and counseling that includes verbal explanation and instructions by a pharmacist to patients and their families on the safe and effective use, administration, and storage of medications.
Written educational information is given in a language and form the patient can understand.
Patient privacy is maintained during education and counseling.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: Medication administration is safely performed by qualified individuals.
elements: Only nurses and other authorized clinical staff administer medications. The hospital defines those who are authorized to administer medication, with or without supervision, in accordance with laws and regulations. The hospital may place limits, when appropriate, on the medication administration of individuals.
Qualifications, experiences, and competency assessments of individuals involved in medication administration are available in their personnel files.

Specific additional guidelines are available for the following: • Safe administration of intravenous push medications • Standard Drug Administration Time • Disposal of the unused portion of narcotic drugs and controlled substances • Safe administration and disposal of chemotherapy

The hospital implements a process for medication administration to verify that the medication is correctly administered in accordance with the medication prescription or order. (See also MMU.05.02, ME 2)

Prior to administration, the individual administering the medication must do the following: • Verify the identity of the patient • Verify that the medication selected matches the medication order or prescription and product

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: Policies and procedures govern medications brought into the hospital by the patient or family, medication prescribed for patient self-administration, and medication samples.
elements: The hospital defines, in writing, when medications brought into the hospital by patients or their families or brought into the hospital as samples can be administered, including checking the integrity of medications brought, and the labeling, ordering, and administration documentation in the patient record.

If self-administration of medications is allowed, the hospital follows the written processes that guide the safe and accurate self-administration of medications or the administration of medications by a family member. The processes address training, supervision, and documentation. 3 The hospital educates patients and families involved in self-administration and documents in the patient’s medical record about the following: • Medication name, type, and reason for use • How to administer the medication, including process, time, frequency, route, and dose • Anticipated actions and potential side effects of the medication administered • Monitoring the effects of the medication • Proper storage of the medication
The hospital determines that the patient or the family member who administers the medication is competent at medication administration before allowing them to administer medications.
When patient’s own medication is not permitted due to the integrity and quality of the medication, both patient and prescriber should be informed.
Medical samples brought by patients are not allowed to be administered at the hospital.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The hospital monitors and responds to the patient’s response to medications and to the actual or potential adverse drug events and adverse drug reactions.
elements: The hospital should establish a multidisciplinary policy and procedure on monitoring the patient response to medications, including the following: • An annual updated list of all formulary medications that cause changes in the patient’s

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The hospital implements a process for identifying, reporting, managing, and tracking all medication errors and near miss events (or close calls).
elements: The hospital adopts definitions of a medication error and a near miss from established and updated guidelines.

The hospital establishes and implements written processes for the following: • Identifying medication errors and near misses • Timely reporting of medication errors and near misses • Timely notification to the treating physician and documentation in the patient medical record • The option for anonymous reporting of medication errors and near misses • Managing medication errors and near misses, including investigating, developing an action

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The hospital implements processes that support patient and family rights during care.
elements: Hospital leaders work collaboratively to protect and advance patient and family rights.
The hospital helps patients exercise their rights and enables them to communicate their concerns or inquiries regarding their rights.

Hospital leaders implement patient and family rights as identified in laws and regulations and through policies and procedures establish and maintain a structure that involves the hospital’s leaders and others to support and oversee all patient rights activities (for example, patient relations, patient rights/patient advocacy committee).

Hospital leaders protect patient and family rights in relation to the cultural practices of the community or individual patients served (for example, providing separate facilities for women, where appropriate).
Hospital leaders develop and maintain a patient rights and responsibilities statement that includes all patient and family rights and responsibilities.
Hospital leaders protect the patient’s right to identify whom the patient wishes to participate in care decisions.
The hospital has a process to determine the patient’s or family’s preferences regarding what and when information is provided to the patient, family, or others.

All clinical staff are trained, through orientation and ongoing courses, on how to support patient and family rights and their participation in care. Staff are aware of their responsibilities in protecting patient and family rights.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The hospital respects, protects, and promotes patient rights.
elements: Information about patient rights and responsibilities is provided to each patient in a language the patient understands. The hospital ensures that the patients are informed about their rights and responsibilities. (See also MOI.02.02, ME 3)

The hospital provides patients appropriate information regarding their responsibilities, including the responsibility to do the following: • Provide complete and accurate information about their health, including medications, dietary

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The hospital protects patient privacy, confidentiality, and access to health information.
elements: Patient privacy is respected for all clinical interviews, examinations, procedures/treatments, and transport. Privacy measures include not exposing patient private parts unnecessarily during care processes and a mandate to get written consent for photographing patients. (See also GLD.09.00, ME 3; HCT.01.03, ME 2; MOI.01.01, ME 1; MOI.01.02, ME 3)
Confidentiality of patient information is maintained, including protection from loss or misuse, according to laws and regulations.
The hospital has a process for patients to give permission for the release of information, including obtaining consent if required, consistent with laws and regulations.
The hospital has a process for providing patients with access to their health information consistent with laws, regulations, and culture.
The hospital provides patients with access to health information, regardless of their ability to pay.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The hospital provides patients with information regarding the safety and security of personal possessions.
elements: The hospital has a process described in a policy for protecting patient belongings.
The hospital has determined its level of responsibility for patients’ possessions. (See also FMS.04.00, ME 2)
Patients receive information about the hospital’s responsibility for safeguarding and protecting their personal possessions.

Patients’ possessions are safeguarded and protected from theft or loss when the hospital assumes responsibility or when the patient is unable to assume responsibility through a process that outlines the following: • Where patient belongings are kept • Who is responsible for obtaining the required signatures on the related form when receiving and

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The hospital identifies its vulnerable populations and the risks to those populations.
elements: The hospital includes the following sources, at a minimum, when defining its vulnerable populations: • Predetermined list of widespread populations as applicable to the hospital’s scope of services • Determined by results of the annual risk assessment • In accordance with laws and regulations

The hospital’s predetermined list includes the following vulnerable populations, as applicable to the hospital’s scope of services: • Disabled and chronically ill • Socioeconomically disadvantaged • Elderly/frail • Children/adolescents • Racial/ethnic minorities​ • Sexual minorities

The hospital performs a vulnerable population risk assessment annually, at a minimum, to identify the following: • Vulnerable populations the hospital serves • Risks associated with each vulnerable population • Specific resources needed to support the care, treatment, and services of these vulnerable

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: Patients and families are engaged in all aspects of their care, treatment, and services.
elements: The hospital supports and promotes patient and family engagement with responsible staff members in care processes and in decision-making and have their questions answered. Patients are informed about how they can actively participate in their care decisions and their choices are respected. Patients are informed of the name and the professional status of the physician or other professional who has the primary responsibility for managing the care process. Staff members identify themselves by introduction and by displaying name.

The health care team informs patients and their families about medical conditions, any confirmed diagnosis, a prognosis, and the planned care and treatment(s) in a manner they can understand to encourage patient engagement and collaboration. When it is medically inadvisable to provide the patient with such information, the information is provided to a legally authorized person or a person designated by the patient. (See also PCC.03.00, ME 1)

Patients are informed of any unanticipated outcomes, including adverse events, that occurred during their care and treatment. The disclosure process is documented in the patient’s medical record. (See also MMU.07.00, ME 1)
The hospital permits and responds appropriately to a patient who seeks a second opinion without compromising the patient’s care.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The hospital informs patients and families about their rights and responsibilities to refuse or discontinue treatment, withhold resuscitative services, and forgo or withdraw life-sustaining treatments.
elements: The hospital identifies its position through a written policy on withholding resuscitative services and forgoing or withdrawing life-sustaining treatments for terminally ill or end-of-life patients, which includes documenting the patient/family decision about the resuscitation order in the patient’s medical record.
The hospital’s position aligns with its community’s religious and cultural norms and any legal or regulatory requirements.

The hospital develops and implements a policy to inform patients and families about their rights to refuse or discontinue treatment and the hospital’s responsibilities related to these decisions. Patient and family choices are respected, and relevant discussion is documented in the patient’s medical record.
The hospital informs patients about the consequences of their decisions.
The hospital informs patients about available care and treatment alternatives.
The hospital provides health care practitioners with resources related to the ethical and legal considerations in carrying out patient wishes.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The hospital evaluates patient experience data and makes improvements to enhance the quality of patient care.
elements: Hospital leaders implement a process (for example, patient satisfaction surveys) for collecting and assessing the patient experience.

Data from the patient experience are collected, aggregated, analyzed, and transformed into information to identify and implement strategies for improving the patient experience. (See also QPS.03.00, ME 2)
Hospital leaders determine priority areas for improving the patient experience that will positively impact patient care.

Data are collected and analyzed following improvements to the patient experience to evaluate their impact on the quality of patient care. The hospital’s quality program should monitor compliance and issue a quarterly report.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The hospital informs patients and families about their right to report complaints and to be notified of errors related to their care and the hospital’s process for acting on them.
elements: The hospital develops and implements a policy for fairly managing patient complaints, including how patients and families are informed about the process for reporting complaints.

The hospital assigns a specific unit or person (for example, patient relations) for managing complaints who investigates and, when possible, resolves complaints within a time frame as defined in hospital policy. If the complaint cannot be resolved immediately, the hospital acknowledges receipt of the complaint and notifies the patient of follow-up to the complaint.
Hospital leaders take quality improvement and strategic actions based on trended data (for example, quarterly and annually).

The hospital develops a written policy that addresses disclosure of clinical errors to patients that includes, at a minimum, the following: • How the hospital defines clinical error • The circumstances under which disclosure of a clinical error is recommended • Who is responsible for notifying a patient of a clinical error • Other individuals or entities that must be notified when applicable
The hospital implements and follows its policy on the disclosure of clinical errors.
The hospital follows its internal process to analyze clinical errors and to prevent the error from occurring again.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: Informed consent is obtained through a process defined by the hospital and carried out by trained staff in a manner and language the patient or their surrogate can understand.
elements: The hospital develops a written policy and implements an informed consent process that includes at least the following: • Defining what information must be discussed and documented as part of the consent process, which includes at least explanation of the nature of the treatment or procedure, expected benefits and risks, alternative courses of action, and the likely consequences of not undergoing the

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The hospital provides an education program that is based on the care, treatment, and services it provides and meets the needs of the patient population it serves.
elements: The hospital, through policies and procedures, plans effective education based on the care, treatment, and services provided and the needs of its patient population. (See also ASC.02.03, ME 2; ASC.03.01, ME 2; HCT.01.01, ME 4)

The hospital has a program with appropriate structure and efficient resources to educate patients throughout the hospital that includes the following: • Oversight by a qualified member(s) of the clinical staff • Access to educational resources, including different teaching methods (such as pamphlets, diagrams, models to practice on, videos, other teaching methods), based on the care, treatment,

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: Each patient’s educational needs and learning ability are assessed and documented in their medical record.
elements: Each patient’s and, when appropriate, family’s educational needs and preferences are assessed and recorded in the patient’s medical record. This must include, at a minimum, the following: • The language the patient prefers for education • The form(s) the patient prefers for education • Who should receive education in addition to the patient (for example, spouse, caregiver) • Any known barriers to learning, including literacy skills, readiness and ability to learn, capability

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: All critical care units operate under qualified medical and nursing leadership appropriate to the unit’s specialty and scope of services.
elements: Each critical and specialized care unit is managed by a qualified individual responsible for overall operations, including the supervision of policy development, implementation, and adherence to infection control guidelines. The specific qualifications required for the individual leading each unit are described in Appendix A.

Each unit is overseen by a nurse manager who collaborates with other departments to develop and implement policies and procedures relevant to the unit, including infection control practices. The nurse manager ensures staff competency and meets specific qualifications based on the unit type as described in Appendix B.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: Critical and specialized care units maintain adequate qualified staff appropriate to unit type, patient acuity, and service scope.
elements: All specialized and critical care units have adequate physician coverage with certification requirements, as described in Appendix C.
All specialized and critical care units have adequate nursing coverage with certification requirements as described in Appendix D.
All specialized and critical care units have adequate staffing of other staff as described in Appendix E.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: Units implement structured processes for patient admission, continued stay, and discharge.
elements: The ICU, PICU, NICU, and CCU; labor and delivery; hemodialysis unit; burn unit; and oncology/ radiation services identify their own population based on age- and diagnosis-related groups consistent with evidence-based practice.
The admission and discharge criteria for the ICU, PICU, NICU, and CCU as well as the burn unit are defined in writing and are implemented.
The criteria for admission are based on physiological parameters (for example, in labor and delivery unit, gestational age of mothers, obstetric department design, available resources).
The criteria are developed collaboratively by relevant staff (for example, obstetricians in case of labor and delivery, nephrologists in case of hemodialysis unit).

In an open ICU, PICU, or CCU, the most responsible physician (MRP) is the admitting consultant, whereas in a closed ICU, the MRP is a member of the medical staff in the ICU, and in the CCU, the MRP is the CCU physician/intensivist.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The intensive care units have an effective handover process that uses the Situation-Background-Assessment- Recommendation (SBAR) tool.
elements: There is documented evidence of handover using the SBAR tool between physicians at change of shift in the ICU, PICU, NICU, and CCU.
There is documented evidence of handover using the SBAR tool between nurses at change of shift in the ICU, PICU, NICU, and CCU.

There is documented evidence of handover using the SBAR tool between intensive care nurse/CCU nurse and the unit/ward nurse at the time of transfer to a lower acuity of care in ICU, PICU, NICU, and CCU.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: Patient care in the critical and specialized care units is provided using a multidisciplinary approach.
elements: The multidisciplinary team for the ICU, PICU, NICU, and CCU includes unit-specific members as well as non-intensive care specialists. The team consists of the ICU/PICU/NICU/CCU physician, unit nurse, clinical pharmacist, respiratory therapist, dietitian, social worker, physiotherapist, and the consultant from the primary service under which the patient was initially admitted.
Medically necessary services are always available and accessible in these units.
Critical care is provided equally and equitably to all patients, whether they are in the unit or other hospital areas (for example, ventilated patients in the emergency department).
Care is developed using evidence-based methods in collaboration with the multidisciplinary team, coordinated among team members, and documented in the patient’s medical record.

A multidisciplinary committee oversees oncology and radiotherapy services and meets at least quarterly. The committee maintains meeting minutes and is responsible for developing, reviewing, and ensuring the implementation of policies, procedures, safety plans, guidelines, and protocols for safe patient care.
Oncology and radiotherapy services include a palliative care unit/service for pain management and treatment-related symptom relief. Staff members receive training in palliative care practices.

The burn unit coordinates with other services, including critical care, anesthesia, social services, pharmaceutical care, and physiotherapy, to meet patient needs. Care is coordinated with different disciplines participating in the plan of care.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: Specialized and critical care units have coordinated admission and discharge processes.
elements: The PICU/ICU/CCU physician and the primary physician jointly make the decision to admit and discharge patients from the unit.
A summary of the intensive care stay is written by the NICU/PICU/ICU/CCU physician and made available at the time of discharge from intensive care to a lower acuity level.
There is documented evidence of handover between the intensive care unit physician and the unit/ ward physician at the time of transfer to a lower acuity of care in ICU, PICU, NICU, and CCU.

When the patient is discharged from the ICU, PICU, NICU, or CCU, the ICU physician ensures that the receiving team on the floor is well informed about the patient’s status and ongoing patient needs, including the following: • The patient’s plan of care and medications are written in detail by the physician, including how to continue them in the floor. • Any special care requirements are documented (for example, watch drainage tubes, tracheotomy care, wound care) in the patient’s medical record.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: Nursing and other staff staffing plans are available in the critical and specialized care units.
elements: The nursing staffing plans demonstrate an evidence-based nursing-to-patient ratio in the ICU, PICU, NICU, and CCU.
The nursing staffing plans are matching the patient volume and patient acuity in the ICU, PICU, NICU, and CCU.
For dental services, dental technicians are available as needed. Moreover, the service ensures that there is one dental assistant per chair.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: Nursing staff in the ICUs receive continuous training with competency assessment.
elements: Nursing and other staff in the critical and specialized care units receive training and education on the general and intensive care–related needs to ensure provision of effective services as relevant to scope of service as defined in Appendix F.
There is a qualified and competent nurse to receive the newborn during delivery, with competencies defined in Appendix F.
There is ongoing competency assessment for the nursing staff (for example, written test, return demonstration).
The competency assessment of the nursing staff is documented.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: Units maintain essential equipment and supplies aligned with patient population needs.
elements: There are isolation rooms with at least one negative pressure room in the ICU, PICU, NICU, and CCU.
There are adequate equipment and medication available in the unit as defined in Appendix G.
The availability and functionality of all tools and equipment are checked daily or when needed.
Equipment is cleaned and disinfected daily and as needed.

All units ensure that equipment and machines are operated within manufacturers’ specifications and periodical preventive maintenance is developed and implemented in accordance with manufacturers’ instructions. All maintenance and repair records are maintained for future reference and inspection.
Portable equipment for safe patient transports is available in at least in the NICU and CCU.
Laboratory and imaging services are available to meet the needs of patients receiving intensive care in the ICU, PICU, NICU, and CCU.

The hemodialysis unit has an equipment management program that includes the following: • All equipment and machines are operated within manufacturers’ specifications, and the periodical preventive maintenance is developed and implemented in accordance with manufacturers’ instructions. • All maintenance and repair are performed by qualified staff/entities, and records are maintained for future reference and inspection. • Staff receive equipment orientation and training to identify malfunctioning equipment or machines and to report to appropriate staff for repair. • Every dialysis machine is equipped with monitors and an alarm system. • The preventive maintenance program includes the water treatment and distribution system.

Safety of specialized equipment, such as linear accelerator and other radiation equipment, is ensured through a safety plan that is implemented and audited. The safety plan includes periodic inspection, maintenance and calibration, guidelines of inspection and monitoring and management of nuclear material used for therapeutic and diagnostic purposes, especially regarding handling, storage, and transportation.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: Policies and procedures are available to guide the work in the critical and specialized care units.
elements: There are policies and procedures for medical and nursing procedures in critical and specialized care units, as listed in Appendix H.
Appropriate staff collaboratively develop the policies and procedures.
Policies and procedures are implemented as evidenced in the daily practice and the patient’s medical record.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The ICU, PICU, and CCU have a process for detecting and notifying potential deceased organ donors.
elements: The ICU, PICU, and CCU establish an effective communication process regarding organ donation and transplantation and work collaboratively with the Saudi Centre for Organ Transplantation (SCOT).
The ICU, PICU, and CCU use criteria to identify, notify, document, and manage potential donors based on the registry of organ donation and transplantation in Saudi Arabia.
The ICU, PICU, and CCU report all cases of potential deceased donors after brain death (DBDs) to SCOT in a timely manner.
The ICU, PICU, and CCU report all cases of potential deceased donors after circulatory death (DCDs) to SCOT in a timely manner.

The hospital establishes and uses criteria that support the effectiveness of the donation process (for example, patient factors, time since perfusion of the tissue stopped, maintenance of viability by appropriate care of the body between death and donation).

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: Infection control standards are developed, strictly implemented, and supervised in the intensive care and specialized units.
elements: The environments of the ICU, PICU, NICU, and CCU are maintained, clean, and neat at all times.
Infection control standards are strictly applied in these ICUs (for example, hand hygiene, personal protective equipment).
Staff members in these ICUs adopt and implement care bundles to prevent epidemiologically significant health care–associated infections.

The hemodialysis unit, burn unit, and dental services follow infection control guidelines developed or adopted from authoritative sources or relevant professional organizations. Implementation is evident from practice and documentation in medical records. The hemodialysis unit also implements protocols to protect staff and patients from bloodborne pathogens. The minimum measures are listed in Appendix I. Appendix A – Specific Requirements for Individuals

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The hospital complies with relevant laws, regulations, building and fire safety codes, and facility inspection requirements.
elements: Hospital leaders implement the national and local laws, regulations, building and fire safety codes, valid Saudi Civil Defense license, and other requirements applicable to the hospital’s facilities (for example, MOMRA’s hospital building requirements, Saudi building code, discharges to drainage systems, safe disposal of waste).

Corrective actions taken to meet the conditions of external facility reports and inspections by national and local authorities are documented, including a valid Saudi Civil Defense report and action plan as applicable.

Hospital leaders and safety committee plan and budget for acquiring, replacing, or upgrading facilities, systems, and equipment through information resulting from safety tours, regular inspection, testing, data monitoring, and maintenance of all operating components needed to meet requirements and for the continued operation of a safe, secure, and effective facility.

When the hospital is located inside a multiuse building, hospital leaders obtain evidence of compliance with relevant laws, regulations, codes, facility inspection reports, utility maintenance requirements, and other requirements related to shared systems and building issues.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: A qualified individual(s) oversees the facility management and safety structure.
elements: Oversight and direction of all aspects of the facility management and safety structure are assigned to a facility management and safety program director qualified by experience and training (for example, bachelor’s degree in engineering science), and evidence of the experience and training in facility management and safety is documented. (See also GLD.06.00, ME 1).
The program director is assisted by qualified staff (for example, safety officer) as required, according to the size and complexity of the hospital services.
Each department has an assigned liaison safety officer to liaise all safety issues within the department.

The program director is responsible for ensuring the following: • Ongoing consultation is provided to all departments. • Recommendations for space, technology, and other resources to support the facility management and safety structure are provided to hospital leaders. • The facility management and safety programs are current and fully implemented. • Staff and others are trained on the programs. • The programs are coordinated, evaluated, and monitored. • The programs are reviewed and revised at least annually, or more frequently if needed (for example, when there are changes to requirements in the country’s laws and regulations, or changes to the hospital’s facilities, systems, or equipment).

There is a multidisciplinary safety committee that oversees the facility management and safety program, which consists of representatives from relevant departments (for example, safety, security, housekeeping, infection control, risk management, biomedical engineering, laboratory, medical staff, emergency department, nursing, radiation safety, maintenance, quality management). The committee meets at least ten times per year on a monthly schedule, and the meeting minutes are documented to be approved by hospital leadership.
When independent business entities are present within the organization, the entities comply with the applicable facility management and safety programs.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The hospital develops and documents a risk assessment based on facility management and safety risks identified throughout the organization, prioritizes the risks, establishes goals, and implements improvements to reduce and eliminate risks.
elements: The hospital develops and implements an annual risk assessment that includes eight facility management and safety programs: • Safety (See also FMS.03.00, ME 2) • Security • Hazardous materials and waste • Fire safety (See also FMS.06.00, ME 3) • Medical equipment • Utility systems • Emergency (internal and external) and disaster management (See also GHI.05.00, ME 4) • Construction and renovation (See also FMS.10.00, ME 1)
The hospital prioritizes the risks, identifies goals and key performance improvements, and implements improvements to reduce and eliminate risks. (See also GLD.06.01, ME 1)
The hospital evaluates the effectiveness of the improvements, and, based on the results, the hospital updates the applicable facility management and safety programs. (See also GLD.06.01, ME 2)

Hospital leaders provide the annual risk assessment report and the effectiveness of the facility management and safety programs to the governing entity, and the governing entity takes actions based on the report. (See also GLD.04.01, ME 1)

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The hospital implements a program to provide a safe physical facility.
elements: The hospital develops and implements a written program to provide a safe physical facility. (See also COP.05.00, ME 1; GLD.07.02, ME 2; HCT.02.00, ME 1; PCI.01.01, ME 2)

The hospital applies safety measures and equipment where needed to ensure safety of patients and staff. Measures include but are not limited to the following: • Non-slip floors, patient support or grab bars, help bell or call system, and lock system that allows

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: Warning and directive signs are posted inside the hospital as appropriate.
elements: There are warning signs posted as appropriate in the hospital and include the following: • Signs for radioactive materials, including warning signs for pregnant women • Signs for wet floors during cleaning • No smoking signs • Signs and warning lights for x-ray room(s) • Signs to restrict cellular phones in sensitive areas as appropriate (for example, MRI or critical care

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The hospital implements a program to provide a secure environment for patients, families, staff, and visitors.
elements: The hospital develops and implements a written program to provide a secure environment.

The hospital develops policies and procedures to support the security program, including but not limited to the following: • Preventing the abduction of children and neonates • Lost and found items • Safekeeping of patient belongings • Involvement of police in cases of trauma, motor vehicle accidents, and medico-legal incidents • Incidents of violence (violence code) • Abuse of women and children

The security program identifies all security risk areas and restricted areas and ensures that they are monitored and kept secure through security personnel or alternative security systems. The high-risk and restricted areas include but are not limited to the following: • Delivery rooms • Neonatal intensive care unit • Nursery • Female wards • Operating rooms • Central sterilization service department • Morgue • Medical records • Hospital roof • Medical equipment and goods stores, including the pharmacy narcotics vault (See also COP.05.00, ME 1; MMU.03.00, ME 6; MMU.03.01, ME 2; PCC.01.03, ME 1)

The hospital has qualified individuals assigned to maintain security, whose number is proportional to the size of the hospital, number of entrances, and availability of supporting security systems. The security personnel have a dress code and conduct hospitalwide security rounds, and significant findings are documented. The security personnel have written job descriptions.

The security program ensures that relevant patients, as well as staff, students, trainees, contract workers, volunteers, vendors, and individuals associated with independent business entities, are identified. The program ensures that hospital staff, temporary employees, and contractor staff wear identification badges.
All security equipment and systems, including devices related to detection, alarm notification, and timely response, are inspected, evaluated, and maintained.
The security program includes education of relevant staff on response to security alerts and roles and responsibilities during a security-related event.

The security personnel of the hospital have their roles clearly defined for the external and internal disaster plan and no-smoking policy. The security personnel receive orientation about their scope of work and job description, emergency codes, and fire safety.
The hospital conducts regular exercises with staff to evaluate the security program and integration with local responders.

The hospital conducts an annual worksite analysis related to its workplace violence prevention program and takes actions to mitigate or resolve the identified workplace violence security risks. (See also GLD.07.02, ME 2)
Based on its process(es), the hospital reports and investigates security incidents involving patients, staff, or others within its facilities.
Based on its process(es), the hospital reports and investigates security incidents related to workplace violence involving patients, staff, or others within its facilities. (See also GLD.07.02, ME 3)

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The hospital implements a program for the management of hazardous materials and waste.
elements: The hospital develops and implements a written program for the management of hazardous materials and waste. (See also HRP.02.01, ME 2)

The hazardous materials and waste program identifies the type, quantities, and locations of hazardous materials and waste, and has a complete inventory, which is updated at least annually, to reflect changes in the hazardous materials used and stored in the organization. Each department has a current list of hazardous materials used in the department, with details that cover purpose of use, responsible person, and permitted quantity. (See also AOP.03.05, MEs 1 and 5; MMU.03.00, ME 2; PCI.05.00, ME 1)

The hazardous materials and waste program establishes and implements procedures for clear labeling, appropriate and safe handling, storage, transporting, use, and disposal of hazardous materials that are consistent with safety data sheets. All hazardous materials are labeled clearly, including, but not limited to, anti-neoplastic drugs, radioactive materials, corrosives, acids, toxic materials, hazardous gases and vapors, anesthetic gases, and flammable liquids.

The hazardous materials and waste program establishes and implements procedures for handling, storing, transporting, and disposing of all kinds of waste (for example, clinical waste, radioactive waste, hazardous gases).

The hazardous materials and waste program establishes and implements the proper protective equipment required during handling and use of hazardous materials, which is available in each department using hazardous materials.

The hazardous materials and waste program establishes and implements procedures for the management of spills and exposures, including the use of proper protective equipment and reporting of spills and exposures.
Eye wash station and emergency water shower are available where hazardous medications and pharmaceutical chemicals are located.

Information about the hazardous materials (for example, Material Safety Data Sheets) related to safe handling, spill-handling procedures, and procedures for managing exposures are always up to date and available in each department handling hazardous materials, relevant to its current list of hazardous materials.

Staff are educated and trained on signs and symptoms of exposure to hazardous materials and appropriate treatment according to Material Safety Data Sheets (MSDS). Staff can describe and/or demonstrate precautions and procedures for handling and managing hazardous materials and waste, as applicable to the staff member’s role and responsibilities. Staff (including contractors’ staff) are trained on dealing with hazardous waste.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The hospital establishes and implements a program for fire safety that complies with national and local codes, laws, and regulations.
elements: The hospital develops and implements a written program for fire safety to protect all occupants of the hospital’s facilities from fire and smoke emergencies.

The fire safety program includes implementing interim measures, when necessary, to ensure that the safety of the hospital’s patients, staff, and visitors is maintained when fire safety risks cannot be immediately addressed.

The hospital’s comprehensive, facilitywide risk assessment as required by FMS.02.00, ME 1 includes evaluation of the following fire-related risks: • Fire separations • Smoke separations/compartments • Hazardous areas (and spaces above the ceilings in those areas) such as soiled linen rooms, trash

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The hospital maintains fire safety equipment and fire safety building features.
elements: The fire safety program includes equipment/systems for the early detection and alarm notification of fire and smoke. The equipment/systems are functioning and regularly inspected per civil defense guidelines.
Elevators, if present in the hospital, are connected to the fire alarm system.

The fire safety program includes equipment/systems for the suppression of fire. Measures taken for suppression include but are not limited to the following: • The hospital ensures procuring materials such as curtains and drapes that are fire retardant. • The hospital ensures separating all dangerous materials or flammables from heat-generating areas. • The hospital ensures installing fire-rated walls as appropriate, especially in high-risk areas such as the laboratory, electrical rooms, and kitchen. • The fire extinguishers are adequate in number per civil defense guidelines. • The fire extinguishers are appropriately distributed throughout the hospital. • The fire extinguishers are appropriately positioned per civil defense guidelines. • The hospital has a functional sprinkler system. • The hospital has a clean agent suppression system. • The hospital has a wet chemical system. • The hospital has standpipes and a hose system.

The fire safety program includes the safe exit from the facility through free and unobstructed access to exits. Measures taken to ensure safe exit include but are not limited to the following: • Fire exits are available and are properly located in the hospital. • Fire exits are not locked. • Fire exits are not obstructed. • Fire exits have panic hardware. • Fire exits are fire resistant. • There are no obstructions to exits, fire extinguishers, fire alarm boxes, emergency or fire blankets, safety showers, and eye wash stations.
The fire safety program includes clearly visible, illuminated exit signage that is understandable to the hospital’s occupants.
The fire safety program includes adequate lighting for emergency exit corridors and stairs.

The fire safety program includes containment of fire and smoke, and these features are maintained to ensure effectiveness and safety. Containment of fire measures include but are not limited to the following: • Fire-rated doors that are available according to the hospital zones with no separation between

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: All fire safety equipment and systems, including devices related to early detection, alarm notification, and suppression, are inspected, evaluated, and maintained.
elements: All fire safety equipment and systems, including those for smoke and fire detection (for example, fire alarm system) and suppression, are inspected, evaluated, and maintained according to manufacturers’ recommendations or as required by local codes, laws, and regulations, whichever sets the more stringent requirement. Fire extinguishers are inspected monthly to assess functionality, and the fire- alarm system is functioning and regularly inspected, with preventive maintenance carried out per civil defense guidelines.
Inspection, testing, and maintenance of all fire safety equipment and systems (including the fire- alarm system) are documented, including results and corrective actions.
Any deficiencies identified in fire safety equipment and systems are immediately corrected, or interim measures are implemented to reduce fire risk until deficiencies can be fully corrected.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The hospital conducts regular exercises with staff to evaluate the fire safety program.
elements: Based on a scheduled training program, all hospital personnel in all departments, including the night shift and weekend shift, are trained in the fire safety program (including the use of fire extinguishers) and participate in drills to evaluate the fire safety program at least annually, or more frequently when required by laws and regulations or other authorities. Fire drills conducted during different shifts test at least the following elements: • Use of Rescue, Alarm, Confine, Extinguish/Evacuate (RACE) procedure • Use of Pull, Aim, Squeeze, Sweep (PASS) procedure • The ability to contain the fire when it starts • Staff performance in the event of fire • Evacuation procedures • Shutoff of oxygen and electricity supplies at the right time
Staff who provide patient care can describe and demonstrate how to bring patients to safety.
A full fire drill is conducted for the internal disaster plan once a year, and this drill is evaluated.

Results of exercises to evaluate the fire safety program are documented and integrated into the quality improvement program, and staff who do not pass are reeducated and retested on the fire safety program.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The fire safety program includes limiting smoking by staff and patients to designated non–patient care areas of the facility.
elements: The fire safety program ensures a strict no smoking policy within the hospital facility.
The program applies to patients, families, visitors, and staff.
The program identifies who may grant patient exceptions for smoking and when those exceptions apply.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The hospital develops and implements a program for the management of medical equipment throughout the organization.
elements: The hospital develops and implements a written program for the management of medical equipment that is hospital owned and non-hospital owned (leased, rented, patient owned) in all areas of the hospital, including dialysis. (See also GLD.05.02, ME 1; HRP.02.01, ME 2)

The equipment program includes the following: • A comprehensive inventory of all medical equipment • Testing according to use and manufacturers’ requirements • Documentation of results, including history record for the maintenance schedule, failure

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The hospital has a process for monitoring and acting on medical equipment hazard notices, recalls, reportable incidents, problems, and failures.
elements: The hospital has a process for monitoring and acting on medical equipment and implantable device hazard notices, recalls, reportable incidents, problems, and failures. (See also AOP.03.04, ME 5; AOP.05.04, ME 5)
The hospital reports any deaths, serious injuries, or illnesses that are a result of medical equipment through the hospital’s incident and adverse event reporting process. (See also GLD.04.00, ME 7)
The medical equipment management program addresses the use of any medical equipment with a reported problem or failure, or that is the subject of a hazard notice or is under recall.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: Hospital staff are trained on safe operation of medical equipment.
elements: Hospital staff are trained to safely operate all medical equipment.
The training includes physicians, nurses, and paramedics.
The training considers the following: • New equipment • Staff transferred from one department to another • Newly hired staff • Recurring misuse of equipment

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The hospital implements a program for the management of utility systems throughout the organization.
elements: The hospital develops and implements a written program for the management of utility systems throughout the hospital that includes management of failure or interruption of the following utilities: • Normal power • Emergency power, no power from sockets in critical areas, and lamp failure in critical areas • Elevators • Water supply • Reverse osmosis plant • Air-conditioning fan coil unit (FCU) in patient rooms • Air-conditioning air handling unit (AHU) in operating rooms • Medical gas system • Sewer lines • Boilers • Telephone service (public address exchange) • Intercom, nurse call, and overhead paging • Fire alarm (See also HCT.01.04, ME 1)
The utility systems program includes description of necessary hospital programs to acquire necessary equipment, upgrade equipment, and upgrade physical condition of the building.

The hospital identifies goals, implements improvements, and monitors data to ensure that the utility systems risks are reduced or eliminated, evaluates performance of the systems, and suggests improvements and upgrades as required.

The hospital inventories its utility systems components and maps their current distribution. Technical utility drawings show the distribution lines for all utilities and how to control them centrally and peripherally so that lines can be controlled as required in case of emergency.

The hospital identifies, in writing, the activities and intervals for inspecting, evaluating, and conducting preventive and routine maintenance on all operating components of the utility systems on the inventory, based on criteria such as manufacturers’ recommendations, risk levels, and hospital experience conducted by qualified and trained staff. The preventive maintenance program covers at least the following: • Electrical system • Elevators • Refrigerators/freezers • Air conditioning system • Medical gas system • Medical suction • Domestic water system, including water pumps and fire hydrants • Fire water system, including fire pumps • Boilers • Plumbing • Low current and communication system • Pavement and ground • Hospital building and ancillaries

The utility systems program supports electrical safety by including measures such as identification of electrical outlets for voltage (110/220V), source of electrical outlets (essential/prime), earthing system in rooftop and sockets used for medical equipment, and annual thermal inspection of circuit breakers in the following: • Operating rooms • Laboratory • Critical care units • Alarm system • Blood storage • Medical gas system

The utility systems program includes preventive maintenance for heating, ventilating, and air- conditioning (HVAC) that covers at least the following: • Periodic preventive maintenance plan (PPM) plan is supported by trained and specialized staff/ contractor. • Maintenance records are maintained. • The HVAC is maintained to control the air quality by cleaning/replacing filters, cleaning diffuser, and cleaning ducts. • HEPA filters are monitored monthly, and the results are documented. • Air change per hour is maintained per national and international guidelines (for example, American Society of Heating, Refrigerating, and Air-Conditioning Engineers [ASHRAE]).
The hospital labels utility system controls to facilitate partial or complete emergency shutdowns.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The hospital utility systems program ensures that essential utilities, including power, water, and medical gases, are available at all times, and alternative sources for essential utilities are tested and evaluated.
elements: The hospital ensures backup availability/continuity of essential utilities (including power, water, and medical gas) 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. Backup/emergency power covers at least the following critical areas: • Operating rooms • Labor and delivery • Critical care units • Alarm system • Fire pumps • Blood storage • Medical gas system • Refrigerators in the pharmacy, laboratory, medication storage, and kitchen • Elevators • Escape routes/corridors • Morgue • Medication storage • Emergency department (See also FMS.09.00, ME 1)

The hospital tests and evaluates the availability and quality of the alternative source(s) of water at least annually or more frequently if required by local laws and regulations or conditions of the source of water. Emergency plans are tested in simulation. The hospital documents the results of the tests, and results are evaluated.

The hospital tests and evaluates alternative sources of power at least quarterly or more frequently if required by local laws and regulations, manufacturers’ recommendations, or conditions of the source of power. The hospital documents the results of the tests. For emergency generators, if applicable, the hospital ensures readiness by ensuring at least the following measures: • The hospital maintains its generator(s) on a periodic basis. The maintenance results are documented. • The hospital performs weekly tests without load for 10 minutes. • The hospital performs monthly on load tests for 30 minutes and should achieve 30% of the nameplate load. The 30-minute time frame does not include the time it takes to warm up or cool down. • The hospital performs full load tests every three years on external load. • The hospital generator starts normally without load for 10 minutes.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: Designated individuals or authorities monitor water quality regularly.
elements: Quality of potable water is tested and evaluated at least quarterly or more frequently in accordance with laws and regulations, conditions of the sources for water, and previous experience with water quality problems. The testing results are documented.

Quality of non-potable water is tested and evaluated at least every six (6) months or more frequently based on local laws and regulations, conditions of the sources for water, and previous experience with water quality problems. The testing results are documented.

Preventive measures and strategies are implemented to reduce the risks of contamination and growth of bacteria in water, including a periodic preventive maintenance plan (PPM) for the water system that is supported by trained and specialized staff/contractor. Records are maintained for water availability 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, and regular checking of the incoming water supply for at least the following: chemicals (once every 6 months) and bacteria (monthly).
Dental unit waterlines are treated, tested, and evaluated according to manufacturer’s guidelines, and treatments and testing are documented.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: Quality of water used in hemodialysis is tested and evaluated for chemical, bacterial, and endotoxin contaminants, and processes for hemodialysis services follow professional standards for water quality and for infection prevention and control.
elements: Hemodialysis services in the hospital follow industry standards and professional guidelines for maintaining water quality and implementing infection prevention and control measures.
There is a written policy defining the periodic checking of water quality for hemodialysis, which is based on manufacturer’s recommendations, regulations, and local experience.

Water used in hemodialysis is tested in accordance with evidence-based guidelines prior to and during treatments and evaluated monthly for bacterial growth and endotoxins and evaluated annually for chemical contaminants, or more frequently if a problem is identified. Hardness and chlorine content of feeding water are monitored on a regular basis by designated staff or authorities. The testing results are documented and reviewed. All physical and monitoring checks are verified and signed off by the nephrologist with recording of any corrective actions taken (for example, in response to out-of-range results for tests of water or dialysate).

The hospital routinely disinfects the hemodialysis water treatment and distribution system as part of the preventive periodic maintenance program. The reverse osmosis system, including the feeding pipelines into the hospital, is disinfected at least once per month, preferably by heat as well as chemical disinfection.
The hospital conducts testing and evaluation on all hemodialysis machines annually, including machines not in use, and testing results are documented.
The hospital establishes and implements procedures for reprocessing dialyzers, including, as applicable, frequency for reusing/replacing dialyzers and processes for cleaning and testing dialyzers.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The hospital reduces the risk of infection in the facility through the use of mechanical and engineering controls.
elements: The hospital operates and maintains negative and positive pressure ventilation systems in accordance with local and national laws and regulations and professional standards. Air flows (positive, negative, balanced) are established and monitored in at least the following locations: • Operating rooms • Labor and delivery • Isolation rooms • Critical care units • Clean and dirty utility rooms • Janitorial closets • Laboratory • Triage and trauma management areas • Central sterilization and supply department
The hospital operates and maintains temperature controls for water, steam, and others in accordance with local and national laws and regulations and professional standards.

The hospital operates and maintains airflow, ventilation systems, and humidity controls in a manner that minimizes infection risk in the hospital in accordance with local and national laws and regulations and professional guidelines. Temperature and humidity are controlled and regularly monitored in at least the following areas: • Recovery rooms • Nursery • Critical care units • Sterile storage supply rooms • Inpatient rooms Sewage handling and disposal are safely conducted in an efficient and sanitary manner according to professional codes of practice.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The hospital ensures proper maintenance of the medical gas system.
elements: The medical gas system is regularly tested for pressure, leaks, and functionality of valves, alarms, pressure gauge, and switches.

There is a policy and procedure that ensures effective use of medical gas system. Areas covered include, but are not limited to, the following: • Following the procedures for taking any part of the system offline • Commissioning and testing new branching or modifications • Following the procedure for ordering and filling liquid oxygen • Documenting all repairs/alterations/tests/filling logs/consumption
Compressed medical air is regularly tested for humidity and purity.
The central medical gas station is in a safe and secure place.
The outlets of medical gases in patient care areas are clearly marked with the type of gas and have different connections according to the gas type.
All medical gas pipes are clearly marked and labeled for the contents and direction of gas flow.

In case of gas pipe repairs or new extensions, outlets are tested for the type of gas to ensure the correct type is delivered through the new pipe. Results of testing are recorded and maintained with engineering and the unit manager.
The hospital keeps standby oxygen and medical air cylinders enough for 48 hours of average consumption.
The gas cylinders are regularly tested for gas type, amount, and leaks.
Emergency shutoff valves are available in all units and clearly marked with areas/rooms affected.
The hospital assigns responsibility for closing shutoff valves to a well-trained individual(s) available in the unit concerned.

The hospital has adequate medical gas outlets in patient care areas as appropriate, and these outlets are error-proof medical gas outlets in accordance with German Institute for Standardization (DIN) standards related to gases piping, outlets, and valves.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The hospital has a documented system for handling the various types of compressed gases.
elements: There is a policy on how to handle various types of compressed gases, which includes the following: • Storing them in a well-ventilated area • Positioning them upright against the wall and secured by a chain • Separating any flammables from oxidizing gases

Exhausts of the following gases are extended to the roof and identified: • Laboratory safety cabinet gases of a certain classes • Central vacuum gases • Scavenger gases of certain types • Bone marrow transplantation (BMT) laboratory gases

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The hospital develops, maintains, and evaluates an emergency management program to respond to internal and external emergencies and disasters that have the potential of occurring within the hospital and community.
elements: The hospital develops, evaluates, and maintains a written emergency and disaster management program that provides processes for the following: • Determining the type, likelihood, and consequences of hazards, threats, and events (See also

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The hospital implements and evaluates an emergency management program to respond to the presentation of global communicable diseases.
elements: The hospital develops and implements an emergency preparedness program to respond to global communicable diseases that includes the following: • A process to determine when emergency management procedures are activated in response to

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The hospital has a mechanism to deal with a bomb threat.
elements: There is a written policy on how to deal with a bomb threat in the hospital, which includes the following: • Defining the code or alert • Defining the role of the person receiving threat alerts • Defining the response team, including the individual responsible for announcing the emergency

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: When planning for construction, renovation, and demolition projects, or maintenance activities that affect patient care, the organization conducts a preconstruction risk assessment.
elements: When planning for construction, renovation, or demolition projects, or maintenance activities that affect patient care, the hospital conducts a preconstruction risk assessment (PCRA) that includes, at a minimum, the following: • Air quality • Infection prevention and control • Utilities • Noise • Vibration • Hazardous materials and waste • Fire safety • Security • Emergency procedures, including alternate pathways/exits and access to emergency services • Other hazards that affect care, treatment, and services (See also FMS.02.00, ME 1)
The hospital acts based on its assessment to minimize risks during construction, renovation, and demolition projects, and maintenance activities that affect patient care.

The hospital develops and implements a policy for safety and security of patients, staff, and visitors during construction, renovation, or demolition that includes at least the following: • Safety and security instructions • Education of contractors • Proper isolation of construction and renovation sites • Procedure for eliminating the risks of fire and spread of dust • Penalties imposed on contractors for violating the policy • Safety rounds on construction/renovation sites by facility management and safety and infection

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: The structure, authority, and responsibilities of the hospital’s governing entity are described in bylaws, policies and procedures, or similar written documents.
elements: The structure, authority, and responsibilities of the hospital’s governing entity are described in a written document, bylaws, and/or policies and procedures, with those responsible for governance of the hospital identified.
The governing entity approves the scope of services of the hospital.
The governing entity approves the hospital’s capital and operating budget(s) that aligns with the hospital’s services and provides for the resources required to meet the hospital’s mission.
The governing entity approves the hospital’s participation in health care professional education and research and in the oversight of the quality of such programs.
The governing entity appoints and annually evaluates the hospital’s chief executive(s), and the evaluation is documented.
The hospital has written policies that describe when and how the authority of the governing entity, and the chief executive(s), can be delegated. The hospital has an effective governing body.

The governing body’s responsibilities reflect its ultimate accountability for the quality of care and patient safety, and include the following: • Working together with the senior management and hospital leaders to create and regularly review

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: A chief executive(s) is responsible for operating the hospital and complying with applicable laws and regulations.
elements: The education and experience of the chief executive(s) match the requirements in the position description, including education, training and experience, and a good command of the English language.
The chief executive(s) recommends policies, strategic plans, and budgets to the governing entity.
The chief executive(s) ensures consistent implementation of the hospital’s approved policies.
The chief executive(s) ensures compliance with applicable laws and regulations.
The chief executive(s) responds to any reports from inspecting, regulatory agencies and accreditation agencies.
The chief executive(s) is accountable to the governing body for the clinical performance and professional conduct of the hospital.

The chief executive(s) participates actively in supporting the safety of patients, staff of patients, staff, and visitors (for example, through leadership safety rounds, review of reported incidents).
The chief executive(s) ensures the availability of adequate resources (for example, human resources, equipment, supplies, medications).
The chief executive(s) ensures all physical properties are kept in a good state of repair and operating condition.
The chief executive(s) ensures the efficient utilization of all resources.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: Hospital leaders are identified and are collectively responsible for defining the hospital’s mission and creating the programs and policies needed to fulfill the mission.
elements: Hospital leaders form an executive management body (for example, an executive management committee), led by the hospital chief executive officer or equivalent, and includes the medical director, the nursing director, the quality director, selected heads of the departments, and other senior staff members as required. • Functions and meetings of the hospital leaders are outlined in specific terms of reference, and they meet at least 10 times per year to evaluate the progress of the overall strategic plan, the quality and safety of care provided to patients, and all other clinical and nonclinical issues related to hospital day-to-day operation. • Discussions, decisions, and actions taken by the hospital leaders are documented in formal meeting minutes.

Hospital leaders establish medical and nonmedical hospitalwide committees, which include the following: • Pharmacy and therapeutics • Morbidity and mortality • Infection prevention and control • Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) • Credentialing and privileging • Operating room • Tissue review • Blood utilization review • Quality and patient safety • Medical records review • Patient rights • Utilization review

Leaders address the formation and terms of reference, including committee functions, chairperson designation and members’ selection with their titles, quorum, meeting frequency, resolution process in case of disagreement, and meeting minutes’ distribution.
The committee chairs submit their respective committee’s accomplishments and unresolved issues annually to executive management, and recommendations are implemented.
Hospital leaders are qualified in health care management by education, training, or experience, and their roles and responsibilities are outlined in their job descriptions.
The hospital has a policy and procedure for delegating function and authority between two qualified peers, which are consistent with other relevant and related policies.

Hospital leaders are responsible for defining and regularly reviewing the hospital’s mission and vision statement, ensuring the following: • The mission reflects the scope of services provided by the hospital and the health needs of the population served. • The mission is communicated to the staff. • The mission is displayed to patients, visitors, and the wider community.
Hospital leaders are responsible for creating the policies and procedures necessary to carry out the mission. • The hospitalwide policies and procedures are identified and combined into a manual that

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: Hospital leaders work collaboratively to develop an effective budgeting process.
elements: The hospital has a finance director qualified by education and experience.
Hospital leaders work together to address both the capital and the operating budgets.
The budgeting process addresses staffing in addition to other financial assets.
The budgeting process allocates resources to all patient care units based on the scope and complexity of care, aiming to ensure a safe, efficient process.
The governing body approves the hospital’s budget.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: Hospital leaders work collaboratively to develop the hospital’s strategic plan.
elements: Hospital leaders work together to develop a strategic plan that is guided by the mission, vision, and values.
Hospital leaders build the strategic plan by aligning it to the national strategy and health holding strategy.

The strategic plan is based on comprehensive evaluation of the internal and external environmental factors (for example, Strengths/Weaknesses/Opportunities/Threats [SWOT] analysis, Political/ Economic/Social/Technological [PEST] analysis).
The strategic plan addresses all clinical and nonclinical services and programs.
The strategic plan spans a period of three to five years and is reviewed on a regular basis.
The strategic plan includes the goals and objectives required to fulfill the hospital’s mission.
Goals and objectives are translated into operational plans with defined projects, clearly delineated responsibilities, and time frames.
Resources required for executing the operational plans are properly allocated.
Operational plans are implemented and closely monitored for progress toward achieving the goals and objectives.
Key performance indicators are developed for each operational plan.
Key performance indicators are reviewed regularly, and corrective actions are taken when required.
Department heads develop annual departmental plans in line with the hospital’s strategic plan.
The strategic plan is communicated to relevant staff.
The governing body approves the strategic plan.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: Hospital leaders identify, plan, and communicate the type of clinical services required to meet the needs of the patients served by the hospital.
elements: Hospital leaders determine and plan with department/service leaders the scope of services and type of care, treatment, and services to be provided by the hospital, consistent with the hospital’s mission and current and future patient needs (planning for health-relevant demographic changes, public health issues, groups with special needs). (See also SQE.01.05, ME 1) This includes the following: • The range of services offered by the hospital (for example, children’s hospital, maternity hospital,

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
statement: Hospital leaders ensure effective communication throughout the hospital.
elements: Hospital leaders ensure that processes are in place for communicating relevant information throughout the hospital in a timely manner. (See also MOI.01.00, ME 1)

Hospital leaders ensure effective communication among clinical and nonclinical departments, services, and individual staff members, as follows: (See also MOI.01.00, ME 1) • Regular departmental staff meetings, with documented minutes • Use of communication tools, such as an intranet site, bulletin boards, periodic reports,

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
group: Leadership for Quality and Patient Safety
statement: Hospital leaders plan, develop, and implement a quality and patient safety program.
elements: Hospital leaders are familiar with the basic concepts and tools used in continuous quality improvement, such as the following: • Basic data analysis and interpretation of quality reports • Basic tools used in quality management (for example, Plan-Do-Check-Act [PDCA] cycle) • Root cause analysis
Hospital leaders participate in developing and implementing a hospitalwide quality and patient safety program. (See also PCI.08.00, ME 1; QPS.01.00, ME 3; QPS.03.03, ME 1)

Hospital leaders select and implement a hospitalwide process to measure, assess data, plan change, and sustain improvements in quality and patient safety, and provide staff education on this quality improvement process. (See also QPS.02.00, ME 2; QPS.04.00, ME 4)
Hospital leaders determine how the program will be directed and managed daily and ensure that the program has adequate resources to be effective. (See also QPS.01.00, ME 1)
Hospital leaders implement a structure and process for the overall monitoring and coordination of the quality and patient safety program. (See also PCI.08.00, ME 3)
Hospital leadership defines sentinel event in writing, and the definition includes all information in the appendix to this chapter.
Hospital leaders report any sentinel event to the relevant authorities – the Ministry of Health, Cluster Leadership, Saudi Health Holding Company, and Saudi Patient Safety Center.

Hospital leaders complete a credible and thorough comprehensive systematic analysis (for example, root cause analysis) of all sentinel events within a time period specified by hospital leadership and it does not exceed 45 days from the date of the event or when made aware of the event.
The root cause analysis identifies all system and process origins that may have contributed to the event.
Hospital leadership considers each identified contributing factor and takes corrective actions for improvement to prevent or reduce the risk of adverse events from recurring.
The hospital monitors the implemented corrective actions for potential process failures (unintended consequences), effectiveness, and sustainability over time.

manual: Hospitals and Academic Medical Centers Standards
group: Leadership for Quality and Patient Safety
statement: Hospital leaders report quality improvement and patient safety information to the governing entity and hospital staff.
elements: The governing entity annually reviews and approves the hospital’s program for quality and patient safety. (See also FMS.02.00, ME 4)
