When contracts are renegotiated or terminated, the ambulatory care organization maintains the continuity of patient services.

statement: Ambulatory care organization leaders ensure that contracts and other arrangements are part of the organization’s quality and patient safety program.
elements: All contracts stipulate which quality data are reported to the ambulatory care organization, how frequently and how reporting will occur, and how the ambulatory care organization will respond when quality requirements or expectations are not met.
Quality data reported under contracts are integrated into the ambulatory care organization’s quality and patient safety program.
The relevant department/service leaders participate with the quality and patient safety program in analyzing quality and safety information from outside contracts.

statement: Ambulatory care organization leaders ensure that independent practitioners not employed by the ambulatory care organization have the right credentials and are privileged for the services they provide to the organization’s patients.
elements: Ambulatory care organization leaders determine those services provided by independent practitioners outside the organization.

All independent practitioners outside the ambulatory care organization who are contracted to provide diagnostic, consultative, and treatment services to the organization’s patients, including services such as telemedicine and teleradiology, are credentialed and privileged by the organization to provide such services and registered with the Saudi Ministry of Health.

Independent practitioners who provide patient care services on the premises of the ambulatory care organization but are not employees or members of the clinical staff of the organization are credentialed, privileged, and evaluated as described in SQE.7.
Any support staff accompanying independent practitioners and providing care and services in the organization are compliant with requirements for primary source verification.
The quality of services by independent practitioners outside the organization is monitored as a component of the ambulatory care organization’s quality and patient safety program.

statement: Ambulatory care organization leaders make decisions about purchasing or using resources—human and technical—with an understanding of the quality and safety implications of those decisions.
elements: Ambulatory care organization leaders use data and information on the quality and safety implications of medical equipment choices.
Ambulatory care organization leaders use data and information on the quality and safety implications of staffing choices.
Ambulatory care organization leaders use the recommendations of professional organizations and other authoritative sources in making resource decisions.
Ambulatory care organization leaders direct, support, and oversee information technology resources.
Ambulatory care organization leaders monitor the results of resource decisions and use the data to evaluate and improve the quality of their resource purchasing and allocation decisions.

statement: The ambulatory care organization seeks and uses data and information on the safety of the supply chain to protect patients and staff from unstable, contaminated, defective, and counterfeit supplies.
elements: The ambulatory care organization outlines the steps in the supply chains for supplies defined as at most risk.
The ambulatory care organization identifies any significant risk points in the steps of the supply chains.
The ambulatory care organization leaders make resource decisions based on their understanding of the risk points in the supply chains.

The ambulatory care organization leaders ensure that all medical devices and supplies contractors and suppliers have a medical device establishment license (MDEL) and that newly purchased medical devices have a medical device marketing authorization (MDMA) certificate.
All newly introduced consumables are formally tested and have a feedback process from the end users.
The ambulatory care organization has a process for retrospective tracing of supplies found to be unstable, contaminated, defective, or counterfeit.

The ambulatory care organization notifies the manufacturer and distributor, as applicable, when unstable, contaminated, defective, or counterfeit supplies are identified. Department/Service Organization and Accountabilities

statement: The ambulatory care organization leaders plan and implement a professional staff structure to support their responsibilities and authority.
elements: There is a professional staff structure that supports the department/service leaders in carrying out their responsibilities and authority.
The structure is appropriate to the ambulatory care organization’s size and complexity.
The structure and processes support a culture of professional communication.
The structure and processes support clinical planning, resource requirements, and policy development.
The structure and processes support oversight of professional ethical issues.
The structure and processes support oversight of the quality of clinical services.

statement: The ambulatory care organization establishes a framework for ethical management that promotes a culture of ethical practices and decision making to ensure that patient care is provided within business, financial, ethical, and legal norms and protects patients and their rights.
elements: The ambulatory care organization establishes a framework for the organization’s ethical management that promotes a culture of ethical practices and decision making to ensure the protection of patients and their rights.
The ethical framework ensures that patient care is provided within business, financial, ethical, marketing, and legal norms.
The ambulatory care organization ensures nondiscrimination in employment practices and provision of patient care in the context of the cultural and regulatory norms of the country.
The ambulatory care organization’s framework for ethical management establishes a mechanism by which health care practitioners and other staff may raise ethical concerns without fear of retribution.
The ambulatory care organization has a process for addressing ethical concerns and provides an effective, timely resolution to any ethical conflicts.

statement: The ambulatory care organization’s framework for ethical management addresses operational and business conduct, including disclosure of ownership and any conflicts of interest, and honestly portrays its services to patients.
elements: The ambulatory care organization discloses its ownership and any conflicts of interest.
The ambulatory care organization honestly portrays its services to patients.
The ambulatory care organization accurately bills for services and ensures that financial incentives and payment arrangements do not compromise patient care.

statement: Ambulatory care organization leaders create and support a culture of safety throughout the organization.
elements: Ambulatory care organization leaders establish and support a culture of safety that promotes accountability and transparency.
Ambulatory care organization leaders develop and document a set of values and code of conduct and identify and correct behaviors that are unacceptable.
Ambulatory care organization leaders provide resources to promote and support the culture of safety within the organization.

Ambulatory care organization leaders implement a simple, accessible, and confidential system for reporting issues relevant to a culture of safety in the organization and prevent retribution against individuals who report issues.
The ambulatory care organization leaders identify and manage systems issues that lead staff to engage in unsafe behaviors.

Ambulatory care organization leaders establish a process to measure the organization’s culture of safety annually. The feedback rate and results are analyzed, actions developed, and reported to the cluster quality committee.
Ambulatory care organization leaders lead the daily safety huddles.
Ambulatory care organization leaders conduct periodic leadership walkarounds.

statement: Health professional education, when provided in the ambulatory care organization, is guided by the educational parameters defined by the sponsoring academic program and the ambulatory care organization’s leaders.
elements: The ambulatory care organization provides a mechanism(s) for oversight of the training program(s).
The ambulatory care organization obtains and accepts the sponsoring academic program’s parameters.
The ambulatory care organization has a complete record of all students and trainees in the organization.
The ambulatory care organization has documentation of the enrollment status, licensure or certifications achieved, and academic classification of the students and trainees.
The ambulatory care organization understands and provides the required level of supervision for each type and level of student and trainee.
The ambulatory care organization integrates students and trainees into its orientation, quality and patient safety, infection prevention and control, and other programs and processes.

statement: Human subjects research, when conducted in the ambulatory care organization, is guided by laws, regulations, and organization leaders.
elements: Ambulatory care organization leaders are responsible for protecting patients, regardless of the research sponsor.

The ambulatory care organization develops and implements a process to guide human subjects research in the organization, which addresses at least the following: • How patients are informed of research relevant to their needs and how to access those activities • The patient’s right to refuse to participate or, later, to withdraw from the research • How patients who participate in research are protected • A process for informed consent for patient participation in research (See also PFR.4.)
Ambulatory care organization leaders identify the official(s) responsible for developing and maintaining compliance with all human subjects research policies and procedures.

statement: The ambulatory care organization has a committee or another way to oversee all research in the ambulatory care organization involving human subjects.
elements: A committee or other mechanism oversees all research that takes place in the ambulatory care organization.
The organization develops a clear statement of purpose for the oversight activities.
Oversight activities include a review process.
Oversight activities include a process to weigh relative risks and benefits for human subjects.

Oversight activities include processes to provide confidentiality and security of human subjects’ information. Appendix A: Sentinel Events (GLD.4) The hospital’s definition of sentinel event includes at least the following information: A sentinel event is a patient safety event (not primarily related to the natural course of a patient’s illness or underlying condition) that reaches a patient and results in any of the following: • Death • Permanent harm • Severe temporary harm Severe temporary harm is defined as critical, potentially life-threatening harm lasting for a limited time with no permanent residual but requires transfer to a higher level of care/monitoring for a prolonged period of time, transfer to a higher level of care for a life-threatening condition, or additional major surgery, procedure, or treatment to resolve the condition. The following are also considered to be sentinel events:

statement: The ambulatory care organization meets the information needs of all those who provide clinical services, those who manage the organization, and those outside the organization who require data and information from the ambulatory care organization.
elements: The ambulatory care organization plans and implements processes to meet the information needs of those who provide clinical services, including how patient demographic and medical information is shared among medical and administrative staff.

The ambulatory care organization plans and implements processes to meet the information needs of the ambulatory care organization’s department/service leaders, including how the types of information are communicated by leaders to staff and vice versa.

The ambulatory care organization plans and implements processes to meet the information needs and requirements of individuals and agencies outside the organization, including Ministry of Health– required information and frequency of reporting, and the patient’s personal and medical information required to refer the patient to a higher organization.
The processes implemented are appropriate to the ambulatory care organization’s size, complexity of services, availability of trained staff, and other human and technical resources.
When data are shared between health care organizations/providers, it is shared using the National Platform for Health Insurance Exchange Services (NPHIES) platform.

statement: Confidentiality, security, and integrity of data and information are maintained.
elements: The ambulatory care organization has implemented processes, including a dedicated, secure storage area for medical records, to ensure the confidentiality of data and information.
The ambulatory care organization has implemented processes to ensure the security of data and information.
The ambulatory care organization has implemented processes to ensure the integrity of data and information.
The ambulatory care organization has identified the level of security for each category of data and information.
The ambulatory care organization has identified those permitted to access each category of data and information and identifies the staff security levels for accessing the information.

statement: The ambulatory care organization determines the retention time of records, data, and information.
elements: The ambulatory care organization determines the retention of patient medical records and other data and information consistent with Ministry of Health rules and regulations.
The retention process provides expected confidentiality and security.
Records, data, and information are destroyed in a manner that does not compromise confidentiality and security.

statement: The ambulatory care organization uses standardized diagnosis codes and procedure codes and ensures the uniform use of approved symbols and abbreviations across the organization.
elements: The ambulatory care organization uses standardized diagnosis codes and procedure codes consistent with Ministry of Health and other regulatory bodies’ requirements.
The ambulatory care organization uniformly uses approved symbols and identifies those not to be used.
If the ambulatory care organization allows abbreviations, it uniformly uses approved abbreviations, and each abbreviation has only one meaning.
If the ambulatory care organization allows abbreviations, it develops and/or adopts a do-not-use list of abbreviations and distributes it to all patient care areas for reference.
Abbreviations are not used on informed consent documents, patient rights documents, discharge instructions, and discharge summaries.
The ambulatory care organization monitors the uniform use of codes, symbols, and abbreviations across the organization and takes action to improve processes when needed.

statement: Records and information are protected against loss, destruction, tampering, and unauthorized access or use.
elements: Records and information are protected from loss by planning how various information is secured and safely stored.
Records and information are protected from damage or destruction.

Records and information are protected from tampering and unauthorized access or use, including in telemedicine, teleradiology, and other diagnostic remote contracted services. The leaders of the ambulatory care organization ensure the security and confidentiality of patient information that may be exposed because of the telecommunication process. Management and Implementation of Documents

statement: Written documents, including policies, procedures, and programs, are managed in a consistent and uniform manner.
elements: There is a written guidance document that defines the requirements for developing and maintaining policies, procedures, and programs, including at least the following: • Developing, reviewing, revising, approving before issue, and terminating all documents by an

statement: The ambulatory care organization fully implements policies, procedures, programs, and other documents that guide consistent and uniform clinical and nonclinical processes and practices.
elements: Required policies, procedures, and programs are available, and staff understand how to access those documents relevant to their responsibilities.
Staff are trained and understand those documents relevant to their responsibilities.
The requirements of the policies, procedures, and programs are fully implemented and evident in the actions of individual staff members.
The implementation of policies, procedures, and programs is monitored, and the information supports full implementation.

statement: The ambulatory care organization initiates and maintains a standardized medical record for every patient assessed or treated and determines the record’s content, format, and location of entries.
elements: A patient medical record is initiated for every patient assessed or treated by the organization. Each patient has only one medical record or historical volumes of the same.
Patient medical records are maintained using an identifier unique to the patient.

The ambulatory care organization standardizes and determines the specific content, format, and location of entries for patient medical records, according to the needs of health care professionals, including those related to telehealth. The organization controls the process through a structure (for example, a forms committee, the medical records review committee).

statement: The medical record contains sufficient information to identify the patient, support the diagnosis, justify the treatment, and document the course and results of treatment.
elements: Patient medical records contain adequate information to identify the patient, including national identification, contact information, emergency contacts, and insurance category.

Patient medical records contain adequate information to support any diagnosis, care, and treatment, including patient allergies, prior adverse reactions, and chronic infections, which are confidentially documented and consistently displayed in a specified area of the patient’s record.
Patient medical records contain adequate information to document the course and results of care and treatment, safely manage the patient, and promote continuity of medical care.

statement: The medical records of patients receiving emergency care, when provided in the ambulatory care organization, include the time of arrival and departure, the conclusions at termination of treatment, the patient’s condition at discharge, and follow-up care instructions.
elements: The medical records of emergency patients treated in the ambulatory care organization include arrival and departure times.
The medical records of discharged or transferred emergency patients include conclusions at the termination of treatment in the ambulatory care organization.
The medical records of emergency patients include the patient’s condition at time of discharge or transfer.
The medical records of discharged emergency patients include any follow-up care instructions.

statement: The ambulatory care organization identifies those authorized to have access to and make entries in patient medical records.
elements: The ambulatory care organization identifies those authorized to have access to patient medical records.
There is a process to ensure that only authorized individuals have access to patient medical records.
The ambulatory care organization identifies those authorized to make entries in patient medical records.
There is a process to ensure that only authorized individuals make entries in the patient medical record.
All entries are legible and signed by the author. Date and time of each entry can be identified.

There is a process that addresses how entries in the patient medical record are corrected or overwritten, where entries written in error are not deleted or erased. Instead, a line is passed through the error text and dated, timed, and signed by the author.
The ambulatory care organization defines a time frame for responding to requests related to the release of patient medical records and monitors compliance.

statement: The ambulatory care organization has a process to address proper use of the copy-and-paste, auto-fill, and auto- correct functions when electronic medical records are used.
elements: The ambulatory care organization develops a process for properly using copy-and-paste, auto-fill, and auto-correct when electronic medical records are used.
The ambulatory care organization provides education and training on properly using copy-and-paste, auto-fill, and auto-correct to all staff who document in the electronic medical record.
The ambulatory care organization monitors compliance with copy-and-paste, auto-fill, and auto- correct guidelines and implements corrective action as needed.
The ambulatory care organization develops a process to monitor the accuracy of the content that has been copied and pasted, auto-filled, or auto-corrected.

statement: As part of its monitoring and performance improvement activities, the ambulatory care organization regularly assesses the content, completeness, and legibility of patient medical records.
elements: There is a process to ensure that patient medical records are regularly checked to ensure their completion. Non-completed medical records are clearly separated from completed ones in the storage area and are completed within a time frame defined by the organization.

A representative sample of active and discharged patient medical records is reviewed at least quarterly or more frequently as determined by laws and regulations, defined in a policy for clinical documentation improvement.
The review is conducted by physicians, nurses, and others authorized to make entries in or manage patient medical records, and they are trained in clinical documentation improvement.
The review focuses on the timeliness, legibility, and completeness of the medical record.
The review includes medical record contents required by laws and regulations.

The review results are incorporated into the ambulatory care organization’s quality oversight mechanism, including a record of the percentage of incomplete records over time, and this information is used to improve staff compliance with record completion.

statement: Health information technology systems are assessed and tested before implementation in the ambulatory care organization and evaluated for quality and patient safety after implementation.
elements: Health information technology stakeholders participate in selecting, implementing, and evaluating health information technology.
Health information technology systems are assessed and tested before implementation.
Health information technology systems are evaluated after implementation for usability, effectiveness, and patient safety.

statement: When electronic communication, such as mobile devices, e-mail, or patient-facing portals, are used to exchange patient information, the ambulatory care organization adopts guidelines to ensure patient care quality and information security and confidentiality.
elements: When ambulatory care organizations allow patient information and/or orders to be transmitted through text messaging, the ambulatory care organization ensures that the process uses a secure text messaging platform that complies with the following: • Secure sign-on process(es) • Encrypted messaging • No unsecured text messaging (for example, short message service [SMS] text messaging) • Delivery and read receipts (for example, printout of a screenshot placed in the medical record) • Date and time stamp (for example, printout of a screenshot placed in the medical record) • Customized message retention time frames • A process for authentication by the ordering physician
When e-mail is used to exchange patient information, the ambulatory care organization adopts guidelines to ensure quality of patient care and information security and confidentiality.

When ambulatory care organizations implement patient portals, the ambulatory care organization complies with the following: • Encryption of patient data/information • Extensive password protection • Audit trails that log and record key activities • Patient consent to participate on the portal

When ambulatory care organizations allow patient information to be exchanged via patient portals and/or orders to be transmitted through text messaging, the ambulatory care organization collects data to monitor the process of communication for clarification when questions arise.

statement: The ambulatory care organization develops, maintains, and tests a program for responding to planned and unplanned downtime of data systems.
elements: The ambulatory care organization develops, maintains, and tests at least annually a program to respond to planned and unplanned downtime of data systems.
The ambulatory care organization identifies the probable impact of planned and unplanned downtime of data systems on all aspects of care and services.

The program includes continuity strategies for providing ongoing safe, high-quality patient care and services, including those provided by outside vendors, during planned and unplanned downtime of data systems. The program describes the manual procedures, where applicable, for the various activities in the event of system failure, maintenance, or repair.
The program identifies internal and, when applicable, external communication strategies for planned and unplanned downtime.

The ambulatory care organization identifies and implements downtime recovery tactics and ongoing data backup processes to recover and maintain data, ensure data integrity, and maintain confidentiality and privacy of patient information.
Staff are trained in the strategies and tactics for planned and unplanned downtime of data systems and can demonstrate procedures for downtime regulation, including manual procedures, if applicable.

statement: One or more individuals oversee all infection prevention and control activities. This individual(s) is qualified in infection prevention and control practices through education, training, experience, or certification.
elements: One or more individuals, acting on a full-time or part-time basis and qualified by education, training, and experience, oversee the infection prevention and control program and ensure that the program complies with local and national laws and regulations and applicable infection control guidelines including: • Demonstrated understanding of infection control principles and patient safety practices • Experience in infection control in a health care organization (at least two years) • Formal education/training in health care infection control and certification in infection control

statement: There is a designated coordination mechanism for all infection prevention and control activities that involves physicians, nurses, and others based on the size and complexity of the ambulatory care organization.
elements: There is a designated mechanism for the coordination of the infection prevention and control program.
Coordination of infection prevention and control activities involves infection prevention and control professionals.
The infection prevention and control program involves physicians, nurses, patients, visitors, and volunteers, based on the size and complexity of the ambulatory care organization.

Program coordination includes the communication of important infection risk and prevention information to all staff, with an infection control manual containing the program’s components accessible to all staff.

statement: The infection prevention and control program is based on current scientific knowledge, accepted practice guidelines, applicable laws and regulations, and standards for sanitation and cleanliness.
elements: The infection prevention and control program is based on current scientific knowledge, accepted practice guidelines, and local laws and regulations.

The infection prevention and control program is based on standards from national or local agencies and publications and professional organizations that address environmental sanitation and cleanliness.

Infection prevention and control program results are reported to public health agencies as required, including the organization’s tabulation and reporting of communicable diseases to the Ministry of Health.
The ambulatory care organization takes appropriate action on reports from relevant public health agencies. Goals of the Infection Prevention and Control Program

statement: The ambulatory care organization designs and implements a comprehensive program to reduce the risks of health care–associated infections in patients and staff.
elements: The ambulatory care organization designs and implements an infection prevention and control program to reduce the risk of health care–associated infections in patients and staff that is based on the organization’s size, geographic location, services, patients, and staff.

The leaders of the ambulatory care organization ensure that the development and implementation of infection control policies and procedures target the most important infection risk processes, including the following: • Disinfection and sterilization • Handling of sharps • Infectious materials and waste disposal • Prevention and management of patients’ and workers’ exposure to health care–associated

statement: The ambulatory care organization identifies the procedures and processes associated with the risk of infection and implements strategies to reduce infection risk.
elements: The leaders develop and implement a policy and procedure for preventing health care–associated infections, including using evidence-based bundles for insertion of devices and regularly collecting and analyzing data on device-related and surgical site infections.

The ambulatory care organization develops and implements policies and procedures to ensure availability and proper use of gloves, protective eyewear, masks, gowns, and other applicable personal protective equipment.

The ambulatory care organization leaders define in a policy and ensure that a process is in place for safely handling, storing, and disposing of infectious waste and potentially infectious waste (including blood, body fluids, and sharps/needles). The policy and process address the following: • Regular waste and infectious waste are differentiated. • Infectious waste is treated and disposed of in accordance with laws and regulations. • Gowns, masks, eyewear, face shields, and other protective equipment are worn during all procedures likely to generate splashes, soiling, or droplets of blood or other body fluids. • Gloves are worn when the potential exists for contact with blood/body fluids. • Needles are not bent, broken, or recapped except in special and approved circumstances. If recapping is necessary, the “scoop method” is used. • At least one puncture-proof and leak-proof sharps container is available in a convenient place in every patient care area. • Sharp containers are not overfilled and are disposed of as medical waste when their contents are three-quarters of their size. They are not opened to facilitate the transfer of sharps into other containers. Needle sticks or sharps injuries are reported in a timely manner and investigated. Data are trended over time and used to develop improvement interventions.
The ambulatory care organization properly manages laundry and linen.
The ambulatory care organization properly stores and handles food and nutrition products.

The ambulatory care organization identifies other processes associated with infection risk and implements policies, procedures, staff education, evidence-based activities, and other strategies to support risk reduction.

statement: The ambulatory care organization reduces the risk of infections associated with medical/surgical/dental equipment, devices, and supplies by ensuring adequate cleaning, disinfection, sterilization, and storage; and implements a process for managing expired supplies.
elements: The ambulatory care organization follows professional practice guidelines for sterilization techniques that best fit the type of situations for sterilization and devices and supplies being sterilized. Qualified staff conduct the sterilization processes.

The ambulatory care organization follows professional practice guidelines for low- and high-level disinfection that best fit the type of devices and equipment being disinfected, including a list of appropriate detergents and disinfectants as defined in policy and approved by the infection control personnel. Detergents and disinfectants are available in all patient care areas.

Staff processing medical/surgical/dental equipment, devices, and supplies are oriented, trained, and competent in cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization and receive proper supervision. In addition: • All units have a cleaning/disinfection schedule that lists all environmental surfaces and items to be cleaned. • Patient care areas are clean, and equipment is properly disinfected. • The infection control staff periodically review the cleaning procedures, schedules, and agents.

Methods for medical/surgical/dental cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization are coordinated and uniformly applied throughout the ambulatory care organization, including the following: • Sterilizers are in good working order, and instructions for their use are available. • Chemical indicators are used in every package. Biological indicators are used at least weekly. Records of results are kept for one year. • Proper sterilization parameters are recorded. Sterilization records are retained for one year. • Personal protective equipment is available and used during decontamination: heavy-duty gloves, waterproof aprons, facemasks, goggles, and face shields. • Adequate space is available for support sterilization processes, and no instrument or equipment sterilization takes place outside this area. Personal protective equipment is available and used during decontamination: heavy-duty gloves, waterproof aprons, facemasks, goggles, and face shields.

Clean and sterile supplies are properly stored in designated storage areas that are clean and dry and protected from dust, moisture, and temperature extremes. Sterilization records are retained for one year.
The ambulatory care organization implements a process consistent with national laws and regulations and professional standards that identify the process for managing expired supplies.
The ambulatory care organization implements a policy and procedure for safely reprocessing single-use items.

statement: The ambulatory care organization develops, implements, and tests strategies to respond to global communicable diseases.
elements: Ambulatory care organization leaders, along with the individual(s) responsible for the infection prevention and control program, develop and implement strategies to respond to global communicable diseases that include at least a) through d) below: a) Development and implementation of segregation and isolation methods, including the

statement: The infection prevention and control program is integrated with the ambulatory care organization’s overall program for quality and patient safety using measures epidemiologically important to the organization.
elements: Infection prevention and control activities are integrated into the ambulatory care organization’s quality and patient safety program.

Monitoring data are collected, analyzed, documented, and used to evaluate and support improvements to the infection prevention and control program that are epidemiologically relevant to the organization’s scope of services. The coordinating multidisciplinary team does an annual evaluation and suggests any necessary additions or changes.
The ambulatory care organization educates all staff and other professionals about infection prevention and control when they begin work in the organization.
All staff receive ongoing education and training related to emerging trends in infection prevention and control, including findings and trends from quality improvement activities.
The ambulatory care organization educates patients and families about infection prevention and control.

group: Management of Quality and Patient Safety Activities
statement: The ambulatory care organization’s program for quality and patient safety includes both patient and staff safety and the organization’s risk management and quality control activities.
elements: The quality and patient safety program is organizationwide.
The quality and patient safety program includes all patients, staff, and visitors.
The quality and patient safety program, which the leaders develop collaboratively, unites all quality and safety activities of the ambulatory care organization.
The program uses an evidence-based quality improvement method such as FOCUS – PDCA.
The ambulatory care organization implements at least one improvement project per year.

The quality and patient safety program implements a training program (formally or through orientation and mentoring) by qualified professionals for all staff on continuous quality improvement that is consistent with staff’s roles in the quality and patient safety program, including, but not limited to, training on quality improvement methodologies and tools (such as Plan-Do-Check-Act [PDCA], Lean Six Sigma, cause-and-effect analysis, process mapping, Pareto charts, and brainstorming), as well as fundamental data competencies such as accurate data collection, interpretation of key performance indicators, basic data analysis, and use of data to monitor trends, evaluate outcomes, and support improvement initiatives.

group: Management of Quality and Patient Safety Activities
statement: The quality and patient safety program includes collecting, aggregating, and analyzing data to support patient care, organization management, and the quality and patient safety program and participation in external databases.
elements: The quality and patient safety program uses key performance indicators and patient and staff surveys to measure performance and improve clinical and managerial areas and has a process to aggregate data.

Aggregate data and information are readily accessible on a timely basis to those responsible for and/ or involved in care and service delivery; are used for making improvements; support leaders’ decision making; and support patient care, organization management, professional practice review, and the overall quality and patient safety program.
Aggregate data and information are provided to outside agencies or external databases in accordance with laws or regulations.
There is a process for comparison with external databases.

group: Management of Quality and Patient Safety Activities
statement: Individuals with appropriate experience, knowledge, and skills systematically aggregate and analyze data in the ambulatory care organization.
elements: Data are aggregated, analyzed, and transformed into useful information to identify opportunities for improvement.
Individuals with appropriate clinical or managerial experience, knowledge, and skills participate in the process.
Results of analysis are reported to those accountable for taking action.

Data analysis supports comparisons internally and externally over time (such as month to month, or one year to the next), including comparisons with reference databases of like organizations; with standards, regulatory requirements, and best practices; and with objective scientific professional sources.
Appropriate technological support is available.

statement: The ambulatory care organization uses an internal process to validate data.
elements: The quality and patient safety program uses data validation as part of the improvement process selected by leaders.

Data are validated when any of the below conditions are met: • A new measure is implemented (in particular, those clinical measures intended to help an ambulatory care organization evaluate and improve an important clinical process or outcome). • Data will be made public on the ambulatory care organization’s website or in other ways. • An existing measure has changed, data collection tools have changed, or the data abstraction process or abstractor has changed. • The data resulting from an existing measure have changed in an unexplainable way. • The data source has changed, such as when part of the patient medical record has been turned into an electronic format and thus the data source is now both electronic and paper. • The subject of the data collection has changed, such as changes in average age of patients or comorbidities; research protocols are altered; new practice guidelines are implemented; or new technologies and treatment methodologies are introduced.
An established methodology for data validation is used.
Ambulatory care organization leaders assume accountability for the validity of the quality and ­outcome data made public. Adverse Event Identification, Analysis, and Prevention

statement: The ambulatory care organization uses a defined process for identifying and managing sentinel events.
elements: Ambulatory care organization leaders define sentinel event, which includes at least the following, as appropriate to the care and services provided by the organization: • An unanticipated death, including, but not limited to, the following: o Death unrelated to the natural course of the patient’s illness or underlying condition (for example, death from a postoperative infection or a health care–associated infection)

statement: The leaders of the ambulatory care organization develop and implement an incident reporting policy.
elements: The policy outlines the types of incidents to be reported internally and to relevant regulatory authorities and the time frame and mechanism for reporting.
The ambulatory care organization uses a risk scoring matrix to categorize the severity of incidences.
Incidences, including near misses, involving patients are documented in the medical record, and the patient and family are informed by the physician of any investigation results.
The ambulatory care organization compiles a report on incidences according to type and severity, and distributes an action plan to staff and governance at least quarterly to prevent their recurrence.

statement: Data are always analyzed when undesirable trends and variation are evident from the data.
elements: Defined data gathering processes are developed and implemented to ensure accurate data collection, analysis, and reporting.
Data are intensely analyzed when there are adverse levels, patterns, or trends.

Data are gathered and analyzed on the following, as applicable to the care and services provided by the ambulatory care organization: • All confirmed transfusion reactions, if applicable to the organization (See also COP.3.1.) • All serious adverse drug events, if applicable and as defined by the organization (See also MMU.4

statement: The ambulatory care organization uses a defined process for identifying and analyzing near misses.
elements: The ambulatory care organization defines near miss.
The ambulatory care organization defines the type of events to be reported.
The ambulatory care organization establishes the process for reporting near misses.
The data are analyzed, and actions are taken to reduce near misses.

statement: An ongoing program of risk management identifies and proactively reduces unanticipated adverse events and other safety risks to patients and staff.
elements: The ambulatory care organization adopts a proactive approach to risk management, including developing risk mitigation strategies.

Leaders identify and prioritize potential risks, including clinical, managerial, and financial risks, which are included in a risk register that is periodically updated. Risks are prioritized through an evidence- based process based on severity, frequency, and/or likelihood of occurrence.
The reporting of incidents and variances, patients’ morbidities, and clinical and financial claims constitute the risk management program’s essential reactive arm.
At least annually, the ambulatory care organization conducts a proactive risk-reduction exercise on one priority risk process.
High-risk processes are redesigned based on the analysis of the test results.
Information from the risk management program, including incidents, analysis, and improvement projects, is communicated to staff and the governing body at least quarterly.

statement: The ambulatory care organization develops a staffing plan that identifies the number of staff and defines the desired education, skills, knowledge, and other requirements of all staff members needed to meet the ambulatory care organization’s mission and provide safe patient care.
elements: The ambulatory care organization’s mission, volume and mix of patients, services, and medical equipment are used in defining the number and qualifications of all required staff.
The staffing plan ensures that services meet the needs of safe patient care.
The staffing plan addresses the roles, assignment, and reassignment of staff.
Applicable laws and regulations are incorporated into staff requirements.
Ambulatory care leaders regularly review and update the staffing plan.

statement: Each staff member’s responsibilities are defined in a current job description.
elements: Each staff member not permitted to practice independently has a job description.

Job descriptions are needed for health professionals appropriate to their activities and responsibilities or who have been privileged if noted as an alternative: • The individual primarily serves in a managerial role, such as a department manager, or in dual clinical and managerial roles, with the managerial responsibilities identified in a job description. • The individual has some clinical responsibilities for which he or she has not been authorized to practice independently, such as an independent practitioner learning a new role or new skills. • The individual is in an educational program and under supervision, and the academic program identifies, for each stage or level of training, what can be done independently and what must be under supervision (the program description can serve as the job description in such cases). • The individual is permitted to temporarily provide services in the ambulatory care organization; for example, a nurse from a temporary staffing agency.
Job descriptions are current according to ambulatory care organization policy.
The job description outlines the knowledge, skills, and attitude necessary to perform the job responsibilities.
The job description clearly defines roles and responsibilities for the position.
Job responsibilities and clinical work assignments are based on evaluation of staff credentials.
The job description is discussed with and signed by the employee upon their hiring and is in their personnel file.

statement: The ambulatory care organization uses a defined process to ensure that clinical and nonclinical staff knowledge and skills are consistent with the requirements of the position.
elements: The ambulatory care organization uses a defined process to match clinical staff knowledge, skills, and competency with patient needs.

The ambulatory care organization uses a defined process to match nonclinical staff knowledge and skills with organization needs and the requirements of the position. The appointment process includes the following: • Receiving resumés, shortlisting, and interview • Acceptance or refusal within a set time frame
New clinical staff members are assessed before they begin their work responsibilities by the department or service to which they are assigned.
New nonclinical staff members are assessed before they begin their work responsibilities by the department or service to which they are assigned.

Prior to or at the time of orientation, an initial employment health screening is performed and documented. Orientation includes but is not limited to the following: • Information about the ambulatory care organization’s mission, vision, values, and organizational structure; patient and family rights; safety and security; the basics of infection prevention and control; and an introduction to the organization’s quality and patient safety and risk

statement: All new clinical and nonclinical staff members are oriented to the ambulatory care organization and to their specific job responsibilities.
elements: All clinical and nonclinical staff members are oriented to the ambulatory care organization, their job responsibilities, and any specific assignments.
Contract workers are oriented to the ambulatory care organization and to their job responsibilities and any specific assignments.
Students/trainees and volunteers are oriented to the ambulatory care organization and their specific assigned responsibilities.

statement: The competence to carry out job responsibilities to meet patient needs is continually assessed, maintained, improved, and documented for each staff member.
elements: Staff members’ abilities to fulfill expectations of their job descriptions are assessed. The competency testing should be conducted as follows: • For all newly hired staff • Based on objective criteria including knowledge, skills and attitude • At the end of the initial probationary period and annually thereafter • Staff participating in the evaluation and any required corrective action • To develop personal goals to achieve for the next year • For newly introduced equipment
The clinical or service area to which the individual is assigned performs the staff evaluation.
There is at least one documented evaluation of each staff member working under a job description each year, or more frequently, as defined by the ambulatory care organization.
Personnel files for each staff member are standardized, current, and maintained and kept confidential according to ambulatory care organization policy.
Personnel files contain the staff member’s job description, qualifications, work history, a record of orientation, and any required health information.
Both the employee and their supervisor sign the performance evaluation, which is kept in the employee’s personnel file.

statement: Each staff member receives ongoing in-service and other education and training to maintain or advance their skills and knowledge.
elements: The ambulatory care organization uses various sources of data and information, including the results of quality and safety measurement activities, to identify staff education needs. Education includes but is not limited to the following: • Proper use and safe operation of current and newly introduced specialized equipment and

statement: The ambulatory care organization develops and implements a staff health and safety program.
elements: The program covers all employees and is consistent with laws and regulations.

The ambulatory care organization provides and incorporates into the quality and safety program and risk management program a staff health and safety program that is responsive to urgent and nonurgent staff needs through direct treatment and/or referral.
The staff health and safety program addresses measures to protect staff and control hazardous conditions and occupational risks.

The ambulatory care organization provides evaluation, counseling, and follow-up for staff who are second victims of sentinel events, experience workplace violence, are exposed to an infectious disease, or experience a work-related injury.
The ambulatory care organization identifies areas for potential workplace violence and implements measures to reduce the risk.

The ambulatory care organization identifies epidemiologically significant infections as well as staff at high risk for exposure to and transmission of infections, and implements a staff vaccination and immunization program that includes health screening, immunization, and postexposure management.
Staff have confidential and secure medical records that reflect their health status.

statement: The ambulatory care organization has a uniform process to gather, verify, and evaluate the credentials (education, licensure/registration, and other credentials) of those medical staff members permitted to provide patient care without supervision.
elements: Medical staff members permitted by laws, regulations, and the ambulatory care organization to provide patient care without supervision are identified as per Saudi Commission for Health Specialties and licensing by the Ministry of Health in accordance with laws and regulations.

Education, licensure/registration, and other credentials, including training, experience, and competence as required by laws or regulations, are copied by the ambulatory care organization and maintained for each medical staff member in his or her personnel file or in a separate credentials file.

Education, licensure/registration, and other credentials required by laws or regulations or issued by recognized education or professional entities as the basis for clinical privileges are verified from the original source that issued the credential.

When third-party verification is used, the ambulatory care organization verifies that the third party (for example, a government agency) implements the verification process as described in policy or regulations.

Medical staff appointments are made after licensure/registration has been verified from the primary source and are consistent with the ambulatory care organization’s patient population, mission, and services.

The credentialing process guides the appointment of health care staff to their appropriate job assignment and is repeated at a minimum every two years to ensure that staff are still capable of performing their job functions.

statement: The ambulatory care organization has a standardized, objective, evidence-based procedure to authorize medical staff members to treat patients and/or to provide other clinical services consistent with their qualifications.
elements: The ambulatory care organization’s privilege delineation process meets the following criteria: • Standardized, objective, and evidence-based • Documented in ambulatory care organization policies • Active and ongoing as the credentials of medical staff members change • Followed for all classes of medical staff membership • Can be demonstrated to show that the procedure is used effectively
Clinical privileges are determined based on the ambulatory care organization’s documented competency and available services.
The medical staff’s clinical privileges are granted as recommended by the medical director and approved by the governing body, either directly or by appropriate delegation.

The clinical privileges of all medical staff members are made available by printed copy, electronic copy, or other means to those individuals or locations (for example, operating room, emergency department) in the ambulatory care organization in which the medical staff member will provide services.
The clinical privileges are reviewed and updated every two years or earlier if needed.
Each medical staff member provides only those services that have been specifically granted by the ambulatory care organization.

statement: The ambulatory care organization uses an ongoing standardized process to evaluate the quality and safety of the patient care provided by each medical staff member and uses this information to continue clinical privileges with or without modification.
elements: There is an ongoing professional practice evaluation of each staff member permitted to practice independently that incorporates available evidence at least annually through a standardized procedure established by the organization that includes evaluation, when indicated by the findings of quality improvement activities.

The monitoring and evaluation process identifies areas of achievement and potential improvement related to the behaviors, professional growth, and clinical results of the medical staff member compared to other department/service medical staff members.
The clinical results of data and information available on medical staff members are reviewed with objective and evidence-based information, as available, for external benchmarking.

The data and information from monitoring are reviewed at least every 12 months by the individual’s department/service head, senior medical manager, or medical staff oversight committee, and the results, conclusions, and any actions taken are documented in the medical staff member’s credentials file and other relevant files.

Based on the ongoing monitoring and evaluation of the medical staff member, the ambulatory care organization determines, at least every three years, if medical staff membership and clinical privileges are to continue with or without modification.

statement: The ambulatory care organization has a uniform process to gather, verify, and evaluate the nursing staff’s credentials (license, education, training, and experience).
elements: The ambulatory care organization has a standardized procedure to gather the credentials of each nursing staff member.
Licensure, education/training, and, when available, experience and competence are documented.

The credentialing process guides the appointment of health care staff to their appropriate job assignment and is repeated every two years to ensure that staff are still capable of performing their job functions.
Licensure and education/training are verified from the original source.
There is a record maintained of the credentials of every nursing staff member.
The ambulatory care organization has a process to ensure that the credentials of contract nurses are valid and complete prior to assignment.
The performance of individual nursing staff members is reviewed when indicated by the findings of quality improvement activities.

statement: The ambulatory care organization has a uniform process to gather, verify, and evaluate other health care practitioners’ credentials (license, education, training, and experience).
elements: The ambulatory care organization has a standardized process to gather the credentials of each health care practitioner, including registration of health care professionals with the Saudi Commission for Health Specialties and licensing by the Ministry of Health, in accordance with laws and regulations.
Licensure, education/training, and, when available, experience and competence are kept securely and updated in the personnel file.
Licensure and education/training are verified from the original source.

The credentialing process guides the appointment of health care staff to their appropriate job assignment and is repeated every two years to ensure that staff are still capable of performing their job functions.
There is a record maintained on other health care practitioners that contains copies of any required license, certification, or registration.
The performance of other health care practitioners is reviewed when indicated by the findings of quality improvement activities.

group: Delineation of the Scope of Primary Care Services
statement: Basic and essential services, as needed by the primary care center’s population, are provided.
elements: Clinical and managerial leaders identify the basic and essential services provided by the primary care center to its population. (See also GLD.3, ME 2.)
Basic and essential services include those needed by the primary care center’s population.
The primary care center provides the basic and essential services identified.
The general clinic (GC) has all necessary equipment and resources available for care, including a well- equipped observation room.

The GC has qualified medical and technical staff, including a family physician and/or general practitioner trained in family medicine basics, and a nurse in charge of GC services who handles administrative and clinical issues related to nursing. There are sufficient medical and nursing staff at all times to meet patient needs, with no significant variation during holidays or weekends, supported by a staffing plan guideline/schedule to cover all GC hours.

group: Delineation of the Scope of Primary Care Services
statement: The primary care center provides additional primary care services and procedures or through agreements with outside organizations and agencies.
elements: The center’s clinical and managerial leaders collaboratively identify additional primary care services. (See also COP.3, ME 1 and GLD.3, ME 2.)
Additional primary care services include the following, as needed by the center’s population: • Screenings, such as for cervical cancer, diabetes, and any other conditions or diseases common to

group: Delineation of the Scope of Primary Care Services
statement: For primary care centers that provide home care services, the center defines and plans for the scope of services required to meet the needs of patients who receive care in their homes.
elements: The primary care center defines and plans for the scope of services it provides to patients in their homes, which are consistent with the patient population’s needs.

Clinical services provided to patients in their home are coordinated and integrated in each department or service of the primary care center, and the care is documented in the patient medical record. (See also IPSG.2.2, ME 1.)
The home care patient, responsible family member, and/or caregiver are educated about preventing injury and maintaining safe conditions in the home for patients, families, and staff.
The primary care center has a process for educating families and caregivers on providing care safely and correctly when they are responsible for providing care to the home care patient.
Home care services provided by the primary care center are included in the center’s quality improvement activities. (See also GLD.4, ME 3.)

statement: The primary care center informs the community about its services and how to obtain care and screens patients to identify if their health care needs match the center’s mission and resources.
elements: Information on the primary care center’s services, its hours of operation, and the process to obtain care is communicated to individuals, agencies, and referral sources in the community.

The center provides mechanisms to ensure effective communication between staff and patients with special communication needs (for example, sign language for hearing-impaired patients, translator services for non-Arabic-speaking patients, assistance for sight-impaired patients) and to identify and handle common barriers that compromise patients’ access to services.

Patients have access to services based on their health needs and the services available. They are screened to identify if their needs match the primary care center’s mission and resources through a standardized process for screening and assessment to ensure that required services are appropriate to their needs. A standardized registration and appointment system is in place to support patient access.
Based on the results of screening, it is determined if the patient’s needs match the primary care center’s mission and resources.

Patients are accepted only if the primary care center can provide the necessary services and appropriate care to meet patient needs, with a clear management process in place when resources are not available.

statement: Enhanced services and procedures requiring special competence and/or facilities are provided by the primary care center or in cooperation with community organizations and agencies.
elements: The primary care center has determined the types of outside services it will take responsibility for arranging for its patients.
The primary care center has a written description of the nature and scope of services provided through contractual agreements. (See also GLD.7, ME 2.)

The primary care center has established and implemented a process for receiving results of tests, consultations, and treatments from contracted services (as applicable) and documenting them in the patient’s medical record.

The primary care center, at least annually, reviews the outside sources and determines and documents whether each source will continue to be used for and by the center’s patients. (See also GLD.7, ME 4.)

statement: The process of care is designed to support the patient.
elements: The primary care center has evaluated its patient flow and designed or redesigned its care processes to support and focus on the patient, as follows: • The patient appointment and registration processes are respectful of patient time and are designed to minimize waiting times for appointments and registration. • The patient information collection process at registration considers the need for confidentiality and privacy. • Patient information collected at registration is provided at each stage of care in the center or to each care site outside the center to eliminate the need to repeatedly collect the same information. • Verbal and written education supports and informs the patient about the process of care. • Communication with each patient is in a language and format they can understand. • When the care plan includes services from outside sites or organizations, or care in the home, the center coordinates and facilitates the patient’s choice, access, and use of those services. • Follow-up office visits, contact via telephone and other means to communicate laboratory and other test results, and other communication between the center and the patient facilitate understanding and compliance.

statement: The primary care center’s routines and processes are designed to support patient care provided by health care practitioners.
elements: The primary care center has evaluated its routines and processes and designed or redesigned the processes to support patient care from health care practitioners.
Planned visit lengths correspond to the type of service being provided, including initial patient visits, follow-up visits, and appointments for complex procedures.
Appropriate staff are available and effectively utilized.
The scheduling system can accommodate lengthy consultations and emergencies.
Care interruptions are minimal and meet defined criteria.

statement: Continuity and coordination of care are provided from initial assessment through care, treatment, and follow-up.
elements: The center provides continuity of care between clinical units and services. (See also IPSG.2.2, ME 1 and GLD.10, ME 3.)
The center coordinates care provided by multiple health care practitioners. (See also IPSG.2.2, ME 1.)
The center coordinates services provided outside the primary care center. (See also IPSG.2.2, ME 1.)
At the end of service, the primary care center identifies the patient’s post-service needs and supports continuity of care, with evidence of this process documented.
Patient information moves with the patient to facilitate coordination of services. (See also IPSG.2.2, ME 1 and CII.5, ME 4.)

statement: Multidisciplinary teams are organized to ensure continuity and coordination of care.
elements: The primary care center designs and implements processes that support continuity and coordination of care among multidisciplinary teams.

The primary care center supports effective team-delivered care consistent with its mission and patient needs through clear role identification and training to enhance team membership and effectiveness.
The patient’s medical record(s) is available to those practitioners who are authorized to have access and need it for patient care. (See also IPSG.2.2, ME 1.)
The patient’s medical record(s) is up to date to ensure communication of the latest information. (See also MOI.7.1, ME 2.)

statement: The records of patients requiring ongoing care or with multiple diagnoses contain profiles of the medical care and are made available to health care practitioners providing care to those patients.
elements: The primary care center identifies the types of patients receiving ongoing care and/or with multiple diagnoses who require a patient profile.
The necessary information in the patient profile is identified by the practitioners who treat those patients.
The primary care center uses a process to ensure the patient profile is easy to retrieve and review.
The process is evaluated to see if it meets practitioner needs and facilitates quality and safety of care.

statement: Patient and family education and instruction are related to the patient’s continuing care needs.
elements: The physician informs and educates the patient about the nature of the illness, diagnosis, treatment plan, and safe and effective use of all medications, including their potential side effects, response to therapy, and prevention of potential interactions with over-the-counter medications and/or food.

The patient and/or family are given the following necessary education and information by health care professionals, as appropriate, and it is documented in the health record: • Information about the patient’s illness and possible complications • Infection prevention and control practices, especially basic handwashing • Necessary treatments and procedures, with pamphlets or diagrams if available • Any surgical procedure needed, along with its benefits and potential risks • X-ray procedures, their benefits, and potential risks • Conditions that require the patient to seek medical assistance • Follow-up clinic appointments to ensure continuity of care

Patients and families are educated how to safely and effectively use medical equipment or appliances (for example, Ventolin inhaler), with return demonstration. Patient/family education is documented in the health record.

Patients and families are educated about proper diet and nutrition, including any dietary restrictions and the reasons for those restrictions. Patient/family education is documented in the health record. (See also PFE.2, ME 2.)
Patients and families are educated about pain management. (See also PFE.2, ME 2.)
Patients and families are educated about rehabilitation techniques.
Patients and families are educated about health promotion, disease prevention, and risk reduction at home, including falls prevention. (See also PFE.3, MEs 2 and 3.)

statement: The primary care center has an established process for referring or transferring a patient to another level of care, health care practitioner, or setting.
elements: There is an established referral system to guide referrals and transfers for care outside the primary care center when patients’ assessed needs require services beyond the center’s scope. The referral system ensures continuity of care in a timely manner and includes policies and procedures to guide referrals, staff roles and responsibilities, approved forms and registries required for referrals, and policies and procedures to receive and document referral results in the patient’s record. A referral manual includes all these elements.

The primary care center has informal or formal arrangements with other institutions to accept patients for referral. These arrangements include a list of referral facilities with the type of services provided, an effective communication process to coordinate referrals with the referral facilities, and a job description for staff assigned to the referral system.
A referral or transfer is based on the patient’s needs for care that can be provided only by sources outside the primary care center. (See also CII.2, ME 3 and COP.7, ME 6.)

Appropriate patient care information is shared with health care practitioners and organizations outside the primary care center, with all referred cases, including all records and forms, completed in the referral registry. Receiving institutions are provided with the necessary information, including the following: • Patient diagnosis • Brief summary of interventions • Medication list and time of the last dose(s) given • Condition at the time of transfer • Reason for transfer • Copy of the patient’s laboratory investigation and X-rays to avoid treatment delays • Referred specialty • Approval for referral • Time of referral
Necessary equipment for referrals is available.

There is a process to receive results from the referral facility and follow up on the care that the primary care center’s patients receive from outside sources. There is evidence of receiving and filing referral feedback, with follow-up from the feedback when required.
Emergency cases are referred to the appropriate facility in a timely manner, with evidence that the referrals occur within an appropriate time frame.

The primary care center leaders identify written indicators to monitor the appropriateness and timeliness of referrals. The results of monitoring are communicated to concerned staff and used for performance improvement.

statement: Transportation services provided or arranged by the primary care center comply with relevant laws and regulations and meet requirements for quality and safe transport.
elements: Transport vehicles owned by the primary care center meet relevant laws and regulations related to their operation, condition, and maintenance.
Transportation services, including owned, contracted, or services provided by the Ministry of Health or other agencies, meet the primary care center’s requirements for quality and safe transport.

Transfers are done quickly and safely, especially in emergency cases (for example, trauma, cardiac emergency), and the medical staff ensures that the patient’s needs are met by: • Assigning a qualified physician or paramedic (as appropriate) to accompany the patient and

statement: All patients cared for by the primary care center have their initial and continuing health care needs identified through an established assessment process.
elements: The primary care center develops and implements an assessment process for initial visits and continuing care visits to identify the health care needs of patients in accordance with laws, regulations, and licensure. (See also IPSG.6.1, ME 1.)
The primary care center identifies who performs which assessments.
The primary care center defines how the information from initial and continuing assessments performed outside the center will be used.
The primary care center defines the time frame for completion of assessment by each discipline.
The primary care center has an established policy on how to triage patients and prioritize their needs.

statement: The primary care center has determined the scope and content of initial and continuing care assessments conducted by different clinical disciplines based on applicable laws and regulations.
elements: The scope and content of initial and continuing assessments by each clinical discipline and care setting are defined in writing.

The assessments include the following, as appropriate to the patient’s needs: • A medical history and physical examination • The patient’s psychological, spiritual/religious, and social needs • A list of current medications and known allergies • An initial psychological assessment as indicated • An initial social and economic assessment and referral to available agencies to assist the patient • Any chronic illnesses (for example, congenital heart disease, rheumatic heart diseases, diabetes) • Any hematological illnesses (for example, hemophilia) • The patient’s chief complaints • Treatment plan • X-rays needed • Dose of local anesthesia, the tooth treated, and the material used • Assistance with the patient’s financial issues/status • The patient’s home situation and noncompliance/adherence to treatment • The patient’s disability and reducing its impact
Only qualified individuals permitted by licensure, applicable laws and regulations, or certification do the assessments. (See also SQE.2, ME 1 and SQE.8, ME 3.)
The primary care center identifies in writing those special patient groups, including age-specific populations, that require modified assessment. (See also CII.3.1, ME 1.)
The assessment process for special patient groups and populations is modified to reflect their needs. (See also CII.3.1, ME 1.)

The primary care center identifies the information to be documented from the assessments. The health record must contain assessment, diagnosis, impression, and plan of care revisions when indicated and therapeutic interventions.

statement: Patients are screened for nutritional status, functional needs, and other special needs as indicated by their condition, and referred for further assessment and treatment when necessary.
elements: Qualified individuals develop screening criteria to identify patients who • require further nutritional or functional assessment; • are in pain; • are at risk of falling; • have psychosocial needs; and/or • have been abused. These criteria are implemented consistently throughout the primary care center where needed.

Patients are screened for nutritional status when indicated by their condition; if needed, they are further assessed and treated in the primary care center or referred or provided with a referral for appropriate follow-up.

Patients are screened for functional status when indicated by their condition; if needed, they are further assessed and treated in the primary care center or referred or provided with a referral for appropriate follow-up. (See also IPSG.6.1, ME 1.)
When the need for additional specialized assessments is identified, patients are referred within the primary care center or to outside services in the community.
Screening and specialized assessments conducted in the primary care center are completed and documented in the patient’s medical record.

statement: All patients are screened for pain and assessed when pain is present.
elements: The primary care center screens patients for pain. (See also COP.6, ME 1.)

When pain is identified from the initial screening exam, the patient is further assessed and treated as needed in the primary care center or provided with a referral for further assessment and treatment.
The assessment or referral is documented in the patient medical record.

statement: There is an emergency assessment sheet/form that is documented for every patient presenting for care in the emergency department.
elements: The emergency assessment includes the following: • Time and means of arrival • Vital signs • History of illness • Allergies to medications, environment, and foods • Physical assessment/reassessment • Suspected diagnosis • Any investigations requested • Treatment given • Time of referral and/or discharge • Documentation of patient condition at time of discharge or referral to other facility

statement: There is an established reassessment process for patients requiring additional services or ongoing care.
elements: The primary care center identifies its patients’ health care needs through an established assessment/ reassessment process.
Patients are reassessed based on their condition, plan of care, and/or individual needs. (See also COP.2.1, ME 3.)
The primary care center defines the scope and content of the reassessment process as well as identifies who may do the reassessments.
Reassessments are documented in the patient’s medical record and available to all those caring for the patient.
