All patients are reassessed at appropriate intervals for the following: • Response to treatment • Compliance with treatment • Complications and side effects • Plan for continued treatment or completion of treatment

statement: Laboratory services are readily available either on site or through arrangements with outside sources to meet patient needs, and all such services meet applicable local and national standards, laws, and regulations.
elements: Basic laboratory services are readily available on site (for example, hematology, basic microbiology and biochemistry) and other services through outside sources through referral and consultation services in the form of agreements. A list of available laboratory services is published and distributed to all departments.

Laboratory services available on site or through outside sources meet applicable local and national standards, laws, and regulations. The laboratory services are provided through a structured program, that includes policies and procedures approved by the laboratory director, known to staff, and reviewed every two years.
Laboratory services provided through outside sources meet quality expectations and professional standards. (See also GLD.7.1, ME 2.)

Laboratory results are available in a timely manner to the patient’s health care practitioner, as defined by the primary care center through a defined turnaround time for all lab services and panic values (critical results) and the reporting method. (See also IPSG.2.1.)
Laboratory results are available in a timely manner to the patient, as defined by the primary care center.

statement: Qualified, trained individuals manage and staff on-site laboratory services, which have adequate supplies, quality control procedures, and a laboratory safety program.
elements: An individual(s) qualified by education and training consistent with applicable laws and regulations manages on-site laboratory services. All laboratory services are identified and under the director’s supervision.
Staff performing on-site laboratory services have adequate training, competence, orientation, and supervision. The chain of command is clearly defined for all staff. (See also SQE.2, MEs 1 and 2.)

Supplies and reagents for on-site laboratory services are consistently available and labeled, as applicable and appropriate, with the following: • Content, quantity, concentration, and/or titer • Storage requirements • Date prepared or reconstituted by laboratory • Expiration date The following are also true for all reagents: • All reagents are used and stored as recommended by the manufacturer. • All reagents must be used within their indicated expiration date. • If there are multiple components of a reagent kit, the laboratory uses components only in the kit lot unless otherwise specified by the manufacturer. • New reagent lots are checked against old reagent lots or with suitable quality control material before or concurrently being placed in service. • Current package inserts are available for all reagents used by the laboratory.

On-site laboratory services have a documented quality control program, approved by the laboratory director and integrated with the center-wide quality program. The quality control program includes the following: • Key quality indicators selected, monitored, and evaluated to detect potential problems • Reporting system for incidents, adverse events, and accidents to avoid recurrence • A proficiency testing (PT) system for each analyte, reported either by participating in external

statement: A qualified individual manages point-of-care testing (POCT) in the primary care center, and trained and competent staff perform the testing.
elements: The person responsible for managing the laboratory services, a designee, or when there are no on-site laboratory services, a qualified individual with the appropriate technical knowledge and experience, oversees and supervises POCT services.
The primary care center identifies those staff who perform POCT, and they are trained and competent to do so.
There is a defined process for reporting abnormal test results, including reporting critical test results, from POCT. (See also IPSG.2.1, ME 1.)
Quality control procedures for POCT are in place, followed, and documented.

statement: The laboratory maintains adequate, well-organized, and safe space that supports quality work and personnel safety, while ensuring all instruments and equipment are properly operated, cleaned, quality controlled, monitored, and maintained through an established system.
elements: The primary care center ensures that its designated laboratory space has adequate water taps, sinks, and drains; electrical outlets and emergency power; ventilation, temperature, and humidity control; lighting; and conveniently located telephones with the option to transfer calls.
The primary care center’s laboratory establishes an instrument and equipment management program, including operations and services manuals, maintenance schedules, and maintenance records.

statement: The laboratory publishes and distributes clear, written instructions for properly collecting, handling, transporting, and preparing specimens.
elements: The primary care center defines its specimen handling procedures, including identifying patients with two identifiers and preparing patients.
The procedures define specimen collection, labeling, preservation, and storage.
The procedures define appropriate transportation conditions and the process for receiving specimens in the laboratory.

statement: Radiology and diagnostic imaging services are readily available on site or through arrangements with outside sources to meet patient needs, and all such services meet applicable local and national standards, laws, and regulations.
elements: Radiology and diagnostic imaging services are readily available on site or through outside sources.

When provided on site, the primary care center ensures that its radiology space is adequate for its function, well maintained, and free of clutter. The space does not compromise the quality of work and staff safety, has a comfortable waiting area that ensures patient privacy, and has appropriate storage.

Radiology services are provided through a structured program, with policies and procedures known to staff, including but not limited to the following: • Scope of radiological services • Staff roles and responsibilities • Required forms and registries for the radiological services • A quality control program • A radiation safety program • Indicators for performance monitoring, evaluation, and improvement
Radiology and diagnostic imaging services provided on site or through outside sources meet applicable local and national standards, laws, and regulations.
Radiology and diagnostic imaging services provided by outside sources meet quality expectations and professional standards. (See also GLD.7.1, ME 2.)
Radiology and diagnostic imaging services establish processes for procedure ordering, ensuring that physicians requesting diagnostic imaging document all necessary information on the request form.

Radiology and diagnostic imaging results are available in a timely manner to the patient’s health care practitioner, as defined by the primary care center. “Panic findings” (for example, air under the diaphragm) are reported immediately to the specialty requesting the examination. Access to all digitally archived previous radiological studies is available to the patient’s health care practitioner. (See also IPSG.2.1.)
Radiology and diagnostic imaging results are available in a timely manner to the patient, as defined by the primary care center.

statement: Trained individuals manage and staff radiology and diagnostic imaging services provided on site at the primary care center. The services have adequate supplies and quality control procedures.
elements: An individual(s) qualified by education and training manages on-site radiology and diagnostic imaging services consistent with applicable laws and regulations.
Registered staff performing radiology and diagnostic imaging procedures on site have adequate training, competency, orientation, and supervision. (See also SQE.2, MEs 1 and 2.)
Equipment and supplies for on-site radiology and diagnostic imaging services, including x-ray film and reagents if used, are consistently available.
On-site radiology and diagnostic imaging services have, follow, and document their quality control procedures. This quality control program is integrated with the center’s overall quality program.

statement: A radiation safety program for staff and patients is in place, is followed, meets infection prevention and control requirements, and is part of the center’s facility management program.
elements: A radiation safety program for patients and staff is in place and addresses potential safety risks and hazards encountered in the primary care center. (See also FMS.2, ME 1.)
The radiation safety program includes educating staff about dosing for radiology and diagnostic imaging tests.
Protocols that identify the maximum dose of radiation for each type of test are adopted and implemented.

Identified radiation safety risks are addressed by processes and safety protective devices, for both staff and patients, that reduce safety risks, including but not limited to the following: • Radiation personal protective measures are available for employees and patients. • Staff are monitored for radiation exposure. • Thermo luminescence dosimeter (TLD) is regularly checked for all radiology staff. • All employees in the radiology department have their white blood cells checked periodically. • Safety warnings are posted on doors in clear and appropriate locations. • Female patients are checked for possible pregnancy before x-ray tests, and the x-ray form requires that the physician ask the patient.

Radiology and diagnostic imaging staff are oriented to safety procedures and practices and receive ongoing education and training for new procedures, equipment, hazardous materials, and so on. (See also FMS.11, ME 1 and SQE.2, MEs 1 and 2.)
The radiation safety program meets infection prevention and control requirements and is part of the center’s facility management program. (See also PCI.4, ME 3 and FMS.4, ME 3.)
All radioactive materials are used according to the guidelines, and the safety officer oversees the activity in the unit.
An experienced safety officer regularly inspects and checks all equipment.

statement: The primary care center provides care and treatment using uniform care processes that follow applicable laws and regulation.
elements: The primary care center has a written, updated General Clinics (GC) manual that is available and well known to concerned staff. The manual defines the scope of services; includes policies and procedures, forms, and registries required; includes a system for patient follow-up; and identifies the roles and responsibilities of concerned staff. It also includes indicators for performance monitoring, evaluation, and improvement.
The center’s clinical and managerial leaders collaborate to provide uniform care processes.

When similar care is provided in more than one place in the center or more than one center site, care delivery is uniform or reflects adaptation to patient needs and is guided by applicable laws and regulations. Patients receive similar care across all settings in the facility.
The provision of uniform care reflects relevant laws and regulations.

Uniform care is provided and meets the following requirements: (See also CII.3.1, ME 2.) • Access to and appropriateness of care and treatment do not depend on the patient’s ability to pay or the source of payment. • The patient’s condition determines the resources allocated to meet their needs. • When the center is open, care does not vary by time of day or day of the week. • When the same care is provided at more than one site, the level of care provided to patients is the same.

statement: There is a process to integrate and coordinate the care provided by each health care practitioner to every patient.
elements: Clinical leaders use tools and techniques to integrate and coordinate the care provided to each patient. (See also IPSG.2.2, ME 2.)
Health care practitioners record observations, test results, treatments, and other pertinent information in the patient’s medical record. (See also MOI.7.1, ME 2.)
Results of patient care team meetings are recorded in the patient’s medical record.

statement: The care provided to a continuing care patient is planned, revised when indicated, and documented in the patient’s record.
elements: The primary care center identifies the disease processes and the patients with complex needs for which a multidisciplinary team is indicated.

The care for each continuing care patient is planned and developed by a multidisciplinary team, including the attending physician, nurse, and other disciplines participating in care. The care plan is based on data from assessments and reassessments, contains measurable goals (desired outcomes), and is documented in the patient’s record.
The patient and, when appropriate, the family are involved in the planned care. (See also PFR.3, ME 1.)

The planned care for a continuing care patient is revised every visit, when indicated by a change in the patient’s condition, and new treatments are added or discontinued. There is evidence of plan-of-care revisions during subsequent visits.

If a procedure is planned, the procedure is explained to the patient, informed consent is taken, clear follow-up instructions are given, and a follow-up appointment is scheduled, all with documentation.
If any local anesthetic is used, the physician is expected to document the dose, the type, and its suitability to the patient’s condition.
The care planned for the patient is provided and noted in the patient’s medical record.
The center has a process to periodically evaluate the effectiveness of multidisciplinary care and address opportunities for improvement.

statement: Clinical practice guidelines and related clinical pathways and/or clinical protocols, as well as other evidence- based recommendations, are used to guide patient assessment and treatment and reduce unwanted variation.
elements: The leaders of the primary care center collaboratively set criteria to select guidelines and any related clinical pathways and/or protocols. (See also IPSG.5, ME 1 and MMU.1.1.)
The center leaders select and implement clinical practice guidelines appropriate to the center’s patients. (See also CII.6.1, ME 2.)
Clinical practice guidelines and any associated clinical pathways and/or clinical protocols are used to guide the assessment and treatment of applicable patients.
Clinical practice guidelines, clinical pathways, and clinical protocols are used to evaluate the quality and safety of services provided by the primary care center.

statement: The care of high-risk patients and the provision of high-risk services are guided by professional practice guidelines, laws, and regulations.
elements: Primary care center leaders identify high-risk patients and services. (See also ACC.1.1, ME 1 and GLD.3, ME 2.)

When the center provides high-risk services, its leaders establish and implement guidelines and procedures for those services and for the care of high-risk patients, including at least the following when the services and/or patients are present in the center: • Emergency patients • Patients with a communicable disease • Immunosuppressed patients • Patients with emotional or psychiatric disorders • Patients receiving dialysis • Patients receiving blood or blood products • Patients receiving radiation therapy • Patients receiving chemotherapy • Vulnerable patient populations, including frail elderly, dependent children, and patients at risk

statement: Resuscitation services are available throughout the primary care center.
elements: Resuscitation services are available during all hours of operation and throughout all areas of the primary care center.
Medical equipment and medications for resuscitation are standardized and available for use based on the needs of the population served. (See also GLD.10, ME 4.)
All staff who provide patient care, including contracted physicians and health care practitioners, are trained to provide basic life support services. (See also SQE.2, ME 1 and SQE.5, ME 3.)

statement: Patients at nutritional risk receive nutrition therapy from the primary care center or are referred to food and nutrition resources in the community.
elements: A qualified individual further assesses patients identified through screening as at nutrition risk.
The center treats patients at nutritional risk or refers them to appropriate food and nutrition resources in the community.
When the primary care center provides nutritional therapy, the patient’s progress is monitored and recorded in their record.
If the patient has been referred to an outside resource, the referral is documented in the patient’s record.

statement: Patients are supported in managing pain effectively.
elements: Based on its scope of services, the primary care center has processes to identify patients in pain. (See also AOP.1.3, ME 1.)
When pain is an expected result of planned treatments, procedures, or examinations, patients are informed about the likelihood of pain and options for pain management. (See also PFR.7.2, ME 1.)
Patients in pain receive care according to pain management guidelines and patient goals for managing pain.

Primary care centers communicating with patients and families about managing pain and symptoms include both pharmacologic and nonpharmacological strategies in the context of the patient’s personal, cultural, and religious beliefs.
Based on its scope of services, the primary care center has processes to educate staff about pain. (See also PFE.2, ME 2.)

statement: When the primary care center provides care and treatment for dying patients, the center addresses end-of-life care appropriate to the patient’s condition and needs, or refers the patient to outside sources of appropriate care.
elements: The center and its staff recognize and respect dying patients’ unique needs. (See also PFR.4, ME 1.)
Assessments and treatment of the dying patient include symptom management related to the disease process or secondary to the treatment provided.
Assessments and reassessments include the dying patient’s and family’s psychological, emotional, spiritual, and cultural concerns. (See also PFR.3, ME 1.)
Care of the dying patient optimizes his or her comfort and dignity. (See also PFR.2, ME 1.)
Pain is managed effectively. (See also PFR.3, ME 1.)
Patients are referred to outside sources of end-of-life care when the center does not provide these services. (See also ACC.9, MEs 1 and 2.)

statement: The primary care center and other health care and civic centers cooperate and partner to identify the health care problems and services needed in the region and community.
elements: The primary care center has defined the geographic region and community it serves.

The primary care center has identified the agencies and organizations with which it will cooperate and partner to identify and meet the health needs of the region or community. (See also GLD.3, ME 2.)
The primary care center has identified its community’s health needs. (See also GLD.3, ME 2.)
The primary care center has identified its mission and scope of services based on community needs. (See also GLD.1.1, ME 1 and GLD.3, ME 2.)
The primary care center updates the needs assessment based on changes in the community and as new information becomes available.

statement: Community hospital backup and medical transportation services are available, if needed, from within the regional health care delivery system.
elements: The primary care center has identified sources of acute medical care available in its community or a nearby community or region and alternatives when acute medical care is not readily available. (See also ACC.10.)
The primary care center has identified sources of transportation necessary to transfer patients to an acute care or other facility and alternatives when transport is not readily available.
When the primary care center is not able to meet the patient’s needs, it has a process for efficiently referring and transferring patients. (See also ACC.9, MEs 1 and 2.)

statement: The primary care center has defined the population(s) for which it will provide access to services that is consistent with its mission and establishes its role in providing services to the identified population(s).
elements: The primary care center has defined the population(s) and/or geographic area for which it will provide services.
The primary care center collaborates with agencies, organizations, and relevant government health planners regarding its role in providing services in the community.
A plan or list of the center’s services is created as a result of the data and information about the population in the community, and meetings and other communications.

statement: The primary care center works collaboratively with other organizations and health agencies to identify and include vulnerable populations in community health programs.
elements: The primary care center has identified the vulnerable populations in its community. (See also AOP.1.1, MEs 4 and 5.)
The primary care center collaborates with other agencies and organizations to ensure that services are provided to vulnerable populations. (See also COP.1, ME 4.)
The primary care center has identified its participation in providing services to vulnerable populations consistent with its mission. (See also PFR.1, ME 3.)

group: Participation of the Primary Care Center in its Community
statement: The primary care center participates actively as a member of its community and region.
elements: Primary care center leaders participate in and/or lead community discussion on health issues, and support and promote community participation by assessing and planning for health care needs, evidenced by their involvement in community activities and attendance at community health committee meetings.
The primary care center understands its role in the event of likely community emergencies, epidemics, pandemics, and natural or other disasters. (See also PCI.6 and FMS.5, ME 3.)

The primary care center participates with the community in health and disease management surveillance, identification, analysis, control, and reporting consistent with its mission. (See also PCI.3, ME 1; GLD.1.2, ME 1; and GLD.2, MEs 4 and 5.)

group: Participation of the Primary Care Center in its Community
statement: One or more primary care center leaders are defined as responsible for speaking on behalf of the primary care center to its community.
elements: The primary care center identifies and documents community representatives and resources related to its scope of services. It also identifies designated individuals to speak to the community on its behalf. (See also MOI.1, ME 3.)

There is a designated committee(s) to coordinate community involvement. The committee must do the following: • Have terms of reference that clearly define its roles and responsibilities, including all relevant

statement: The primary care center’s commitment to health promotion and disease prevention is evident in its mission statement, values statement, collaborative agreements with local and regional agencies, and relevant policies and community participation.
elements: The mission statement, values statement, and other policies and documents reflect the primary care center’s commitment to community health promotion and disease prevention, with leadership support evidenced in the implementation of health promotion and education concepts.
The center leads or participates in health screenings, immunizations, and special public health programs consistent with its mission and community needs.

The center leads or participates in community health education activities and assesses the effectiveness of those programs, with written health promotion and education plans and programs developed by primary care center leaders with assistance from professionals and effective community participation.

The primary care center has approved and implemented health promotion and education plans that do the following: • Identify the health needs and priorities of individuals and the community • Identify behaviors and social and environmental factors that positively or negatively affect health • Focus on the health priorities of the catchment area, addressing habits, activities, and concerns of

statement: The primary care center participates in a variety of health promotion and disease prevention programs with its community.
elements: Primary care center leaders and staff collaborate with relevant sectors to implement health promotion and disease prevention programs, which are documented and include the following: • Immunizations • Healthy children’s programs • Fitness screenings • Health screenings (for example, breast cancer screening, colon/rectal cancer screening) • Family planning • Primary disease prevention and health promotion, including smoking, drugs, alcohol, physical activity, and nutrition. A written healthy nutrition program is in place that encourages balanced nutrition, discourages the intake of soft drinks and foods that affect oral and dental health in schools, encourages milk as an essential component in school nutrition, ensures safe food provision, and educates on the risks of obesity. • Secondary and tertiary disease prevention and health promotion (for example, cardiovascular

statement: The primary care center has a program to provide ongoing care and support to patients with chronic diseases.
elements: The primary care center develops and implements a chronic disease management program that includes patient and family education and promotion of self-management.
The center partners with other health care practitioners and organizations to facilitate the coordination of services to improve the management of patients with chronic conditions.
The center evaluates the efficacy of its chronic disease management program.

statement: In conjunction with community planning, each primary care center defines and measures its achievement in meeting community goals of care.
elements: The primary care center involves community members in setting goals for improving health promotion and disease prevention.
The primary care center prioritizes areas for improvement. (See also QPS.1, ME 2 and GLD.5, ME 1.)
The primary care center collects data and reports data related to these internal and community goals. (See also QPS.1, ME 3.)
The primary care center involves the community in developing action plans for improving outcomes based on data related to internal and community goals.

statement: The primary care center, at least quarterly, solicits community perceptions related to its services, community presence, and activities.
elements: The primary care center has a means to solicit community perceptions related to its services, community presence, and activities. (See also GLD.6.)
The primary care center requests the information in a manner defined by the center, at least quarterly.
The primary care center uses a process to receive, analyze, and use the information to influence its programs and services.

statement: The primary care center develops and implements a process to improve accuracy of patient identification.
elements: Patients are identified using two patient identifiers, not including the use of the patient’s examination room number and location in the primary care center. (See also MOI.7, ME 2.)
Patients are identified before providing treatments, conducting procedures, taking blood samples, and administering medications. (See also IPSG.4, ME 1; IPSG.4.1, ME 1; and MMU.4.)
The primary care center ensures the correct identification of patients in special circumstances, such as those without identification or with the same name.

statement: The primary care center develops and implements a process to improve the effectiveness of verbal and/or telephone communication among caregivers.
elements: The complete verbal order is documented and read back by the receiver and confirmed by the individual giving the order.
The complete telephone order is documented and read back by the receiver and confirmed by the individual giving the order.
There is an implemented process for the attending physician or his designee to sign off on the entire verbal and telephone orders.
The complete test result is documented and read back by the receiver and confirmed by the individual giving the result.

statement: The primary care center develops and implements a process for reporting critical results of diagnostic tests.
elements: The primary care center has defined critical values for each type of diagnostic test. (See also AOP.3.2, ME 3.)
The primary care center has identified by whom and to whom critical results of diagnostic tests are reported.
The primary care center has identified what information is documented in the medical record.

statement: The primary care center develops and implements a process for handover communication.
elements: Standardized critical content is communicated between health care practitioners during handovers of patient care. (See also ACC.1.2, ME 2; ACC.3, ME 5; ACC.5, MEs 1-4; and ACC.6, MEs 1 and 3.)
Standardized forms, tools, or methods support a consistent and complete handover process. (See also COP.2, ME 1.)

Data from adverse events resulting from handover communications are tracked and used to identify ways in which handovers can be improved, and improvements are implemented. Goal 3: Improve the Safety of High-Alert Medications

statement: The primary care center develops and implements a process to improve the safety of high-alert medications.
elements: The primary care center identifies in writing its list of high-alert medications and develops and implements a process for managing these high-alert medications.
The primary care center has a list of look-alike/sound-alike medications and develops and implements a process for managing look-alike/sound-alike medications.

The process for managing high-alert medications and the process for managing look-alike/sound-alike medications are uniform throughout the primary care center. Goal 4: Ensure Correct-Site, Correct-Procedure,

statement: The primary care center develops and implements a process for the pre-procedure verification and procedure site-marking.
elements: The primary care center implements a pre-procedure verification process using a checklist or other mechanism to document, before the procedure, that the informed consent is appropriate to the procedure; that the correct patient, correct procedure, and correct site are verified; and that all required documents, blood products, medical equipment, and implantable medical devices are on hand, correct, and functional. (See also IPSG.1, ME 2.)
The primary care center uses an instantly recognizable, standardized, and unambiguous mark with permanent ink for identifying the procedure site that is consistent throughout the primary care center.
The person performing the procedure does the site marking and involves the patient in the marking process whenever possible.

statement: The primary care center develops and implements a process for the time-out that is performed immediately prior to the start of the invasive procedure.
elements: The full team actively participates in a time-out process, in the area in which the procedure will be performed, immediately before starting the procedure. The time-out process ensures the following: • Correct patient identity • Correct procedure to be done • Correct procedure site
Completion of the time-out and time of completion are documented.
When invasive procedures are performed, regardless of location in the primary care center, uniform processes are used to ensure the correct site, correct procedure, and correct patient.

statement: The primary care center adopts and implements evidence-based hand-hygiene guidelines to reduce the risk of health care–associated infections.
elements: The primary care center has adopted current evidence-based hand-hygiene guidelines. (See also COP.2.2, ME 1.)
The primary care center implements a hand-hygiene program throughout the center.
Handwashing and hand-disinfection procedures are used in accordance with hand-hygiene guidelines throughout the primary care center. (See also PCI.4, ME 2.)

statement: Not applicable to primary care centers
The primary care center develops and implements a process to reduce the risk of patient harm resulting from falls for the center’s patient population.
elements: The primary care center implements a process for screening patients whose condition, diagnosis, situation, or location may put them at risk for falls and uses screening tools/methods appropriate for the patients being served. (See also AOP.1, ME 1; AOP.1.2, ME 3; and COP.3, ME 4.)

When fall risk is identified from the screening process, measures and/or interventions are implemented to reduce fall risk for those patients identified at risk, and the screening and interventions are documented.
Measures and/or interventions to reduce fall risk are implemented in situations and locations assessed to be a risk for falls.

statement: Medication use in the primary care center is organized to meet patient needs, is appropriate to the center’s mission and services, and complies with applicable laws and regulations.
elements: The pharmacy head is experienced, certified, and registered pharmacist with a bachelor’s degree in pharmacy and a current Saudi Commission for Health Specialties license.
All pharmacy staff have evidence of a valid Saudi Commission for Health Specialties license to practice in Saudi Arabia.
Medications available in the center for prescribing and use are appropriate to the center’s mission, patient needs, and services.
The primary care center develops and implements a program to guide medication management and use that meets applicable laws and regulations.

Health care practitioners involved in ordering, dispensing, administering, and patient-monitoring processes are involved in the development and ongoing evaluation of the medication management and use program.

The program addresses the following elements as appropriate to the center: (See also IPSG.3.) • Planning • Selection and procurement • Storage • Ordering • Preparing and dispensing • Administration • Monitoring • Annual evaluation

The primary care center establishes an interdisciplinary committee for overseeing and monitoring the medication management processes. The committee has defined terms of reference, and meeting minutes reflect its functions.
The space of the pharmacy allows the principal functions to be carried out efficiently and effectively.
The pharmacy hours of operation are announced and posted at the pharmacy entrance.
Pharmacy areas have adequate drug information resources to contact a poison control center when needed

statement: The primary care center develops and implements a program for prudent use of antibiotics based on the principles of antibiotic stewardship.
elements: The primary care center develops and implements a program for antibiotic stewardship that involves, as applicable, physicians, nurses, pharmacists, trainees, patients, families, and others.
The program is based on scientific evidence, accepted practice guidelines, and local laws and regulations. (See also PCI.2 ME 1.)
The program includes guidelines for optimal use of antibiotic therapy for treating infections, including proper use of prophylactic antibiotic therapy.

The program includes educating patients, families, caregivers, and the community about use and misuse of antibiotics, including individualized counseling and public awareness training. (See also CII.4, ME 1.)
There is a mechanism to oversee the program for antibiotic stewardship. (See also GLD.9, ME 6.)
The effectiveness of the antibiotic stewardship program is monitored.

statement: There is a method for overseeing the primary care center’s medication list, availability of medications, and medication use.
elements: There is a method for overseeing medication use in the primary care center.

There is a list (drug formulary) of medications stocked in the primary care center or, if applicable, readily available from outside sources, and it includes at least the following: • Generic name, formulation, strength, therapeutic, and brief prescribing information for each

statement: Medications, including emergency medications and medications that require special handling, are properly and safely stored.
elements: Medications are stored under conditions suitable for product stability (continuously controlled temperature 18 and 25 degrees centigrade), including medications stored on ambulances (as applicable).

The pharmacy has refrigerators for storing vaccines and cold medications. Other requirements for these pharmacy refrigerators include the following: • A list of the refrigerator’s contents (medications and pharmaceutical products) with expiration dates is posted on the refrigerator. • A refrigerator’s temperature is recorded daily. Appropriate refrigerator temperature is maintained between 2 and 8 degrees centigrade. • All medication refrigerators and freezers are equipped with appropriate thermometers or an equivalent device for temperature recording and temperature log sheets. • The vaccine refrigerator is connected to an emergency power source (electric outlets are marked). The temperature is recorded daily, or an equivalent process is in place to monitor temperature around the clock. • There are written and implemented policies and procedures for handling medications in case of failure of electrical power or whenever temperature is out of range. • Food, drinks, biological samples, and culture media are not allowed inside medication refrigerators.

The primary care center has a policy for identifying and handling expired medications including the following: • Process for identifying expired medications • Frequency of inspection • Documentation of the returned expired drugs to the supplier or manufacturer and/or evidence of

statement: The primary care center has a system for ensuring preparedness of crash carts, emergency bags, and emergency medications.
elements: There is a standardized list of crash cart medications, which complies with and is updated in accordance to Saudi Heart Association recommendations.
Crash cart medications are inspected monthly and replaced in a timely way after use or when expired. The monthly inspection and any actions taken as a result are documented.

statement: An individual authorized by laws and regulations prescribes medications.
elements: Only authorized medical staff, by laws and regulations, are allowed to prescribe medications.

There is a list of medical staff including the following for each member: name, specialty, prescribing privileges (that is, for narcotics and psychotropics), signature, and identification number, and stamp or code available to all clinical staff. This list includes pharmacy staff in the drug dispensing area and is updated annually and whenever a new medical staff member joins.
The primary care center ensures that only authorized individuals are allowed to prescribe medications within the accepted prescribing privileges.

statement: The primary care center has a system for handling prescriptions and dispensing medications.
elements: There is a uniform medication dispensing and distribution system; medications are dispensed by a licensed pharmacist as identified and permitted by the primary care center and relevant licensure, laws, and regulations. (See also SQE.2, ME 1.)

The licensed pharmacist should verify the availability of the following information prior to the prescription: • Patient’s name • Medical record number • Age • Gender • Body weight • Diagnosis • Allergies • Name of the prescribing physician, stamp, and license number • Date and time

A pharmacist verifies the physician’s prescription or order for diagnosis, approved indications for the diagnosis, dosing, frequency, route, duration, and interactions (drug to drug and drug to food).

There is a mechanism in place that allows the pharmacist to stop dispensing the medication and seek clarification when the order is missing elements and/or when patient is identified as allergic to the prescribed medication.
All prescriptions are double-checked by another qualified professional prior to dispensing.
The primary care center has a policy for filling and refilling prescriptions.

The records of patients on multiple medications contain a list of current medications that includes the name of the medication, dose, frequency, and route of administration. Patient records also indicate the patient use of any herbs or supplements. (See also AOP.1.1 and MMU.5, ME 2.)
Patients and families are offered education about dispensed medications.
Written drug counseling materials are available in an easily understandable language.
The pharmacist explains to the patient how to use their medications (dose, route, frequency, time in relation to meals, and any side effects).

statement: Medication administration in the primary care center follows standardized processes to ensure patient safety.
elements: Medications are administered by qualified individuals as identified and permitted by the primary care center and relevant licensure, laws, and regulations. (See also SQE.2, ME 1.)
The medication, dosage amount, and route of administration are verified with the prescription or order.
Medications prescribed and/or administered within the primary care center are noted in the patient’s record. (See also MOI.7.1, ME 2.)

statement: Medications are monitored for patient adherence, clinical effectiveness, and adverse medication effects.
elements: Patient adherence in taking medications, medication effectiveness, and adverse medication effects are monitored.
The record of each patient who receives medications in the primary care center contains a list of the current medications prescribed or ordered. (See also AOP.1.1 and MMU.4, ME 5.)

The primary care center has a written policy and procedures covering the following: • Definition of significant adverse drug reaction and time frame and procedure for reporting, including the format that needs to be used to report the adverse drug reaction (ADR) • Mechanism to inform the treating physician of the ADR • Adverse effects and any required immediate care are documented in the patient’s medical record, and the record is flagged adequately. • All significant ADRs are intensively reviewed and analyzed, as defined in the primary care center’s policy and procedure. • All significant or unexpected ADRs are reported to the relevant authorities per rules and regulations.

statement: The primary care center establishes and implements a process for reporting and acting on medication errors and near misses.
elements: The primary care center establishes a definition of medication error and near miss. (See also QPS.6, ME 1.)
The primary care center establishes and implements a process for reporting and acting on medication errors and near misses. (See also GLD.1.1, ME 6; GLD.4, ME 4; and GLD.12, ME 4.)
The primary care center identifies those individuals accountable for acting on medication error and near miss reports.
The primary care center uses medication error and near miss reports to improve its medication use processes.

statement: The primary care center provides education that supports patient, family, and caregiver participation in care decisions and processes.
elements: The center plans education consistent with its mission, services, and patient population.
There is an established structure or mechanism for education throughout the center.
The education structure and resources are organized effectively.

statement: Each patient’s educational needs related to immediate and long-term health conditions are assessed and recorded in the patient’s medical record.
elements: The educational needs of the patient, family, and/or caregiver are assessed.
Patients are educated to meet their ongoing health needs and/or achieve their health goals. (See also ACC.8, MEs 1-4 and 6; and COP.6, ME 5.)
Education supports patients in making care decisions, participating in their care, and continuing care at home. (See also ACC.8, ME 6.)
Educational needs assessment findings and patient’s response are recorded in the patient’s medical record in a uniform manner. (See also MOI.7, ME 3.)

statement: The patient’s and family’s or caregiver’s ability to learn and willingness to learn are assessed.
elements: The patient’s learning/educational needs, literacy skills (including health care literacy) educational level, and language are assessed and documented in their health record.
The patient’s emotional barriers and motivations are assessed.
The patient’s physical and cognitive limitations are assessed.
The assessment findings are used to plan the education.
The patient’s and family’s or caregiver’s readiness and ability to learn are assessed.

statement: Education methods consider the patient’s and family’s or caregiver’s values and preferences and allow sufficient interaction among the patient, family or caregiver, and staff for learning to occur.
elements: The education process considers the patient’s and family’s or caregiver’s values and preferences.
There is a process to verify that patients, families, and caregivers receive and understand the education provided.
Those who provide education encourage patients and their families or caregivers to ask questions and speak up as active participants.
Patient, family, and caregiver education is provided collaboratively by the patient’s health care practitioners, when indicated.
Those who provide education have the subject knowledge and communication skills to do so and use educational materials (written, verbal, pictures, demonstration, and so on).

The patient, family, and/or caregiver are educated about the following: • The nature of the illness and any complications • Diagnosis • Treatment plan • Any medications, including frequency, side effects, precautions, and response to therapy • Infection prevention and control practices, especially basic handwashing • Any necessary treatments and surgical procedures, with pamphlets or diagrams if available • Appropriate use of any medical equipment or appliances (for example, ventolin inhaler) with

statement: There are guidelines for primary care center staff (nurses, physicians, dietitians, and so on) on how to teach the patient/family or caregiver, including but not limited to the items in the measurable elements.
elements: Staff should use simple language, so the patient/family/caregiver understands the education.
Staff should give the patient/family/caregiver sufficient time to understand the information given to them.
Staff should provide enough time to interact with the patient/family/caregiver during the education.
Staff should use pamphlets, diagrams, models to practice on, or other teaching methods.
Staff should obtain feedback (repeating or demonstrating) from the patient/family/caregiver to ensure that they understand.

statement: The primary care center’s health promotion program includes periodic health assessments for its age-specific patient population.
elements: The periodic health assessments for age-specific patient populations are based on updated scientific guidelines.
Periodic health assessments are documented in the patient’s health record.

statement: The primary care center is responsible for providing processes that support patient and family rights during care.
elements: The primary care center works to protect equitable health care services and advance patient and family rights.
The primary care center understands patient and family rights as identified in laws and regulations.
Primary care center leaders are involved in supporting and protecting patient and family rights by: • Developing and maintaining a patient rights and responsibilities statement and policies to

statement: The primary care center provides care that respects the patient’s dignity, personal values, beliefs, and privacy as well as confidentiality of care and information.
elements: Staff provide care that is respectful and considerate of the patient’s dignity and self-worth. (See also COP.7, ME 4 and GLD.12, ME 2.)
Staff provide care that respects the patient’s values and beliefs.
Staff identify, respect, and protect patient expectations and needs for privacy during care and treatment.
A patient’s expressed need for privacy is respected for all clinical interviews, examinations, procedures/ treatments, and transport.
Confidentiality of patient information is maintained according to laws and regulations. (See also GLD.11, ME 1; MOI.3, MEs 2 and 3; and MOI.12, MEs 1–3.)

statement: The primary care center supports and promotes patient and family participation in care processes, the patient’s right to assessment and management of pain, and the needs of the dying patient.
elements: The center supports and promotes patient and family participation in care processes. (See also COP.2.1, ME 3; COP.7, ME 3; and COP.7, ME 5.)

The center respects and supports the patient’s right to assessment and management of pain as follows: • Assessing the patient during visits for pain • Providing quick pain relief for the patient as possible • Assessing the patient’s response to pain medications • Dealing with side effects from pain medications administered • Providing advice on how to deal with chronic pain • Referring the patient to other health care settings, as appropriate • Educating the patient about their pain and how to minimize it
The center respects and supports the dying patient’s right to compassionate care and assesses and manages the patient’s needs.
Staff are trained in the policies and procedures and their role in supporting patient and family participation in care processes. (See also SQE.3, ME 1.)

statement: The primary care center informs patients and families about their rights to refuse or discontinue treatment and the center’s responsibilities related to such decisions.
elements: As appropriate to the patient’s needs and preferences, the primary care center informs patients and families about their rights to refuse or discontinue treatment including the following: (See also COP.7, ME 1.) • The consequences of treatment refusal are explained to patients. • Patients are informed about available care and treatment alternatives. • Family members, when appropriate, are involved in the process. • Patient and family choices are respected. • The discussion is documented in the patient’s record.

The primary care center informs patients about fully participating in decisions about their care, treatment, and services, including consequences of their decisions, by giving them accurate and honest information, and the following occur: • Patients are informed of their diagnosis; options for care, treatment, and services (in simple layman’s terms); and how they can participate in care decisions. • Patients discuss their plan of care with the physician and have all their questions answered. • Staff members respond appropriately to patients’ requests for a second consultation. • Patients’ preferences and choices are respected.
The primary care center informs patients and families about their responsibilities related to such decisions.
The primary care center truthfully informs patients about available care and treatment alternatives.

statement: The primary care center informs patients and families about its process to receive and act on complaints, conflicts, and differences of opinion about patient care and the patient’s right to participate in these processes.
elements: Patients are informed about the process for voicing complaints, conflicts, and differences of opinion.
The primary care center investigates patient complaints, conflicts, and differences of opinion.
Complaints, conflicts, and differences of opinion that arise during the care process are resolved in a timely manner.
Patients and families participate in the resolution process.
The primary care center has a system (including a policy, forms, and a process) to conduct ongoing patient satisfaction surveys and makes improvements based on the trended survey results.

The primary care center has an effective structure to handle patient complaints that includes the following: • A specific unit or person in the organization (for example, patient relations, social worker, quality department) is responsible for managing complaints. • A committee oversees the patient complaint process and outcomes, and its membership includes staff from at least medical, nursing, patient relations, and quality management departments. • The unit or person responsible for patient complaints routes patient complaints that have a non- medical implication to the concerned department/section leader who will investigate and help resolve the issues. • The unit or person responsible for patient complaints routes patient complaints that have a medical implication to the medical director to handle the clinical review process of the case. • The medical director routes all complaints, identified as mortality and/or morbidity cases by the clinical review process, to the mortality and morbidity committee. • The primary care center investigates immediately and finalizes the medical cases by no later than one month from receiving the complaint and gives feedback to the complainant. • The committee that oversees patient complaints receives a confidential summary report of the complaint cases reviewed from the mortality/morbidity committee chair, with copies to the center’s director, medical director, and quality management committee. • The chair of the committee that oversees patient complaints routes trended reports to department heads as needed and receives written feedback from them. • The chair of the committee that oversees patient complaints routes the minutes to the center’s director, medical director, and quality management coordinator. • The center’s leaders ensure taking quality improvement and strategic actions based on monthly, quarterly, and annual trended report data.

statement: All patients are informed about their rights and responsibilities in a manner and language they can understand.
elements: Information about patient rights and responsibilities is provided to each patient in a language the patient understands. (See also ACC.3, ME 4 and PFR.7, ME 3.)
Information about patient rights and responsibilities is provided in writing or in another manner the patient understands.
The statement of patient rights and responsibilities is always posted or otherwise available from staff.

statement: Patient informed consent is obtained through a process defined by the primary care center and carried out by trained staff in a manner and language the patient can understand.
elements: The center develops and implements a clearly defined informed consent process and trains designated staff in that process. (See also MOI.4, ME 5.)

Physicians and nurses involve the patient/designee/family as appropriate, to assist the patient in making informed decisions about treatment offered, by giving them accurate and honest information about the following: • The patient’s illness • The proposed treatment • Potential benefits • Potential complications • Likelihood of success of treatment • The attending physician’s name and other consultants’ names involved in the patient’s care • The patient’s change or transfer of care from one physician to another
Patients are informed about how the informed consent process works, when informed consent is required, and when individuals other than the patient can grant informed consent.
The informed consent process and related education are provided in a manner and language the patient or surrogate decision-maker understands, and it includes verbal language and non-verbal language.
Each patient/family receives education to help them give informed consent, participate in care processes, and understand any financial implications of care choices.
Informed consent is obtained in a manner and language that the patient understands. (See also PFR.6, ME 1.)
Patients give informed consent consistent with the process.
Informed consent is uniformly recorded.
The identity of the individual providing the information to the patient and family, and witnessed for all high-risk procedures, is documented in the patient’s medical record.
There is proper identification and a clearly written name when any other family member signs the consent on the patient’s behalf.

statement: The primary care center identifies the high-risk treatments and procedures that require informed consent and obtains consent before those treatments and procedures.
elements: The primary care center has identified those procedures and treatments that require informed consent.

The list includes at least the following: • Invasive procedures, such as surgery under local anesthesia, as defined by the center • Blood and blood products given to the patient • Practitioner-initiated testing (for example, HIV testing, genetic testing) • Other high-risk procedures and treatments, as defined by the center, with exceptions for

statement: Patients and families receive adequate information about the patient’s condition, proposed treatment(s) or procedure(s), and health care practitioners so that they can grant consent and make care decisions.
elements: Patients are informed of the following as part of the informed consent process when informed consent is required for the treatment(s) or procedure(s): (See also COP.6, ME 2.) • The patient’s condition • The proposed treatment(s) or procedure(s) • The name of the person providing the treatment • Potential benefits and drawbacks/risks • Possible alternatives • The likelihood of success • Possible problems related to recovery • Possible results of nontreatment
Patients know the identity of the physician or other health care practitioner responsible for their care.

The primary care center develops and implements a process to respond to a patient’s request for additional information about the physician or other health care practitioner responsible for their care.

statement: The primary care center implements general principles of patient and family rights as listed in the measurable elements.
elements: The primary care center always treats patients and their families with respect and dignity.
The primary care center always respects patients’ and their families’ cultural, psychosocial, spiritual, and personal values and beliefs.
The primary care center provides patients and families information regarding the identity and professional status of their treating physician and how to contact them.
Primary care center staff respect patients’ need for privacy and do not expose any private parts unnecessarily during treatment or care.
The primary care center respects patients’ right to pain assessment and management.

Primary care center staff ensure complete confidentiality of all patients’ treatment by never discussing patients in public and never revealing or publicizing patients’ names or any information about their illness.
Primary care center staff do not neglect patient demands and/or needs and respect their right to complain.
The primary care center allows its patients to submit verbal or written complaints or proposals with no effect on the quality of care provided.
The primary care center allows its patients to refuse to talk to any individual who has no relationship to their care.
The primary care center protects its patients from verbal abuse by physicians, nurses, or any other staff.
The primary care center provides patients with their complete medical report and accurate check-up results.

statement: The primary care center develops and implements an administrative policy and procedure for protecting patient belongings.
elements: The policy and procedure for protecting patient belongings address at least the following: • The location where patient belongings are kept and secured • The person(s) responsible for obtaining the required signatures on the form when receiving and

statement: The primary care center leaders develop and/or adopt the ethical standard in dealing with patients and their supporters and sponsors.
elements: The primary care center accurately bills for its services and makes a price list available to patients and their sponsors.
The primary care center honestly portrays its services to patients.
The primary care center ethically markets its care, treatment, and services.
The primary care center ensures that the provision of care is not affected by the patient’s inability to pay.

statement: Primary care center leaders develop a set of values and professional code of conduct for all staff that describes expectations of staff regarding their behavior and communication with each other and with their patients.

The primary care center has a defined process for informing patients and, when appropriate, families of the outcome of care, including significant adverse medical events and unanticipated negative outcomes.
The primary care center informs staff and educates patients and their families about the choices and procedures of organ donation.

The primary care center has an approved process or a research committee or team that decides on research, new procedures, or new drugs that involve patients, to ensure that the research is appropriate and safe.
elements: The committee or team meets to discuss and evaluate the scientific evidence related to the new research.
The committee or team studies the potential benefits and risks of the new drug, equipment, or procedure for the patient.
The committee or team has a process to explain the benefits and risks of the research protocol, and the patient signs the research consent if they are willing to participate.
Patient wishes are respected.

statement: Patients are informed about their responsibilities.
elements: The primary care center communicates its policies and procedures (for example, patient rights and responsibilities, working hours, smoking policy, use of electrical appliances, safety of personal belongings) via a patient information handbook or other appropriate tools.
The primary care center communicates the plan of care to the patient and their family (preferably by patient education handout/form).

statement: The primary care center adopts a system of providing emergency medical care in the emergency department for all life-threatening cases.
The primary care center ensures comprehensive programs with current manuals, qualified staff, essential equipment, and an adequate supply of medications and vaccines for safe, effective care.
elements: The primary care center maintains a current and approved program manual that is regularly updated, readily available, and effectively communicated to all relevant staff. The manual includes policies and procedures covering all aspects of each program, as listed in Appendix A to this chapter.
Adequate and qualified staff are available to manage each program, with specific program requirements listed in Appendix B to this chapter.
Necessary tools, essential equipment, materials, medications, vaccines, and immunoglobulin are available for each program.

Emergency services are available 24 hours and maintain at least the following: • An equipped room to manage common injuries, accidents, and emergency cases • Medical bags containing all essential medications, updated and checked daily and after each use • Electrocardiogram (ECG) machine, monitor, defibrillator, pulse oximetry, chest tubes of different sizes, intubation equipment for adults, and intubation equipment for children in emergency department documented and checked on a daily basis, and emergency and cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) drugs in emergency department with routine (minimum

statement: The primary care center implements a structured education plan to ensure the population receives appropriate and effective health education.
elements: A well-structured education plan is implemented for each program with components listed in Appendix C to this chapter.
Each program’s population is educated on the identified topics.

statement: The programs are implemented in the primary care center and surveillance systems implemented.
elements: Programs are fully implemented in the primary care center and evident in staff’s knowledge and actions. Specific implementation requirements are listed in Appendix D to this chapter.
Surveillance systems are developed and implemented in the primary care center for each program. Appendix A – Specific Requirements for

statement: The primary care center complies with relevant laws, regulations, building and fire safety codes, and facility inspection requirements.
elements: The primary care center’s leaders understand the national and local laws, regulations, building and fire safety codes, and other requirements that apply to the center’s facilities. (See also GLD.2, ME 4.)

The primary care center’s leaders implement the national and local laws, regulations, standards, building and fire safety codes, recommendations of professional organizations, and other requirements or approved alternatives, including applicable environmental protection standards, laws, and regulations (for example, discharges to drainage systems, safe disposal of waste, and the like).
The primary care center’s leaders ensure that the center meets the conditions of facility reports or citations from inspections by national and local authorities. (See also GLD.2, ME 5.)

One or more qualified individuals oversee the primary care center’s facility management program to reduce and control risks in the care environment. An interdisciplinary committee for overseeing and monitoring the facility management and safety program is established that ensures the following: • Regular inspection, testing, and maintenance of all operating components of the program • Review, analysis, and aggregation of data related to safety issues • Recommending of appropriate solutions (including education) when safety issues are identified

statement: The primary care center plans and implements a program to provide a safe physical facility through inspection and planning to reduce risks.
elements: The primary care center has an integrated program to provide a safe physical facility that covers major disasters, utility failures, hazardous materials, fire safety, medical equipment, building safety, and security. (See also AOP.4.2, ME 1.)

The primary care center has a documented, accurate inspection of its physical facilities, which is conducted at least quarterly. The inspection includes examining the physical plant, checking staff knowledge, and implementing facility management and safety (FMS) plans and ensures building and surroundings are free from hazards.

The primary care center has an ongoing program for monitoring data on incidents, injuries, and other events in an effort to further plan and reduce risks to ensure a safer physical facility, including planning and budgeting long-term facility upgrading and replacements. (See also FMS.3, ME 2.)

statement: The primary care center plans and implements a program to provide a secure environment for patients, families, staff, and visitors.
elements: The primary care center has a program to provide a secure environment (including equipment and data), including monitoring and securing areas identified as security risks. (See also MMU.3, MEs 2 and 6.)
The program ensures that all staff, contract workers, and vendors are identified.
All security risk areas and restricted areas are identified, documented, monitored, and kept secure. (See also MMU.3, MEs 2 and 6.)
The program ensures that security personnel are available.
The program ensures that patient privacy is respected.

statement: The primary care center environment is user friendly.
elements: The center has adequate amenities (for example, parking, waiting areas, toilets).
The center is equipped for people with special needs (for example, the disabled, elderly, children).
The center has directional signs.

statement: When planning for demolition, construction, or renovation, the primary care center conducts a preconstruction risk assessment (PCRA).
elements: When planning for demolition, construction, or renovation, the primary care center conducts a PCRA for at least the following: • Air quality • Infection control (Infection Control Risk Assessment [ICRA]) • Utilities, such as water and power • Fire hazards, such as smoking • Noise • Vibration • Hazardous materials • Emergency response, such as response to codes • Other hazards that affect care, treatment, and services
The primary care center takes action based on its assessment to minimize risks during demolition, construction, and renovation. (See also FMS.2, ME 3.)
The primary care center ensures that contractor compliance is monitored, enforced, and documented.

statement: The primary care center has a program for the inventory, handling, storage, use, control, and disposal of hazardous materials and waste.
elements: Hazardous materials and waste are identified in the primary care center.
Hazardous materials and waste are safely managed through the hazardous materials and waste program.

The program includes at least the following: • Inventory of hazardous materials and waste that includes the material, quantity, and locations • Handling, storage, and use of hazardous materials • Proper personal protective equipment (PPE) and procedures during use, spill, or exposure

statement: The primary care center develops, maintains, and evaluates an emergency management program to respond to potential internal and external emergencies and disasters in the center and/or community.
elements: The primary care center has identified the major internal and external disasters, such as community emergencies, and natural or other disasters that pose significant risks of occurring, considering the primary care center’s geographic location.
The primary care center identifies the probable impact of each type of disaster on all aspects of care and services. (See also MOI.13, MEs 2 and 3.)

The primary care center establishes and implements a disaster program that identifies its response to internal and external disasters, including at least the following actions: • Determining the type, likelihood, and consequences of hazards, threats, and events • Determining the primary care center’s role in such events • Determining communication strategies for events • Managing resources during events, including alternative sources • Managing clinical activities during an event, including alternative care sites and nearest health

statement: The primary care center establishes and implements a program for the prevention, early detection, suppression, abatement, and safe exit from the facility in response to fires and nonfire emergencies.
elements: The primary care center establishes and implements a program to ensure that all center occupants are safe from fire, smoke, or other nonfire emergencies.
The program includes the documented assessment of fire risks, including when construction is p ­ resent in or adjacent to the facility.
The program includes early detection of fire and smoke.
The program includes abatement of fire and containment of smoke.
The program includes safe exit (including egress routes free from obstruction) from the facility when fire and nonfire emergencies occur.
The program includes proper storage practices in the primary care center.

statement: The primary care center regularly tests its fire and smoke safety program, including any devices related to early detection and suppression, and documents the results.
elements: All staff are trained on the fire evacuation plan and participate in at least one fire and smoke safety program test per year.
Staff can demonstrate how to bring patients to safety. (See also FMS.11, ME 1.)

Fire detection and abatement equipment and systems (including fire systems, fire alarms, and fire equipment) are in place, functioning, inspected, tested, and maintained according to manufacturers’ recommendations.

statement: The fire safety program includes limiting smoking by staff and patients to designated non–patient care areas of the facility.
elements: The fire safety program addresses eliminating or limiting smoking in the primary care center.
The program applies to patients, families, visitors, and staff.
The program identifies who may grant patient exceptions for smoking and when those exceptions apply.

statement: The primary care center establishes and implements a program for inspecting, testing, and maintaining medical equipment and documenting the results.
elements: The primary care center establishes and implements a medical equipment program, which includes an inventory of all medical equipment.
Medical equipment is inspected and tested when new and according to age, use, and manufacturers’ recommendations thereafter.
The medical equipment program covers preventive maintenance, including equipment tagging.
Staff providing these services are qualified and trained for the services being provided. (See also FMS.11, ME 1.)
The primary care center has a system in place for monitoring and acting on medical equipment and implantable device hazard notices, recalls, reportable incidents, problems, and failures.
The primary care center has a system to ensure that all defective medical equipment is labeled accordingly, and no obsolete equipment is kept in the center.
There are temperature chart logs in all pharmacy and laboratory refrigerators and freezers.

statement: The primary care center has emergency processes to protect facility occupants in the event of water, power, and other utility system disruption, contamination, or failure.
elements: The center has identified the areas and services at greatest risk when water, power, and other utilities fail, are contaminated, or are interrupted.
The center seeks to reduce the risks of such events.
The center plans for and tests alternative sources of water, power, and other utilities in emergencies, when appropriate to the center, and documents the results of tests.

statement: Utility systems, including electrical and mechanical systems, are inspected, maintained, and improved.
elements: Utility systems and components are inspected based on center-developed criteria.
Utility systems and components are tested based on center-developed criteria.
Utility systems and components are maintained based on center-developed criteria.
Utility systems and components are improved when necessary.
The primary care center inventories its utility systems components and maps their distribution.
Utility systems are appropriately located and labeled.

statement: Designated individuals or authorities monitor water quality regularly.
elements: Water quality is monitored at least annually or more frequently based on local laws and r­ egulations, conditions of the water sources, and previous experience with water quality problems. The monitoring is documented.
Measures are implemented to prevent and reduce the risks of contamination and growth of bacteria in water. The effectiveness of the measures is monitored.
Actions are taken and documented when water quality is found to be unsafe.

statement: The primary care center educates and trains all staff about their roles in providing a safe, effective patient care facility.
elements: For each component of the center’s facility management and safety program, there is planned education to ensure that staff can effectively carry out their responsibilities. Staff training includes but is not limited to training in safe practices, certification in emergency drills, and dealing with hazardous materials and waste. (See also AOP.4.2, ME 5; FMS.5; FMS.6.1, ME 2; and FMS.7, ME 4.)
The education includes all staff, vendors, contract workers, and others as identified by the primary care center.
Training, testing, and the results of testing are documented for each staff member.

statement: The structure and authority of the primary care center’s governing entity are described in bylaws, policies and procedures, or similar documents.
elements: The structure of the primary care center’s governing entity is described in a written document, with those responsible for governing the center identified.

The center’s governing entity and management structure are represented or displayed in an organizational chart that identifies names, titles, and lines of authority and responsibility of the primary care center’s leaders or another document that shows lines of authority and accountability.
The authority of the primary care center’s governing entity is described in bylaws, policies and procedures, or similar documents.
The delegation of authority of the primary care center’s governing body is defined in writing
The governing entity is evaluated annually to ensure its own effectiveness, and the results are documented.

statement: The governing entity’s operational responsibilities and accountabilities are described in a written document(s).
elements: The governing entity approves and periodically reviews the primary care center’s mission statement. (See also CII.1, ME 4.)
The governing entity ensures communication of the primary care center’s mission, vision, and values to all staff and to the community (including patients, community leaders, and other stakeholders).
The governing entity approves the primary care center’s strategic and operational plans and the policies and procedures needed to operate the center on a daily basis.
The governing entity approves the primary care center’s capital and operating budget(s) and allocates other resources required to meet the center’s mission.
Those responsible for governance allocate the resources required to meet the center’s mission.
The governing entity is responsible for approving the primary care center’s scope of services and ensuring that the scope of services meet its community’s needs.

The governing entity appoints or approves, and annually evaluates, the primary care center’s senior manager/director; the evaluation is documented, and reappointment is based on the evaluation results.
The governing entity is accountable for the primary care center’s quality of care and services and patient safety.

The governing entity annually approves the primary care center’s program for quality and patient safety and regularly receives and acts on reports of the program, including reports of adverse and sentinel events. (See also MMU.5.1, ME 2; QPS.4; and PCI.7, ME 3.)

statement: The primary care center includes community participants in its governance structure.
elements: The primary care center includes community participants in its governance structure and relevant governance committees. (See also CII.4, ME 3.)
The primary care center determines the scope of community members’ participation in the governance activities.
There is a clearly defined role for the participants in governance discussions and decisions.

statement: A senior manager/director is responsible for operating the primary care center and complying with applicable laws and regulations.
elements: The senior manager/director has the education and experience to carry out their responsibilities and manage the center’s daily operations.
