The senior manager/director carries out their responsibilities and manages the center’s daily operations based on the delegated authorities and responsibilities by the governing entity.
The senior manager/director recommends policies, strategic plans, and budgets to the governing entity.
The senior manager/director ensures compliance with approved policies.

The senior manager/director ensures compliance with applicable laws and regulations related to the primary care centers in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia (for example, Ministry of Health regulations, building safety certificate forms). (See also CII.4, ME 3 and FMS.1, ME 1.)
The senior manager/director responds to any reports from inspecting and regulatory agencies. (See also CII.4, ME 3; PCI.2, ME 4; and FMS.1, ME 3.)
The senior manager/director manages human, financial, and other resources.

statement: Primary care center leaders are identified and collectively responsible for defining the center’s mission and creating the programs and policies needed to fulfill its mission.
elements: The primary care center’s leaders are formally identified and include the medical director, nursing director, quality leader, and department heads.
The primary care center’s leaders’ scope of responsibilities is defined in current job descriptions.
The primary care center’s leaders are collectively responsible for defining the center’s mission, creating programs and policies, and planning care and services consistent with its mission.

The primary care center’s leaders plan with community leaders, patients, staff, and other identified stakeholders to meet the current and future needs of the population(s) it serves, including the following actions: • Assessing community health needs • Defining the range of services (preventive, promotive, curative, and rehabilitative) and age

group: Leadership for Quality and Patient Safety
statement: Primary care center leaders plan, develop, and implement a quality improvement and patient safety program and communicate quality improvement and patient safety information to the governing entity.
elements: Primary care center leaders participate in developing and implementing a centerwide quality improvement and patient safety program.
Primary care center leaders determine how the quality improvement and patient safety program will be directed and managed on a daily basis and ensure adequate technology and other needed resources.

Primary care center leaders identify and implement a structure and process for overall monitoring and coordination of the quality improvement and patient safety program. (See also ACC.1.2, ME 5; COP.3, ME 5; PCI.7, ME 1; GLD.7.1, ME 3; GLD.7.2, ME 5; and MOI.10.)

Primary care center leaders report on the quality improvement and patient safety program, including information on adverse and sentinel events, at least every six months or more frequently to the governing entity. (See also MMU.5.1, ME 2; QPS.2.1, ME 3; and GLD.7.1, ME 1.)

group: Leadership for Quality and Patient Safety
statement: Primary care center leaders prioritize which centerwide clinical and managerial processes and outcomes will be measured and which improvement and patient safety activities will be implemented.
elements: Primary care center leaders use available data to set collective priorities for centerwide measurement and improvement activities. (See also CII.8, ME 2.)
Primary care center leaders ensure that priorities include full compliance with the International Patient Safety Goals.
Primary care center leaders set priorities for improvement activities and the sequence of implementing improvements.

group: Leadership for Quality and Patient Safety
statement: The individuals leading the clinical departments and services improve quality and safety by participating in centerwide improvement priorities and monitoring and improving the services specific to the department/ service.
elements: Department/service leaders implement quality and patient safety measures relevant to the services provided, including any contracted services for which they are responsible. (See also GLD.7.1, ME 3.)

The quality monitoring specific to the department/service area is integrated with the center’s quality program. Examples of clinical measures may include the following: • Completeness and appropriateness of patient assessments • Laboratory safety and quality control program • Radiology safety and quality control program • Use of science-based tests and treatments (for example, ACE inhibitors, blood pressure control,

statement: Primary care center leaders are accountable for the review, selection, and monitoring of clinical and nonclinical contracts.
elements: Primary care center leaders are accountable for contracts to meet patient and management needs. (See also ACC.10, ME 4.)
The primary care center has a written description of the nature and scope of those services provided through contractual agreements. (See also ACC.2.1, ME 2.)
Health care practitioner contracts require credentials review comparable to the primary care center’s review process. (See also SQE.10, ME 5.)
Department/service leaders share accountability for the review, selection, and monitoring of clinical and nonclinical contracts. (See also ACC.2.1, ME 4.)
When contracts are renegotiated or terminated, the primary care center maintains the continuity of patient services.

statement: Primary care center leaders ensure that contracts and other arrangements are part of the center’s quality improvement and patient safety program.
elements: All contracts stipulate the quality data to be reported to the primary care center, the reporting frequency and mechanism, and how the primary care center will respond when quality requirements or expectations are not met. (See also GLD.4, ME 4.)
Quality data reported under contracts are integrated into the primary care center’s quality monitoring program. (See also AOP.3, ME 3 and AOP.4, ME 3.)
The relevant department/service leaders participate with the quality improvement program in analyzing quality and safety information from outside contracts. (See also GLD.4, ME 3 and GLD.6, ME 1.)

statement: The primary care center ensures that independent practitioners not employed by the center have the right credentials and are privileged for the services that they provide to its patients.
elements: The primary care center determines those services that will be provided by independent practitioners outside the center.

All independent practitioners outside the center who are contracted to provide diagnostic, consultative, and treatment services to the center’s patients, including services such as telemedicine and teleradiology, are credentialed and privileged by the center to provide such services.

Independent practitioners who provide patient care services on the premises of the primary care center but are not employees or clinical staff members of the center are credentialed, privileged, and evaluated.
Any support staff accompanying independent practitioners and providing care and services in the center comply with requirements for primary source verification.
The quality of services by independent practitioners outside the center is monitored as a component of the center’s quality improvement program. (See also GLD.4, ME 3.)

statement: The primary care center seeks and uses data and information on its supply chain safety to protect patients and staff from unstable, contaminated, defective, and counterfeit supplies.
elements: The primary care center outlines the steps in its supply chains for supplies defined as at most risk.
The primary care center identifies any significant risk points in the steps of its supply chains.
Primary care center leaders make resource decisions based on their understanding of the risk points in the supply chains.
The primary care center has a process for retrospectively tracing supplies found to be unstable, contaminated, defective, or counterfeit.

The primary care center notifies the manufacturer and/or distributor when unstable, contaminated, defective, or counterfeit supplies are identified. Department/Service Organization and Accountabilities

statement: Primary care center leaders plan and implement a professional staff structure to support their responsibilities and authority.
elements: There is a professional staff structure that supports the department/service leaders in carrying out their responsibilities and authority. (See also SQE.1, ME 1.)
The structure is appropriate to the primary care center’s size and complexity. (See also SQE.1, ME 1.)
The structure and processes support a culture of professional communication.
The structure and processes support clinical planning, resource requirements, and policy development.
The structure and processes support the oversight of professional ethical issues. (See also GLD.11, ME 4.)
The center’s structure and processes support the oversight of the quality of clinical services. (See also MMU.1.1, ME 5.)

statement: One or more qualified individuals provide leadership for each clinical or service unit in the primary care center and identify, in writing, the services to be provided and the integration and coordination of those services with other departments.
elements: An individual with appropriate training, education, and experience leads each clinical or service unit.
Written documents describe each department or service’s current and planned services.
The written documents identify the coordination and integration of services with other departments or services. (See also ACC.5, ME 1.)
Department/service leaders recommend space, medical equipment, staffing, technology, and other needed resources. (See also COP.4, ME 2.)
Department/service leaders recommend criteria for selecting staff and participate in selecting and recruiting staff. (See also SQE.1, ME 2.)
Department/service leaders orient and train all staff on the duties and responsibilities for the department or service to which they are assigned. (See also SQE.3, ME 1.)

Primary care center leaders consider the establishment of an interdisciplinary committee(s) to oversee at least the following: medication management, safety, morbidity and mortality, cardiopulmonary resuscitation, health record review, utilization review, and credentialing and privileging. • The committee’s functions, membership, quorum, and frequency of meeting (at least quarterly) are defined. • The committee develops and submits an annual report of accomplishments to the reporting authority (as per the committee’s structure).

statement: The primary care center establishes a framework for ethical management that promotes a culture of ethical practices and decision-making to ensure that patient care is provided within business, financial, ethical, and legal norms and protects patients and their rights.
elements: The primary care center establishes a framework for the center’s ethical management that promotes a culture of ethical practices and decision-making to ensure that patients and their rights are protected. (See also PFR.2, ME 5.)
The ethical framework ensures that patient care is provided within business, financial, ethical, and legal norms.
The primary care center ensures nondiscrimination in employment practices and provision of patient care in the context of the country’s cultural and regulatory norms.

The primary care center’s framework for ethical management establishes a mechanism by which health care practitioners and other staff may raise ethical concerns without fear of retribution. (See also GLD.9, ME 5.)
The primary care center has a process for addressing ethical concerns and provides an effective and timely resolution to ethical conflicts that arise. (See also PFR.5.)

statement: The primary care center’s framework for ethical management addresses operational and business conduct, including disclosing ownership and any conflicts of interest and honestly portraying its services to patients.
elements: The primary care center discloses its ownership and any conflicts of interest.
The primary care center honestly portrays its services to patients.
The primary care center accurately bills for services and ensures that financial incentives and payment arrangements do not compromise patient care.

statement: The primary care center creates and supports a culture of safety throughout the center.
elements: The primary care center establishes and supports a culture of safety that promotes accountability and transparency.

Primary care center leaders should establish a process to measure the center’s culture of safety annually. The feedback rate and results are analyzed, actions developed, and the findings are reported to the cluster quality committee.
Primary care center leaders lead the daily safety huddles.
The primary care center develops and documents a code of conduct and identifies and corrects unacceptable behaviors. (See also PFR.2, ME 1.)
The primary care center provides resources to promote and support a culture of safety in the center.

The primary care center provides a simple, accessible, and confidential system for reporting issues relevant to a culture of safety in the center and prevents retribution against individuals who report issues. (See also MMU.5.1, ME 2 and QPS.6, ME 3.)
The primary care center identifies and manages systems issues that lead staff to engage in unsafe behaviors.

statement: Health professional education, when provided in the primary care center, is guided by the educational parameters defined by the sponsoring academic program and the center’s leadership.
elements: The primary care center provides a mechanism(s) for overseeing the training program(s).
The primary care center obtains and accepts the sponsoring academic program’s parameters.
The primary care center has a complete record of all students and trainees in the primary care center.
The primary care center documents enrollment status, licensure or certifications achieved, and academic classification of students and trainees.
The primary care center understands and provides the required level of supervision for each type and level of student and trainee.

The primary care center integrates students and trainees into its orientation, quality, patient safety, infection prevention and control, and other programs and processes. (See also QPS.1, ME 1; PCI.1, ME 2; and SQE.3, ME 4.)

statement: Informed consent is obtained before a patient participates in clinical research, clinical investigations, and clinical trials.
elements: Informed consent is obtained when a patient decides to participate in clinical research, clinical investigations, or clinical trials.
Consent decisions are documented and dated on the informed consent document and stored in the research files.
The identity of the individual(s) providing the information and obtaining the consent is noted on the informed consent document and stored in the research files.

statement: To protect patient rights, the primary care center has a committee or another way to oversee all research in the primary care center involving human subjects.
elements: The primary care center has a committee or other mechanism such as an Institutional Review Board (IRB) to oversee all research in the center.
Committee activities include a review process.
Committee activities include a process to weigh relative risks and benefits to subjects.
Committee activities include processes to provide confidentiality and security of research information.

statement: The primary care center meets the information needs of all those who provide clinical services, those who manage the primary care center, and those outside the center who require data and information from the primary care center.
elements: The primary care center plans and implements processes to meet the information needs of those who provide clinical services; the center also assesses information needs of its clinical staff.

The primary care center plans and implements processes to meet the information needs of its managers and leaders, including assessing their information needs. The center also describes the various kinds of information reports, their frequency, and their recipients.

The primary care center plans and implements processes to meet the information needs and requirements of individuals and agencies outside the center according to Saudi laws and regulations. (See also CII.5, ME 1.)

The processes implemented are appropriate to the primary care center’s size, complexity of services, availability and description of trained staff, and other human and technical resources, including internet access for staff to obtain information that supports safe patient care.
Information management processes include an education/training schedule for decision makers and other appropriate staff on the principles of data management for decision-making.

Information management processes include a description of the roles and responsibilities of leadership and department heads in relation to implementing and evaluating information management processes.

statement: Primary care center leaders establish roles and responsibilities for data collection, entry, analysis, and report generation, ensuring a designated person prepares statistical reports in a timely manner and collaborates with department heads to identify essential data for decision-making.
elements: There is a responsible person who prepares the required statistical reports in a timely manner.
The primary care center has sufficient resources including equipment and forms required for statistical reports.

Primary care center leaders identify necessary data and determine the roles and responsibilities for data entry (completion of forms), data collection, data analysis, and reports generation, and this includes the following: • Identifying necessary data based on the center’s scope of services and complexity of care • Defining data elements and developing forms for designated staff to enter the necessary data • Establishing time frames for collecting data • Displaying and analyzing data using software programs • Deciding the routing of the reports
Primary care center leaders analyze the information with the quality coordinator’s assistance.
Primary care center leaders use the information to make decisions, strategically plan, identify, and prioritize quality improvement projects based on patient demographics and services.
Primary care center leaders are educated on data management appropriate to their roles and responsibilities in the center.

statement: Confidentiality, security, and integrity of data and information are maintained.
elements: The center has implemented processes to ensure confidentiality of data and information. (See also CII.5, ME 2 and QPS.2, ME 5.)
The center has implemented processes to ensure security of data and information. (See also QPS.2, ME 5.)
The center has implemented processes to ensure integrity of data and information.
The center has identified the level of security for each category of data and information (both manual and computerized).

The center has adopted the principle of “need-to-know basis” access to patient information, has identified those permitted to access each category of data and information, and determines the penalties for staff who violate the security and confidentiality of data and information.

statement: The primary care center determines the retention time of patient medical record information based on law and regulation and on its use for patient care, legal, research, and educational activities.
elements: The primary care center determines the retention of patient medical records and other data (including x-rays) and information consistent with laws and regulations (minimum five years).
The retention process provides expected confidentiality, integrity, and security. (See also PFR.2, ME 5.)
Records, data, and information are destroyed in a manner that does not compromise confidentiality and security. (See also PFR.2, ME 5.)

statement: The primary care center uses standardized diagnosis and procedure codes and ensures the standardized use of approved symbols and abbreviations across the center.
elements: The primary care center uses standardized diagnosis codes (such as International Classification of Diseases [ICD], International Classification of Primary Care [ICPC], Current Procedural Terminology [CPT], or Diagnostic Related Groups [DRGs), and procedure codes so that data can be aggregated and transformed into information.
The primary care center implements uniform use of approved symbols and definitions, and those not to be used are identified.

If the primary care center allows abbreviations, it implements uniform use of approved abbreviations as required by regulating agencies; each abbreviation has only one meaning, and the list is recommended by the health records review committee.

If the primary care center allows abbreviations, it develops and/or adopts a “do-not-use” list of abbreviations, which is recommended and approved by related committees such as the pharmacy and therapeutic committee and health records review committee.

Abbreviations are not used on informed consent and patient rights documents, discharge instructions, summaries, and other documents patients and families receive from the primary care center about the patient’s care. (See also ACC.8; PFR.4; and PFR.7, ME 1.)
Uniform use of codes, symbols, and abbreviations across the primary care center is monitored and actions taken to improve processes when needed.

statement: Records and information are protected against loss, destruction, deliberate tampering, and unauthorized access or use.
elements: Records and information are protected from loss.
Records and information are protected from damage or destruction.
Records and information are protected from tampering and unauthorized access or use. Processes are developed describing the disciplinary action if staff make any deliberate alterations (tampering).
There is a health records tracking system that can identify the location of any record not in the health records department. Management and Implementation of Documents

statement: Written documents, including policies, procedures, and programs, are managed in a consistent and uniform manner.
elements: There is a written guidance document that defines the requirements for developing and maintaining policies, procedures, programs, and other important documents (for example, organizational plans) including at least the following: • Development, review, approval, and termination of all documents by an authorized person

statement: The policies, procedures, programs, and other documents that guide consistent, uniform clinical and nonclinical processes and practices are fully implemented.
elements: Required policies, procedures, and programs are available, and staff understand how to access those documents relevant to their responsibilities.
Staff are trained and understand those documents relevant to their responsibilities.
The requirements of the policies, procedures, and programs are fully implemented and evident in the actions of individual staff members.
The implementation of policies, procedures, and programs is monitored, and the information supports full implementation.

statement: The primary care center initiates and maintains a medical record for every patient assessed or treated and determines the record’s content, format, and location of entries.
elements: A medical record is initiated for every patient assessed or treated by the primary care center. The center has processes for managing medical records, including but not limited to the following: • Initiating a new health record • Transferring a health record to another primary care center • Receiving a health record from another primary care center • Archiving the responses to the patients’ referrals • Retrieving and replacing an individual file from a family record • Documenting and exchanging information related to treatment of visitors from outside the

statement: Patient medical records contain sufficient information to identify the patient, support the diagnosis, justify the treatment, and document the course and results.
elements: Patient medical records contain the patient’s name, address, date of birth, and next of kin. The name must include family name, first name, and middle name. Essential information about the patient is legible and located on the face sheet along with other information, such as allergies.

Patient medical records contain adequate information to support any diagnosis and justify the care and treatment and include at least: • The patient’s medical history • Details of the present illness, including, when appropriate, assessment of the patient’s emotional,

statement: The medical records of patients receiving emergency care, when provided in the primary care center, include time of arrival and departure, conclusions at termination of treatment, patient’s condition at discharge or transfer, and follow-up care instructions.
elements: The medical records of all emergency patients treated in the primary care center include arrival and departure time.
The medical records of discharged or transferred emergency patients contain conclusions at termination of treatment in the primary care center.
The medical records of emergency patients include the patient’s condition at time of discharge or transfer.
The medical records of discharged emergency patients include any follow-up care instructions.

statement: The health records department maintains defined staffing roles with clear job descriptions based on service scope and workload, led by a qualified department head who participates in the quality management program.
elements: The health records department has the following categories of staff and clear job descriptions for the positions (per the scope of services and volume of work): • Coders • Assemblers/analysts • Medical secretaries • File clerks
The health records department head is qualified by education, training, and experience.
The health records department head participates in the quality management program.

statement: The primary care center identifies those authorized to have access to and make entries in patient medical records.
elements: Those authorized to have access to the patient medical record are identified by the primary care center.
There is a process to ensure that only authorized individuals have access to patient medical records.

Those authorized to make entries in the patient medical record are identified by the primary care center. There is a unique identifier (name and/or number) for each staff member that they use when making entries in the records.
There is a process to ensure that only authorized individuals make entries in the patient medical record.
Each entry in the patient’s medical record during a visit is dated, timed, and signed by the responsible staff member for identification.
There is a process that addresses how entries in the patient medical record are corrected or overwritten.

statement: Patient medical records are accessible within 15 minutes of request, available 24/7, and released only in accordance with a policy approved by primary care center leaders.
elements: Patient medical records are available within 15 minutes of being requested.
Patient medical records can be retrieved any time of the day.

Medical records are released out of the health records department only according to a policy approved by primary care center leaders, which includes the following: • Records can be released to nurses in the general clinics. • Records can be released to emergency department nurses for a patient in the emergency department. • Records are released to chair of morbidity and mortality committee, and they sign for it. • The primary care center director or medical director must approve all other requests for release of the health record.

statement: The primary care center has a process for proper use of the copy-and-paste and auto-complete functions when electronic medical records are used.
elements: The primary care center develops a process for proper use of copy-and-paste and auto-fill when electronic medical records are used.
The primary care center educates and trains all staff who document in the medical record how to properly use copy-and-paste and auto-fill.
The primary care center monitors compliance with copy-and-paste and auto-fill guidelines and implements corrective action as needed.
The primary care center develops a process to ensure that the accuracy of the electronic medical record is monitored. (See also MOI.10.)

statement: Patient medical records are reviewed for completeness, accuracy, legibility, and timely completion of all information, and action is taken, as necessary, to improve.
elements: A representative sample of patient medical records is reviewed at least quarterly or more frequently as determined by laws and regulations. The process includes quality checks of the following documentation: • History and physical • Patient assessments • Laboratory results • Progress notes • Plan of care • Documentation of patient education and health promotion activities
The review is conducted by those authorized to make entries in patient medical records or manage patient medical records.
The review focuses on the timeliness, legibility, and completeness of the patient medical record.
Medical record contents required by law or regulation are included in the review process.
The results of the review process are incorporated in the primary care center’s quality oversight mechanism.

statement: The center has a process for completing patient medical records.
elements: The completion of patient medical records includes documentation of all relevant diagnoses and procedures.

When required, a typewritten summary concisely restates the significant findings and diagnosis, treatments, current medications, and follow-up instructions provided to the patient and, as appropriate, to the practitioner responsible for the patient’s continuing or follow-up care.
The attending physician is responsible for completing their own records.
Physicians who do not complete their records in a timely manner receive disciplinary action as outlined in the primary care center’s delinquent record policy.
A physician sees and signs all laboratory results before they are filed in the patient’s record.

statement: Health information technology systems are assessed and tested before implementation in the primary care center and evaluated for quality and patient safety after implementation.
elements: Health information technology stakeholders (appropriate clinical and managerial staff) participate in selecting, implementing, integrating, and evaluating information technology.
Health information technology systems are assessed and tested prior to implementation and when changes are made.
Health information technology systems are evaluated following implementation for usability, effectiveness, and patient safety.

statement: When electronic communication, such as mobile devices, e-mail, or patient-facing portals, is used for exchanging patient information, the primary care center adopts guidelines to ensure quality of patient care; and security and confidentiality of information are maintained.
elements: When a primary care center allows patient information and/or orders to be transmitted through text messaging, it ensures use of a secure text messaging platform that complies with the following: • Secure sign-on process(es) • Encrypted messaging • Prohibited use of unsecured text messaging (for example, short message service [SMS] text

statement: The primary care center develops, maintains, and tests a program for response to planned and unplanned downtime of data systems.
elements: The primary care center develops, maintains, and tests at least annually a program for responding to planned and unplanned downtime of data systems.
The primary care center identifies the probable impact of planned and unplanned downtime of data systems on all aspects of care and services. (See also FMS.5, ME 2.)
The program includes continuity strategies for providing ongoing safe, high-quality patient care and services during planned and unplanned downtime of data systems. (See also FMS.5, ME 2.)
The primary care center identifies and implements downtime recovery tactics and ongoing data backup processes to recover and maintain data and ensure data integrity.
Staff are trained in the strategies and tactics for planned and unplanned downtime of data systems.

statement: The primary care center designs and implements a comprehensive program for all infection prevention and control (IPC) activities that includes a qualified individual(s) to oversee the program and involves all staff.
elements: The primary care center designs and implements a comprehensive IPC program that does the following: • Involves all staff, patients, visitors, and volunteers • Covers all patient care areas and support services such as the laboratory, housekeeping, and

statement: The infection prevention and control (IPC) program is based on current scientific knowledge, accepted practice guidelines, applicable laws and regulations, and standards for sanitation and cleanliness.
elements: The IPC program is based on current scientific knowledge, accepted practice guidelines, and local laws and regulations. (See also MMU.1.1, ME 2.)
The IPC program is based on standards from national or local agencies and publications and professional organizations that address environmental sanitation and cleanliness.

The IPC program is documented in a manual that includes all administrative and practice guidelines. The manual contains the following: • A written statement of authority • Written policies and procedures for performing disinfection and sterilization, handling sharps, managing infectious materials and waste disposal, and preventing patient and worker exposure to

statement: Case findings and identification of demographically important infections provide surveillance data and data for reporting, when appropriate, within the primary care center and to public health agencies.
elements: The center has a process to collect and analyze surveillance information, case findings, and other sources of information to monitor the risk and presence of infections in the center. Communicable diseases are tabulated and reported in compliance with laws, with a policy and evidence of implementation.
Infection prevention and control (IPC) information is reported to staff of the center.
IPC information is used to guide staff in-service education.

statement: The primary care center identifies the procedures and processes associated with the risk of infection and implements strategies to reduce infection risks.
elements: The primary care center identifies processes associated with infection risk.

The primary care center identifies which processes require policies, procedures, staff education, practice changes, evidence-based activities, and other strategies to support risk reduction. (See also IPSG.5, ME 3.)

The primary care center implements strategies in compliance with applicable laws and regulations to reduce the risk of infection. These strategies include the following: • Availability and proper use of infection control tools and supplies o Disinfectants and personal protective equipment (PPE) (gowns, gloves, masks, and protective eyewear) are readily accessible in all required areas. o Written policies and procedures guide the appropriate use of PPE. • Proper use of PPE • Gloves are worn when there is a potential risk for blood/body fluid contact, removed immediately after use, and discarded properly. • Contaminated gloves are not used to touch uncontaminated surfaces. • Gowns or other protective clothing are worn during procedures likely to generate splashes or soiling from blood or other body fluids. • Masks, protective eyewear, or face shields are worn during procedures likely to generate droplets of blood or body fluids. • A system to handle blood/body fluid spills and wastes • Staff are proficient in cleaning blood/body fluid spills. • Spill kits are available in every patient care unit, containing necessary equipment, with written policies on their use. • Proper management of laundry and linen

statement: The primary care center reduces the risk of infections associated with medical/surgical equipment, devices, and supplies by ensuring adequate cleaning, disinfection, sterilization, and storage; and implements a process for managing expired supplies.
elements: The primary care center follows professional practice guidelines for sterilization techniques that best fit the type of situations for sterilization and devices and supplies being sterilized. Equipment and supplies used for sterilization and disinfection, as stated in the infection prevention and control program, are available, along with a comprehensive list of all such equipment and supplies.

The primary care center defines and implements policies and procedures for cleaning, decontamination, and disinfection processes in all patient care areas, including the following: • A defined and approved list of appropriate detergents and disinfectants • Availability of detergents and disinfectants in all patient care areas

A sterilization room (unit) must be available with the following structural and functional specifications: • Written policies and procedures guide disinfection and sterilization processes. • The sterilization unit is available and operational, with designated areas for decontamination, packing, sterilization, and storage. • Personal protective equipment (PPE) is used during decontamination, including heavy-duty gloves, waterproof aprons, facemasks, goggles, or face shields. • Sterilization service staff have adequate knowledge and training. • All cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization of medical equipment is performed in the sterilization unit, not in respective departments. • Uni-directional flow of traffic from dirty to clean areas is as follows: decontamination > packing > sterilization > storage. • Proper sterilization parameters are recorded, with sterilization records kept for one year for inspection. • Sterilizers are in good working order, with operating instructions available. • Chemical indicators are used in every package, and biological indicators are used at least weekly. Records of results are kept for one year. • Complete and comprehensive monitoring of the sterilization process is documented, including sterilization records, spore results, and biological indicator results.
The primary care center follows professional practice guidelines for low- and high-level disinfection that best fit the type of devices and equipment being disinfected.

Staff processing medical/surgical equipment, devices, and supplies are oriented, trained, and competent in cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization and receive proper supervision. The sterilization process is conducted by qualified staff, including central sterilization service staff who are either central sterile services department (CSSD) technicians or nurses with adequate experience and training in sterilization.
Methods for medical/surgical cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization are coordinated and uniformly applied throughout the primary care center.
Clean and sterile supplies are properly stored in designated storage areas that are clean and dry and protected from dust, moisture, and temperature extremes. (See also ACC.10, ME 4.)

The primary care center implements a process consistent with national laws and regulations and professional standards that identifies the process for managing expired supplies. (See also ACC.10, ME 4.)

statement: The primary care center develops, implements, and tests a program to respond to the presentation of potential global communicable diseases.
elements: The primary care center develops and implements a program to respond to the presentation of potential global communicable diseases. This program includes the following: • Communication with centers participating in worldwide surveillance activities • Development and implementation of segregation and isolation strategies, including the

statement: The infection prevention and control (IPC) program is integrated with the quality improvement and patient safety program, using measures that are epidemiologically important to the primary care center.
elements: IPC activities are integrated into the quality improvement and patient safety program. (See also GLD.4, ME 3.)
Monitoring data are collected and analyzed and are used to evaluate and support improvements to the IPC program. (See also QPS.2, ME 1.)
Monitoring data are documented, and reports of data analysis and recommendations are provided to leadership at least every six months. (See also GLD.1.1, ME 6.)

group: Management of Quality and Patient Safety Activities
statement: The primary care center’s program for quality and patient safety includes both patient and staff safety and includes the center’s risk management and quality control activities.
elements: The quality and patient safety program involves the entire primary care center and includes all patients, staff, and visitors. The program is systematic, continuous, and organizationwide; supports innovation; and covers all aspects of performance including but not limited to the following: • Identifying goals and objectives • Defining the scope of activities • Identifying all levels of staff roles and responsibilities, including the individual leading the program who can apply the quality concepts and principles. The leader of the program reports to the primary care center director. • Outlining the educational activities about quality concepts • Describing the criteria for selection of indicators, collection of data, data analysis,

group: Management of Quality and Patient Safety Activities
statement: There is a quality improvement (QI) committee that consists of at least the leadership group that implements and oversees the primary care center’s program for quality and patient safety.
elements: The QI committee approves all quality management initiatives and oversees the quality management program.
The QI committee receives reports from all teams, department heads, and other members assigned for QI projects.
The QI committee approves all centerwide teams formed to solve a particular issue.
The QI committee provides feedback to their staff on QI projects.

The QI committee identifies and prioritizes recommendations for QI projects based on the organization’s prioritization criteria, and the analysis of trends and sustained performance improvements (including accreditation status) are communicated to center staff, the public, the community, and other customers.

group: Management of Quality and Patient Safety Activities
statement: The primary care center leaders promote staff participation in the quality management program and ensure ongoing, coordinated education on quality concepts and tools, delivered by qualified personnel.
elements: The primary care center leaders encourage staff to participate in quality management and patient safety educational activities and quality improvement (QI) teams.

There are coordinated, comprehensive, and continuous educational activities on quality concepts and tools taught by staff who are qualified in the field. These educational activities include the following: • Quality management concepts • How to work in teams • Use and display of data • QI tools • QI cycle model such as FOCUS – PDCA or other methodology • Decision-making tools

group: Management of Quality and Patient Safety Activities
statement: The primary care center leaders select quality management teams, which use quality improvement (QI) tools to improve processes.
elements: Leadership determines the membership of the QI teams.
The teams include a facilitator.
The teams include a designated team leader who is an identified leader in the primary care center.
The teams use the QI cycle.
The teams use QI tools (Pareto charts, brainstorming, affinity diagrams, fishbone charts, multivoting, and so on).

group: Management of Quality and Patient Safety Activities
statement: The quality and patient safety program in the primary care center includes the collection, aggregation, and analysis of data to support patient care, primary care center management, the quality management and patient safety program, and participation in external databases.
elements: The center’s leaders develop and implement a set of indicators that are collected regularly and used for quality improvement (QI), as well as strategic and operational planning. The indicators represent key care and service structures, processes, and outcomes; focus on important managerial and clinical areas; and reference current evidence-based practice.

The center’s data collection process ensures that data are gathered from qualitative and quantitative sources and coordinated with other performance monitoring activities such as patient safety and risk management. The process ensures that each indicator has a definition, sample size, data collection method, frequency, analysis, and expression (for example, expressed as a ratio, with defined numerator and denominator).
The quality and patient safety program has a process to aggregate and convert data into useful information for trends and variances.

Aggregate data and information support patient care, organization management, professional practice review, and the overall quality and patient safety program in a manner that recipients can understand and use.
Aggregate data and information are provided to agencies outside the primary care center in accordance with law or regulation.
There is a process to contribute to and learn from external databases for comparison purposes.
Security and confidentiality are maintained when contributing to or using external databases. (See also MOI.2, MEs 1 and 2.)
Information about the quality and performance of the center’s services are provided to the public in an appropriate format.

group: Management of Quality and Patient Safety Activities
statement: Individuals with appropriate experience, knowledge, and skills systematically aggregate and analyze data in the primary care center.
elements: Data are aggregated, analyzed, and transformed into useful information to identify opportunities for improvement. (See also PCI.7, ME 2.)
Individuals with appropriate clinical or managerial experience, knowledge, and skills participate in the process. (See also SQE.1.1, ME 1.)
Results of analysis are reported to those accountable for taking action. (See also GLD,4, ME 4 and GLD.6, ME 3.)

Data analysis supports comparisons internally and externally over time, including comparisons with databases of like centers, best practices, and objective scientific professional sources. 5 Appropriate technological and administrative support is available, including but not limited to the following: • Sufficient working and meeting space • A sufficient quantity of computers, photocopiers, printers, phones, and faxes • Internet access • Appropriate software

group: Management of Quality and Patient Safety Activities
statement: The primary care center selects structure, process, and outcome indicators for data collection based on its mission.
elements: Data are on structure indicators, which include but are not limited to the following: • Availability of essential supplies and equipment • Availability of health records • Availability of emergency medications • Vacancy rates in all departments
Data are on process indicators, which include but are not limited to the following: • The timing and use of antibiotics • Documentation in health records • Physician delays in answering calls

Data are on outcome indicators, which include but are not limited to the following: • Staff satisfaction • Patient satisfaction • Unplanned patient returns to the primary care center • Patient resuscitation (cardiac/respiratory arrest) • Adverse events (falls, injuries) • Sentinel events • Patient complaints • Medication errors • Common procedures

group: Management of Quality and Patient Safety Activities
statement: The primary care center uses an internal process to validate data.
elements: The quality program validates data as part of the improvement process selected by leadership.

Data are validated when any of the following conditions are met: • A new measure is implemented (in particular, those clinical measures intended to help a primary care center evaluate and improve an important clinical process or outcome). • Data will be made public on the primary care center’s website or in other ways. • An existing measure has changed, such as the data collection tools have changed, or the data abstraction process or abstractor has changed. • The data resulting from an existing measure have changed in an unexplainable way. • The data source has changed, such as when part of the patient medical record has been turned into an electronic format and thus the data source is now both electronic and paper. • The subject of the data collection has changed, such as changes in average age of patients or comorbidities, research protocol alterations, new practice guidelines implemented, or new technologies and treatment methodologies introduced.
The quality program uses an established method to validate data.
Primary care center leadership assumes accountability for the validity of the quality and outcome data made public. Adverse Event Identification, Analysis, and Prevention

group: Management of Quality and Patient Safety Activities
statement: The primary care center uses a defined process for identifying and managing sentinel events.
elements: The primary care center’s leaders establish a definition of sentinel event that includes at least the following: • An unanticipated death, including but not limited to, o A death unrelated to the natural course of the patient’s illness or underlying condition (for example, death from a postoperative infection or health care–associated infection)

group: Management of Quality and Patient Safety Activities
statement: Data are always analyzed when undesirable trends and variation are evident from the data.
elements: Defined data-gathering processes are developed and implemented to ensure accurate data collection, analysis, and reporting.
Data are intensely analyzed when adverse levels, patterns, or trends occur.

Data are gathered and analyzed on the following items as applicable to the care and services provided by the primary care center: • All confirmed transfusion reactions, if applicable to the center • All serious adverse drug events, if applicable and as defined by the center • All significant medication errors, if applicable and as defined by the center • Other events, for example, health care–associated infections and infectious disease outbreaks (See also QPS.7.)
Results of analyses are used to implement actions to improve the quality and safety of the service, treatment, or function.

group: Management of Quality and Patient Safety Activities
statement: The primary care center uses a defined process for the identification and analysis of near-miss events.
elements: The primary care center establishes a definition of near miss. (See also MMU.5.1, ME 1.)
The primary care center defines the type of events to be reported through an incident (occurrence/ variance/accident) reporting system (policy and form).

The primary care center establishes a process for reporting and processing near misses and incidents. The process includes identifying the staff member responsible for the near misses and incident reporting system, and educating staff on the near misses and incident reporting system. (See also GLD.12, ME 4.)
All reported incidents and near misses are investigated in a timely manner.

The primary care center takes immediate actions as well as actions to prevent recurrence of near misses and incidents. The center monitors incidents over time, analyzes data, and takes actions to reduce near-miss events and incidents and improve processes. (See also QPS.7.)
Patients are informed when involved in near-miss incidents, and this is documented in their health records.

group: Management of Quality and Patient Safety Activities
statement: An ongoing risk management program identifies and proactively reduces unanticipated adverse events and other safety risks to patients and staff.
elements: The primary care center’s risk management program includes the following: • Identifying risks through a systematic process • Prioritizing risks to analyze for severity and likelihood of occurrence • Reporting risks • Analyzing and managing risks by developing interventions to address potential risks (that is, to

statement: The primary care center develops a staffing plan that identifies the number of staff and defines the desired education, skills, knowledge, and other requirements of staff needed to meet its mission and provide safe patient care.
elements: The primary care center’s mission, volume, and mix of patients, services, and medical equipment are used in defining the number and qualifications of required staff. (See also GLD.9, MEs 1 and 2.)
The desired education, skills, and knowledge are defined for staff. (See also GLD.10, ME 5.)
Applicable laws and regulations are incorporated into the requirements for staff. (See also GLD.3, ME 4.)
The desired education, skills, and knowledge are defined for all staff.
There is a qualified individual assigned to managing human resources activities.

statement: Each staff member’s responsibilities are defined in a current job description.
elements: Each staff member not permitted to practice independently has a job description. (See also QPS.2.1, ME 2 and PCI.5, ME 3.)

Those individuals have job descriptions appropriate to their activities and responsibilities or have been privileged if noted as an alternative. Job descriptions are also needed for health professionals when any of the following applies: • The individual serves in primarily a managerial role, such as a department manager, or in dual clinical and managerial roles, with the managerial responsibilities identified in a job description. • The individual has some clinical responsibilities for which he or she has not been authorized to practice independently, such as an independent practitioner learning a new role or new skills. • The individual is in an educational program and under supervision, and the academic program identifies, for each stage or level of training, what can be done independently and what must be under supervision (the program description can serve as the job description in such cases). • The individual is permitted to temporarily provide services in the primary care center (for example, a nurse from a temporary staffing agency).

Job descriptions are current according to primary care center policy that requires all categories of staff to have clearly written job descriptions that are reviewed and revised at least every three (3) years and as needed and all the following apply: • The job description is used when selecting staff for hire, internal promotions, and transfer. • The job description outlines the necessary knowledge, skills, and attitude to perform the role. • The job description is provided to every staff member at time of hire and is in the employee’s personnel file and department manual. • All job descriptions follow a prescribed format. • All job descriptions are competency based.

statement: The primary care center uses a defined process to ensure that clinical and nonclinical staff knowledge and skills are consistent with the requirements of the position.
elements: The primary care center uses a defined process to match clinical staff knowledge, skills, and competency with patient needs. (See also AOP.1.1, ME 3; AOP.3.1, ME 2; AOP.4.1, ME 2; AOP.4.2, ME 5; COP.4, ME 3; and MMU.4, ME 2.)

The primary care center uses a defined process to match nonclinical staff knowledge and skills with its needs and the requirements of the position. (See also AOP.3.1, ME 2; AOP.4.1, ME 2; and AOP.4.2, ME 5.)

New clinical staff are registered in the Saudi Commission for Health Specialties and evaluated at the time they begin their work responsibilities by the department or service to which they are assigned. (See also SQE.4, ME 1.)
New non-clinical staff members are evaluated at the time they begin their work responsibilities by the department or service to which they are assigned. (See also SQE.4, ME 1.)

There is at least one documented evaluation of each clinical and nonclinical staff member working under a job description each year or more frequently as defined by the primary care center. (See also SQE.4, MEs 3 and 6.)
There is a staff record that contains the individual’s qualifications, results of evaluations, and work history. (See also SQE.4, MEs 4 and 5; SQE.7, ME 2; and SQE.11, ME 4.)

statement: All clinical and nonclinical staff members are oriented to the primary care center and their specific job responsibilities, and their capability to perform their specific job responsibilities is assessed.
elements: All clinical and nonclinical staff members are oriented to the primary care center, their job responsibilities, and their specific assignments. (See also PFR.1, ME 5; PFR.3, ME 4; QPS.1, ME 1; PCI.1, ME 2; PCI.5, ME 3; and GLD.10, ME 6.)
A human resources employee manual is given to all new employees during their primary care center orientation.
Each new staff member’s competency to perform their job responsibilities is evaluated during orientation.

The primary care center has a comprehensive, mandatory general orientation for all new employees, and the orientation includes, but is not limited to, the following: • The primary care center’s mission, vision, values, and organizational chart • Staff role in disasters and emergencies (for example, fire) • General information about hazardous materials including material safety data sheets (MSDSs) • General information on infection prevention and control and sharps disposal • Electrical safety • General information on communication devices: paging, telephone system, and beepers • General information on staff evaluation process • The definitions of adverse events and sentinel events, along with the process for reporting such events, including who should report, when to report, how to report, and to whom the report is

statement: Each staff member’s competence to carry out job responsibilities to meet patient needs is continually assessed, maintained, improved, and documented.
elements: Staff members’ abilities to fulfill expectations of their job descriptions are assessed. (See also SQE.2, MEs 3 and 4.)
The clinical or service area to which the staff member is assigned does the evaluation.
Department heads recommend, implement, and evaluate the necessary courses and skills to update and maintain staff competence to provide care.
There is at least one documented evaluation of each staff member working under a job description each year, or more frequently, as defined by the primary care center. (See also SQE.2, ME 5.)
The evaluation form covers all aspects of expected performance levels as outlined in the staff member’s job description (for example, competence, attitude, and so on).
All staff read and sign their evaluations.
Personnel files for each staff member are standardized, current, maintained, and kept confidential according to primary care center policy. (See also SQE.2, ME 6.)
Personnel files contain the staff member’s job description, qualifications, work history, record of orientation, and any required health information. (See also SQE.2, ME 6 and SQE.6, ME 2.)
Personnel files contain the results of performance reviews. (See also SQE.2, ME 5.)

statement: Each staff member receives ongoing in-service and other education and training to maintain and/or advance staff knowledge, skills, and competence.
elements: The primary care center uses several sources of data and information, including the results of quality and safety measurement activities, to identify staff education needs.

The needs identified for training and education are based on the following, as appropriate: • The primary care center’s mission, vision, and values • The primary care center’s patient population, type and nature of care provided, and the

statement: The primary care center develops and implements a staff health and safety program.
elements: The primary care center provides, and incorporates into its quality and safety program, a staff health and safety program that responds to urgent and nonurgent staff needs through direct treatment and referral.

The staff health and safety program includes the following: (See also SQE.4, ME 5.) • An initial employment health screening • Measures to control harmful occupational exposures, such as exposure to toxic drugs and

statement: The primary care center has a uniform process to gather, verify, and evaluate the credentials (licensure, education, training, and experience) of those staff permitted by law and the primary care center to provide patient care without supervision.
elements: Medical staff members permitted by laws, regulations (Saudi Commission for Health Specialties), and the primary care center to provide patient care without supervision are identified. (See also SQE.1.1.)

The primary care center has a process for gathering, verifying, and evaluating the credentials of those medical staff, including licensure/registration, education, training, experience, and other credentials required by laws or regulations. The center copies and maintains those credentials for each medical staff member (for example, full time, part time, locum, and so on) in their personnel file or in a separate credentials file. (See also SQE.2, ME 6.)

The primary care center uses education, licensure/registration, and other credentials required by laws or regulations or issued by recognized education or professional entities as the basis for clinical privileges; the center verifies this information from the original source that issued the credential.

When third-party verification is used, the primary care center verifies that the third party (for example, a government agency) implements the verification process as described in policy or regulations.

Medical staff appointments are made after the licensure/registration has been verified from the primary source and are consistent with the primary care center’s patient population, mission, and services.
There is a standardized procedure to review, initially and every three years, the qualifications of each independent practitioner.

statement: The primary care center has a standardized, objective, evidence-based procedure to authorize medical staff members to treat patients and/or to provide other clinical services consistent with their qualifications.
elements: The primary care center’s privilege delineation process complies with laws and legal requirements and is as follows: • Standardized, objective, and evidence based • Documented in primary care center policies • Active and ongoing as medical staff members’ credentials change • Followed for all classes of medical staff membership • Can be demonstrated to show its effectiveness

The primary care center has clearly defined and documented processes for appointing and granting privileges to medical staff. The medical staff includes licensed physicians, dentists, and other licensed individuals permitted by law to provide patient care services independently in the center. • Medical staff appointments and granting privileges are based on evaluation of verified credentials (license, education, training, and experience) as well as physical and mental health. • Medical staff appointments and privileges are recommended by the medical staff leaders (for example, credentialing and privileging committee, medical executive committee), and approved by the governing body, either directly or by appropriate delegation. • Physician privileges are reviewed and updated every two (2) years and as needed.

The clinical privileges of all medical staff members are made available by printed copy, electronic copy, or other means to those individuals or locations (for example, operating room, emergency department) in the primary care center in which the medical staff member will provide services.
Each medical staff member provides only those services specifically granted by the primary care center. (See also AOP.1.1, ME 3.)

statement: The primary care center has an ongoing, standardized process to evaluate the quality and safety of the patient care provided by each medical staff member and uses this information to continue clinical privileges with or without modification.
elements: There is an ongoing professional practice evaluation of each medical staff member permitted to practice independently that incorporates available evidence at least annually through a standardized procedure established by the primary care center that includes evaluation, when indicated by the findings of quality improvement activities. (See also GLD.6, ME 3.)

The medical director, together with the department heads, evaluates the performance of each medical staff member for the following at a minimum: • Mortality and morbidity • Appropriateness of referrals • Outcomes of procedures • Utilization, such as appropriateness of interventions and medications, and waiting time • Medication use • Treatment according to the guidelines • Performance is reviewed at least annually and when indicated by findings of the performance improvement activities.

For each medical staff member, the monitoring and evaluation process identifies areas of achievement and potential improvement related to their behaviors, professional growth, and clinical results compared to other department/service medical staff members.
The clinical results of data and information available on medical staff members are reviewed with objective and evidence-based information, as available, for external benchmarking.

The data and information from the monitoring are reviewed at least every 12 months by the individual’s department or service head, senior medical manager, or medical staff body, and the results, conclusions, and any actions taken are documented in the medical staff member’s credentials or other relevant files.

Based on the medical staff member’s ongoing monitoring and evaluation, the primary care center determines, at least every three years, if medical staff membership and clinical privileges are to continue with or without modification.

statement: The primary care center has a uniform process to gather, verify, and evaluate nursing staff credentials (license, education, training, and experience).
elements: The primary care center has a standardized procedure to gather the credentials of each nursing staff member.
Licensure, education, training, and when available, experience are documented, and information is updated as appropriate.
Licensure, education, experience and training are verified from the original source.

A separate credentials record for every nursing staff member is maintained and includes copies of any required license, certification, registration, and other documents required by the center. (See also SQE.2, ME 6.)
The primary care center has a process to ensure that contract nurses’ credentials are valid and complete prior to assignment. (See also GLD.7, ME 3.)
The performance of individual nursing staff members is reviewed when indicated by the findings of quality improvement activities. (See also GLD.6, ME 3.)

statement: The primary care center has a uniform process to gather, verify, and evaluate other health care practitioners’ credentials (license, education, training, and experience).
elements: The primary care center has a standardized process to gather each health care practitioner’s credentials.
Licensure, education/training, and, when available, experience, are documented, and information is updated as appropriate.
The primary care center verifies licensure, experience, and education/training from the original source.
The primary care center maintains a record for each other health care practitioner that includes copies of any required license, certification, or registration. (See also SQE.2, ME 6.)
The performance of other health care practitioners is reviewed when indicated by the findings of quality improvement activities. (See also GLD.6, ME 3.)

statement: The primary care center’s employee manual includes a policy for handling staff complaints and/or dissatisfaction.
The primary care center has a policy that addresses methods for resolving conflicts between staff.
The primary care center leaders develop and implement a program for recruitment, retention, development, and continuing education for all staff.

All staff who provide direct patient care (medical staff, nursing staff, and other health professionals) receive training in basic cardiopulmonary resuscitation (basic life support), and the training is repeated every two (2) years.

The primary care center has a nurse leader (nursing director/nurse executive) who is a registered nurse qualified by appropriate education and experience and does the following: • The nurse leader/designee participates in the primary care center’s interdisciplinary structures (for example, relevant committees). • The nurse leader develops and maintains a current standard of practice for each nursing unit. • The nurse leader develops a staffing plan that maintains an adequate staffing level on all units. • The nurse leader allocates nursing staff according to the following: o Skill level and appropriate qualifications based on laws and regulations o Patient type and acuity on units
Patients have access to services based on their identified health care needs and the home care organization’s mission, resources, and scope of services.
elements: Based on the results of screening, patients are accepted for care if the patient’s needs match the home care organization’s mission and resources.
The organization follows its written process for accepting a patient for care, treatment, or services.

The home care organization accepts a patient for care when the patient’s medical, nursing, social, physical, cognitive functional, and/or personal health and independence goals can be met in the home, through a standardized process based on the patient’s needs and available services.

A visit schedule is in place to organize patient visits, and staff is aware of the services provided. An on-call coverage list is maintained to ensure patient access to care for non-emergency circumstances after availability hours.

The home care organization will share referral information (with patient consent) to alternate/ additional services when multidisciplinary or multiservice procedures and care are required in the home.

statement: The home care organization designs and carries out processes to provide continuity of patient care services in the organization, coordination among health care practitioners, and access to information related to the patient’s care.
elements: The service leaders design and implement processes that support continuity and coordination of care, including the following: • Palliative care and hospice care services • Physical/occupational therapy and ambulatory care • Home care and community care • Outpatient care programs • Other organizations and other care settings
The patient’s medical record(s) is available to those practitioners who are authorized to have access and need it to care for the patient.
The patient’s medical record(s) is up to date to ensure communication of the latest information.
The patient’s medical record(s) or a summary of patient care information is transferred with the patient to another service in the home care organization.

The summary of information, if transferred with the patient, contains at least the following: • The reason for admission • Significant findings • Diagnosis • Procedures performed • Medications • Other treatments • The patient’s condition at transfer
The home care organization supports continuity and coordination of care processes through tools, such as care plans, guidelines, or other such tools.

statement: During all phases of patient care, a qualified individual is identified as responsible for the patient’s care.
elements: Each patient is registered under the care of a specific physician of the home care organization, referred to as the “most responsible physician.” A qualified individual responsible for coordinating the patient’s care is identified in the patient’s medical record and available through all phases of care, and patients or families are provided with the contact information of healthcare professionals providing care.
There is a process for transferring the responsibility for coordination of care from individual to individual.
The process identifies how these individuals assume the transferred responsibility and documents their participation or coverage.

statement: The home care organization develops and implements a discharge planning and referral process that is based on the patient’s readiness for discharge.
elements: The home care organization develops and implements a discharge planning and referral process that starts at the beginning of care and is based on the patient’s readiness for discharge.

The patient’s readiness for discharge is determined by the most responsible physician based on identifiable clinical criteria and relevant indications that ensure patient safety. The physician also specifies the estimated date of discharge or service termination and ensures the patient’s suitability and stability for discharge.
The discharge planning process includes the need for both support services and continuing medical needs.
Patients not directly referred or transferred are provided with the name and location of a site(s) for continuing care if appropriate.
Patients not directly referred or transferred are provided written instructions on when and whom to contact, if appropriate, and when and how to obtain urgent care.
Discharge planning and instructions are documented in the patient record and provided to the patient in writing.

statement: The home care organization’s discharge planning process addresses patient, family, and caregiver education and instruction related to the patient’s ongoing need for continuing care and services.
elements: Patient, family, and caregiver education and instruction are related to the patient’s ongoing need for continuing care and services, and all necessary support services for a safe discharge should be organized and documented in the discharge summary.

Patients, families, and caregivers are provided with a complete list of medications to be taken at home when provided as a part of the organization’s services, and these medications should be documented in the discharge summary.

Patients, families, and caregivers are educated about the safe and effective use of all medications, potential side effects, and prevention of potential interactions with over-the-counter medications and/ or food when provided as a part of the organization’s services.
Patients, families, and caregivers are educated about proper diet and nutrition.
Patients, families, and caregivers are educated about pain management as appropriate.
Patients, families, and caregivers are educated about safe and effective use of medical equipment and rehabilitation techniques as appropriate.
Patients, families, and caregivers are informed about how to communicate and obtain assistance post discharge, if needed.

statement: The home care organization develops a process to transfer patients to other health care organizations based on their status, their continuing care needs, and the receiving organization’s ability to meet patients’ needs.
elements: The home care organization develops and implements a transfer process based on criteria to address patients’ needs for continuing care.

The transfer process addresses how and when responsibility for continuing care is moved to another practitioner or setting and determines that the receiving organization can meet the needs of the patient to be transferred.
The transfer process identifies who is responsible for monitoring the patient during transfer and the staff qualifications required for the type of patient being transferred.
The transfer process identifies the medications, supplies, and medical equipment required during transport.
The transfer process addresses a follow-up mechanism that provides information about the patient’s condition upon arrival at the receiving organization.
The transfer process addresses the situations in which transfer is not possible.

statement: The receiving organization is given a written summary of the patient’s clinical condition and the interventions provided by the referring home care organization, and the process is documented in the patient’s medical record.
elements: A patient clinical summary document is transferred with the patient and includes at least the following: • The patient’s clinical condition or status • The procedures and other interventions provided • The patient’s continuing needs
Transferred patients’ medical records identify the receiving health care organization and the individual agreeing to receive the patient.
Transferred patients’ medical records contain documentation or other notes as required by the transferring home care organization’s policy.
Transferred patients’ medical records state the reason(s) for transfer and any special conditions related to transfer.

statement: The process for referring, transferring, or arranging needed services outside the home considers transportation needs.
elements: The process for transferring patients considers transportation needs.
The home care organization assists in arranging for transportation as part of its planned services when the patient has no family or friends able to provide transportation.
The type of transportation considers the patient’s needs.

statement: The home care organization’s patients have their health care needs identified through an assessment process defined by the home care organization.
elements: A policy and procedures define the process for assessing and reassessing home care patients.

The home care organization defines the minimum content of assessments for patients, in a collaborative manner, for each clinical discipline that performs assessments and specifies the required elements of the history and physical examination prior to providing care and including the following: • Collecting information and data on the patient’s physical, psychological, and social status, and

statement: Each patient’s initial assessment includes a physical examination and health history as well as an evaluation of psychological, spiritual/cultural (as appropriate), social, and economic factors.
elements: All patients have an initial assessment, documented within 24 hours in the medical record, that includes a health history and physical examination consistent with the requirements defined in the home care organization’s policy.
The assessment includes a list of the patient’s current medications and known allergies.
The physician or a qualified licensed individual(s) (such as a nurse) documents the assessment of pain, medications, allergy, and code status at the initial assessment.
