The initial assessment includes the following: • An initial psychological assessment, as indicated by the patient’s condition • An initial social and economic assessment, as indicated by the patient’s needs • An initial spiritual and cultural assessment, as indicated by the patient’s needs
Each patient assessment includes an environmental and occupational health and safety assessment at their home.
The initial assessment results in an initial diagnosis.

statement: The home care organization has a process for accepting initial medical and other assessments conducted in a physician’s private office or other outpatient setting prior to admission to the home care organization.
elements: Initial medical and other assessments conducted prior to admission to the home care organization are less than or equal to 30 days old.

For initial medical assessments less than or equal to 30 days old, any significant changes in the patient’s condition since the assessment or “no change” are documented in the patient’s medical record at the time of admission to the home care organization.
If the medical assessment is more than 30 days old at admission to the home care organization, the medical history is updated and the physical examination repeated.
The findings of all assessments performed outside the home care organization are reviewed and/or verified at admission to the home care organization.

statement: Patients are screened for nutritional status and functional needs and referred for further assessment and treatment when necessary.
elements: Qualified individuals develop criteria to identify patients who require further nutritional assessment, and the criteria are implemented consistently throughout the home care organization where needed.
Patients at risk for nutritional problems receive a nutritional assessment.
Assessment includes screening patients for malnutrition and referring patients who are malnourished or at risk for malnutrition for a nutritional assessment and management.

Qualified individuals develop criteria to identify patients who require further functional assessment, and the criteria are implemented consistently throughout the home care organization where needed.
Patients in need of a functional assessment are referred for such an assessment.
Patients with physical limitations who are at risk of falls or pressure ulcers are provided with adequate measures and precautions to reduce associated risks.
The health team recognizes patients’ physical and mental limitations and assists the patient and family in incorporating the patient’s remaining abilities into daily activities.
Patients are referred within the home care organization or outside the home care organization when additional specialized assessments are needed.
Specialized assessments conducted within the home care organization are completed and documented in the patient’s medical record.

statement: All patients are screened for pain and assessed when pain is present.
elements: All patients are screened for pain, the screening is documented, and the following questions are asked: • Are you having pain right now? • Does pain keep you from sleeping at night? • Does pain keep you from participating in activities? • Do you experience pain every day?
The patient is referred if needed, or the home care organization performs a comprehensive assessment when pain is identified.
The assessment is recorded in a way that facilitates regular reassessment and follow-up according to criteria developed by the home care organization and the patient’s needs.

statement: The home care organization conducts individualized initial assessments for special populations cared for by the organization.
elements: The home care organization defines, in writing, those special patient groups and populations that require modifications to its assessment, including but not limited to the following: • Infants • Children • Adolescents • Frail elderly • Terminally ill/dying patients • Patients with intense or chronic pain • Patients with emotional or psychiatric disorders • Patients suspected of drug and/or alcohol dependency • Victims of abuse or neglect • Patients with infectious or communicable diseases • Patients receiving chemotherapy or radiation therapy • Patients with compromised immune systems • Patients requiring complex medical equipment for sustainment such as ventilators or dialysis
The assessment process for special patient populations is modified to reflect their needs.
The modified assessment process is consistent with local laws and regulations and incorporates professional standards related to such populations.
Individualized medical, nursing, and/or other allied health care practitioner assessments are performed and documented.

statement: The home care organization has a process to identify, report, and refer suspected or alleged victims of abuse or neglect, according to local laws and regulations.
elements: The home care organization uses a process for identifying and reporting victims of alleged or suspected abuse or neglect, according to laws and regulations.
The home care organization has established referral criteria for possible victims of abuse or neglect.
Staff members know how to apply the criteria.
Possible victims of abuse or neglect are referred to community agencies when needed.
The information is documented in the patient’s record and available to those caring for the patient.

statement: The initial assessment includes determining the need for discharge planning.
elements: The home care organization begins the discharge planning process early in the assessment process to identify those patients for whom discharge planning is critical.
Discharge planning includes identifying special needs and developing and implementing a plan to address those needs.
Patients, family and caregivers as appropriate, and staff involved in the patient’s care participate in the discharge planning process. (See also ACC. 4.1.)

statement: All patients are reassessed at intervals to determine their response to care and services and plan for continued care and services or discharge.
elements: The home care organization defines the frequency of reassessment based on the clinical needs and condition of the population served, and patients are reassessed to determine their response to treatment and plan for continued treatment and/or discharge.

Patients are reassessed at intervals based on their condition and when there is a significant change in their condition, plan of care, or individual needs and to ensure the effectiveness of the care planning.
Reassessments are documented in the patient’s record.

statement: Qualified individuals conduct the assessments and reassessments.
elements: Policies and procedures are developed collaboratively and highlight the reassessment requirements.
Individuals qualified to conduct patient assessments and reassessments are identified, and their responsibilities are defined in writing.
Only those individuals permitted by licensure, applicable laws and regulations, or certification perform patient assessments.
Nursing assessments (if provided by the home care organization) are conducted by individuals qualified to do so.

statement: Medical, nursing, and other allied health care practitioners and services responsible for patient care collaborate to analyze and integrate patient assessments and prioritize the most urgent/important patient care needs.
elements: Patient assessment data and information are analyzed and integrated.
Those responsible for the patient’s care and services participate in the process.
Patient needs are prioritized based on assessment results.

statement: Laboratory services are readily available through arrangements with outside sources to meet patient needs.
elements: Laboratory services meet applicable local and national standards, laws, and regulations.
Laboratory services are available to meet the needs related to the home care organization’s mission and patient population, and the community’s health care needs, including after normal hours.
The laboratory results are available to the patient on a timely basis, as defined by the home care organization in a turnround document.
Experts in specialized diagnostic areas are contacted when needed.
If the home care organization does not provide laboratory services, it selects outside sources based on an acceptable record and compliance with laws and regulations.

statement: A qualified individual is responsible for overseeing and supervising the point-of-care testing (POCT) program.
elements: The person responsible for coordinating laboratory services, or a designee, oversees and supervises the POCT program.
Staff performing point-of-care testing have the required qualifications and training and are competent to perform POCT.
The POCT program includes a defined process for reporting abnormal test results, including critical results.
The POCT program includes quality control performance, documentation, and evaluation as per manufacturer’s recommendation.
The POCT program is monitored, evaluated, and included in quality improvement activities.

statement: The home care organization establishes and implements procedures for collecting, identifying, handling, safely transporting, and disposing of specimens.
elements: Policies and procedures are developed and implemented for ordering tests, including POCT.
Policies and procedures are developed and implemented for collecting and identifying specimens.
Policies and procedures are developed and implemented for transporting, storing, and preserving specimens.
Procedures are developed and implemented for receiving and tracking specimens.
Policies and procedures are developed and implemented for disposing of specimens.
The procedures are followed when reference/contract laboratory services are used.
The most responsible physician acknowledges reviewing the expected test results within 24 hours from issuing the report.

statement: Radiology and diagnostic imaging services are available to meet patient needs, and all such services meet applicable local and national standards, laws, and regulations.
elements: Radiology and diagnostic imaging services meet applicable local and national standards, laws, and regulations.

Radiology and diagnostic imaging services are available to meet the needs related to the home care organization’s mission and patient population, the community’s health care needs, and emergency needs, including after normal hours.
If the home care organization does not provide radiology and diagnostic imaging services, it recommends outside sources of radiology and diagnostic imaging services.

The individual(s) coordinating radiology and diagnostic imaging services is responsible for the following: • Developing, implementing, and maintaining policies and procedures • Providing administrative oversight • Maintaining any necessary quality control program • Recommending outside sources of radiology and diagnostic imaging services • Monitoring and reviewing all radiology and diagnostic imaging services
Transportation is arranged for any diagnostic imaging services not available on site.
The home care organization maintains a roster of experts in specialized diagnostic areas and ensures that the roster is accessible to staff who need it.
The process includes contacting the most responsible physician for a referral to an expert in specialized diagnostic tests when needed.

statement: Diagnostic imaging services are available within a time frame to meet the patient’s needs as defined by the home care organization.
elements: The home care organization has defined expected report times for diagnostic imaging results.
Diagnostic imaging results are reported within a time frame to meet the patient’s needs.
The individual(s) responsible for the diagnostic imaging program reviews and evaluates data related to diagnostic imaging time frames as defined by the organization.

statement: The home care organization provides uniform care of all patients and follows applicable laws and regulations.
elements: The home care organization’s clinical and managerial leaders collaborate to provide uniform care processes.
The provision of uniform care reflects local and regional laws and regulations.

The home care organization provides uniform care, which meets the following requirements: • Access to and appropriateness of care and treatment do not depend on the patient’s ability to pay or the source of payment. • Access to appropriate care and treatment by qualified practitioners do not depend on the day of the week or time of day within the hours of operation identified by the home care organization. • Acuity of the patient’s condition determines the resources allocated to meet the patient’s needs.

statement: There is a process to integrate and coordinate the care provided to each patient, including a uniform process for prescribing patient orders.
elements: Care planning and care delivery are integrated and coordinated among settings, departments, and services.

The home care organization develops and implements a uniform process for prescribing written/ documented patient orders that includes identifying orders that may be received verbally, via telephone, and via text, with established policies for telephone orders and escalation.
Diagnostic imaging and clinical laboratory test orders include a clinical indication/rationale when required for interpretation.
Only those qualified to do so prescribe orders.
Orders are found in a uniform location in medical records.
The patient and/or family is provided with the plan of care and schedule of services to be provided, including service contact details.

statement: Care and treatment provided to the patient maintain the patient’s daily routine when possible and meet the patient’s identified needs.
elements: Care and treatment provided are consistent with those identified during the care and treatment planning process.
Planned care and services are provided at the frequency and on the days and times that meet the patient’s needs.
Scheduling care and services involves the patient and/or family to maintain the patient’s daily routine.

The home care organization ensures that home visit bags are properly prepared and maintained to support safe and effective care delivery, including the following: • Contents appropriate to the patient’s needs • Preparation according to a standardized list, with expiry dates clearly indicated • A process for regularly cleaning and disinfecting the bag

statement: An individualized plan of care is developed and documented for each patient.
elements: The care for each patient is planned by the most responsible physician, nurse, and/or other allied health care practitioners after admission to the home care organization within a time frame identified by the organization but not to exceed five days.

The plan of care is individualized based on the patient’s initial assessment data and identified home care needs, covers all health aspects (including prevention, treatment, rehabilitation, and end-of-life care), aims to achieve measurable goals, and is documented by the most responsible physician in the patient’s medical record.

The plan of care is updated or revised by the multidisciplinary team based on any changes in the patient’s condition identified from the patient’s reassessment, and is documented in the patient’s medical record. Updates to the care plan are made only by the most responsible physician, based on outcome measures assessed by the visiting staff. An escalation policy is in place.
The results or conclusions of any patient care team meetings or other collaborative discussions are documented in the patient’s medical record.
The plan of care is provided to each patient and is evident in the patient’s medical record through documentation by the health care practitioners providing the care.

The home care organization has an established policy and procedure to detect early warning signs that warrant referring the patient to a higher health care setting. When such signs are identified, the following occurs: • The health care practitioners providing the care, in coordination with the family, arrange with medical transport services to safely transfer the patient to the appropriate service or facility. • The health care practitioners providing the care hand over the patient to the emergency response team and document the handover in the patient’s medical record.

statement: The care of high-risk patients and the provision of high-risk services are guided by professional practice guidelines, laws, and regulations.
elements: Home care leadership identifies the high-risk patients and services, including the following, when provided by the home care organization: • Handling, use, and administration of high-risk medications or treatments • Care of patients who are on life support or are comatose • Care of patients with communicable diseases and immune-suppressed patients • Care of patients on dialysis • Administration of blood and blood products • Use of sedation • Care of vulnerable elderly patients, disabled patients, infants and children, and populations at

statement: Based on the patient’s nutritional status and/or need, patients, families, and caregivers are provided with nutritional education and support.
elements: Patients, family members, and caregivers in the home are supported in providing nutritional support.
Nutritional needs are identified and monitored.
Patients, family members, and caregivers are educated about the patient’s diet.

When parenteral or enteral tube nutrition is provided in the home, the home care organization monitors the patient’s nutritional status, including the following: • The patient’s response to the nutrition therapy • The effectiveness of the therapy or the patient’s nutritional intake related to achieving care and

statement: Patients at nutrition risk receive nutrition therapy.
elements: Patients assessed at nutrition risk receive nutrition therapy.
A collaborative process is used to plan, deliver, and monitor nutrition therapy.
The patient’s response to nutrition therapy is monitored and documented in the medical record.

statement: Patients are supported in managing pain effectively.
elements: The home care organization has processes to identify patients in pain based on its scope of services.
Patients are informed about the likelihood of pain and options for pain management when pain is an expected result of planned treatments, procedures, or examinations.
Patients in pain receive care according to pain management guidelines and patient goals for pain management.
The home care organization has processes to communicate with and educate patients, families, and caregivers about pain based on its scope of services.
The home care organization has processes to educate staff about pain based on its scope of services.

Patients in pain are referred to the pain management team or outside source for further assessment and management when pain management is outside the home care organization’s mission or care and services.

statement: The home care organization provides end-of-life care that addresses the dying patient’s and family’s needs and optimizes the patient’s comfort and dignity.
elements: Staff are educated about the unique needs of patients and their families at the end of life.
The patient’s health care needs and the patient’s and family’s support service needs are identified as appropriate to their religious and cultural preferences.
End-of-life care addresses the symptoms, conditions, and health care needs of the dying patient as indicated by their assessment.
End-of-life care addresses the dying patient’s pain.
End-of-life care addresses the patient’s and family’s psychosocial, emotional, cultural, and spiritual needs, as appropriate, regarding dying and grieving.
The patient and family are involved in care decisions.

statement: The home care organization develops and implements a process to improve the accuracy of patient identification.
elements: At least two patient identifiers, that do not include the patient’s location (such as an address), are used to identify the patient and label elements associated with the patient’s care and treatment plan.
Patients are identified by at least two identifiers including their full name, as in a valid identification document, and a unique medical record number.
Patients/families are actively involved in the process of patient identification.
Patients are identified before diagnostic procedures, treatments, and other procedures (for example, withdrawing blood, administering medications).
The home care organization ensures the correct identification of patients in special circumstances, such as the comatose or nonverbal patient.

statement: The home care organization develops and implements a process to improve the effectiveness of verbal and/or telephone communication among caregivers.
elements: The receiver documents and reads back complete verbal/telephone orders, and the individual giving the order confirms the order and escalation policies.
The receiver documents and reads back complete telephone orders, and the individual giving the order confirms the telephone orders.
The receiver documents and reads back complete test results, and the individual giving the result confirms the test results.

statement: The home care organization develops and implements a process for reporting critical results of diagnostic tests.
elements: The home care organization defines critical results that may represent urgent or emergent life- threatening values for diagnostic tests.

The home care organization develops a formal reporting process, used throughout the organization, that identifies how critical results of diagnostic tests are reported/communicated to health care practitioners.
The policy defines which staff are responsible for receiving critical test results.
The process involves the receiver writing down the result and reading back the findings to the result provider.
The read-back process and the physician’s intervention are documented in the patient’s medical record.
The home care organization identifies what information is documented in the medical record.

statement: The home care organization develops and implements a process for handover communication.
elements: Standardized critical content is communicated between health care practitioners during handovers of patient care.
Standardized forms, tools, or methods that support a consistent and complete handover process are used.
Data from adverse events resulting from handover communications are tracked and used to identify ways in which handovers can be improved, and improvements are implemented.
The home health care service implements a standardized process to improve the effectiveness of communication between the most responsible physician and the visiting staff.

statement: The home care organization develops and implements a process to improve the safety of high-alert medications.
elements: The home care organization identifies in writing its list of high-alert medications.

The home care organization develops and implements a process for reducing the risk and harm of high-alert medications that is uniform throughout the organization when these medications are stored in the home care organization.
When high-alert medications are stored in the patient’s home, home care staff educate the patient, family, and other caregivers about preventing medication errors.
The home care organization annually reviews and, as necessary, revises its list of high-alert medications.

statement: The home care organization develops and implements a process to improve the safety of look-alike/sound-alike medications.
elements: The home care organization identifies in writing its list of look-alike/sound-alike medications.

The home care organization develops and implements a process for managing look-alike/sound-alike medications that is uniform throughout the organization when these medications are stored in the home care organization and during transportation to the patient’s home.
When look-alike/sound-alike medications are stored in the patient’s home, home care staff educate the patient, family, and other caregivers about preventing medication errors.
The home care organization annually reviews and, as necessary, revises its list of look-alike/sound-alike medications.

statement: The home care organization adopts and implements evidence-based hand hygiene guidelines to reduce the risk of health care–associated infections.
elements: The home care organization has an established and implemented policy on hand hygiene.
The home care organization has adopted or adapted current evidence-based hand-hygiene guidelines.
The home care organization implements and monitors an effective hand-hygiene program.
Handwashing and hand-disinfection procedures are used in accordance with hand hygiene guidelines throughout the home care organization.

statement: Home care organization leaders identify care processes that need improvement and adopt and implement evidence-based interventions to improve patient outcomes and reduce the risk of health care–associated infections.
elements: Home care organization leaders identify priority areas for improving health care–associated infections.
Home care organization leaders identify and implement evidence-based interventions (such as bundles) for all applicable patients.

Evidence-based interventions (such as bundles) used to reduce the risk of health care–associated infections are evaluated by health care practitioners for compliance and improvement in clinical outcomes.
The home health care service leaders allocate adequate and appropriate resources to support the infection prevention and control program.
A qualified individual, acting on a full-time or part-time basis, is responsible for the infection control program.
The infection prevention and control program is updated annually based on current scientific knowledge, accepted practice guidelines, and applicable laws and regulations.
The infection prevention and control program is integrated with the quality and patient safety and risk management programs.
The infection prevention and control program’s components are contained in a manual that is available to all staff members.

statement: The home care organization develops and implements a process to reduce the risk of patient harm resulting from falls for the home care patient population.
elements: The home care organization implements a process for initially assessing patients for fall risk and reassessing patients when indicated by a change in patient condition or environment.

The home care organization implements a process for reassessing patients who may become at risk for falls due to a change in condition or are already at risk for falls based on the documented assessment.

Measures and/or interventions to reduce fall risk are implemented for those identified patients, situations, and locations in the home environment assessed to be at risk. Patient interventions are documented.

statement: Medication use in the home care organization is organized to meet patient needs, complies with applicable laws and regulations, and is under the direction and supervision of a licensed pharmacist or other qualified professional.
elements: A written document addressing the aspects below, as appropriate, identifies how medication use is organized, managed, and overseen throughout the home care organization: • Planning • Selection and procurement • Storage • Ordering • Preparing and dispensing • Administration • Monitoring • Medication error and adverse event reporting • Evaluation
All settings, services, and individuals who manage medication processes are included in the organizational structure.
A licensed pharmacist or other qualified individual directly supervises the activities of the pharmacy or pharmaceutical service if the organization has a fully owned or contracted pharmacy.
The home care organization documents at least one review of the medication management system annually.
The process for dispensing and distribution of medications in the home environment complies with applicable laws and regulations.
Appropriate sources of drug information are readily available to those involved in medication use.

statement: The home care organization has a method for overseeing its medication list, including how listed medications are used; a method for ensuring that medications for prescribing or ordering are stocked; and a process for medications not stocked or not normally available to the home care organization or for times when the pharmacy is closed.
elements: When full pharmacy services are provided, the home care organization has a list of medications, identified by both brand name and generic name, that it stocks or that are readily available from outside sources, and the list is reviewed annually.

The process for developing and monitoring the list (unless determined by regulation or an authority outside the home care organization) includes representation from health care practitioners involved in ordering, dispensing, administering, and patient-monitoring processes in the home care organization.

When full pharmacy services are not provided, the home care organization has a list of medications, identified by both brand name and generic name, that home care staff can administer and/or prescribe.

Home care staff educate patients and families about how to obtain medications during the night or when the pharmacy is closed and how to obtain medications not stocked or not normally available to the home care organization.

statement: Medications are properly and safely stored.
elements: Patients, families, and caregivers are educated about how to properly and safely store medications, and this is documented in the patient’s medical record.
Controlled substances are accurately accounted for according to applicable laws and regulations.
There is a process for managing medications or products requiring special handling, such as hazardous medications, radioactive medications, and investigational medications.
Medications stored in the home care facility are stored under conditions suitable for product stability.
All medication storage areas, including medication storage areas in patient homes (as applicable), are periodically inspected to ensure that medications are stored properly.
Medications are protected from loss or theft throughout the home care organization.

statement: Emergency medications are available, uniformly stored, monitored, and secure when stored outside the pharmacy.
elements: The home care organization determines which emergency medications and associated supplies will be available in the home and which will be available from clinical staff.

The home care organization establishes and implements a process for how emergency medications are uniformly stored; maintained; replaced when used, damaged, or out of date; and protected from loss or theft.
Access to emergency medications does not require a specific individual or keys to unlock the emergency medication box.
Emergency medications are monitored and replaced in a timely manner after use or when expired or damaged.
The home care organization uses a risk-based approach to identify and implement strategies to improve the efficiency and accuracy of medication administration during emergency resuscitation.

statement: The home care organization has a medication recall system.
elements: The home care organization establishes and implements a process for receiving and acting on notifications of medication recalls.
The process includes identifying, retrieving, and returning, or safely and properly destroying, medications recalled by the manufacturer, supplier, or regulatory agency.
The recall process includes medications compounded in the home care organization, if applicable, and identifies which products that have been recalled have been used.
The home care organization establishes and implements a process for use of unopened, expired medications and outdated medications.
The home care organization establishes and implements a process for destroying medications known to be expired or outdated.

statement: The home care organization identifies those qualified individuals permitted to prescribe or order medications and develops and implements a medication reconciliation process.
elements: Only those permitted by the home care organization and by relevant licensure, laws, and regulations prescribe or order medications.
Individuals permitted to prescribe and order medications are known to the pharmaceutical service (depending on the services provided) or others who dispense medications.
The home care organization identifies the information needed to reconcile current and newly ordered medications.
The patient’s medical records contain a list of current medications, and this information is made available to the patient’s health care practitioners and the pharmaceutical services as needed.

Initial medication orders are compared to the list of medications taken prior to admission, according to the home care organization’s established process for medication reconciliation by the most responsible physician.

statement: The home care organization identifies safe prescribing, ordering, and transcribing practices and defines the elements of a complete order or prescription.
elements: The home care organization establishes, implements, and trains staff about safe prescribing and ordering of medications by the most responsible physician and for transcribing of medications.
All orders and prescriptions contain the name of the drug, dose, and frequency, route, and duration of administration.

Additional elements of complete medication orders or prescriptions include at least the following as appropriate to the order: • The data necessary to accurately identify the patient (See also IPSG.1.) • When generic or brand names are acceptable or required (See also MMU.2.) • Specific guidelines for PRN (pro re nata, or “as needed”) orders, including indications for use and detailed directions for overlapping orders, such as more than one medication for pain • The types of orders that are weight based or otherwise adjusted, such as for children, frail elderly,

statement: Medications are prepared and dispensed in a safe, clean environment.
elements: Medication preparation and dispensing adhere to laws, regulations, and professional standards of practice.
Medications are prepared and dispensed in clean, uncluttered, safe, and functionally separate areas with appropriate medical equipment and supplies.

Staff preparing/compounding sterile products/medications are trained and competent in the principles of medication preparation and aseptic techniques and are provided resources to support medication preparation (depending on the services provided).
Guidelines for single-use and multidose vials are identified and implemented in the medication processes (depending on the services provided).

When medications are stored, prepared, and dispensed from areas outside the pharmacy (for example, in the patient home), staff educate the patient, family, and caregivers about safely preparing medications.

statement: Qualified individuals permitted to administer medications are identified and document the medications administered in the patient’s medical record.
elements: The home care organization identifies those individuals, by job description of the privileging process, authorized to administer medications.
The home care organization places limits, when appropriate, on the medication administration of individuals.
Medications administered by home care staff are recorded for each dose.

statement: Medication administration performed by the home care organization’s staff includes a process to verify the medication is correct based on the medication order.
elements: Medications are verified with the prescription or order.
Medications are compared against the patient’s allergies.
The dosage of the medication is verified with the prescription or order.
The route of administration is verified with the prescription or order.
Patients are informed about the medications that they are going to be given and have an opportunity to ask questions.
Medications are administered as prescribed on a timely basis and noted in the patient’s medical record.

statement: Medications are safely and accurately administered by patients, families, and/or caregivers in the home.
elements: The home care organization develops and implements a process for ensuring safe medication administration by patients, families, and/or caregivers in the home.

The process includes educating patients, families, and/or caregivers about the following: • Medication name, type, and reason for use • Administration process, frequency, route, and dose • Anticipated actions • Potential side effects • Monitoring of the effects of medications (See also MMU.7.)
The home care organization supervises patients, families, and/or caregivers until they determine the patients, families, and/or caregivers can administer the medications safely and correctly.

statement: Medication effects on patients are monitored.
elements: Medication effects on patients are monitored and documented when appropriate.
The monitoring process includes patients, families, physicians, nurses, and other health care providers (depending on the services provided).
Medication adverse effects on patients are monitored and documented.

The home care organization uses a standardized process for recording in the patient medical record any adverse effects related to medication use and for reporting adverse effects to the physician responsible for the patient’s care, and to the relevant local authorities as per the applicable laws and regulations.
The home care organization uses a standardized process for reporting adverse medication effects as part of the home care quality improvement and patient safety program.

Patients, families, and caregivers are educated about any monitoring for medications that are self- administered or administered by families or caregivers, and this education is documented in the patient medical record.

statement: The home care organization establishes and implements a process for reporting and acting on medication errors and near misses (or close calls).
elements: The home care organization defines medication error and near miss.
The home care organization establishes and implements a process for reporting and acting on medication errors and near misses.
Staff, patients, families, and/or home care providers are educated on the importance of and process for reporting medication errors and near misses.
The home care organization uses medication errors and near misses reporting information to improve medication use processes.

statement: The home care organization is responsible for providing processes that support the patients’ and families’ rights during care.
elements: Home care leadership works collaboratively to protect and advance patient and family rights and responsibilities statement.
Home care leadership implements patient and family rights as identified in laws and regulations.
Home care leadership protects patient and family rights in relation to the cultural practices of the community or individual patients served.
Home care leadership ensures that patients/families have the right to accurate billing for provided services.
Home care leadership protects the patient’s right to identify whom they wish to participate in care decisions.

The home care organization has a process to determine the patient’s preference, and in some circumstances the patient’s family’s preference, as to what information regarding the patient’s care would be provided to family or others, and under what circumstances.
All health care practitioners are trained in the processes and their role in supporting patient and family rights and participation in care.

statement: The home care organization seeks to reduce physical, language, cultural, and other barriers to access and delivery of services and provides information and education to patients, families, and caregivers in a language and manner they can understand.
elements: Home care organization service leaders and staff identify their patient population’s most common and challenging barriers to accessing and receiving care and develop processes that support their implementation.
The service leaders develop and implement a process for overcoming or limiting barriers to access to care and their impact on service delivery for patients seeking care.
Information about aspects of the patient’s medical care and treatment is provided in a manner and language the patient understands.
Information about patient rights and responsibilities is provided to each patient, in writing or another method, in a language the patient understands.
The statement of patient rights and responsibilities is always posted or otherwise available from staff.

statement: The home care organization provides care that supports patient dignity, respects the patient’s values and beliefs, and responds to requests for spiritual and religious observance.
elements: Staff provide care that is respectful and considerate of the patient’s dignity and self-worth.
The patient’s spiritual and cultural beliefs and values are respected.
The home care organization responds to routine as well as complex requests related to religious or spiritual support.
Staff recognize patients’ physical and mental losses and assist the patient and family in incorporating the patient’s remaining abilities into daily activities.

statement: The home care organization establishes a process to ensure patient privacy and confidentiality of care and information and allows patients to have access to their health information within the context of existing law and culture.
elements: Staff meet patient expectations and needs for privacy, when expressed, during care and treatment.
A patient’s expressed need for privacy is respected for all clinical interviews, examinations, procedures/ treatments, and transport.
Confidentiality of patient information is maintained according to laws and regulations.
The home care organization has a process for patients to grant permission for the release of information not covered by laws and regulations.
The home care organization has a process for providing patients with access to their health information within the context of existing laws, regulations, and culture.
Access to health information is timely, and cost does not prevent access to this information for the purpose of maintaining continuity of care.

statement: The patient has the right to receive protection from neglect, exploitation, and abuse.
elements: The home care organization develops and implements a process to protect the patient from neglect, exploitation, and abuse while receiving care, treatment, or services.
This process considers infants, vulnerable children, the elderly, patients in comas, and others less able or unable to protect themselves.
Staff are educated on their responsibilities in the protection processes.

statement: Patients and families are engaged in all aspects of their medical care and treatment through education and participation in care and treatment decisions and care processes.
elements: The home care organization assists patients and, when appropriate, their families in participating in care and decision-making to the extent they wish.
Participation in the care process includes educating patients, family, and caregivers about their medical conditions, any confirmed diagnosis, and the planned care and treatment(s).
Patients and families are educated about the expected outcomes of care and treatment based on their health care needs.
Patients and families receive education to help them participate in the care process and understand any financial implications of their care choices.
Patients are told of any unanticipated outcomes during their care and treatment.
Patients and families participate in decisions about transfer to another service or setting or discharge from the home care program.

Staff provide patients/families with truthful, accurate information, in a manner they can understand, about their illness, treatment options, proposed treatment, potential benefits, potential complications, and likelihood of success of treatment.
Patients and families are provided with the identity and professional status of the treating physician or other practitioners and the contact details of the home health care providers.
Patient and family education is evaluated for effectiveness through demonstrated learning or verbalized understanding.

The home health care service has a process for patient discharge or termination of services, including the following: • Estimated date of discharge or service termination • Identifiable clinical criteria for discharge and the patient’s suitability and stability for discharge • A discharge summary with medications and support services necessary for a safe discharge • How to communicate and obtain assistance if needed, post-discharge

statement: The home care organization informs patients and families about their rights and responsibilities to refuse or discontinue treatment, withhold resuscitative services, and forgo or withdraw life-sustaining treatments.
elements: The home care organization has identified its position on calling for emergency assistance when the patient is in extremis and forgoing or withdrawing life-sustaining treatments and informs the patient.
Health care providers are vigilant in detecting early warning signs warranting the patients’ referral to a hospital. If needed, the patient is safely transferred through the Red Crescent.
The treating physician develops a care plan to meet patient needs, considering cultural and/or religious needs as well as legal or regulatory requirements.

The home care organization informs patients and families about their rights to refuse or discontinue treatment or ask for a second opinion as well as the home care organization’s responsibilities related to such decisions.
The home care organization informs patients about the consequences of their decisions.
The home care organization informs patients about available care and treatment alternatives.
The home care organization guides health care practitioners on the ethical and legal considerations in carrying out patient wishes regarding treatment alternatives.

statement: The home care organization supports the patient’s right to assessment and management of pain and respectful compassionate care at the end of life.
elements: The home care organization respects and supports the patient’s right to pain assessment and management.

The home care organization respects and supports the patient’s right to assessment and management of the dying patient’s needs. 3 The home care organization’s staff understand the personal, cultural, and societal influences on the patient’s experiences with pain.
The home care organization’s staff understand the personal, cultural, and societal influences on the patient’s experiences with death and dying.

statement: The home care organization measures, analyzes, and, when necessary, improves the patient experience to enhance the quality of patient care.
elements: Leadership develops and implements a process for assessing the patient experience (periodic satisfaction surveys) and its impact on patient care.
Data from the patient experience are aggregated, analyzed, and transformed into information to identify strategies for improving the patient experience.
Leadership determines a priority area for improving the patient experience that will positively impact patient care.
Identified strategies for improving the patient experience are implemented.
Improvements to the patient experience are analyzed and revised to optimize their impact on quality of patient care.

statement: The home care organization informs patients and families about its process to receive and act on complaints, conflicts, and differences of opinion about patient care and services and about the patient’s right to participate in these processes.
elements: Patients and families are informed about internal and external processes for voicing complaints, conflicts, concerns, and suggestions, or differences of opinion.
The home care organization investigates complaints, conflicts, or differences of opinion.
Complaints, conflicts, or differences of opinion that arise during the care process are resolved in a time frame described in the policy.
Patients and, when indicated, families participate in the resolution process.
The home health care service assigns a staff member to be responsible for managing complaints.
Data collected from surveys and complaints are analyzed, used for improvement, and integrated into the quality and safety program.

statement: General consent for treatment, if obtained when a patient is admitted to the home care organization’s services, is clear in its scope and limits.
elements: The home care organization informs the patient and family on the scope of the general consent (when obtained prior to treatment).
The home care organization defines how a general consent, when used, is documented in the patient medical record.
Whether or not a general consent is obtained, all patients and families are informed about which tests and treatments require informed consent.
Whether or not general consent is obtained, all patients receive information about the likelihood of students and trainees participating in care processes.

statement: Patient informed consent is obtained through a process defined by the home care organization and carried out by trained staff in a manner and language the patient can understand.
elements: The home care organization develops and implements a clearly defined consent process and trains designated staff in the process.
The home care organization educates patients about the informed consent process and when informed consent is required.
The home care organization has listed those procedures and treatments that require separate consent.

Patients give informed consent consistent with the process. The informed consent process and related education are provided in a manner and language the patient or surrogate decision-maker understands, and it includes verbal language and non-verbal language.
There is uniform documentation of informed consent.
The identity of the individual providing the information to the patient and family is documented in the patient’s medical record.

statement: Patients and families receive adequate information about the patient’s condition, proposed treatment(s) or procedure(s), and health care practitioners so that they can make care and services decisions.
elements: Patients are informed of the following as part of the informed consent process when informed consent is required for the treatment(s) or procedure(s): • The patient’s condition • The proposed treatment(s) or procedure(s) • The name of the person providing the treatment • Potential benefits and drawbacks • Possible alternatives • The likelihood of success • Possible problems related to recovery • Possible results of nontreatment
When informed consent is not required, patients are informed as relevant to their condition and planned treatment(s) or procedure(s).
Patients know the identity of the physician or other practitioner responsible for their care.

The home care organization develops a process to respond to a patient’s and/or responsible family member’s request for additional information on the health care practitioner coming into the patient’s home.

statement: The home care organization establishes a process, within the context of existing law and culture, for when others can grant consent.
elements: The home care organization develops and implements a process for when others can grant informed consent.
The process respects law, culture, and custom.
The patient’s medical record lists the individual(s) granting consent.

statement: The home care organization provides an education program based on its mission, services, and patients, and health care practitioners collaborate to provide education.
elements: The home care organization plans education consistent with its mission, services, and patient population.
There is an established structure or mechanism for adequate education resources throughout the home care organization.
Patient, family, and caregiver education is provided collaboratively when indicated.
Those who provide education have the subject knowledge and communication skills to do so.
Those who provide education have adequate time to do so.

statement: Each patient’s educational needs and ability and willingness to learn are assessed and recorded in their record.
elements: Each patient’s and, when appropriate, family’s or caregiver’s educational needs are assessed and documented in the patient medical record.
The patient’s, family’s, and caregiver’s barriers to learning are assessed and documented.
Home care staff educate patients, families, and caregivers in a manner that accommodates their identified needs.
Education provided to patients, families, and caregivers is documented in the patient medical record.

statement: Education methods consider the patient’s, family’s, and caregiver’s values and preferences and allow sufficient interaction among the patient, family, caregiver, and staff for learning to occur.
elements: The education process considers the patient’s, family’s, and caregiver’s values and learning preferences.
There is a process to verify that patients, families, and caregivers receive and understand the education provided.
Those who provide education encourage patients and their families or caregivers to ask questions and speak up as active participants.
Verbal information is reinforced with written material that is related to the patient’s needs and consistent with the patient’s and family’s learning preferences. Section II:

statement: The home care organization complies with relevant laws, regulations, building and fire safety codes, and facility inspection requirements.
elements: Home care leadership and the facility management and safety structure understand and implement national and local laws, regulations, building and fire safety codes, national standards, environmental protection standards, recommendations of professional centers, and other requirements applicable to the organization’s facilities.

Home care leadership and the facility management and safety structure document corrective actions taken to meet the conditions of external facility reports or citations from inspections by national and local authorities.

Home care leadership plans and budgets for the replacement or upgrade of facilities, systems, and equipment as needed to meet applicable requirements and for the continued operation of a safe, secure, and effective facility.
Home care leadership approves and allocates budgeted resources or implements alternative strategies to reduce risks until the resources can be allocated.

When the home care organization is inside a multiuse building, home care leaders obtain evidence of compliance with relevant laws, regulations, codes, facility inspection reports, utility maintenance requirements, and other requirements related to shared systems and building issues, and when the home care organization is part of a hospital (that is, a department within the hospital), the hospital FMS standards apply.

statement: A qualified individual oversees the facility management and safety structure to reduce and control risks in the patient home environment and the home care facility.
elements: An individual qualified, as a full-time or part-time employee, by experience and training is responsible for overseeing and directing the facility management and safety structure, and evidence of their experience and training is documented.
The qualified individual is responsible for the following: • Making recommendations to home care leadership about space, medical equipment, technology,

statement: The home care organization develops and documents a comprehensive risk assessment based on facility management and safety risks identified throughout the organization’s facility and the environment in which patient care and services are provided, prioritizes the risks, establishes goals, and implements improvements to reduce and eliminate risks.
elements: The risk assessments from all the following facility management and safety programs are integrated to develop and document a comprehensive, organizationwide risk assessment, at least annually: • Safety • Security • Hazardous materials and waste • Fire safety • Medical equipment • Utility systems • Emergency and disaster management
The home care organization prioritizes the risks, identifies goals and improvements, and implements improvements to reduce and eliminate risks.
The home care organization evaluates the effectiveness of the improvements, and based on the results, updates the applicable facility management and safety programs.
The patient, responsible family member, and/or caregiver are educated about preventing injury and maintaining safe conditions for patients, families, and staff.

statement: Data are collected and analyzed from each of the facility management and safety programs to reduce risks in the facility and patient home environment, track progress on goals and improvements, and support planning for replacing and upgrading facilities, systems, and equipment.
elements: Monitoring data are collected and analyzed for each of the facility management and safety programs, actions taken, and used to reduce risks in the facility and the patient home environment and support planning for replacing or upgrading facilities, systems, and equipment.
Monitoring data for the facility management and safety programs are documented and integrated into the home care organization’s quality improvement and patient safety program.

The individual who oversees the facility management and safety structure provides monitoring data reports that address the effectiveness of each program and progress on goals to home care leadership on a quarterly basis, and leadership takes action.

The individual who oversees the facility management and safety structure provides the comprehensive, organizationwide risk assessment and planned and implemented improvements to home care leadership at least annually.
Home care leadership provides an annual report to the governing entity on the effectiveness of the facility management and safety programs, and the governing entity takes action.

statement: The home care organization develops and implements a program to ensure physical safety in the home care facilities and patient home environment.
elements: The home care organization develops and implements a written program to provide a safe physical facility and decrease risks in the patient’s home environment. Measures adopted to ensure such include, but not limited to, the following: • Adequate parking spaces, waiting areas, and toilets • Appropriate storage area for medical supplies and medical equipment • Medical supplies and consumables stored in an organized way, with labels showing the item’s

statement: The home care organization develops and implements a program to provide a secure environment for patients, families, staff, and visitors.
elements: The home care organization develops and implements a written program to provide a secure environment.
A security risk assessment is conducted and documented annually throughout the organization, and security risks are identified and prioritized from the risk assessment.
The security program identifies all security risk areas and restricted areas in the home care facility and ensures that they are monitored and kept secure.
The security program ensures that all staff, students, trainees, contract workers, volunteers, and vendors, are identified.
The home care organization identifies goals, implements improvements in the security program, and monitors data to ensure that security risks are reduced or eliminated.
The home care organization develops and implements a process to maintain staff security while in the patient’s home.

statement: The home care organization develops and implements a program for managing hazardous materials and waste.
elements: The home care organization develops and implements a written program for managing hazardous materials and waste.

A hazardous materials and waste risk assessment is conducted and documented annually throughout the facility and the patient’s home environment, and risks related to hazardous materials and waste are identified and prioritized from the risk assessment.
The home care organization identifies goals, implements improvements, and monitors data to ensure that risks related to hazardous materials and waste are reduced or eliminated.

statement: The home care organization’s program for managing hazardous materials and waste includes inventorying, handling, storing, using, and disposing of hazardous materials and waste.
elements: The hazardous materials and waste program identifies the type, quantities, and locations of hazardous materials and waste, and maintains a complete inventory along with the appropriate safety data sheets (SDSs). The inventory is updated at least annually to reflect changes in the hazardous materials used and stored in the organization.

The hazardous materials and waste program establishes and implements procedures for safely handling, storing, using, and disposing of hazardous materials and waste. Fire-rated cabinets are used for flammable hazardous materials.
The hazardous materials and waste program establishes and implements the proper protective equipment required while handling, using, and disposing of hazardous materials and waste.
The hazardous materials and waste program establishes and implements proper and clear labeling of hazardous materials that is consistent with information from the safety data sheets (SDSs).
The hazardous materials and waste program establishes and implements procedures for managing spills and exposures, including using proper protective equipment and reporting spills and exposures.
Information about safe handling and spill and exposure procedures for hazardous materials and waste is up to date and available at all times.

statement: The home care organization establishes and implements a fire safety program, including an ongoing assessment of risks and compliance with national and local codes, laws, and regulations for fire safety.
elements: The home care organization develops and implements a written fire safety program to protect all occupants of the organization’s facilities from fire, smoke, and non-fire emergencies.

The home care organization performs and documents an ongoing fire safety risk assessment related to the following (as applicable), and fire safety risks are identified and prioritized from the risk assessment: • Fire separations • Smoke separations/compartments • Hazardous areas (and spaces above the ceilings in those areas) such as soiled linen rooms, trash

statement: The fire safety program includes fire response and potential fire hazards in the facility and the home care environment.
elements: The fire safety program for the patient’s home environment includes escape procedures (if applicable) and other interim measures.
The fire safety program for the patient’s home environment includes identifying hazards related to medical equipment or supplies, including oxygen safety when indicated.
The fire safety program for the patient’s home environment includes recommending the use of smoke detectors.
The fire safety program for the patient’s home environment includes educating the patient on hazards such as smoking in bed.
The fire safety program for the patient’s home environment includes notifying the fire department of a disabled person(s), when this service is available.
The fire safety program for the patient’s home environment includes ensuring the patient’s ability to summon emergency assistance.

statement: The home care organization involves staff in regular exercises to evaluate the fire safety program.
elements: All staff are trained annually on emergency drills, fire drills, and evacuation plans and participate in an exercise to evaluate the fire safety program.
Staff are knowledgeable about the fire safety program and can describe how to bring themselves and patients to safety.
Results of exercises to evaluate the fire safety program are documented in staff personnel files, and staff who do not pass are reeducated and retested on the fire safety program.

statement: All fire safety equipment and systems, including devices related to early detection, alarm notification, and suppression, are inspected, tested, and maintained.
elements: All fire safety equipment and systems in the home care facility, including fire alarms, fire equipment, and smoke and fire detection and suppression, are in place, functioning, inspected, tested, and maintained according to manufacturers’ recommendations or as required by local codes, laws, and regulations, whichever sets the more stringent requirement.
Egress routes, corridors, and fire escapes are marked and free from obstacles.

Inspection, testing, and maintenance of all fire safety equipment and systems in the home care facility, including fire alarm system, are documented, including results and corrective actions. Fire extinguishers are tested and distributed according to the type of extinguisher required.

Any deficiencies identified in the home care facility’s fire safety equipment and systems are immediately corrected, or interim measures are implemented to reduce fire risk until deficiencies can be fully corrected.

statement: The fire safety program includes limiting smoking.
elements: A “no smoking” policy is approved and enforced.
“No Smoking” signs are posted at all entrances and waiting areas.

statement: When the home care organization supplies medical equipment in the home, it develops and implements a program for inspecting, testing, and maintaining medical equipment and documents the results.
elements: The home care organization develops and implements a medical equipment program.
The home care organization completes a risk assessment, at least annually, as part of the medical equipment program.

The medical equipment program does the following: • Takes inventory of all medical equipment • Tracks the location of each piece of equipment in the patient’s home • Regularly inspects all medical equipment • Tests all medical equipment according to its use and requirements • Provides preventive maintenance to equipment supplied by the home care organization according to the supplied and available manufacturer’s service manual, and documents this

statement: Equipment received and stored by the home care organization for use in the patient’s home is stored appropriately.
elements: Storage areas for clean and dirty medical equipment supplied by the organization are separate and clearly identified.
A separate area for cleaning and disinfecting equipment supplied by the organization is clearly identified.
A separate area for storing equipment supplied by the organization for maintenance and repair is clearly identified.
A separate area for equipment supplied by the organization ready for use is clearly identified.
Equipment supplied by the organization and ready for use remains clean during storage.
Equipment supplied by the organization is stored so that required temperatures, expiration requirements, and battery charge requirements are maintained.

statement: Medical equipment is delivered and set up according to the patient’s needs for care and services.
elements: Medical equipment is delivered at a frequency to meet the patient’s needs.
Clean and dirty equipment are separated during transport.
Delivery methods are related to the patient’s needs.
Medical equipment is set up in the home to accommodate the equipment’s physical, electrical, and other requirements.
Medical equipment is adapted or fit to the setting or the patient during setup.
Medical equipment is unpacked, assembled, and checked for safe operation during setup in the home.

statement: When the home care organization provides equipment, it provides emergency maintenance, replacement, or backup equipment if needed.
elements: The home care organization completes a risk assessment, at least annually, of equipment requiring 24-hour emergency repair.
Equipment that requires emergency maintenance, replacement, or backup is identified.
Emergency maintenance, replacement, or backup equipment is provided when needed.

statement: The home care organization provides 24-hour emergency services and/or a backup system when an equipment malfunction may threaten the patient’s health.
elements: Patients whose health may be threatened by a medical equipment malfunction have access to emergency services 24 hours a day, 7 days per week, from the home care organization, or a contracted service approved by the home care organization.

When the patient, responsible family member, or caregiver reports a medical equipment malfunction, the home care organization, or an approved contracted service, provides backup medical equipment or emergency maintenance or replacement before the patient’s health is affected.

The backup system or emergency plan for repair or replacement is sufficient for the patient to receive continued therapy or equipment function beyond the maximum time it will take for home care organization response.
If the home care organization is not able to respond in a time frame to meet the patient’s needs, an alternative arrangement is planned.

statement: The home care organization develops and implements a program for managing utility systems throughout the organization.
elements: The home care organization conducts and documents a risk assessment, at least annually, of the facility’s utility systems.
The home care organization has a process for assessing the patient’s home prior to placing equipment, which includes identifying power requirements for specific brands and types of equipment.
The home care organization has a process for determining if the utility systems in the patient’s home are appropriate or can be adapted, including ensuring a clean and adequate water supply.
The home care organization has a process for ensuring adequate refrigeration facilities for heat- degradable items.
The home care organization has a process for assessing heat, ventilation, and air-conditioning in the patient’s home.

statement: The utility systems program inspects, tests, and provides maintenance, and/or collaborates with the building’s ownership, to ensure that its facility’s utilities operate effectively and efficiently to meet staff and visitor needs.
elements: The home care organization inventories its utility systems components and maps the current distribution of them in the home care facility.

The home care organization identifies, in writing, the activities and intervals for inspecting, testing, and conducting preventive and routine maintenance in the home care facility on all operating components of the utility systems on the inventory, based on criteria such as manufacturers’ recommendations, risk levels, and home care experience.

The home care organization updates or replaces or collaborates with the building’s ownership to update or replace utility systems and components as needed when identified through inspection, testing, and maintenance in the home care facility.
The home care organization labels utility systems controls to facilitate partial or complete emergency shutdowns in the home care facility.

statement: The home care organization develops, maintains, and tests an emergency management program to respond to internal and external emergencies and disasters that may occur in the home care organization and community.
elements: The home care organization develops, evaluates, and maintains a written emergency management program that identifies its response to likely emergencies and disasters, including the following: • Determining the type, likelihood, and consequences of hazards, threats, and events • Planning for alternative sources of power and water in emergencies and disasters • Determining the organization’s role in such events • Determining communication strategies for events • Managing resources during events, including alternative sources • Managing clinical activities during events, including alternative care sites • Identifying and assigning staff roles and responsibilities during events (including contract staff,

statement: Staff and others are trained and knowledgeable about the home care organization’s facility management and safety programs and their roles in ensuring a safe and effective facility.
elements: All staff, including new hires, receive annual training and testing (including drills) on each facility management and safety program to ensure that they can safely and effectively carry out their responsibilities, and testing results are documented in staff personnel files.

Training on the facility management and safety programs includes vendors, contract workers, volunteers, students, trainees, and others, as applicable to the individuals’ roles and responsibilities, and as determined by the home care organization.
Staff can describe and/or demonstrate their roles in response to a fire.
Staff can describe and/or demonstrate actions to eliminate, minimize, or report safety, security, and other risks.

Staff can describe and/or demonstrate precautions and procedures for handling and managing medical gases and hazardous materials and waste, as applicable to the staff member’s role and responsibilities.
Staff can describe and/or demonstrate procedures for and their roles in internal and community emergencies and disasters.

statement: The structure and authority of the home care organization’s governing entity are described in bylaws, policies and procedures, or similar documents.
elements: The structure and authority of the home care organization’s governing entity are described in a written document, bylaws, and/or policies and procedures, with those responsible for governance of the organization identified.
The document(s) describes when and how the authority of the governing entity and the chief executive can be delegated through approval authority delegation.
The governing entity is evaluated annually, and the results are documented.

statement: The operational responsibilities and accountabilities of the governing entity are described in a written document(s).
elements: The governing entity approves the home care organization’s strategic plans, operational plans, scope of services, key policies, and procedures, and approves, periodically reviews, and makes public the organization’s mission and vision statement and values.

The governing entity approves the home care organization’s capital and operating budget(s) and allocates other resources required to meet the organization’s mission and execute the operating plan efficiently.
The governing entity approves the home care organization’s participation in research when applicable and the oversight of the quality of such programs.
The governing entity appoints, and annually evaluates, the home care organization’s chief executive(s)/ director(s), and the evaluation is documented.

statement: The governing entity approves the home care organization’s program for quality improvement and patient safety and regularly receives and acts on reports of the quality improvement and patient safety program.
elements: The governing entity annually approves the home care organization’s program for quality improvement and patient safety and risk management initiatives.

At least quarterly, the governing entity receives, evaluates, and acts on reports of the quality improvement and patient safety program, including reports of adverse and sentinel events, corrective actions, and outcomes from the home health care service, including risk management.

Minutes reflect the governing entity’s actions, any follow-up on those actions, and the recommended corrective actions, which are documented and received by the home health care service chief executive(s)/director(s) for implementation.

statement: A chief executive(s) is responsible for operating the home care organization and complying with applicable laws and regulations.
elements: The education and experience of the chief executive(s) match the requirements in the position description.
The chief executive(s) manages the home care organization’s day-to-day operations, including those responsibilities described in the position description.
The chief executive(s) ensures availability of adequate and proper resources for the planned services in accordance with the approved operating budget.
The chief executive(s) recommends policies to the governing entity.
The chief executive(s) ensures compliance with approved policies.
The chief executive(s) ensures compliance with applicable laws and regulations.
The chief executive(s) responds to any reports from inspecting and regulatory agencies.
The chief executive(s) ensures a safe and functional home health services facility environment for staff.

statement: Home care leadership is identified and is collectively responsible for defining the organization’s mission and vision and creating the programs and policies needed to fulfill the mission and vision.
elements: The chief executive(s) and home care leadership are identified by title and name, and their collective accountabilities are described in written documents.
Home care leadership, including the chief executive(s), is responsible for defining the organization’s mission, vision, and values and communicates them to all staff.
Home care leadership is responsible for creating the policies and procedures necessary to carry out the mission and vision.
Home care leadership ensures that policies and procedures are followed.

statement: Home care leaders plan with community leaders and leaders of other organizations to meet the community’s health care needs.
elements: Home care leaders meet with recognized community leaders to develop and revise strategic and operational plans to address community needs. The strategic plan is based on a comprehensive evaluation of internal and external environmental factors and includes the goals and objectives required to fulfill the home health care service’s mission.
Home care leaders plan with the leaders of other health care organizations in the community.

Home care leaders seek the input of individual and group stakeholders, including patients/service users, their families, staff, and, where possible, the wider community, as part of the home care organization’s strategic and operational planning. The strategic plan is guided by the organization’s mission and vision.
The strategic plan addresses all clinical and non-clinical services and programs, spans a period of three to five years, and is reviewed regularly.
The home care organization participates in community education on health promotion and disease prevention.

statement: The leaders transform the approved strategic plan into an operational plan.
elements: Leaders translate the center’s goals and objectives into operational plans with defined projects, clearly delineated responsibilities, required resources, and time frames.
Leaders communicate the plans to all staff.
