The long-term care organization has a policy and procedure for registering outpatient services.

statement: The long-term care organization considers residents’ clinical needs and informs them of unusual delays for diagnostic and/or treatment services.
elements: Residents are informed of any delays in care and/or treatment.
Residents are informed of the reasons for the delay and available alternatives consistent with their clinical needs.
The information on unusual delays and reasons for the delay are documented in the resident’s health record.

The long-term care organization leaders address all variations contributing to waits, delays, and cancellations that impact smooth and timely flow of residents through long-term care organization departments.

statement: The long-term care organization has a process for managing resident flow throughout the long-term care organization, including admission and registration, as applicable to the care setting.
elements: The long-term care organization leaders implement strategies to maximize the efficiency of resident flow by ensuring the following: • Availability of appropriate beds • Enough medical staff at all times, with no significant variation during holidays and weekends • Properly trained staff • Expected movement and progression throughout care areas • Availability of nonclinical services
The long-term care organization has an admission process for residents, regardless of their origin of arrival, including a registration process for residents who do not require admission.
The flow processes are reviewed for effectiveness, and process improvements are identified and implemented. Admission to the Long-Term Care Organization

statement: At admission to the long-term care organization, the resident and family or caregiver receive education and orientation to the ward and organization, the proposed care, any expected costs for care, and expected outcomes of care.
elements: On admission, the resident and family receive education and orientation to the ward and organization, including information about fire safety, safety, security, and infection prevention and control measures.
The resident and family receive information on the proposed care, treatment, and/or services.
The resident and family receive information on the expected outcomes of care.
The resident and family receive information on any expected costs related to proposed care, treatment, and/or services.
Residents and families are informed as to the scope of general consent, if used by the long-term care organization.
The long-term care organization defines, in writing, how general consent is documented in the resident’s health record, if used by the long-term care organization.
All residents receive information about the likelihood of students and trainees participating in care processes.

statement: The long-term care organization designs and carries out processes to provide continuity of resident care services in the organization, coordination among health care practitioners, and access to information related to the resident’s care. P
elements: The leaders of departments and services design and implement processes that support continuity and coordination of care, including the following: • Palliative care and hospice care services • Diagnostic services and treatment services • Physical/occupational therapy and skilled nursing • Dementia care programs • Other organizations and other care settings
The resident’s health record(s) is available to those practitioners who are authorized to have access and need it for care of the resident.
The resident’s health record(s) is up to date to ensure communication of the latest information.
The most responsible physician assesses the need for transfer and matches the resident’s condition with the unit’s admission criteria.
The most responsible physician assesses the transfer requirements, both staff and equipment.
The physician and nurse at the receiving unit assess the resident at arrival to ensure safe and smooth handover.
The resident’s health record(s) or a summary of resident care information is transferred with the resident to another service or unit in the long-term care organization.

A summary of information transferred with the resident includes the following: • Reason for admission • Significant findings • Diagnosis • Procedures performed • Medications • Other treatments • Condition at transfer • Code status (for example, do not resuscitate)
Continuity and coordination of care processes are supported using tools such as care plans, guidelines, or other such tools.

statement: During all phases of resident care, a qualified individual is identifed as responsible for the resident’s care.
elements: A qualified individual(s) responsible for coordinating the resident’s care is identified in the resident’s health record and is available through all phases of care.
There is a process for transferring responsibility for coordinating care from individual to individual.
The transfer of care and coordination is documented in the health record.
The process identifies how these individuals assume the transferred responsibility and document their participation or coverage.

statement: The long-term care organization develops and implements a discharge planning and referral process based on the resident’s readiness for discharge. P
elements: The long-term care organization develops and implements a discharge planning and referral process that starts at the beginning of care and is based on the resident’s readiness for discharge.
The resident’s readiness for discharge is determined using relevant criteria or indications that ensure resident safety.
The discharge planning process includes the need for both support services and continuing medical needs.
Residents not directly referred or transferred are provided with the name and locations of a site(s) for continuing care.

Residents not directly referred or transferred are provided with instructions, in writing, on when to return to the organization for continued care, if appropriate, and when and how to obtain urgent care.
Residents, family as appropriate, and staff involved in the resident’s care participate in discharge planning.
Discharge planning and instructions are documented in the resident record and provided to the resident in writing.

statement: The long-term care organization’s discharge planning process addresses resident and family education and instruction related to the resident’s need for continuing care and services.
elements: Resident and family education and instruction are related to the resident’s ongoing need for continuing care and services.
Residents and families are provided with a complete list of medications to be taken at home.

Residents and families are educated about the safe and effective use of all medications, potential side effects, and prevention of potential interactions with over-the-counter medications and/or food.
Residents and families are educated about proper diet and nutrition.
Residents and families are educated about pain management as appropriate.
Residents and families are educated about safe and effective use of medical equipment and rehabilitation techniques as appropriate.

Resident and family education is documented in the resident’s health record and includes the following: • The information and education provided • The delivery method of the information and education (for example, in writing, verbally, by

statement: A complete discharge summary is prepared for all residents, a copy of which is in the resident’s health record.
elements: A qualified individual prepares the discharge summary.

The discharge summary contains at least the following: • Reason for admission, diagnoses, and comorbidities • Significant physical and other findings • Diagnostic and therapeutic procedures performed • Medications administered during admission with the potential for residual effects after the

statement: The long-term care organization has a process for managing and following up with residents who notify long- term care staff that they intend to leave against medical advice. P
elements: There is a process for managing residents who notify staff that they are leaving against medical advice.
The process includes informing the resident of the medical risks of incomplete treatment.
The resident is discharged according to the long-term care organization discharge process.
If the primary care practitioner of a resident leaving against medical advice is known and has not been involved in the process, the practitioner is notified.
The process is consistent with applicable laws and regulations, including reporting cases of infectious disease and cases in which residents may be a threat to themselves or others.

When consistent with regional laws and regulations, the long-term care organization develops a process for allowing residents to leave the organization during the planned course of treatment on an approved pass for a defined period of time.

statement: The long-term care organization has a process for managing residents who leave the organization against medical advice without notifying long-term care staff. P
elements: There is a process for managing residents who leave the long-term care organization against medical advice without notifying long-term care staff, including the following: • Residents who leave with and without informing long-term care organization staff • Residents who have absconded • Residents receiving complex treatment who do not complete or do not return for treatment

statement: The long-term care organization develops a process to transfer residents to other health care organizations based on their status and continuing care needs as well as the receiving organization’s ability to meet residents’ needs. P
elements: The long-term care organization develops a transfer process based on criteria to address residents’ needs for continuing care.

The transfer process addresses how and when responsibility for continuing care is moved to another practitioner or setting and determines that the receiving organization can meet the needs of the resident to be transferred.
The receiving provider/organization accepts, in writing, the transfer of responsibility for the resident’s care.
The long-term care organization communicates with all potential receiving organizations, and necessary arrangements are made whenever applicable.
The most responsible physician ensures that all the resident’s health needs during transportation are met, and the transfer occurs at the most suitable time.
The transfer process identifies who is responsible for monitoring the resident during transfer and the staff qualifications required for the type of resident being transferred.
The transfer process identifies the medications, supplies, and medical equipment required during transport.
The transfer process includes a follow-up mechanism that provides information about the resident’s condition upon arrival to the receiving organization.
The transfer process addresses situations in which transfer is not possible.

statement: The referring organization gives the receiving organization a written summary of the resident’s clinical condition and interventions provided, and the process is documented in the resident’s health record.
elements: A resident clinical summary document is transferred with the resident and includes at least the following: • The resident’s clinical condition or status • The procedures and other interventions provided • The resident’s continuing needs
Transferred residents’ health records identify the name of the receiving health care organization and the name of the individual agreeing to receive the resident.
Transferred residents’ health records contain documentation or other notes as required by the transferring organization’s policy.
Transferred residents’ health records state the reason(s) for transfer and any special conditions related to transfer.

statement: The long-term care organization’s transportation services comply with relevant laws and regulations and meet requirements for quality and safe transport.
elements: A qualified and licensed paramedic is assigned to the long-term care organization’s transportation services.
The process for referring and/or discharging residents includes the most responsible physician assessing transportation needs for residents who may require assistance.

Transportation services, including contracted services, and transport vehicles owned by the organization meet relevant laws and regulations and the organization’s requirements for quality and safe transport.

All vehicles used for transportation, contracted or organization owned, comply with the infection prevention and control program and have appropriate medical equipment, supplies, and medications to meet the needs of the resident being transported.
The transportation provided or arranged is appropriate to the resident’s needs and condition.
There is a process in place to monitor the quality and safety of transportation provided or arranged by the organization, including a complaint process.

statement: All residents cared for by the long-term care organization have their health care needs identified through an assessment process defined by the organization.
elements: The long-term care organization defines the minimum content of assessments for residents for each clinical discipline that performs assessments and specifies the required elements of the history and physical examination.

The long-term care organization policy defines, in writing, the assessment process and its scope and content for all categories of residents and its scope and content for all disciplines (physicians, nurses, physiotherapists, social service, and others).
Only qualified individuals permitted by licensure, applicable laws and regulations, experience, or certification perform the assessments.

The long-term care organization identifies the information to be documented for the assessments with an aim to identify the general resident’s medical and nursing needs and a provisional diagnosis so that it can initiate care and treatment.

statement: Each resident’s initial assessment includes a health history and physical examination as well as an evaluation of psychological, spiritual/cultural, social, and economic factors.
elements: All residents have an initial assessment that includes a health history and physical examination consistent with the requirements defined in organization policy.

The assessment includes the following: • List of the resident’s current medications and known allergies • System review • Present illness • Pain (screening followed by assessment if required) • Risk for fall (screening followed by assessment if required) • Physical status and functionality (screening followed by assessment if required)

The following assessments may also be performed as appropriate to the resident’s needs: • An initial psychological assessment as indicated by the resident’s condition • An initial social and economic assessment, as indicated by the resident’s needs • An initial spiritual/religious and cultural assessment, as indicated by the resident’s needs

The long-term care organization policy identifies, in writing, criteria for those resident groups and populations it serves that require additions or modifications to their initial assessment and documented in the resident’s health record. The special resident population includes but is not limited to the following: • Residents in severe or chronic pain • Children • Frail elderly (pressure ulcers, geriatric depression screening) • Suspected victims of abuse, neglect, and domestic violence • Drug abuse • Psychiatric disorders • Terminally ill and dying residents • Residents with dental, hearing, eye, or speech defects
Initial nursing assessment is completed within 8 hours and medical assessment is completed within 24 hours of admission.
The initial assessment results in an initial or provisional diagnosis or diagnoses that require treatment and monitoring.

statement: The long-term care organization has a process for accepting initial medical assessments conducted in a physician’s private office or other outpatient or inpatient settings prior to admission.
elements: Initial medical assessments conducted prior to admission to the long-term care organization are less than or equal to 30 days old.

For assessments less than or equal to 30 days old, any significant changes in the resident’s condition since the assessment or “no change” are documented in the resident’s health record at the time of admission.
If the medical assessment is greater than 30 days old at the time of admission, the health history is updated and the physical examination repeated.
The findings of all assessments performed outside the long-term care organization are reviewed and/or verified at the time of admission.

statement: Residents are screened for nutritional status, functional needs, and other special needs and are referred for further assessment and treatment when necessary.
elements: The long-term care organization policy defines, in writing, the evidence-based screening tools developed by qualified individuals.

Qualified individuals (licensed dietitian) develop screening tools to identify residents who require further nutritional assessment, and the criteria are implemented consistently throughout the long- term care organization where needed.

Nutritional assessment, as defined in the policy, includes but is not limited to the following: • Body mass index (BMI) • Eating habits • Food allergies • Need for therapeutic diet • Physical difficulties with eating and drinking and the need for any assistive devices

A qualified dietitian does the following: • Develops a nutritional plan of care • Highlights food-drug interactions to clinical staff • Makes recommendations related to resident dietary needs • Monitors residents who are on nil per os (NPO), or nothing by mouth, orders • Educates other health staff, residents, and families • Ensures documentation in the health record for nutritional activities
Residents at risk of nutritional problems receive a nutritional assessment within 24 hours of referral.
The long-term care organization policy defines, in writing, the screening tools developed by qualified individuals (licensed therapists).

Qualified individuals develop screening tools to identify residents who require further functional assessment, and the criteria are implemented consistently throughout the long-term care organization where needed.
Residents who need a functional assessment are referred for such an assessment within 24 hours of referral.
When the need for additional specialized assessments is identified, residents are referred in the long- term care organization or outside the organization.
Specialized assessments conducted in the long-term care organization are completed and documented in the resident’s health record.

statement: All residents whose condition, diagnosis, or situation may indicate they are at risk of pain are screened for pain and assessed when pain is present.
elements: All residents are screened for pain at times and intervals defined by long-term care organization policy, and the screening is documented.

When pain is identified, a comprehensive assessment of the resident’s pain is performed. The assessment process clearly defines the following: • Requirements for a comprehensive pain assessment and management • Role of staff in pain assessment • Items included in pain assessment (intensity, type, duration, frequency, location, and progress) • Pain-relieving measures, including medications and their dosage, frequency, and route
Residents are reassessed for pain after any pain management interventions as defined by the long-term care organization policy.

statement: All residents are reassessed at intervals based on their condition and treatment to determine their response to treatment and to plan for continued treatment or discharge. P
elements: Long-term care organization policy defines, in writing, how often various members of the health care team reassess residents and other circumstances requiring reassessment, including the following: • Defined intervals by various members of the care team, including physicians, nurses, and other

statement: Qualified individuals conduct the assessments and reassessments. P
elements: Individuals qualified to conduct resident assessments and reassessments are identified and have their responsibilities defined in writing.
Only those individuals permitted by licensure, applicable laws and regulations, or certification perform resident assessments.
Qualified individuals conduct assessments and reassessments, including physicians, nurses, and other clinical staff (for example, therapists, social workers).

statement: Medical, nursing, and other individuals and services responsible for resident care collaborate to analyze and integrate resident assessments and prioritize the most urgent/important resident care needs.
elements: Resident assessment data and information are analyzed and integrated.
Those responsible for the resident’s care participate in the process.
Resident needs are prioritized based on assessment results.

statement: Laboratory services are available to meet resident needs, and all such services meet applicable local and national standards, laws, and regulations.
elements: Laboratory services have a clearly defined scope of services and meet applicable local and national standards, laws, and regulations.

Laboratory services are available to meet the needs related to the long-term care organization’s mission and resident population, the community’s health care needs, and emergency needs, including after normal hours.
Experts in specialized diagnostic areas are contacted when needed.
All laboratory staff have the required qualifications, training, and experience to perform and interpret tests.
Outside sources are selected based on an acceptable record and compliance with laws and regulations.

statement: A qualified individual is responsible for overseeing and supervising the point-of-care testing (POCT) program. P
elements: The person responsible for managing the laboratory services, or a designee, oversees and supervises the POCT program.
Staff performing POCT are qualified, trained, and competent to do so.
The POCT program includes a defined process for reporting abnormal test results, including critical results.
The POCT program includes quality control performance, documentation, and evaluation and maintenance of POCT devices.
The POCT program is monitored, evaluated, and included in quality improvement activities.

statement: Laboratory results are available in a timely way as defined by the long-term care organization. P
elements: The long-term care organization establishes the expected report time for results.
The long-term care organization measures the timeliness of reporting of urgent/emergency test results.
Laboratory results are reported within a time frame to meet resident needs, and the long-term care organization takes corrective action.
Laboratory results are monitored as part of the quality program.

statement: Procedures for collecting, identifying, handling, safely transporting, and disposing of specimens are established and implemented. P
elements: Procedures are established and implemented for ordering tests.

Procedures are established and implemented for collecting and identifying specimens to ensure the performance and documentation of the following: • Date and time of specimen receipt • Check for proper packaging • Check for specimen quality and quantity • Check for adequate specimen labeling • Check for request completion • Check for label/request discrepancies • Any suboptimal specimen clearly highlighted in the reported results • Final decision (accept/reject)
Procedures are established and implemented for transporting, storing, and preserving specimens.
Procedures are established and implemented for receiving and tracking specimens.

Procedures are established and implemented for disposing of specimens that comply with national laboratory safety standards, as well as the long-term care organization safety and infection control plan, to ensure disposal using prick-proof containers and leak-proof bags.
The procedures are followed when using reference/contract laboratory services.

The procedures are followed when using contracted laboratory services. The laboratory develops a services/specimen collection manual that includes available tests and services on and off site (reference laboratory) and their turnaround times.

statement: Established norms and ranges are used to interpret and report clinical laboratory results.
elements: The laboratory establishes reference ranges for each test performed.
The range is included in the health record when test results are reported.
Ranges are provided when contracted laboratory services perform tests.
Ranges are appropriate to the long-term care organization and resident demographics.
The laboratory reviews and updates ranges as needed.

statement: Radiology and diagnostic imaging services are available to meet resident needs, and all such services meet applicable local and national standards, laws, and regulations.
elements: Radiology and diagnostic imaging services meet applicable local and national standards, laws, and regulations.

Radiology and diagnostic imaging services are available to meet the needs related to the long-term care organization’s mission and resident population, the community’s health care needs, and emergency needs, including after normal hours.
The long-term care organization maintains a roster of experts in specialized diagnostic areas and ensures that the roster is accessible to staff who need it.

Outside sources are selected based on recommendations of the individual responsible for radiology and diagnostic imaging services and have an acceptable record of timely performance and compliance with applicable laws and regulations.

statement: Radiology and diagnostic imaging study results are available in a timely way as defined by the long-term care organization. P
elements: The long-term care organization establishes the expected report time for diagnostic imaging results.
Radiology and diagnostic imaging study results are reported within a time frame to meet resident needs.

The radiology reports follow the following format and content: • Identification of the resident • Type of procedure • Identification of the ordering physician • Reporting date and time • Identification of the reporting radiologist
The long-term care organization measures the timeliness of reporting urgent/emergency study results.
When radiology and diagnostic imaging results are not reported within the expected time frame, the long-term care organization takes corrective action.
Radiology results are monitored as part of the quality program.

statement: Uniform care of all residents is provided and follows applicable laws and regulations. P
elements: The long-term care organization’s department/service leaders collaborate to provide uniform care processes.
The provision of uniform care reflects local and regional laws and regulations.

Uniform resident care is provided and meets the following requirements: • Access to and appropriateness of care and treatment do not depend on the resident’s ability to pay or the source of payment. • Access to appropriate care and treatment by qualified practitioners does not depend on the day of the week or time of day. • Acuity of the resident’s condition determines the resources allocated to meet the resident’s needs.

statement: There is a process to integrate and coordinate the care provided to each resident, including a uniform process for prescribing resident orders.
elements: Care planning and care delivery are integrated and coordinated among settings, departments, and services.

The long-term care organization develops and implements a uniform, written process for prescribing written/documented resident orders that includes identifying orders that may be received verbally, via telephone, and via text.
The long-term care organization process includes medication and non-medication orders.

The long-term care organization has a process that defines situations for accepting verbal or telephone orders and staff who are allowed to accept such orders, including the time frame for order authentication.
Complete verbal orders, including telephone orders, are documented and read back by the receiver and confirmed by the individual giving the order.
Diagnostic imaging and clinical laboratory test orders include a clinical indication/rationale when required for interpretation.
Orders are prescribed only by those qualified to do so.
Orders are found in a uniform location in health records.

statement: Clinical and diagnostic procedures and treatments are carried out and documented as ordered, and the results or outcomes are recorded in the resident’s health record.
elements: Procedures and treatments are carried out as ordered and documented in the resident’s health record.
The person requesting and the reason for requesting the procedure or treatment are documented in the resident’s health record.
The results of procedures and treatments performed are documented in the resident’s health record.

statement: An individualized plan of care is developed and documented for each resident.
elements: The care for each resident is planned by the responsible physician, nurse, and other health care practitioners within 24 hours of admission.
The plan of care is individualized based on the resident’s initial assessment data and identified needs and is documented in the resident’s health record.
The plan of care contains the measurable goals/desired outcomes toward discharge.

The interdisciplinary team updates or revises the plan of care based on any changes in the resident’s condition identified from the reassessment of the resident by the health care practitioners; the updates or revisions are documented in the resident’s health record.
The results or conclusions of any resident care team meetings or other collaborative discussions are documented in the resident’s health record.
The plan of care is provided to each resident and documented in the resident’s health record by the health care practitioners providing the care.
The resident and family are involved in the planning process when applicable.

statement: Professional practice guidelines, laws, and regulations guide the care of high-risk residents and the provision of high-risk services. P
elements: Long-term care leaders identify the following high-risk residents and services provided by the organization: • Comatose residents • Residents on life support • Residents with a communicable disease • Immunosuppressed residents • Administration of blood and blood products • Residents receiving dialysis • Residents in restraints • Vulnerable resident populations, including frail elderly, dependent children, and residents at risk

group: Recognition of Changes to Resident Condition
statement: Clinical staff are trained to recognize and respond to changes in a resident’s condition.
elements: The long-term care organization develops and implements a systematic process for staff recognition of and response to a resident whose condition appears to be worsening.
The long-term care organization develops and implements documented age-specific criteria describing early warning signs of a change or deterioration in a resident’s condition.
The long-term care organization develops and implements a process for identifying when and how to seek further assistance.
Based on the organization’s early warning criteria, staff seek additional assistance when they have concerns about a resident’s condition.
The long-term care organization informs the resident and family how to seek assistance when they have concerns about a resident’s condition.
The long-term care organization evaluates the activities and outcomes of the rapid response teams as part of the quality program.

statement: Resuscitation services are available throughout the long-term care organization.
elements: Resuscitation services are available and provided to all residents 24 hours a day, every day, throughout all areas of the organization.
The long-term care organization has a policy and procedure for cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) across all the organization areas.
Medical equipment for resuscitation and medications for basic and/or advanced life support are standardized and available based on the needs of the population served.
The long-term care organization has standardized crash carts readily available in all areas suitable to the resident populations.

In all areas of the organization, basic life support is implemented immediately upon recognition of cardiac or respiratory arrest, and advanced life support is implemented in fewer than five minutes (if applicable to the services provided).
The long-term care organization evaluates the activities and outcomes of the resuscitation services as part of its quality program.
The long-term care organization conducts regular drills covering all patient care areas and shifts and evaluates the activities and roles and responsibilities during the drill.

group: Management of Residents at Risk of Suicide or Self-Harm
statement: The long-term care organization has a process for identifying residents at risk of suicide and self-harm. P
elements: The long-term care organization establishes criteria for which residents are screened for suicide and self-harm, as clinically indicated.

The long-term care organization uses evidence-based tools to assess residents for suicidal ideation based on established criteria. Residents who screen positive are identified as “at risk” of suicide and/or self-harm based on the established criteria.

The long-term care organization conducts an environmental risk assessment that identifies features in the physical environment that could be used in a suicide or self-harm attempt; the organization takes necessary action to minimize the risk(s).
The long-term care organization implements protocols and procedures to mitigate the risk of resident suicide and/or self-harm.
The long-term care organization follows written policies and procedures for counseling and follow-up care at discharge for residents identified as at risk of suicide and self-harm.

The long-term care organization monitors implementation and effectiveness of protocols and procedures for preventing resident suicide and/or self-harm by analyzing data regarding self-harm, incidents, or deaths.
Staff are trained in screening tools and suicide and self-harm risk-reduction protocols and procedures.
Suicide screenings and assessments are documented in the resident’s health record or in accordance with laws and regulations when applicable.

statement: The long-term care organization implements policies and procedures for the safety of clinical alarm systems.
elements: Long-term care organization leaders implement a written management program for alarm signals that pose a risk to resident safety.
The program identifies the most important alarm signals to be managed based on the risk to resident safety.

Long-term care organization leaders develop and implement strategies for managing alarms that include the following: • Clinically appropriate settings for alarm signals • Situations in which alarm signals can be disabled • Circumstances under which alarm parameters must be reviewed and/or changed (for example, when the resident’s condition significantly changes, when residents are transferred to different

statement: A variety of food choices, appropriate for the resident’s nutritional status and consistent with their clinical care, is available.
elements: A variety of food choices or nutrition, consistent with the resident’s condition, care, and needs, is regularly available.
Prior to residents being fed, there is an order for food in the resident’s health record based on their nutritional status and needs.
Food preparation, handling, storage, and distribution are safe and timely, and special requests are met and guided by professional guidelines.
The distribution of food is timely, and special requests are met.
When a family provides food, they are educated about the resident’s diet limitations.
Food provided by family or others is stored under proper conditions to prevent contamination.
Residents are encouraged to maintain adequate fluid intake.

statement: Residents at nutritional risk receive nutrition therapy.
elements: Residents assessed at nutrition risk receive nutrition therapy.
A collaborative process is used to plan, deliver, and monitor nutrition therapy.
The resident’s response to nutrition therapy is monitored and documented in the health record.

statement: Residents are supported in managing pain effectively. P
elements: Based on the scope of services provided, the long-term care organization has processes for identifying residents in pain.
When pain is an expected result of planned treatments, procedures, or examinations, residents are informed about the likelihood of pain and options for pain management.
Residents in pain receive care according to pain management guidelines and resident goals for pain management.
Based on the scope of services provided, the long-term care organization has processes for communicating with and educating residents and families about pain.
Based on the scope of services provided, the long-term care organization has processes for educating staff about pain.

statement: The long-term care organization provides end-of-life care for the dying resident that addresses the resident’s and family’s needs and optimizes the resident’s comfort and dignity.
elements: The long-term care organization has a process for assessing and managing the needs of residents receiving end-of-life care.
All clinical staff are educated about the unique needs of residents and their families at the end of life.
The resident’s and family’s health care needs are identified as appropriate to their religious and cultural preferences.
End-of-life care addresses the dying resident’s symptoms, conditions, and health care needs as indicated by their assessment.
The long-term care organization provides care and support for residents and their family, considering their personal, spiritual/religious, and cultural preferences.
End-of-life care addresses the resident’s pain.
End-of-life care addresses the resident’s and family’s psychosocial, emotional, cultural, and spiritual needs, as appropriate, regarding dying and grieving.
The resident and family are involved in care decisions.

statement: The long-term care organization engages residents and families in decisions related to its operational aspects as appropriate.
elements: The long-term care organization has a process for engaging with residents and their families to develop processes and procedures that allow for deinstitutionalization of its operations.
The long-term care organization regularly monitors processes and procedures for collecting resident and family feedback.
The long-term care organization identifies goals and implements improvements based on the data collected.

statement: The long-term care organization has a process for providing evidence-based care to residents with dementia or memory issues.
elements: The long-term care organization establishes criteria for which residents are screened for dementia, as clinically indicated.
The long-term care organization uses evidence-based tools to assess residents for dementia based on established criteria.
The long-term care organization develops, implements, and uses clinical pathways and/or protocols for residents with dementia.
Staff are trained to use the clinical pathways and/or protocols for residents with dementia.

statement: The long-term care organization develops and implements a process to improve the accuracy of resident identification. P
elements: At least two resident identifiers that do not include the use of the resident’s room number or location in the organization are used to identify the resident and to label elements associated with the resident’s care and treatment plan.
Residents are identified before diagnostic procedures, treatments, and other procedures.
The long-term care organization ensures that residents are correctly identified in special circumstances, such as the comatose or confused resident.
Residents are actively involved in the process of resident identification.

statement: The long-term care organization develops and implements a process to improve the effectiveness of verbal and/ or telephone communication among caregivers. P
elements: Complete verbal orders are documented and read back by the receiver and confirmed by the individual giving the order.
Complete telephone orders are documented and read back by the receiver and confirmed by the individual giving the order.

statement: The long-term care organization develops and implements a process for reporting critical results of diagnostic tests. P
elements: The long-term care organization defines, in writing, critical results that may represent urgent or emergent life-threatening values for diagnostic tests.

The long-term care organization develops a formal reporting process, used throughout the organization, that identifies how critical results of diagnostic tests are reported/communicated to health care practitioners and the expected time frame for reporting the critical results.

The long-term care organization policy on critical results of diagnostic tests includes the following: • Identification of results that should be reported as critical • Identification of the notified party • Identification of the means of communicating critical results • Description of the sequence of conveying the result and read-back

The long-term care organization identifies what information is documented in the health record, including the following: • Date and time of notification • Resident identification • Test results • Documentation of read-back • Identification of the notifying person • Identification of the notified person
Critical test results are documented and read back by the receiver and confirmed by the individual giving the result.
The long-term care organization monitors compliance with the defined time frames for reporting and acting on critical results, and it documents actions taken when time frames are not met.

statement: The long-term care organization develops and implements a process for handover communication. P
elements: Standardized critical content is communicated between health care practitioners during handovers of resident care.
Standardized forms, tools, or methods that support a consistent and complete handover process are used.
The long-term care organization collects, analyzes, tracks, and trends data for resident safety events related to handovers.

Data from adverse events resulting from incomplete or inadequate handover communications are tracked and used to identify ways in which handovers can be improved, and improvements are implemented. Goal 3: Improve the Safety of High-Alert Medications

statement: The long-term care organization develops and implements a process to improve the safety of high-alert medications. P
elements: The long-term care organization identifies in writing its list of high-alert medications including but not limited to the following: • Controlled medications and narcotics • Neuromuscular blockers • Chemotherapeutic agents • Concentrated electrolytes (for example, hypertonic sodium chloride, concentrated potassium

statement: The long-term care organization develops and implements a process to improve the safety of look-alike/sound- alike medications. P
elements: The long-term care organization identifies in writing its list of look-alike/sound-alike medications.
The long-term care organization develops and implements a uniform process for managing look-alike/ sound-alike medications.
The long-term care organization reviews and, as necessary, revises its list of look-alike/sound-alike medications at least annually.

The long-term care organization takes actions to prevent errors involving look-alike/sound-alike medications, including the following, as applicable: • Educating health care professionals about look-alike/sound-alike medications at orientation and

statement: The long-term care organization adopts and implements evidence-based hand hygiene guidelines to reduce the risk of health care–associated infections. P
elements: The long-term care organization has adopted current evidence-based hand hygiene guidelines.
The long-term care organization implements a hand hygiene program throughout the organization.
Handwashing and hand disinfection procedures are used consistently with hand hygiene guidelines throughout the long-term care organization.

statement: The long-term care organization develops an approach to reduce the risk of resident harm resulting from falls. P
elements: The long-term care organization screens all residents for fall risk, using evidence-based screening tools appropriate for the residents being served as well as for those residents whose condition, diagnosis, situation, or location may put them at risk for falls.

Evidence-based interventions to reduce fall risk are implemented for those identified residents, situations, and locations in the long-term care organization assessed to be at risk, and the interventions are documented.

The long-term care organization implements a process for initial assessment of residents for fall risk and reassessment of residents when indicated by a change in resident condition or environment, among others.
Measures are implemented to reduce fall risk for those assessed to be at risk. Resident interventions are documented.
Measures are monitored for results, both successful fall injury reduction and any unintended related consequences.
Policies and/or procedures support continued reduction of risk of resident harm resulting from falls in the long-term care organization.

statement: Medication use in the long-term care organization is organized to meet resident needs, complies with applicable laws and regulations, and is under the direction and supervision of a licensed pharmacist or other qualified professional. P
elements: A written document identifies how medication use is organized, managed, and overseen throughout the long-term care organization. The document addresses the following (as applicable): • Planning • Selection and procurement • Storage • Ordering/prescribing and transcribing • Preparing and dispensing • Administration • Monitoring • Medication error and adverse event reporting • Evaluation

The medication management interdisciplinary team (medical, nursing, and management staff) is called the pharmacy and therapeutics committee and develops the policies and processes for overseeing and ensuring uniform medication management in the long-term care organization.
All settings, services, and individuals who manage medication processes have an adequate number of staff qualified by education, training, and experience as per the organizational structure.
A licensed pharmacist or other qualified individual directly supervises the activities of the pharmacy or pharmaceutical service and ensures compliance with applicable laws and regulations.
The long-term care organization (pharmacy and therapeutics committee) documents at least one review of the medication management system annually.
A uniform medication dispensing and distribution system is available and complies with applicable laws and regulations.
Appropriate sources of drug information are readily available to those involved in medication use (including books, manuals, and online subscriptions to drug information resources).

statement: The long-term care organization develops and implements a program for the prudent use of antibiotics based on the principle of antibiotic stewardship. P
elements: The long-term care organization develops and implements a program for antibiotic stewardship that involves infection prevention and control professionals, physicians, nurses, pharmacists, trainees, residents, families, and others.

The program is based on scientific evidence, accepted practice guidelines, and local laws and regulations and, at a minimum, includes the following: • Documentation indicating that the scope of the antimicrobial stewardship program includes all

statement: The long-term care organization has a method for overseeing its medication list, including how listed medications are used, a method for ensuring medications for prescribing or ordering are stocked, and a process for obtaining medications not stocked or not normally available to the organization or for times when the pharmacy is closed. P
elements: There is a list (formulary) of medications, by both brand name and generic name, stocked in the long-term care organization or readily available from outside sources, and the list is reviewed at least annually.
An interdisciplinary team develops policy and procedure criteria for selecting, approving, and procuring non-formulary medications within an acceptable time frame,

The process for developing and monitoring the list (unless determined by regulation or an authority outside the long-term care organization) includes representation from health care practitioners involved in ordering, dispensing, administering, and resident-monitoring processes in the organization.
There is a process for obtaining medications during the night or when the pharmacy is closed and for obtaining medications not stocked or not normally available to the organization.

statement: Medications are properly and safely stored. P
elements: Medications are stored under conditions suitable for product stability, including medications stored on individual resident care units and ambulances, as applicable.
Controlled substances are accurately accounted for according to applicable laws and regulations.
There is a process for managing medications or products requiring special handling, such as hazardous medications, radioactive medications, and investigational medications.

There is a policy and procedure on proper storage and temperature control of medications including controlled substances, nutrition products, and free medical samples (from the point of receipt until the point of administration).
Medications and chemicals used to prepare medications are accurately labeled with contents, expiration dates, and warnings.
All medication storage areas, including medication storage areas on resident care units and ambulances (as applicable), are periodically inspected to ensure that medications are stored properly.
Medication storage areas have controlled access and are protected from loss or theft throughout the long-term care organization. Only authorized individuals have access to stored medications.
Medications are stored according to manufacturer’s recommendations (temperature, light, humidity, sanitation).
The long-term care organization stores (locks) narcotics and psychotropic and other controlled medications in accordance with relevant laws and regulations.

statement: Emergency medications are available; uniformly stored; monitored every shift; replaced when used, damaged, or out of date; and secure, including when stored outside the pharmacy.
elements: Emergency medications are immediately available in the units where they will be needed or are readily accessible in the long-term care organization to meet emergency needs (as applicable to the services provided) based on the current Saudi Heart Association recommendations.

The long-term care organization establishes and implements a process for how emergency medications are uniformly stored; maintained; monitored every shift; replaced when used, damaged, or out of date; and protected from loss or theft.
Access to emergency medications does not require a specific individual or keys to unlock the emergency cart.
Emergency medications are monitored and replaced in a timely manner after use or when expired or damaged.
The long-term care organization uses a risk-based approach to identify and implement strategies to improve the efficiency and accuracy of medication administration during emergency resuscitation.

statement: The long-term care organization has a process for recalled, expired, and/or outdated medications. P
elements: The long-term care organization establishes and implements a process for receiving and acting on notifications of medication recalls.
The process includes identifying, retrieving, and returning, or safely and properly destroying, medications recalled by the manufacturer, supplier, or regulatory agency.
The recall process includes medications compounded in the long-term care organization using products that have been recalled.
The long-term care organization notifies residents who received recalled medication and provides them with appropriate guidance.
The long-term care organization has a process to inform health care providers about the recall and advise them on alternative treatments, if necessary.
The process includes documenting all actions taken related to the medication recall, including the recall notice, affected lot numbers, actions taken, communications sent, and any responses received.
The process includes maintaining on file all drug recall memoranda from the Saudi Food and Drug Authority, manufacturers, and/or other relevant legal bodies.
The long-term care organization establishes and implements a process for using unopened, expired medications and outdated medications.

The long-term care organization isolates expired medications from the rest of the medication stock to prevent accidental use or distribution and clearly labels them as “expired” until they are removed or properly destroyed.
The process includes documenting all actions taken related to expired medications.
The long-term care organization establishes and implements a process for destroying medications known to be expired or outdated.

statement: The long-term care organization identifies and documents the resident’s current list of medications and reviews the list against all new medications prescribed or dispensed. P
elements: The long-term care organization identifies the information needed to reconcile current and newly ordered medications.

The resident’s health record contains a list of current medications taken prior to admission, and this information is made available to the resident’s health care practitioners and the pharmacy as needed.
Initial medication orders are compared to the list of medications taken prior to admission, according to the long-term care organization’s established process.
A medication review is conducted when there are changes to the resident’s level of care, unit, or health care practitioner service, including the discharge planning process for medication management.

statement: The long-term care organization identifies those qualified individuals permitted to prescribe or order medications.
elements: Only those permitted by the long-term care organization and by relevant licensure, laws, and regulations prescribe or order medications.
The long-term care organization establishes and implements a process to place limits, when appropriate, on the prescribing or ordering practices of individuals.
Individuals permitted to prescribe and order medications are known to the pharmaceutical service or others who dispense medications.

statement: The long-term care organization identifies safe prescribing, ordering, and transcribing practices and defines the elements of a complete order or prescription. P
elements: The long-term care organization establishes, implements, and trains staff on a process for the safe prescribing, ordering, and transcribing of medications in the facility.
All orders and prescriptions contain the name of the drug, the dose, and the frequency and route of administration. A diagnosis, condition, or indication for use exists for each medication ordered.

Complete medication orders or prescriptions include as appropriate to the order the following elements: • The data necessary to accurately identify the resident (See also IPSG.1.) • When generic or brand names are acceptable or required (See also MMU.2.) • Specific guidelines for using PRN (pro re nata, or “as needed”) orders that include indications for use and detailed directions for overlapping orders, such as more than one medication for pain • The types of orders that are weight based or otherwise adjusted, such as for children, frail elderly,

statement: Medications are prepared and dispensed in a safe, clean environment.
elements: Medication preparation and dispensing adhere to laws, regulations, and professional standards of practice.
Medications are prepared and dispensed in clean, uncluttered, safe, and functionally separate areas with appropriate medical equipment and supplies.

Staff preparing/compounding sterile products/medications are trained and competent in the principles of medication preparation and aseptic techniques and are provided resources to support the medication preparation process.
During preparation, staff visually inspect the medication for particulates, discoloration, or other loss of integrity.
Guidelines for using single-use and multidose vials are identified and implemented in the medication processes.
All open multidose medications are labeled with open date, expiration date, initials, and time.
Medications stored, prepared, and dispensed from areas outside the pharmacy (for example, resident care wards) comply with the same cleanliness measures required in the pharmacy.

statement: A system is used to safely dispense medications in the right dose to the right resident at the right time.
elements: The long-term care organization dispenses medications and maintains records in accordance with laws and regulations, licensure, and professional standards of practice.
Medications are dispensed in the most ready-to-administer form available.
The system supports accurate and timely dispensing and documentation of dispensing practices.

After preparation, medications not immediately administered are labeled with the name of the medication, the dosage/concentration, the date prepared, the expiration date, and two resident identifiers.
Medication quality issues are reported to the Saudi Food and Drug Administration, as required.

statement: Qualified individuals permitted to administer medications are identified and document the medications administered in the resident’s health record.
elements: The long-term care organization identifies those individuals, by job description or the privileging process, authorized to administer medications.
The long-term care organization places limits, when appropriate, on the medication administration of individuals.
Medication administration is recorded for each dose.

statement: Medication administration includes a process to verify the medication is correct based on the medication prescription or order.
elements: Medications are verified with the prescription or order.
The dosage of the medication is verified with the prescription or order.
The route of administration is verified with the prescription or order.
Residents are informed about the medications that they are going to be given and have an opportunity to ask questions.
Medications are administered as prescribed on a timely basis and noted in the resident’s health record.

statement: Policies and procedures govern medications brought into the long-term care organization by the resident or family and medication prescribed for resident self-administration. P
elements: The long-term care organization establishes and implements a process that addresses any medications brought in by the resident/family and sample medications. The process is documented, including the following: • Receipt (noting how the organization received the medication from the resident or other source) • Identification • Labeling • Storage • Control and distribution

The long-term care organization performs a risk assessment for any medications brought in by the resident/family that addresses where and when the medication was obtained and how the medication was stored at home.
The long-term care organization establishes and implements a process to govern resident self- administration of any medications.
The long-term care organization establishes and implements a process to govern the management, use, and documentation of any medication brought in by the resident/family.

The long-term care organization educates residents and families involved in self-administration and documents in the resident’s health record the following: • Medication name, type, and reason for use • Medication administration, including process, time, frequency, route, and dose • Anticipated actions and potential side effects of the medication administered • Monitoring of the medication’s effects • Proper storage of the medication

statement: Policies and procedures govern medications brought into the long-term care organization as samples. P
elements: The long-term care organization establishes and implements a process for receiving, identifying, labeling, storing, and controlling and distributing medication samples.

The long-term care organization performs a risk assessment for any sample medications brought in by the resident or provided by other sources that addresses where and when the medication was obtained and how the medication was stored prior to arrival.
The long-term care organization establishes and implements a process to govern the availability, management, use, and documentation of medication samples.

statement: Medication effects on residents are monitored. P
elements: Medication effects on residents are monitored and documented when appropriate.
Medication adverse effects on residents are monitored and documented.
The long-term care organization uses a standardized process for recording in the resident health record any adverse effects related to medication use and reporting adverse effects to the prescriber.
The long-term care organization uses a standardized process for reporting adverse medication effects as part of its quality improvement and resident safety program.
Adverse effects are reported as identified by the process in the time frame required.
The long-term care organization conducts a root cause analysis of data when adverse drug event patterns or undesirable trends occur.
The long-term care organization uses the analysis of adverse drug-related events to improve its medication use processes.

All adverse drug reactions are documented in the resident’s health record, and the long-term care organization reports all serious or unexpected adverse drug reactions to the Saudi Food and Drug Authority.

statement: The long-term care organization establishes and implements a process for reporting and acting on medication errors and near misses (or close calls). P
elements: The long-term care organization defines medication error and near miss.

The long-term care organization establishes and implements a process for reporting and acting on medication errors and near misses, including the following steps: • Identifying medication errors and near misses • Timely reporting of medication errors and near misses • Notifying in a timely way the treating physician and Saudi Food and Drug Authority and

statement: The long-term care organization is responsible for providing processes that support the residents’ and families’ rights during care.
elements: Long-term care leaders work collaboratively to protect and advance a statement of resident and family rights and responsibilities.
Long-term care leaders implement resident and family rights as identified in laws and regulations and through policies and procedures.
Long-term care leaders protect resident and family rights in relation to the cultural practices of the community or individual residents served.
Long-term care leaders protect the resident’s right to identify who the resident wishes to participate in care decisions.

The long-term care organization has a process to determine the resident’s preference, and in some circumstances the resident’s family’s preference, in determining what information regarding the resident’s care would be provided to family or others and under what circumstances.
All health care practitioners are trained on the processes for and their role in supporting resident and family rights and participation in care.

statement: The long-term care organization respects, protects, and promotes resident rights and seeks to reduce physical, language, cultural, and other barriers to access and delivery of services and provides information and education to residents and families in a language and manner they can understand.
elements: The department/service leaders and staff of the long-term care organization identify their resident population’s most common and challenging barriers to accessing and receiving care.
The department/service leaders develop and implement a process to overcome or limit barriers to access to care and their impact on service delivery for residents seeking care.
Information about aspects of the resident’s medical care and treatment is provided in a manner and language the resident understands.
Information about resident rights and responsibilities is provided to each resident in writing, in a language the resident understands.
The statement of resident rights and responsibilities is posted or otherwise available from staff at all times.

statement: The long-term care organization provides care that supports resident dignity, is respectful of the resident’s personal, spiritual/religious, and cultural values and beliefs, and responds to requests for spiritual and religious observance.
elements: Staff provide care that is respectful and considerate of the resident’s dignity and self-worth.
The resident’s spiritual and cultural beliefs and the resident’s values and preferences are respected.
The long-term care organization responds to complex requests related to religious or spiritual support, advice, or care that meet the needs of different populations served.

statement: The long-term care organization establishes a process to ensure resident privacy and confidentiality of care and information and allows residents the right to have access to their health information within the context of existing law and culture. P
elements: Staff meet resident expectations and needs for privacy, when expressed, during care and treatment.
A resident’s expressed need for privacy is respected for all clinical interviews, examinations, procedures/treatments, and transport.
Confidentiality of resident information is maintained according to laws and regulations.
The long-term care organization has a process for residents to grant permission for the release of information not covered by laws and regulations.
The long-term care organization has a process for providing residents with access to their health information within the context of existing laws, regulations, and culture.
Access to health information is timely, and cost does not prevent access to this information for the purpose of maintaining continuity of care.

statement: The long-term care organization protects residents’ possessions from theft or loss.
elements: The long-term care organization has a process described in a policy and has determined its level of responsibility for residents’ possessions.
Residents receive information about the long-term care organization’s responsibility for protecting personal belongings.

Residents’ possessions are safeguarded when the long-term care organization assumes responsibility or when the resident is unable to assume responsibility through a process that outlines the following: • Where resident belongings are kept • Who is responsible for obtaining the required signatures on the related form when receiving and

statement: Residents are protected from physical assault, and populations at risk are identified and protected from additional vulnerabilities.
elements: The long-term care organization develops and implements a process to protect all residents from assault.

The long-term care organization identifies its vulnerable populations, as applicable to its scope of services: • Disabled and chronically ill • Socioeconomically disadvantaged • Elderly/frail • Children/adolescents • Racial/ethnic minorities • Sexual minorities

The long-term care organization performs a vulnerable population risk assessment annually, at a minimum, to identify the following: • Vulnerable populations the long-term care organization serves • Risks associated with each vulnerable population • Resources to support the care, treatment, and services of these vulnerable populations, including

statement: Residents and families are engaged in all aspects of their medical care and treatment through education and participation in care, treatment decisions, and care processes. P
elements: The long-term care organization supports and promotes resident and family engagement through participation in care processes and decision making to the extent they wish.

Participation in the care process includes educating residents and families about how they can actively participate in their care decisions and their choices related to medical conditions, any confirmed diagnosis, and the planned care and treatment(s).
Residents are informed about the expected outcomes of care and treatment.
Residents are told of any unanticipated outcomes, including adverse events, that may have occurred during their care and treatment.
The long-term care organization facilitates a resident’s request to seek a second opinion without fear of compromise to their care within or outside the organization.

statement: The long-term care organization informs residents and families about their rights and responsibilities to refuse or discontinue treatment, withhold resuscitative services, and forgo or withdraw life-sustaining treatments. P
elements: The long-term care organization identifies its position on withholding resuscitative services and forgoing or withdrawing life-sustaining treatments.
The long-term care organization’s position conforms to its community’s religious and cultural norms and any legal or regulatory requirements.

The long-term care organization informs residents and families about their rights to refuse or discontinue treatment and the organization’s responsibilities related to such decisions. Resident and family choices are respected, and relevant discussion is documented in the resident’s health record.
The long-term care organization informs residents about the consequences of their decisions.
The long-term care organization informs residents about available care and treatment alternatives.

The long-term care organization guides health care practitioners on the ethical and legal considerations in carrying out resident wishes regarding treatment alternatives and supports the health care team when the resident’s wishes do not align with the health care team members’ personal, spiritual/religious, and cultural beliefs.

statement: The long-term care organization supports the resident’s right to pain assessment and management and respectful, compassionate care at the end of life.
elements: The long-term care organization respects and supports the resident’s right to pain assessment and management.
The long-term care organization respects and supports the dying resident’s right to assessment and management of their needs.
The long-term care organization’s staff understand the personal, spiritual/religious, and cultural influences on the resident’s experiences with pain.
The long-term care organization’s staff understand the personal, spiritual/religious, and cultural influences on the resident’s experiences with death and dying.

statement: The long-term care organization informs residents and families about its process to receive and act on complaints, conflicts, and differences of opinion about resident care and the resident’s right to participate in these processes. P
elements: Residents are informed about how to voice complaints, conflicts, and differences of opinion.
The long-term care organization investigates complaints, conflicts, and differences of opinion.
Complaints, conflicts, and differences of opinion that arise during the care process are resolved.
Residents and families participate in the resolution process as appropriate.

The long-term care organization develops a written policy that addresses disclosure of clinical errors to residents that includes, at a minimum, the following: • Definition of clinical errors • Who is responsible for notifying a resident/family of a clinical error • Entities that must be notified when applicable • Disclosure of clinical errors
The long-term care organization leaders take quality improvement and strategic actions based on trended data (for example, quarterly and annually).

statement: The long-term care organization allows residents and/or families to meet as an organized group to discuss issues of importance related to resident care and services provided by the organization.
elements: The long-term care organization offers a forum for residents to meet in a group to express and resolve issues and concerns.
Residents are informed of meetings and invited to attend.
When residents are not able to attend group meetings, family members or individual advocates can attend in the resident’s place.

statement: General consent for treatment, if obtained when a resident is admitted to the organization, is clear in its scope and limits.
elements: Residents and families are informed as to the scope of a general consent when used by the long-term care organization, and this information is also conveyed in non-verbal language.
The long-term care organization’s general consent process honors the resident’s and family’s rights to withhold informed consent.
The long-term care organization defines how a general consent, when used, is documented in the resident’s health record.
Whether or not a general consent is obtained, all residents and families are informed about which tests and treatments require informed consent.
Whether or not general consent is obtained, all residents are informed about the likelihood of students and trainees participating in care processes.

statement: Resident informed consent is obtained through a process defined by the long-term care organization and carried out by trained staff in a manner and language the resident can understand. P
elements: The long-term care organization develops and implements a clearly defined informed consent process and trains designated staff in that process.

The long-term care organization’s policy identifies what information must be discussed and documented as part of the consent process, including at least explanation of the nature of the treatment or procedure, expected benefits and risks, alternative courses of action, and likely consequences of not undergoing the treatment.
The long-term care organization’s policy identifies what tests, procedures, and treatments require consent.
The long-term care organization educates residents about the informed consent process and when informed consent is required.
Residents learn about the process for granting informed consent in a manner and language that they understand.
Residents give informed consent consistent with the process.
There is a uniform documentation of informed consent.
The identity of the individual providing the information to the resident and family is documented in the resident’s health record.

statement: The long-term care organization establishes a process, in the context of existing law and culture, for when others can grant consent.
elements: The long-term care organization develops and implements a process for when others can grant informed consent.
The process respects law, culture, and custom.
The resident’s health record lists the individual(s) granting consent.

statement: The long-term care organization provides an education program based on its mission, services, and resident population, and health care practitioners collaborate to provide education.
elements: The long-term care organization plans education consistent with its mission, services, and resident population.
There is an established structure or mechanism and adequate resources for education throughout the long-term care organization.

The long-term care organization provides the resident with the necessary education and information in language easily understood by the resident/family about the following, where applicable: • The primary illness and all possible complications • Infection prevention and control practices, emphasizing basic handwashing • Required treatments and procedures • Appropriate, safe use of medical equipment or appliances • The care (for example, breathing exercises, diet, wound care, and so on) • Necessary medications and their frequency, potential side effects, and food-drug interactions • Follow-up clinical appointments • How to carry out activities of daily living • Community resources for additional care and how to access emergency services if necessary
Resident and family education is provided collaboratively when indicated.
Those who provide the education have the subject knowledge and communication skills to do so.
Those who provide the education have the resources and time to do so.

statement: Each resident’s educational needs and ability and willingness to learn are assessed and recorded in the resident’s health record.
elements: Each resident’s and, when appropriate, family’s educational needs are assessed and recorded in the resident’s health record. This must include, at a minimum, the following: • The language the resident prefers for education • The form(s) the resident prefers for education • Who should receive education in addition to the resident (for example, spouse, caregiver) • Any known barriers to learning, including literacy skills, readiness and ability to learn, and

statement: Education methods consider the values and preferences of the resident and their family and allow sufficient interaction among the resident, family, and staff for learning.
elements: The education process considers the values and learning preferences of the resident and their family.
There is a process to verify that residents and families receive and understand the education provided.
Those who provide education encourage residents and their families to ask questions and speak up as active participants.
Verbal information is reinforced with written material related to the resident’s needs and consistent with the learning preferences of the resident and their family when needed. Section II:

statement: The long-term care organization complies with relevant laws, regulations, building and fire safety codes, and facility inspection requirements.
elements: Long-term care leadership and the facility management and safety structure understand and comply with national and local laws, regulations, building and fire safety codes, a valid Saudi Civil Defense license, and other requirements applicable to the organization’s facilities (for example, Ministry of Municipal and Rural Affairs’ long-term care building requirements, Saudi building code, discharges to drainage systems, safe disposal of waste).
