Long-term care leadership and the facility management and safety structure document corrective actions taken to address conditions in external facility reports or citations from inspections by national and local authorities, including a valid Saudi Civil Defense report and action plan as applicable.
Long-term care leaders plan and budget for replacing or upgrading facilities, systems, and equipment to meet applicable requirements and to continue operating a safe, secure, and effective facility.
Long-term care leaders approve and allocate budgeted resources or implement alternative strategies to reduce risks until resources can be allocated.

When the organization is located in a multiuse building, long-term care leaders obtain evidence of compliance with relevant laws, regulations, codes, facility inspection reports, utility maintenance requirements, and other requirements related to shared systems and building issues.

statement: A qualified individual oversees the facility management and safety structure to reduce and control risks in the care environment.
elements: Oversight and direction of the facility management and safety structure are assigned to a facility management and safety program director qualified by experience and training (for example, bachelor’s degree in engineering science), and evidence of their experience and training in facility management and safety is documented.
The program director is assisted by qualified staff (for example, safety officer) as required, according to the size and complexity of the long-term care organization’s services.

The qualified individual is responsible for the following: • Providing ongoing consultation to all departments • Making recommendations to long-term care leaders about space, medical equipment, technology, and other resources to support the facility management and safety structure • Planning and developing facility management and safety programs for safety, security, hazardous materials and waste, fire safety, medical equipment, utility systems, emergency and disaster

statement: The long-term care organization develops and documents a comprehensive risk assessment based on facility management and safety risks identified throughout the organization, prioritizes the risks, establishes goals, and implements improvements to reduce and eliminate risks.
elements: The risk assessments from all the following facility management and safety programs are integrated to develop and document a comprehensive, facilitywide risk assessment, at least annually: • Safety • Security • Hazardous materials and waste • Fire safety • Medical equipment • Utility systems • Emergency and disaster management • Construction and renovation
The long-term care organization prioritizes the risks, identifies goals and improvements, and implements improvements to reduce and eliminate risks.
The long-term care organization evaluates the effectiveness of the improvements, and based on the results, the organization updates the applicable facility management and safety programs.

statement: Data are collected and analyzed from each of the facility management and safety programs to reduce risks in the environment, track progress on goals and improvements, and support planning for replacing and upgrading facilities, systems, and equipment.
elements: Monitoring data are collected and analyzed for each of the facility management and safety programs and used to reduce risks in the environment and support planning for replacing or upgrading facilities, systems, and equipment.
Monitoring data for the facility management and safety programs are documented and integrated into the organization’s quality improvement and resident safety program.

The individual who oversees the facility management and safety structure provides monitoring data reports that address each program’s effectiveness and progress on goals to long-term care leaders on a quarterly basis, and leaders take action.

The individual who oversees the facility management and safety structure provides the comprehensive facilitywide risk assessment and planned and implemented improvements to long-term care leaders at least annually.
Long-term care leaders provide an annual report to the governing entity on the effectiveness of the facility management and safety programs, and the governing entity takes action.

statement: The long-term care organization develops and implements a program to provide a safe physical facility through inspection and planning to reduce risks. P
elements: The long-term care organization develops and implements a written program to provide a safe physical facility.

The long-term care organization applies safety measures and equipment where needed to ensure resident and staff safety. Measures include but are not limited to the following: • Non-slip floors, resident support or grab bars, help bell or call system, and lock system that

statement: Warning and directive signs are posted inside the long-term care organization’s building as appropriate. P
elements: Warning signs are posted as appropriate in the long-term care organization’s building and include the following: • Signs for radioactive materials, including warning signs for pregnant women • Signs for wet floors during cleaning • “No Smoking” signs • Signs and warning lights for x-ray room(s) • Signs to restrict cellular phones in sensitive areas as appropriate

Directive signs are posted as appropriate in the long-term care organization’s building and include the following: • Signs indicating the organization’s name and main entrances/exits • Directional signs • Signs to direct staff and residents to the different services in the organization • Fire exit signs • Signs to identify floor level in staircases and in front of elevators • Signs to instruct staff, residents, and visitors in restricted areas • Signs for populations with special needs

statement: The long-term care organization develops and implements a program to provide a secure environment for residents, families, staff, and visitors. P
elements: The long-term care organization develops and implements a written program to provide a secure environment.

The long-term care organization develops policies and procedures to support the security program, including but not limited to the following: • Prevention of the abduction of children and neonates • Lost and found items • Safekeeping of resident belongings • Involvement of police in cases of trauma, motor vehicle accidents, and medico-legal incidents • Incidents of violence (violence code) • Abuse of women and children
A security risk assessment is conducted and documented at least annually throughout the facility, and security risks are identified and prioritized from the risk assessment.
The security program identifies all security risk areas and restricted areas and ensures that they are monitored and kept secure through security personnel or alternative security systems.

The organization assigns qualified individuals to maintain security whose number is proportional to the organization’s size, number of entrances, and availability of supporting security systems. The security personnel have a dress code and conduct organizationwide security rounds, and significant findings are documented. The security personnel have written job descriptions.

The security program ensures that all staff, students, trainees, contract workers, volunteers, vendors, and individuals associated with independent business entities are identified. The program ensures that the organization’s staff, temporary employees, and contractor staff wear identification badges.
The security program includes educating relevant staff on response to security alerts and roles and responsibilities during a security-related event.

The organization’s security personnel have their roles clearly defined for the external and internal disaster plan and no-smoking policy. The security personnel are oriented about their scope of work and job description, emergency codes, and fire safety.
The organization conducts regular exercises with staff to evaluate the security program and integration with local responders.
The long-term care organization identifies goals and implements improvements in the security program, and monitors data to ensure that security risks are reduced or eliminated.

statement: The long-term care organization develops and implements a program for managing hazardous materials and waste. P
elements: The long-term care organization develops and implements a written program for managing hazardous materials and waste.

A hazardous materials and waste risk assessment is conducted and documented at least annually throughout the facility, and risks related to hazardous materials and waste are identified and prioritized from the risk assessment.
The long-term care organization identifies goals, implements improvements, and monitors data to ensure that risks related to hazardous materials and waste are reduced or eliminated.

statement: The long-term care organization’s program for managing hazardous materials and waste includes inventorying, handling, storing, and using hazardous materials. P
elements: The hazardous materials and waste program identifies the type, quantities, and locations of hazardous materials and waste, and has a complete inventory, updated at least annually, to reflect changes in the hazardous materials used and stored in the organization. Each department has a current list of its hazardous materials, with details that cover purpose of use, responsible person, and permitted quantity.
The hazardous materials and waste program establishes and implements procedures for safely handling, storing, and using hazardous materials.

The hazardous materials and waste program establishes and implements the proper protective equipment for handling and using hazardous materials, which is available in each department with hazardous materials.
The hazardous materials and waste program establishes and implements proper and clear labeling of hazardous materials, consistent with information from the safety data sheets (SDS).
The hazardous materials and waste program establishes and implements procedures for managing spills and exposures, including using proper protective equipment and reporting spills and exposures.
Information about safely handling and managing spills of and exposures to hazardous materials and waste are up-to-date and available at all times.

statement: The long-term care organization establishes and implements a program for fire safety, including ongoing assessment of risks and compliance with national and local codes, laws, and regulations for fire safety. P
elements: The long-term care organization develops and implements a written program for fire safety to protect all occupants of the organization’s facilities from fire, smoke, and non-fire emergencies.

The long-term care organization performs and documents an ongoing fire safety risk assessment related to at least the following, and fire safety risks are identified and prioritized from the risk assessment: • Fire separations • Smoke separations/compartments • Hazardous areas (and spaces above the ceilings in those areas) such as soiled linen rooms, trash

statement: The fire safety program includes early detection, suppression, and containment of fire and smoke. P
elements: The fire safety program includes equipment/systems for early detection and alarm notification of fire and smoke. The equipment/systems are functioning and regularly inspected per civil defense guidelines.
Elevators, if present in the facility, are connected to the fire alarm system.

The fire safety program includes equipment/systems for suppressing fire, including at least the following measures: • Procuring materials such as curtains and drapes that are fire retardant • Separating all dangerous materials or flammables from heat-generating areas • Installing fire-rated walls as appropriate, especially in high-risk areas such as the laboratory,

statement: The fire safety program includes measures to ensure safe exit from the facility in case of fire and non-fire emergencies. P
elements: The fire safety program includes the safe exit from the facility through free and unobstructed access to exits.

The fire safety program includes clearly visible exit signage that is understandable to the long- term care organization’s occupants. Measures to ensure safe exit include but are not limited to the following: • Fire exits are available and are properly located in the organization. • Fire exits are unlocked. • Fire exits are unobstructed. • Fire exits have panic hardware. • Fire exits are fire resistant. • There are no obstructions to exits, fire extinguishers, fire alarm boxes, emergency or fire blankets, safety showers, and eye wash stations.
The fire safety program includes lighting for emergency exit corridors and stairs.

statement: All fire safety equipment and systems, including devices related to early detection, alarm notification, and suppression, are inspected, tested, and maintained. P
elements: All fire safety equipment and systems, including those for smoke and fire detection and suppression, are inspected, tested, and maintained according to manufacturers’ recommendations or as required by local codes, laws, and regulations, whichever sets the more stringent requirement. Fire extinguishers are inspected monthly to assess functionality, and the fire-alarm system is functioning and regularly inspected, with preventive maintenance carried out per civil defense guidelines.
Inspection, testing, and maintenance of all fire safety equipment and systems are documented, including results and corrective actions.
Any deficiencies identified in fire safety equipment and systems are immediately corrected, or interim measures are implemented to reduce fire risk until deficiencies can be fully corrected.

statement: The long-term care organization involves staff in regular exercises to evaluate the fire safety program. P
elements: Based on a scheduled training program, personnel in all departments, including the night shift and weekend shift, are trained in the fire safety program (including the use of fire extinguishers) and participate in drills to evaluate the fire safety program at least annually, or more frequently when required by laws and regulations or other authorities. Fire drills conducted during different shifts test at least the following elements: • Use of Rescue, Alarm, Confine, Extinguish/Evacuate (RACE) procedure • Use of Pull, Aim, Squeeze, Sweep (PASS) procedure • The ability to contain the fire when it starts • Staff performance in the event of fire • Evacuation procedures • Shutoff of oxygen and electricity supplies at the right time
Clinical staff are knowledgeable of the fire safety program and can describe how to bring residents to safety.
A full fire drill is conducted for the internal disaster plan once a year, and this drill is evaluated.
Results of exercises to evaluate the fire safety program are documented, and staff who do not pass are reeducated and retested on the fire safety program.

statement: The fire safety program includes limiting smoking by staff and residents to designated non–resident care areas of the facility. P
elements: The fire safety program ensures a strict “no smoking” policy within the long-term care facility.
The program applies to residents, families, visitors, and staff.
The program identifies who may grant resident exceptions for smoking and when those exceptions apply.
Smoking is prohibited in all areas under construction or renovation.

statement: The long-term care organization develops and implements a program for managing medical equipment throughout the organization. P
elements: The long-term care organization develops and implements a written program for managing medical equipment throughout the facility.
A medical equipment risk assessment is conducted and documented at least annually throughout the organization, and medical equipment risks are identified and prioritized from the risk assessment.
The long-term care organization identifies goals, implements improvements, and monitors data to ensure that medical equipment risks are reduced or eliminated.

statement: The medical equipment program includes inspection, testing, preventive maintenance, and documenting the results. P
elements: The medical equipment program addresses organization-owned and non-organization-owned medical equipment in the organization, such as equipment that is leased, rented, brought in by physicians and other health care practitioners, brought in by residents, and so on.

The medical equipment program includes the following: • A comprehensive inventory of all medical equipment • Testing according to use and manufacturers’ requirements • Documentation of results, including history record for the maintenance schedule, failure

statement: The long-term care organization has a process for monitoring and acting on medical equipment hazard notices, recalls, reportable incidents, problems, and failures. P
elements: The long-term care organization has a process for monitoring and acting on medical equipment and implantable device hazard notices, recalls, reportable incidents, problems, and failures.
The long-term care organization reports any deaths, serious injuries, or illnesses that are a result of medical equipment through the organization’s incident and adverse event reporting process.
The medical equipment management program addresses the use of any medical equipment with a reported problem or failure, or that is the subject of a hazard notice or under recall.

statement: The long-term care organization develops and implements a program for managing utility systems throughout the organization. P
elements: The long-term care organization develops and implements a written program for managing utility systems throughout the facility, including how to handle failure or interruption of the following utilities: • Normal power • Emergency power, power from sockets in critical areas, and lamps in critical areas • Elevators • Water supply • Reverse osmosis plant • Air-conditioning fan coil unit (FCU) in resident rooms • Air-conditioning air handling unit (AHU) in operating rooms • Medical gas system • Sewer lines • Boilers • Telephone service (public address exchange) • Intercom, nurse call, and overhead paging • Fire alarm

The long-term care organization conducts and documents the utility systems risk assessment at least annually throughout the facility and prioritizes the utility systems risks identified from the risk assessment.
The long-term care organization identifies goals, implements improvements, and monitors data to ensure that the utility systems risks are reduced or eliminated.

statement: The utility systems program includes inspection, testing, and maintenance to ensure that utilities operate effectively and efficiently to meet resident, staff, and visitor needs. P
elements: The long-term care organization inventories and maps the current distribution of its utility systems components. Technical utility drawings show the distribution lines for all utilities and how to control them centrally and peripherally so that lines can be controlled as required in case of emergency.

The long-term care organization identifies, in writing, the activities and intervals for inspecting, testing, and conducting preventive and routine maintenance on all operating components of the utility systems on the inventory, based on criteria such as manufacturers’ recommendations, risk levels, and organization experience. This work is conducted by qualified and trained staff. The preventive maintenance program covers at least the following: • Electrical system • Elevators • Refrigerators/freezers • Air conditioning system • Medical gas system • Medical suction • Domestic water system, including water pumps and fire hydrants • Fire water system, including fire pumps • Boilers • Plumbing • Low current and communication system • Pavement and ground • Facility building and ancillaries

The utility systems program supports electrical safety by including measures such as identification of electrical outlets for voltage (110/220V), source of electrical outlets (essential/prime), earthing system in rooftop and sockets used for medical equipment, and annual thermal inspection of circuit breakers in the following: • Operating rooms • Laboratory • Critical care units • Alarm system • Blood storage • Medical gas system
The long-term care organization updates or replaces utility systems and components when the need for improvement is identified through inspection, testing, and maintenance.

The utility systems program includes preventive maintenance for heating, ventilating, and air- conditioning (HVAC) that covers at least the following: • Periodic preventive maintenance plan (PPM) plan is supported by trained and specialized staff/ contractor. • Maintenance records are maintained. • The HVAC is maintained to control air quality by cleaning/replacing filters, cleaning diffuser, and cleaning ducts. • HEPA filters are monitored monthly, and the results are documented. • Air change per hour is maintained per national and international guidelines (for example, American Society of Heating, Refrigerating, and Air-Conditioning Engineers [ASHRAE]).
The long-term care organization labels utility system controls to facilitate partial or complete emergency shutdowns.

statement: The long-term care organization’s utility systems program ensures that essential utilities, including power, water, and medical gases, are available at all times and that alternative sources for essential utilities are established and tested. P
elements: The long-term care organization identifies the areas and services at greatest risk when essential utilities (including power, water, and medical gas) become unavailable.

The long-term care organization ensures backup availability/continuity of essential utilities (including power, water, and medical gas) 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. Backup/emergency power covers at least the following critical areas: • Operating rooms • Alarm system • Fire pumps • Blood storage • Medical gas system • Refrigerators in the pharmacy, laboratory, medication storage, and kitchen • Elevators • Escape routes/corridors • Morgue • Medication storage
The long-term care organization assesses for and reduces the risks of interruption, contamination, and failure of essential utilities (including power, water, and medical gas).

The long-term care organization tests the availability and quality of the alternative source(s) of water at least annually or more frequently if required by local laws and regulations or conditions of the source of water. Emergency plans are tested in simulation. The organization documents the results of the tests.

The long-term care organization tests alternative sources of power at least quarterly or more frequently if required by local laws and regulations, manufacturers’ recommendations, or conditions of the source of power. The organization documents the results of the tests. For emergency generators, if applicable, the long-term care organization ensures readiness by ensuring at least the following measures: • Generator(s) is maintained periodically, and results are documented. • Weekly tests are done without load for 10 minutes. • Load tests are done monthly for 30 minutes and achieve 30% of the nameplate load. (The 30-minute time frame does not include the time it takes to warm up or cool down.) • Full load tests are done every three years on external load. • Generator(s) starts normally without load for 10 minutes.
When emergency sources of power require a fuel source, the organization establishes and stores on site the necessary amount of fuel.

statement: The organization ensures proper maintenance of the medical gas system.
elements: The medical gas system is regularly tested for pressure, leaks, and functionality of valves, alarms, pressure gauge, and switches.

Policies and procedures ensure effective use of medical gas system. Areas covered include, but are not limited to, the following: • Following the procedures for taking any part of the system offline • Commissioning and testing new branching or modifications • Following the procedure for ordering and filling liquid oxygen • Documenting all repairs/alterations/tests/filling logs/consumption
Compressed medical air is regularly tested for humidity and purity.
The central medical gas station is in a safe, secure place.
Medical gas outlets in resident care areas are clearly marked with the type of gas and have different connections according to the gas type.
All medical gas pipes are clearly marked and labeled for the contents and direction of gas flow.

In case of gas pipe repairs or new extensions, outlets are tested for type of gas to ensure the correct type is delivered through the new pipe. Testing results are recorded and maintained with engineering and the unit manager.
The organization keeps enough standby oxygen and medical air cylinders for 48 hours of average consumption.
The gas cylinders are regularly tested for gas type, amount, and leaks.
Emergency shutoff valves are available in all units and clearly marked with areas/rooms affected.
The long-term care organization assigns responsibility for closing shutoff valves to a well-trained individual(s) available in the unit concerned.

The long-term care organization has adequate medical gas outlets in resident care areas as appropriate, and these outlets are error-proof medical gas outlets in accordance with German Institute for Standardization (DIN) standards related to gases, piping, outlets, and valves.

statement: The long-term care organization develops, maintains, and tests an emergency management program to respond to internal and external emergencies and disasters that potentially can occur in the organization and community. P
elements: The long-term care organization develops, evaluates, and maintains a written emergency and disaster management program that identifies its response to likely emergencies and disasters, including the following items: • Determining the type, likelihood, and consequences of hazards, threats, and events • Identifying the structural and nonstructural vulnerabilities of the organization’s resident care environments and how the organization will perform in the event of an emergency or disaster • Planning for alternative sources of power and water in emergencies and disasters (See also

statement: When planning for construction, renovation, and demolition projects, or maintenance activities that affect resident care, the organization conducts a preconstruction risk assessment. P
elements: When planning for construction, renovation, or demolition projects, or maintenance activities that affect resident care, the organization conducts a preconstruction risk assessment (PCRA) for at least the following: • Air quality • Infection prevention and control (See also PCI.11.) • Utilities • Noise • Vibration • Hazardous materials and waste • Fire safety • Security • Emergency procedures, including alternate pathways/exits and access to emergency services • Other hazards that affect care, treatment, and services
The long-term care organization takes action based on its assessment to minimize risks during construction, renovation, and demolition projects, and maintenance activities that affect resident care.

The organization develops and implements a policy for safety and security of residents, staff, and visitors during construction, renovation, or demolition that includes at least the following: • Safety and security instructions • Education of contractors • Proper isolation of construction and renovation sites • Procedure for eliminating the risks of fire and spread of dust • Penalties imposed on contractors for violating the policy • Safety rounds on construction/renovation sites by facility management and safety and infection

statement: Staff and others are trained and knowledgeable about the long-term care organization’s facility management and safety programs and their roles in ensuring a safe, effective facility.
elements: All staff receive annual training and testing on each facility management and safety program to ensure that they can safely and effectively carry out their responsibilities, and testing results are documented.

Training on the facility management and safety programs includes vendors, contract workers, volunteers, students, trainees, and others, as applicable to the individuals’ roles and responsibilities, and as determined by the organization.
Staff can describe and/or demonstrate their roles in response to a fire.
Staff can describe and/or demonstrate actions to eliminate, minimize, or report safety, security, and other risks.

Staff can describe and/or demonstrate precautions and procedures for handling and managing medical gases and hazardous materials and waste, as applicable to the staff member’s role and responsibilities.
Staff can describe and/or demonstrate procedures for and their roles in internal and community emergencies and disasters.

group: Governance of the Long-Term Care Organization
statement: The structure and authority of the long-term care organization’s governing entity are described in bylaws, policies and procedures, or similar documents. P
elements: The structure and authority of the long-term care organization’s governing entity is described in a written document, bylaws, and/or policies and procedures with those responsible for governance of the organization identified.
The governing entity ensures that the long-term care organization has an effective organizational structure displayed in an organizational chart with titles (or names) and reporting relationships.
The document(s) describes when and how the authority of the governing entity and the chief executive can be delegated. The governing entity approves delegation of authority.
The governing entity is evaluated annually, and the results are documented.

group: Governance of the Long-Term Care Organization
statement: The operational responsibilities and accountabilities of the governing entity are described in a written document(s). P
elements: The governing entity approves the long-term care organization’s strategic plans, operational plans, policies, and procedures, scope of services, and medical staff by-laws, and approves, periodically reviews, and makes public the organization’s mission statement.
The governing entity approves the long-term care organization’s capital and operating budget(s) and allocates other resources required to meet the organization’s mission.
The governing entity approves the long-term care organization’s participation in health care professional education and research and in the oversight of the quality of such programs.
The governing entity appoints and annually evaluates the long-term care organization’s chief executive(s), and the evaluation is documented.

group: Governance of the Long-Term Care Organization
statement: The governing entity approves the long-term care organization’s program for quality and resident safety and regularly receives and acts on reports of the quality improvement and resident safety program. P
elements: The governing entity annually approves the long-term care organization’s program for quality and resident safety.
The governing entity ensures monitoring, evaluating, and continuously improving the outcome of the quality and resident safety plans and programs.
The governing entity at least quarterly receives and acts on reports of the quality improvement and resident safety program, including reports of adverse and sentinel events.
Minutes reflect actions taken and any follow-up on those actions.

statement: A chief executive(s) is responsible for operating the long-term care organization and complying with applicable laws and regulations. P
elements: The education and experience of the chief executive(s) matches the requirements in the position description.
The chief executive(s) manages the long-term care organization’s day-to-day operations, including those responsibilities described in the position description.
The chief executive(s) recommends policies, strategic plans, and budgets to the governing entity.
The chief executive(s) ensures compliance with approved policies.
The chief executive(s) ensures compliance with applicable laws and regulations.
The chief executive(s) responds to any reports from inspecting and regulatory agencies.
The chief executive(s) is accountable to the governing entity for the clinical performance and professional conduct of the long-term care organization’s staff.
The chief executive(s) actively participates in supporting the safety of residents, staff, and visitors (for example, through leadership safety rounds, review of reported incidents).
The chief executive(s) ensures the availability of adequate resources (for example, human resources, equipment, supplies, medications).
The chief executive(s) ensures all physical properties are kept in a good state of repair and operating condition.
The chief executive(s) ensures efficient utilization of all resources.

statement: Long-term care leaders are identified and collectively responsible for defining the organization’s mission and creating the programs and policies needed to fulfill the mission.
elements: The chief executive(s) and long-term care leaders are identified by title and name, and their collective accountabilities are described in written documents.
Long-term care organization leaders are qualified in health care management by education, training, or experience, and their roles and responsibilities are outlined in their job descriptions.

Long-term care organization leaders form an executive management body (for example, an executive management committee), led by the chief executive officer or equivalent, and includes the medical director, nursing director, quality director, selected heads of the departments, and other senior staff members as required. • Functions and meetings of the long-term care leaders are outlined in specific terms of reference, and they meet at least 10 times per year to evaluate the progress of the overall strategic plan, the quality and safety of care provided to residents, and all other clinical and nonclinical issues related to the organization’s day-to-day operation. • Discussions, decisions, and actions taken by the organization’s leaders are documented in formal meeting minutes.

Long-term care leaders establish medical and nonmedical organizationwide committees and address the formation and terms of reference, including committee functions, chairperson designation and members’ selection with their titles, quorum, meeting frequency, resolution process in case of disagreement, and meeting minutes’ distribution. The committees include but are not limited to the following: • Pharmacy and therapeutics • Morbidity and mortality • Infection prevention and control • Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) • Credentialing and privileging • Operating room • Tissue review • Blood utilization review • Quality and resident safety • Medical records review • Resident rights • Utilization review
The committee chairs submit their respective committee’s accomplishments and unresolved issues annually to executive management, and recommendations are implemented.

Long-term care leaders are responsible for defining the organization’s values and mission, ensuring the following: • The mission reflects the scope of services provided by the long-term care organization and the health needs of the population served. • The mission is communicated to the staff. • The mission is displayed to residents, visitors, and the wider community.

Long-term care leaders are responsible for creating the policies and procedures necessary to carry out the mission. The organizationwide policies and procedures are identified and combined into a manual that includes the following: • A brief general description of the long-term care organization • The organization’s vision, mission, and values • Organizational chart • The organization’s scope and organization of services • Standing meetings and committees • Staff code of conduct and ethics • Conflict of interest policy • Admission/discharge and referral processes • Visiting hours • Smoking policy • Parking
Long-term care leaders ensure that policies and procedures are followed.

Long-term care leaders ensure compliance with all relevant laws and regulations, waste management, food management, infection prevention and control, medication management, resident rights, radiation safety, and physical environment safety.

statement: Long-term care organization leaders work collaboratively to develop an effective budgeting process.
elements: The long-term care organization has a finance director qualified by education and experience.
Long-term care organization leaders work together to address both the capital and the operating budgets.
The budgeting process addresses staffing in addition to other financial assets.
The budgeting process allocates resources to all resident care units based on the scope and complexity of care, aiming to ensure a safe, efficient process.
The governing entity approves the long-term care organization’s budget.

statement: Long-term care organization leaders work collaboratively to develop the organization’s strategic plan.
elements: Long-term care organization leaders work together to develop a strategic plan that is guided by the mission, vision, and values.

The strategic plan is based on comprehensive evaluation of the internal and external environmental factors (for example, Strengths/Weaknesses/Opportunities/Threats [SWOT] analysis, Political/ Economic/Social/Technological [PEST] analysis).
The strategic plan addresses all clinical and nonclinical services and programs.
The strategic plan spans a period of three to five years and is reviewed regularly.
The strategic plan includes the goals and objectives required to fulfill the long-term care organization’s mission.
Goals and objectives are translated into operational plans with defined projects, clearly delineated responsibilities, and time frames.
Resources required for executing the operational plans are properly allocated.
Operational plans are implemented and closely monitored for progress toward achieving the goals and objectives.
Key performance indicators are developed for each operational plan.
Key performance indicators are reviewed regularly, and corrective actions are taken when required.
Department heads develop annual departmental plans in line with the long-term care organization’s strategic plan.
The strategic plan is communicated to relevant staff.
The governing body approves the strategic plan.

statement: Long-term care leaders plan with community leaders and leaders of other organizations to meet the community’s health care needs. P
elements: Long-term care leaders meet with recognized community leaders to develop and revise strategic and operational plans to address community needs.
Long-term care leaders plan with the leaders of other health care organizations in the community.
Long-term care leaders seek the input of individual and group stakeholders in the community as part of the organization’s strategic and operational planning.
The long-term care organization participates in community education on health promotion and disease prevention.

statement: Long-term care leaders identify and plan for the type of clinical services required to meet their residents’ needs. P
elements: Long-term care leaders determine and plan with department/service leaders the type of care and services to be provided by the organization, consistent with the organization’s mission and resident needs. This includes the following: • The range of services offered by the long-term care organization • The scope of services for the targeted age groups • The scope of services, including the principal diagnostics and therapeutic modalities used in the

statement: Long-term care leaders ensure effective communication throughout the organization. P
elements: Long-term care leaders ensure that processes are in place for communicating relevant information throughout the organization in a timely manner.

Long-term care leaders ensure effective communication among clinical and nonclinical departments, services, and individual staff members through regular departmental staff meetings, with documented minutes, and communication tools, such as an intranet site, bulletin boards, periodic reports, newsletters, and website.
Long-term care leaders communicate the organization’s vision, mission, goals, policies, and plans to staff.

Long-term care leaders develop and implement a policy that outlines roles and responsibilities for handling all incoming requests from other long-term care organizations and external organizations, and the responses sent to the organizations are timely and informative.

statement: Long-term care leaders ensure uniform programs for the recruitment, retention, development, and continuing education of all staff.
elements: The long-term care organization develops and implements a process for staff recruitment.
The long-term care organization develops and implements a process for staff retention.
The long-term care organization develops and implements a process for staff personal development and continuing education.
The planning is collaborative and includes all departments and services in the organization.

statement: Long-term care leaders plan, develop, and implement a quality improvement and resident safety program. P
elements: Long-term care leaders are familiar with the basic concepts and tools of continuous quality improvement, such as basic data analysis and interpretation of quality reports, quality management tools (for example, Plan-Do-Check-Act [PDCA] cycle), and root cause analysis.
Long-term care leaders participate in developing and implementing an organizationwide quality improvement and resident safety program.

Long-term care leaders select and implement an organizationwide process to measure, assess data, plan change, and sustain improvements in quality and resident safety, and provide for staff education on this quality improvement process.
Long-term care leaders determine how the program will be directed and managed on a daily basis and ensure that the program has adequate technology and other resources to be effective.
Long-term care leaders implement a structure and process for the quality improvement and resident safety program’s overall monitoring and performance.

statement: Long-term care leaders regularly communicate quality improvement and resident safety information to the governing entity and organization staff.
elements: Long-term care leaders report on the quality improvement and resident safety program at least quarterly to the governing entity.

Long-term care leaders’ report to the governing entity includes, at least quarterly, the number and type of sentinel events and root causes, whether the residents and families were informed of the sentinel event, actions taken to improve safety in response to sentinel events, and if the improvements were sustained.
Long-term care leaders regularly communicate information on the quality improvement and resident safety program to staff, including progress on meeting the International Patient Safety Goals.

statement: The chief executive and long-term care leaders prioritize which organizationwide processes will be measured, which organizationwide quality improvement and resident safety activities will be implemented, and how success of these organizationwide efforts will be measured.
elements: The chief executive and long-term care leaders use available data to set collective priorities for organizationwide measurement and improvement activities and consider potential system improvements.
The chief executive and long-term care leaders ensure that, when present, clinical research and health professional education programs are represented in the priorities.
The chief executive and long-term care leaders set priorities for compliance with the International Patient Safety Goals.
The chief executive and long-term care leaders assess the impact of organizationwide and departmental/service improvements on efficiency and resource use.

statement: Long-term care leaders are accountable for reviewing, selecting, and monitoring clinical and nonclinical contracts and inspecting compliance with contracted services as needed. P
elements: Long-term care leaders are accountable for contracts to meet resident and management needs.
The long-term care organization has a written description of the nature and scope of those services to be provided through contractual agreements.
Department/service leaders share accountability for the review, selection, and monitoring of clinical and nonclinical contracts.
Long-term care leaders inspect compliance with contracted services as needed.
When contracts are renegotiated or terminated, the organization maintains the continuity of resident care services.

statement: Long-term care leaders ensure that contracts and other arrangements are part of the organization’s quality improvement and resident safety program.
elements: All contracts stipulate the quality data to be reported to the long-term care organization, the reporting frequency and mechanism, and how the organization will respond when quality requirements or expectations are not met.
Quality data reported under contracts are integrated into the long-term care organization’s quality monitoring program.
The relevant clinical and managerial leaders participate with the quality improvement and resident safety program in analyzing quality and safety information from outside contracts.

statement: Long-term care leaders ensure that licensed health care professionals and independent health care practitioners not employed by the organization have the appropriate credentials and are competent and/or privileged for the services provided to the organization’s residents. P
elements: Long-term care leaders determine those services provided by independent health care practitioners outside the organization.

All diagnostic, consultative, and treatment services provided by independent health care practitioners outside the organization, such as telemedicine, teleradiology, and interpretations of other diagnostics, such as electrocardiogram (ECG), electroencephalogram (EEG), pathology, and the like, are credentialed and privileged by the organization to provide such services.

Independent health care practitioners who provide resident care services on the premises of the long-term care organization but are not employees or members of the clinical staff are credentialed, privileged, and evaluated as required in Standards SQE.9 through SQE.12.
Any support staff accompanying independent health care practitioners and providing care and services in the organization comply with requirements for primary source verification.

The quality of services by independent health care practitioners outside the long-term care organization is monitored as a component of the organization’s quality improvement and resident safety program.

When the long-term care organization uses staff contracts for licensed health care professional staff, the organization ensures that a credential review comparable to the organization’s review process is conducted. Long-Term Care Leadership for Resource Decisions

statement: Long-term care leaders make decisions related to the purchase or use of resources—human and technical— with an understanding of the quality and safety implications of those decisions.
elements: Long-term care leaders use data and information on the quality and safety implications to make decisions about medical equipment.
Long-term care leaders use data and information on the quality and safety implications to make decisions on staffing.
Long-term care leaders use the recommendations of professional organizations and other authoritative sources in making resource decisions.
Long-term care leaders provide direction, support, and oversight of information technology resources.
Long-term care leaders provide direction, support, and oversight of the emergency and disaster management program(s).
Long-term care leaders monitor the results of their decisions and use the data to evaluate and improve the quality of resource purchasing and allocation decisions.

statement: Long-term care leaders seek and use data and information on the safety of the supply chain to protect residents and staff from unstable, contaminated, defective, and counterfeit supplies.
elements: Long-term care leaders define which supplies are most at risk, and outline the steps in the supply chain, including risk points, for supplies defined as most as risk.
Long-term care leaders make resource decisions based on their understanding of the risk points in the supply chain.
The long-term care organization has a process for performing retrospective tracing of supplies found to be unstable, contaminated, defective, or counterfeit.
The long-term care organization notifies the manufacturer and/or distributor when unstable, contaminated, defective, or counterfeit supplies are identified.
Long-term care leaders and relevant heads of departments identify all medical supplies and devices essential for providing safe, quality care.
Suppliers of medical supplies and devices are qualified and carefully selected and evaluated.
Medical supplies and devices are stored safely and in accordance with manufacturer’s recommendations.
Medical supplies and devices are protected against theft, damage, contamination, and deterioration.
Long-term care leaders conduct regular inspections to ensure the safety of medical supplies and devices (for example, storage conditions, integrity, contamination, expiration).
Long-term care leaders respond to any adverse effects resulting from medical supplies and devices through prompt investigation and the use of recurrence prevention measures.
Long-term care leaders ensure that adverse effects resulting from medical supplies and devices are reported to the relevant regulatory authorities.
The long-term care organization has a process for safely segregating and disposing of expired, damaged, or contaminated medical supplies and devices.
The long-term care organization has a process to retrieve dispensed supplies and devices when recalled or discontinued by the manufacturer or relevant regulatory authorities for safety reasons.

group: Direction of Long-Term Care Departments and Services
statement: One or more qualified individuals provide direction for each department or service in the long-term care organization. P
elements: Each department or service in the long-term care organization is directed by an individual with the training, education, and experience comparable to the services provided. The department head does the following: • Ensures that workflow and resident safety are not compromised during their absence • Ensures that department functions are well managed through regular scheduled visits, the

group: Direction of Long-Term Care Departments and Services
statement: Each department/service leader identifies, in writing, the services provided by the department and integrates or coordinates those services with the services of other departments. P
elements: Department/service leaders have selected and use a uniform format and content for planning documents.
The departmental or service documents describe the current and planned services provided by each department or service.
The departmental or service documents guide the provision of identified services.
The departmental or service documents address the staff knowledge and skills needed to assess and meet resident needs.
There is coordination and/or integration of services within and with other departments and services.

group: Direction of Long-Term Care Departments and Services
statement: Measures selected by the department/service leaders that are applicable to evaluating the performance of physicians, nurses, and other professional staff participating in the clinical care processes are used in the staff’s performance evaluation.
elements: When applicable, assessment of participation in quality activities and the results of measurement activities are included in the ongoing professional practice evaluation of the physicians of the department or service.
When applicable, assessment of participation in quality activities and the results of measurement activities are included in the performance evaluation of nursing staff.
When applicable, assessment of participation in quality activities and the results of measurement activities are included in the performance evaluation of other health care practitioners.

group: Direction of Long-Term Care Departments and Services
statement: Department/service leaders select and implement clinical practice guidelines, and related clinical pathways and/or clinical protocols, to guide clinical care. P
elements: On an annual basis, department/service leaders collectively determine at least five organizationwide priority areas on which to focus the use of clinical practice guidelines.

Department/service leaders follow the process described in the following when selecting and implementing clinical practice guidelines: • Select from among those applicable to the organization’s services and residents (mandatory

statement: Long-term care leaders establish a framework for ethical management that promotes a culture of ethical practices and decision making to ensure that resident care is provided within business, financial, ethical, and legal norms and protects residents and their rights. P
elements: Long-term care leaders establish a framework for the organization’s ethical management that promotes a culture of ethical practices and decision making to ensure the protection of residents and their rights.
The ethical framework ensures that resident care is provided within business, financial, ethical, and legal norms.
The long-term care organization ensures nondiscrimination in employment practices and provision of resident care in the context of the cultural and regulatory norms of the country.
Long-term care leaders examine national and international ethical norms for incorporation when developing the organization’s framework for ethical conduct.

statement: The long-term care organization’s framework for ethical management addresses operational and business issues, including marketing, admissions, transfer, discharge, and disclosure of ownership and any business and professional conflicts that may not be in residents’ best interests. P
elements: The long-term care organization discloses its ownership and any conflicts of interest.
The long-term care organization honestly portrays its services to residents.
The long-term care organization accurately bills for services and ensures that financial incentives and payment arrangements do not compromise resident care.

statement: The long-term care organization’s framework for ethical management addresses ethical issues and decision making in clinical care. P
elements: The long-term care organization’s framework for ethical management establishes a mechanism by which health care practitioners and other staff may raise ethical concerns without fear of retribution.
The organizational structure(s) and processes support oversight of professional ethical issues.
Support for identifying and addressing ethical concerns is readily available and includes ethics resources and training for health care practitioners and other staff.
The long-term care organization provides an effective, timely resolution to ethical conflicts that arise.

statement: Long-term care leaders create and support a culture of safety program throughout the organization. P
elements: Long-term care leaders establish and support an organizational culture that promotes accountability and transparency.
Long-term care leaders establish and document a code of conduct and identify and correct unacceptable behaviors.
Long-term care leaders provide education and information (such as literature and advisories) relevant to the organization’s culture of safety to all individuals who work in the organization.
Long-term care leaders define how issues related to a culture of safety in the organization are identified and managed.
Long-term care leaders provide resources to promote and support the culture of safety in the organization.

statement: Long-term care leaders implement, monitor, and take action to improve the program for a culture of safety throughout the organization.
elements: Long-term care leaders provide a simple, accessible, and confidential system for reporting issues relevant to a culture of safety in the organization.
Long-term care leaders ensure that all reports related to the organization’s culture of safety are investigated in a timely manner.
The long-term care organization identifies systems issues that lead health care practitioners to engage in unsafe behaviors.
Long-term care leaders use measures to evaluate and monitor the safety culture in the organization and implement improvements identified from measurement and evaluation.
Long-term care leaders implement a process to prevent retribution against individuals who report issues related to the culture of safety.

statement: Human subjects research, when provided within the organization, is guided by laws, regulations, and long- term care leaders. P
elements: Long-term care leaders identify the official(s) responsible for maintaining the development of and compliance with all human subjects research policies and procedures.
Long-term care leaders assume responsibility for resident protection regardless of the research sponsor.
Long-term care leaders recognize and establish mechanisms for complying with all regulatory and professional requirements related to research.
Long-term care leaders ensure that a source of indemnity insurance is in place to adequately compensate residents participating in clinical research who experience an adverse event.
The long-term care organization establishes entry and/or transfer criteria for admission to a specialized ward due to research and/or another specialized program to meet resident needs.

statement: The long-term care organization plans and designs information management processes to meet the information needs of those who provide clinical services, the long-term care leaders, and those outside the organization who require data and information from the organization.
elements: The long-term care organization plans and implements processes to meet the information needs of those who provide clinical services.
The long-term care organization plans and implements processes to meet the information needs of the organization’s leadership and department/service leaders.

The long-term care organization plans and implements processes to meet the information needs and requirements of individuals, services, and agencies outside the organization (for example, Ministry of Health, accrediting bodies, national research and databases).
The processes implemented are appropriate to the organization’s size, complexity of services, availability of trained staff, technical resources, and other resources.

Relevant clinical and managerial staff participate in selecting, integrating, and using information management technology, which is identified and integrated with existing information management processes. Adequate resources are provided for an effective information management system.

statement: The long-term care organization maintains the confidentiality, security, privacy, and integrity of data and information through processes to manage and control access.
elements: The long-term care organization develops and implements processes consistent with laws and regulations to ensure the confidentiality, security, and integrity of data and information.

The long-term care organization identifies those authorized to access data and information, including those authorized to make entries in the resident health record, and determines their level of access based on each individual’s role and responsibilities.
The long-term care organization has a process in place to grant authorized individuals access privileges to data and information consistent with their level of access.
The long-term care organization implements processes to ensure that only authorized individuals access data and information that is consistent with their level of access.
The long-term care organization implements processes to ensure that only authorized individuals make entries in the resident health record that is consistent with their level of access.
The long-term care organization monitors compliance with the processes and takes action when confidentiality, security, or data integrity are violated or compromised.

statement: The long-term care organization maintains the confidentiality, security, privacy, and integrity of data and information through processes that protect against loss, theft, damage, and destruction.
elements: The long-term care organization conducts and documents an annual information security risk assessment throughout the organization, and data security risks are identified and prioritized from the risk assessment.

Data and information are stored in a manner that protects against loss, theft, damage, destruction, ransomware, and other cyberattacks through processes that include, but are not limited to, the following: • Regularly backing up and retrieving information system data • Protecting medical records from loss, theft, and deliberate alterations or destruction • Ensuring confidentiality, integrity, and security of medical records during storage

The long-term care organization implements data security best practices to protect and secure data and information through processes that include, but are not limited to, the following: • Safeguarding data and information against loss, destruction, tampering, damage, and

statement: The long-term care organization determines the retention time of resident health records, data, and other information. P
elements: The long-term care organization determines the retention time of resident health records and other data and information and complies with laws and regulations.

The retention process of medical records takes into account at least the following: • The medical records are retained for a minimum of five years after the resident was last seen, unless otherwise specified by laws and regulations. For minors, records shall be kept until they are 18 years of age, and then for a minimum additional five years. • The process addresses the retention period of different types of the medical records as well as the permanent types (for example, records of medical-legal cases). • The process addresses the retention period of different parts of the medical record as well as the permanent parts (master resident index, admission and discharge dates, name of the most responsible physician, diseases treated, operations performed, and a discharge summary for each admission).
The retention process provides expected confidentiality and security.
Resident health records, data, and other information are destroyed or deleted in a manner that does not compromise confidentiality and security.

When the long-term care organization discontinues operation, it stores the medical records in a facility offering retrieval services for the specified retention periods. Residents or their representatives are informed.

statement: The long-term care organization uses standardized diagnosis and procedure codes and ensures the uniform use of approved symbols and abbreviations across the organization.
elements: The long-term care organization uses standardized diagnosis codes and procedure codes. For diagnosis coding, the long-term care organization uses the International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, 10th Revision, Australian Modification (ICD-10-AM), and for procedure coding, Australian Classification of Health Interventions (ACHI).
The long-term care organization implements the uniform use of approved symbols and identifies those not to be used.
If the long-term care organization allows abbreviations, the organization uniformly uses only approved abbreviations, and each abbreviation has only one meaning.
If the long-term care organization allows abbreviations, the organization develops and/or adopts a list of do-not-use abbreviations.

If the long-term care organization allows abbreviations and symbols, it adopts the following measures: • The lists are consistent with national standards and professional organizations concerned with resident safety. • The lists are developed and approved by the medical staff and other relevant structures (for example, medical records review committee, pharmacy and therapeutics committee). • The lists are revised periodically (for example, annually).
Abbreviations are not used on informed consent and resident rights documents, discharge instructions, and discharge summaries.
The long-term care organization monitors the uniform use of codes, symbols, and abbreviations throughout the organization and takes actions to improve processes when needed.

statement: The data and information needs of those in and outside the long-term care organization are met on a timely basis in a format that meets user expectations and with the desired frequency.
elements: Data and information dissemination meets the needs of individuals and organizations within and outside the long-term care organization, including residents, health care practitioners, long-term care leadership, health care services and organizations, and regulatory agencies.

When individuals or organizations need data and information for the care of a resident, the long- term care organization has processes to ensure that it is received in a timely manner that supports continuity of care and resident safety.
Individuals and organizations within and outside the long-term care organization receive data and information in a format that facilitates their intended use.
Staff providing resident care have access to the data and information needed to carry out their job responsibilities and provide resident care safely and effectively.

statement: Clinical staff, decision-makers, and other staff members are educated and trained on information systems, information security, and the principles of information use and management.
elements: Clinical staff, decision-makers, and others are educated and trained on information systems, information security, and the principles of information use and management, as appropriate to their role and responsibilities. The education and training include, but are not limited to, the following: • Selection and use of indicators (measures) in assessing and improving work processes • Data collection and analysis • Use of data and information for decision making • Data and information confidentiality and security

Staff who use an electronic health record system receive education, ongoing training, and assessment to ensure that they can effectively and efficiently use the system to carry out their job responsibilities.
Clinical and managerial data and information are integrated as needed to support decision making. Management and Implementation of Documents

statement: Documents, including policies, procedures, and programs, are managed in a consistent and uniform manner. P
elements: There is a written guidance document that defines the requirements for developing and maintaining policies, procedures, and programs, including at least the following: • Review and approval of all documents by an authorized person before issue • The process and frequency of review and continued approval of documents (every two to three

statement: The policies, procedures, plans, and other documents that guide consistent and uniform clinical and nonclinical processes and practices are fully implemented. P
elements: Required policies, procedures, and plans are available, and staff understand how to access those documents relevant to their responsibilities.
Staff are trained and understand those documents relevant to their responsibilities.
The requirements of the policies, procedures, and plans are fully implemented and evident in individual staff members’ actions.
The implementation of policies, procedures, and plans is monitored, and the information supports full implementation.

statement: The long-term care organization initiates and maintains a standardized, accurate health record for every resident assessed or treated and determines the record’s content, format, and location of entries. P
elements: A health record with at least two identifiers unique to the resident is initiated for every resident on their first contact who has been assessed or treated by the long-term care organization.
The long-term care organization ensures only one medical record for each resident.

The long-term care organization has a process to ensure complete and accurate medical records by adopting at least the following measures: • A policy identifies all staff members authorized to make entries in medical records. • All entries in the medical records must be legible, indelibly verified, and authenticated. • Clinical staff authorized to make entries in the medical record receive formal training in clinical documentation improvement per the national/international guidelines. • The medical record must be completed within 30 days of resident discharge and before any elective vacation or period of absence of the staff member entering the notes in the medical record. • The long-term care organization has a policy to deal with delinquent medical records. • The most responsible physician must complete their medical records.

The long-term care organization determines and standardizes the specific content, format, and location of entries for resident health records according to the needs of health care professionals. The long-term care organization controls the process through a structure (for example, a forms committee, the medical records review committee).

The long-term care organization establishes and implements guidelines on proper use of copy-and- paste, autofill, autocorrect, and templates and provides education and training on the guidelines to all staff who document in the electronic health record.

The long-term care organization has a process to monitor compliance with the guidelines on proper use of copy-and-paste, autofill, autocorrect, and templates and implements corrective action as needed.
The long-term care organization establishes and implements processes and guidelines to facilitate accurate and complete documentation in resident health records.

statement: The health record contains sufficient information to identify the resident, support the diagnosis, justify the treatment, and document the course and results of treatment.
elements: Resident health records contain adequate information to identify the resident.
Resident health records contain adequate information to support the diagnosis and promote continuity of care.
Resident health records contain adequate information to justify and document the course and results of the resident’s care, treatment, and services.

statement: Every resident health record entry identifies its author and when the entry was made in the health record.
elements: The author of each entry in the resident health record can be identified and authenticated by official stamp, signature, written initials, or computer entry.
The date of each entry in the resident health record can be identified.
The time of each entry in the resident health record can be identified.
There is a process that addresses how entries in the resident health record are corrected or overwritten.

When scribes assist with documentation in the resident health record, they sign, date, and time their entries, and there is a process for the physician/health care practitioner to review and authenticate the scribe’s entries.

statement: As part of its monitoring and performance improvement activities, the long-term care organization regularly assesses resident health record content.
elements: A representative sample of health records, including active and discharged health records and health records of current residents, is reviewed at least quarterly or more frequently as determined by laws and regulations.
Physicians, nurses, and others authorized to make entries in resident health records or manage resident health records conduct the review.
The review focuses on the resident health records’ timeliness, accuracy, completeness, and legibility.
The review process includes health record content required by laws or regulations.
The results of the review process are incorporated into the long-term care organization’s quality oversight mechanism.

statement: The health information management (medical records) department has adequate qualified staff.
elements: An individual qualified by education (bachelor’s degree in health information management) and experience directs the health information management (medical records) department.
The department director is credentialed in health information management through formal training per the national/international guidelines.
The department has adequate staff to carry out its functions.
Staff working in the department are credentialed in health information management through formal training per the national/international guidelines.
Clinical coding staff working in the department are credentialed/certified in clinical coding through formal training per the national/international guidelines.
The department has one or more staff members credentialed in clinical documentation improvement (CDI) through formal training per the national/international guidelines.

statement: The long-term care organization maintains a master resident index (either manual or computerized) of all residents admitted to or treated by the long-term care organization.
elements: The master resident index is used to identify a resident’s medical record number.

The master resident index provides basic resident demographic information (identification information collected during registration) as well as resident activity (visit) information as follows: • The resident demographic information (identification information) includes medical record number, resident’s full name, date of birth, sex, marital status, address, national identification number, next of kin (and their contacts) and/or a person that the resident wishes to be contacted in an emergency, or authorized representative/designee. • The resident activity (visit) information includes admission and discharge/transfer dates for admission, date of death when a death occurs, and most responsible physician.
The resident demographic information (identification information) of the master resident index is recorded on the front sheet of the medical record.
The master resident index is updated for each new episode of care for any change in information.
The master resident index is retained permanently to provide historical access to basic resident information and dates of stay in the long-term organization.

statement: The long-term care organization maintains the medical records in one central place.
elements: The long-term care organization has a medical records department that accommodates all medical records.

The long-term care organization has processes to manage the different parts of the medical records, including ensuring the following: • The different parts of multiple records are cross-referenced to the resident’s unique identifier to enable records linkage. • The different parts can be easily located when not stored together. • The long-term care organization ensures that all information is available and accessible when needed.

The processes include, but are not limited to, the following: • Records that are partly paper-based and partly electronic • Records that include items requiring incompatible storage systems such as videos and audio

statement: The long-term care organization has a process to ensure medical records are available in a timely manner.
elements: The long-term care organization determines in a policy all disciplines that may access the medical records.
Care providers have access to current and past medical records.
Medical records are readily retrievable for each resident encounter.
Medical records are available within 30 minutes of being requested.
Medical records can be retrieved any time of the day.

statement: Medical records are consistently organized.
elements: Individual medical records are securely compiled.
Medical records are organized into sections (for example, a section for test results, operative reports, consultations, discharge summary).

The different sections of the medical record are organized chronologically (for example, physician orders start with the initial set written when the resident was admitted to the long-term care organization and end with the discharge order).

statement: The long-term care organization has a system to manage voluminous medical records.
elements: The long-term care organization has a system that enables medical record linkage.
When the medical record is divided into volumes, the number of each volume should be clearly visible on the folder and on the sign-out slip (for example, Volume 1 of 2, Volume 2 of 2).

When the long-term care organization practices thinning of voluminous medical records: • The long-term care organization develops thinning guidelines that remain consistent for the type of documentation contained. • The long-term care organization retains documentation in the medical record that reflects the current plan of care and services provided. • The long-term care organization removes parts of the medical record older than a certain date and moves them into a secondary record (the overflow record).

statement: The long-term care organization develops and implements a policy for releasing medical records from the medical record department.
elements: The long-term care organization has a policy that describes the process for releasing medical records for resident care encounters.

The long-term care organization determines when to release medical records for reasons not related to direct resident care (for example, research, utilization management, quality improvement, morbidity and mortality, government requests).
The long-term care organization has an approval mechanism for releasing medical records for reasons not related to resident care. The approval mechanism is implemented.

statement: The long-term care organization has a system for tracking medical records.
elements: The long-term care organization has a medical records tracking system to identify the location of any record not in the medical records department and its date and time of movement as well as subsequent movements, when applicable.
The medical records tracking system includes all components of the medical records.

statement: Long-term care leaders identify a qualified individual to oversee the organization’s health information technology systems and processes.
elements: Long-term care leaders provide direction, support, and resources for health information technology in the organization.
