Long-term care leaders identify a qualified individual to oversee health information technology systems in the organization with responsibility for at least the following: • Recommending space, equipment, technology, and other resources to organization leadership to

statement: When mobile devices are used for texting, e-mailing, or other communications of resident data and information, the long-term care organization implements processes to ensure quality of resident care and maintains security and confidentiality of resident information. P
elements: When the long-term care organization allows resident data and information to be transmitted through text messaging, the organization ensures that the process uses a secure messaging platform and complies with the following: • Secure, encrypted sign-on process(es) is followed to authenticate users (sign-on processes are password protected and unique to each user). • Only authorized individuals in the platform’s directory of users can receive messages. • Messages have delivery and read receipts. • Messages are dated and time stamped. • Processes are followed to protect and secure resident information against unauthorized access and use (for example, automatic logout after a period of inactivity, ability for the organization to remotely deactivate mobile devices or wipe data from devices if lost or stolen).
When mobile devices are used for communicating resident data and information, the organization implements guidelines and processes to protect and secure resident information.

The organization establishes processes to ensure that text messages and e-mails on mobile devices that have data and information relating to a resident’s care are documented in the resident’s health record.

When the organization implements a resident portal or communicates with residents via text messages or e-mails, the organization first obtains consent from residents to participate in the portal and/or receive text messages or e-mails.

When the long-term care organization allows resident information to be communicated via text messages, e-mail, and resident portals, the organization ensures that questions about information exchanged are addressed in a timely manner and monitored for improvements needed to the communication processes.

statement: The long-term care organization develops, maintains, and tests a program for responding to planned and unplanned downtime of data systems. P
elements: The long-term care organization develops and maintains, and tests at least annually, a program for response to planned and unplanned downtime of data systems. The program is supported by procedures and forms to be used during planned and unplanned downtime.
The long-term care organization identifies the probable impact of planned and unplanned downtime of data systems on all aspects of care and services.

The program includes continuity strategies for providing ongoing safe, high-quality resident care and services, including services provided by outside vendors, during planned and unplanned downtime of data systems. The program supports documentation and reporting of resident information (for example, reporting of laboratory results) during the downtime.
The program identifies internal and, when applicable, external communication strategies for planned and unplanned downtime.

The long-term care organization identifies and implements downtime recovery tactics and ongoing data backup processes to recover and maintain data and to ensure data integrity and maintain confidentiality and security of resident information.
Staff are trained in the strategies and tactics for planned and unplanned downtime of data systems.
A downtime assessment report is generated and reviewed.

statement: One or more individuals oversee all infection prevention and control (IPC) activities. This individual(s) is qualified in IPC practices through education, training, experience, certification, and/or clinical authority.
elements: One or more individuals oversee the IPC program and ensure that the program complies with local and national laws and regulations.
The individual(s) is qualified for the organization’s size, complexity of activities, and level of risks as well as the program’s scope.
The individual(s) fulfills program oversight responsibilities as assigned or described in a job description.

The individual(s) coordinates with long-term care leaders regarding priorities, resources, and quality improvement opportunities related to the infection prevention and control program. This individual(s) is responsible for the following: • Developing the annual IPC plan and ensuring its implementation • Reviewing the daily activities of the structure responsible for IPC (for example, IPC department

statement: There is a designated coordination mechanism for all infection prevention and control (IPC) activities that involves physicians, nurses, and others based on the long-term care organization’s size and complexity.
elements: The designated mechanism coordinates the IPC program and involves IPC professionals.
There is a formal interdisciplinary coordination mechanism, such as a committee for the IPC program, that involves IPC professionals.
Each member of the committee acts as an advocate of IPC in their department, trying to promote its principles, and ensures the application of its rules.

The function and activities of the coordination mechanism are documented and include, but are not limited to, the following: • Reviewing the long-term care organization’s IPC policies and procedures • Reviewing the reports of health care–associated infection surveillance submitted regularly by the

statement: Long-term care leaders provide resources to support the infection prevention and control (IPC) program.
elements: The IPC program is staffed according to the long-term care organization’s size, complexity of activities, and level of risks as well as the program’s scope.
Long-term care leaders approve and assign staff required for the IPC program.
Long-term care leaders approve and allocate resources required for the IPC program (including equipment and supplies, and so on).
Information management systems support the IPC program. Goals of the Infection Prevention and Control Program

statement: The long-term care organization designs and implements a comprehensive infection prevention and control (IPC) program that identifies the procedures and processes associated with the risk of infection and implements strategies to reduce infection risk. P
elements: The IPC program is comprehensive and crosses all levels of the organization to reduce the risk of health care–associated infections in residents.
The IPC program is comprehensive and crosses all levels of the organization to reduce the risk of health care–associated infections in long-term care staff, visitors, and vendors.
The long-term care organization identifies those processes associated with infection risk.
The long-term care organization implements strategies, education, and evidence-based activities to reduce infection risk in those processes.

statement: The long-term care organization uses a risk-based, data-driven approach in establishing the focus of the health care–associated infection prevention and control (IPC) program. P
elements: The long-term care organization establishes the program’s focus by collecting and tracking data related to the following relevant infections and sites: • Respiratory tract—such as the procedures and medical equipment associated with intubation,

statement: The long-term care organization identifies high-risk areas for infections by conducting a risk assessment, develops interventions to address these risks, and monitors the effectiveness.
elements: The long-term care organization completes and documents a risk assessment, at least annually, to identify and prioritize high-risk areas for infections.
The long-term care organization identifies and implements interventions to address infection risks identified through the risk assessment.
The long-term care organization evaluates the effectiveness of the interventions and makes appropriate changes to the infection prevention and control program as needed.
The long-term care organization monitors ongoing data to ensure that risks are reduced or eliminated.

statement: The long-term care organization reduces the risk of infections associated with medical equipment, devices, and supplies by ensuring adequate cleaning, disinfection, sterilization, and storage. P
elements: The long-term care organization follows professional practice guidelines and manufacturers’ guidelines for sterilization techniques that best fit the type of situations for sterilization and devices and supplies being sterilized.

The long-term care organization follows professional practice guidelines and manufacturers’ guidelines for low- and high-level disinfection that best fit the type of devices and equipment being disinfected.

A qualified individual(s) who has experience, knowledge, and certification by the Saudi Commission for Health Specialties oversees cleaning, disinfection, sterilization, and storage of medical equipment, devices, and supplies.
Staff processing medical equipment, devices, and supplies are oriented to, trained in, and demonstrate competency in cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization, and they receive proper supervision.
Methods for medical cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization are coordinated and uniformly applied throughout the organization.
Clean and sterile supplies are properly stored in designated storage areas that are clean and dry and protected from dust, moisture, and temperature extremes to prevent contamination prior to use.
The long-term care organization has written policies and procedures for cleaning, disinfection, sterilization, and storage.

statement: The long-term care organization identifies and implements a process for managing the reuse of single-use devices consistent with regional and local laws and regulations and implements a process for managing expired supplies. P
elements: The long-term care organization identifies single-use devices and materials that may be reused in accordance with local and national laws and regulations and implements a process for managing expired supplies.
The long-term care organization uses a standardized process for identifying when a single-use device is no longer safe or suitable for reuse.

The long-term care organization has a process for cleaning, disinfecting, or sterilizing each reusable, single-use device in accordance with laws and regulations, manufacturer’s requirements, or other applicable requirements.
The long-term care organization identifies and tracks residents on whom reusable medical devices have been used.
When adverse events result from reusing single-use devices, residents using these devices are tracked and an analysis is performed, with results used to identify and implement improvements.
The long-term care organization implements a process, including storage, evaluation, and use, to manage expired supplies to prevent contamination or damage.

statement: The infection prevention and control (IPC) program identifies and implements standards from recognized IPC programs to address cleaning and disinfecting the environment and environmental surfaces.
elements: The long-term care organization selects evidence-based cleaning and disinfection standards and procedures from recognized IPC programs to maintain environmental cleanliness.
Long-term care leaders identify high-risk areas and situations for transmitting infections and implement additional cleaning and disinfection procedures as indicated.
Cleaning of infectious rooms during the resident’s admission and after discharge follows IPC guidelines, including a cleaning/disinfection schedule to cover all environmental surfaces and areas.
The long-term care organization monitors and documents its environmental cleaning and disinfection processes and then uses the data to make changes to the process when applicable.

statement: The infection prevention and control (IPC) program identifies standards from recognized IPC health agencies related to cleaning and disinfecting laundry, linens, and scrub attire provided by the long-term care organization.
elements: Laundering methods comply with local and national laws and regulations and follow guidelines from recognized IPC agencies. Policies and procedures guide linen management and cover all steps starting from collecting linens from residents’ rooms until completion of the cleaning process.
Standard precautions are used when handling laundry, linens, and organization-issued scrub attire, and appropriate transmission-based precautions are used as indicated.
Laundry, linens, and organization-issued scrub attire are transported, processed, and stored in a manner that prevents cross contamination of soiled and clean items.
Staff wear organization-issued scrub attire where required in accordance with applicable IPC guidelines, national health care industry standards, and long-term care organization policy.

statement: The long-term care organization has a process to protect residents and staff from bloodborne pathogens related to exposure to blood and body fluids. P
elements: The long-term care organization identifies processes that could result in resident or staff exposure to blood and body fluids and implements practices to reduce exposure risk.
The long-term care organization uses an expeditious, timely process for reporting resident and staff exposures to blood and body fluids.
The long-term care organization uses a process for acting upon resident and staff exposures to blood and body fluids.
Staff are educated about how to report an exposure incident.
The long-term care organization tracks and monitors incidents of resident and staff exposures to blood and body fluids and documents such in the staff files.
Reports of exposure incidents are reviewed, and actions are taken to minimize the risk of future exposures to blood and body fluids.

statement: The long-term care organization reduces infection risks associated with food and dietetics services.
elements: The long-term care organization stores food and nutrition products in a manner that reduces infection risk, including those stored outside the kitchen and food preparation areas. Infection prevention and control (IPC) measures include the following: • Kitchen design supports its function. • Refrigerator temperatures are checked daily and documented on log sheets. • The kitchen environment and functions are addressed in policies and procedures that are reviewed by the IPC team. • The kitchen environment is clean.

The long-term care organization adopts and implements kitchen sanitation measures and guidelines for preparation areas to prevent cross-contamination and infection risks. IPC measures include the following: • Kitchen areas are separated based on assigned function (separate areas for vegetables, meat, dessert preparation, and so on). • Each kitchen area has an adequate number of handwashing facilities. • Food containers are properly labeled and expiry dates noted. • Food is protected from the environment during storage, preparation, display, and transportation. • Garbage containers or receptacles are adequate in number, insect and rodent proof, and covered. • Cutting boards for meat, poultry, chicken, or vegetables are identifiably separated and immediately washed after use. • Fruits and vegetables are washed and disinfected thoroughly. • Food containers are washed immediately after being emptied of food. • Policies and procedures address staff hygiene and health in the kitchen and are reviewed by the infection prevention and control team. • While handling food, staff wash their hands, cover their hair, and wear gloves. • Personnel with respiratory infections or gastroenteritis are restricted from handling food. • Stool tests and cultures are performed routinely upon hiring, every six months, and after returning from vacation. • The IPC practitioner reviews the results of stool analysis and cultures.
The long-term care organization prepares food and nutrition products using proper sanitation and temperature.
The long-term care organization uses a process to ensure that proper food temperature is maintained during preparation, transportation, and distribution.
Professional guidelines are adopted for nutritional products with special storage and preparation requirements.

statement: The long-term care organization reduces infection risk in the facility through mechanical and engineering controls.
elements: The long-term care organization operates and maintains positive and negative pressure ventilation systems consistent with local and national laws and regulations and professional standards. The organization establishes and monitors airflow (positive, negative, balanced) in the following locations as indicated: • Isolation rooms • Clean and dirty utility rooms • Janitorial closets • Laboratory • Central sterilization and supply department
The long-term care organization operates and maintains temperature controls for water, steam, and others consistent with local and national laws and regulations and professional standards.

The long-term care organization operates and maintains airflow, ventilation systems, temperature, and humidity controls in a manner that minimizes infection risk in the organization consistent with local and national laws and regulations and professional guidelines. Temperature and humidity are controlled and regularly monitored in at least the following areas: • Sterile storage supply rooms • Resident rooms

statement: The long-term care organization reduces infection risk in the facility associated with demolition, construction, and renovation.
elements: The long-term care organization has a program that uses risk criteria to assess the impact of renovation or new construction and implements the program when demolition, construction, or renovation take place.

The long-term care organization assesses the risks and impact of demolition, renovation, or construction activities on air quality and infection prevention and control activities throughout the facility.
The risks and impact of the demolition, renovation, or construction are managed to protect residents, staff, and visitors from infection.

statement: The long-term care organization provides barrier precautions and isolation procedures that protect residents, visitors, and staff from communicable diseases and protects immunosuppressed residents from acquiring infections to which they are uniquely prone.
elements: The long-term care organization uses a process to isolate residents with infectious diseases, and staff use transmission-based precautions consistent with recommended guidelines.

The long-term care organization protects residents with immunosuppression or other increased risks from contracting a communicable disease through isolation and reverse/protective isolation consistent with recommended guidelines.

The long-term care organization routinely monitors and makes available negative pressure rooms for infectious residents who require isolation for airborne infections. Negative pressure rooms should have the following: • The ventilation system serving airborne isolation facilities provides pressure patterns that prevent airborne pathogens from being distributed to other areas of the long-term care organization. • The entry of the isolation room is through a work area or anteroom that serves as a site for handwashing, gowning, and storage of protective clothing (gloves, aprons, masks). • Toilet, shower or tub, and hand-washing facilities are provided for each isolation room. • Transmission-based precaution cards (isolation signs) are consistent with the resident’s diagnosis, are posted in Arabic and English, and indicate the type of precautions required. • Staff wear respirator (high-filtration) masks (N95, N99) during direct care of residents on airborne precautions; these masks are available on all units likely to admit residents on airborne precautions. • Respirator (high-filtration) masks (N95, N99) can be reused by the same resident caregiver per the period specified by the manufacturer.
When negative pressure rooms are not immediately available, temporary negative pressure rooms that follow acceptable guidelines and adhere to building and fire codes may be created.

statement: The long-term care organization develops and implements policies and procedures to manage a sudden influx of residents with airborne infections and when negative pressure rooms are not available.
elements: The long-term care organization develops and implements policies and procedures to address managing residents with airborne infections for short periods of time when negative pressure rooms are not available by using high efficiency particulate air (HEPA) filters.
The long-term care organization develops and implements policies and procedures for managing an influx of residents with contagious diseases.
Staff are educated in managing infectious residents when there is a sudden influx or when negative pressure rooms are not available.

statement: The long-term care organization develops, implements, and evaluates an emergency preparedness program to respond to the presentation of global communicable diseases.
elements: Long-term care leaders, along with the individual(s) responsible for the infection prevention and control program, develop and implement an emergency preparedness program to respond to global communicable diseases. The program provides processes for the following: • Communicating with organizations participating in worldwide surveillance activities • Developing and implementing segregation and isolation strategies (See also ACC.1, PCI.12, and

statement: Gloves, masks, eye protection, other protective equipment, soap, and disinfectants are available and used correctly when required. P
elements: The long-term care organization identifies situations in which personal protective equipment is required and ensures that it is available at any site of care at which it could be needed.
Staff are trained and correctly use personal protective equipment in each identified situation.
The long-term care organization implements surface disinfecting procedures for areas and situations in the organization identified as at risk for infection transmission.
Liquid soap, disinfectants, and towels or other means of drying are in areas where handwashing and hand-disinfecting procedures are required.
Residents and visitors are educated on when they must disinfect their hands and how to correctly use personal protective equipment.

statement: The infection prevention and control (IPC) process is integrated with the long-term care organization’s overall program for quality improvement and resident safety, using measures epidemiologically important to the organization.
elements: The long-term care organization integrates IPC activities into the quality improvement and resident safety program.

The long-term care organization collects and analyzes data for the IPC activities, and the data includes epidemiologically important infections. Data collection process includes at least the following: • The long-term care organization selects indicators based on the projected use of data (internal and external benchmarking). • The long-term care organization defines the data collection methods and sources. • Policies and procedures define the types of surveillance for health care–associated infections. • There are written standardized definitions for identifying health care–associated infections. • Policies and procedures define how data will be collected, analyzed, and used. • The monitoring process includes using indicators related to infection issues that are epidemiologically important to the long-term care organization.
The long-term care organization uses monitoring data to evaluate and support improvements to the IPC program at least annually.
The long-term care organization uses risk, rate, and trend information, and monitoring data include benchmarking infection rates.
The IPC program documents monitoring data and provides quarterly data analysis reports to leaders.

statement: The long-term care organization provides education on infection prevention and control (IPC) practices to staff, physicians, residents, families, and other caregivers when indicated by their involvement in care.
elements: The long-term care organization provides IPC education to all staff and other professionals at orientation when they begin work in the organization.

The long-term care organization provides ongoing education and training to all staff related to the organization’s IPC program and emerging trends in IPC at least annually. Education and training records are maintained in staff files.
The long-term care organization educates residents and families about IPC.
The long-term care organization communicates findings and trends from quality improvement activities to all staff and as part of staff education.

statement: A qualified individual(s) guides the implementation of the long-term care organization’s program for quality improvement and resident safety and manages the activities needed to carry out an effective program of continuous quality improvement and resident safety in the organization. P
elements: An individual(s) who is experienced in quality improvement methods and processes is selected to guide the implementation of the long-term care organization’s quality improvement and resident safety program. The implementation is guided through: • A quality management director, qualified by education, training, and experience in quality, who is responsible for directing all aspects of the quality management program and reporting to the

statement: Long-term care leaders support an organizationwide continuous quality improvement program.
elements: Long-term care leaders provide resources required for the continuous quality improvement program, including human, financial, and time resources.
Long-term care leaders actively participate in quality improvement activities, including improvement teams.
Long-term leaders support staff to make and participate in quality improvement initiatives and attend quality improvement educational activities.

statement: Quality improvement and resident safety program staff support the measure selection process throughout the long-term care organization and coordinate and integrate measurement activities throughout the organization.
elements: The quality improvement and resident safety program supports the selection of measures throughout the long-term care organization at the organizationwide level and the department or service level. Indicators selected represent key care and service structures, processes, and outcomes based on the mission and scope of services. Measures and indicators that the long-term care organization uses may include, but are not limited to, the following: Structure • Availability of essential supplies and equipment • Availability of medical records • Availability of emergency medications • Vacancy rates in all departments • Staffing ratios Process • Documentation in medical records • Delay of physicians answering nurses’ phone calls and pages • Waiting times for treatment • Neuropathy testing in diabetic residents Outcome • Mortality rates • Health care–associated infections • Staff satisfaction • Resident satisfaction • Unplanned transfer to the critical care unit • Resuscitation of residents (cardiac/respiratory arrest) • Readmission to the organization within 30 days of discharge • Various adverse events (for example, falls, injuries, pressure ulcers) • Medication errors • Sentinel events • Resident complaints • Length of stay
For each indicator, there is a clear definition, sample size, data collection method, frequency, analysis, and expression (for example, a ratio, with defined numerator and denominator).

The quality improvement and resident safety program provides coordination and integration of measurement activities throughout the long-term care organization, including information developed from risk management activities integrated and coordinated with the quality improvement and resident safety activities.
The quality improvement and resident safety program provides for the integration of event reporting systems, safety culture measures, and others to facilitate integrated solutions and improvements.
The quality improvement and resident safety program tracks the progress on the planned collection of measurement data for the priorities selected.

statement: The long-term care organization develops a quality improvement program that provides a structured framework for monitoring and improving performance as well as supporting innovation.
elements: The quality improvement program covers processes of care involving high-risk, high-volume, problem-prone, and high-cost areas.
The quality improvement program is in line with the long-term care organization’s strategic plan.
The quality improvement program is based on a documented quality improvement plan that is revised at least annually, with defined scope, goals, and objectives.

statement: The long-term care organization develops and maintains a resident safety program.
elements: Long-term care leaders adopt a just culture that promotes both professional accountability and reporting of adverse events/near misses.
Long-term care leaders define sentinel event in writing, and the definition includes all information in the appendix to this chapter.
Long-term care leaders report any sentinel event to the relevant authorities, including the Ministry of Health, Cluster Leadership, Saudi Health Holding Company, and Saudi Patient Safety Center.

Long-term care leaders complete a credible and thorough comprehensive systematic analysis (for example, root cause analysis) of all sentinel events within a time period specified by leadership, and it does not exceed 45 days from the date of the event or when made aware of the event.
The root cause analysis identifies all system and process origins that may have contributed to the event.
Long-term care leaders consider each identified contributing factor and take corrective actions to prevent or reduce the risk of adverse events from recurring.
The long-term care organization monitors the implemented corrective actions for potential process failures (unintended consequences), effectiveness, and sustainability over time.

Long-term care leaders establish a multidisciplinary resident safety committee (can be integrated with quality improvement committee) to provide direction and oversight of the resident safety program.
Long-term care leaders conduct a resident safety culture assessment at least once annually, analyze the data, and make improvements accordingly.

Long-term care leaders conduct regular leadership resident safety rounds in resident care services and lead safety huddles to encourage reporting of incidents/near misses and identify potential risks and hazards.

The long-term care organization adopts safe practices that have been proven to improve resident safety and reduce harm to residents, such as those from the World Health Organization (WHO) and other national and international organizations concerned with resident safety.
The long-term care organization provides equipment/devices with technological features proven to reduce errors and improve safety.
Resident safety activities and their results are communicated to staff and other relevant groups and used to improve the long-term care organization’s processes.

statement: Long-term care leaders build a culture and environment that supports evidence-based care through the use of current scientific knowledge and information to support resident care, health professional education, clinical research, and management.
elements: Long-term care leaders build a culture and environment that supports evidence-based care.
Current scientific knowledge and information support resident care.
Current scientific knowledge and information support clinical education.
Current scientific knowledge and information support research.
Current professional knowledge and information support management.
Information is provided in a time frame that meets user expectations.

group: Analysis and Validation of Measurement Data
statement: Individuals with appropriate experience, knowledge, and skills systematically aggregate and analyze data in the long-term care organization.
elements: Data are aggregated, analyzed, and transformed from multiple qualitative and quantitative sources into useful information to identify improvement opportunities. Aggregate data and information include information requirements for key functions specified in this manual (for example, facility management and safety, infection control, clinical data and information, identified organizationwide indicators, department-specific indicators, physician-specific information).
Individuals with appropriate clinical or managerial experience, knowledge, and skills participate in the process.
Statistical tools and techniques are used in the analysis process when suitable (for example, brainstorming, fishbone diagrams).

The frequency of data analysis is appropriate to the process or outcome studied, in accordance with laws and regulations and national health care industry standards, and in a manner long-term care leaders can understand and use.
Results of analysis are reported to those accountable for taking action.
Data analysis supports comparisons internally over time, including comparisons with like organizations, with best practices, and with objective scientific professional sources.

group: Analysis and Validation of Measurement Data
statement: The data analysis process includes at least one determination per year of the impact of organizationwide priority improvements on cost and efficiency.
elements: Data on the amount and type of resource use are collected on at least one organizationwide priority improvement project per year before and after the improvement.
The quality improvement and resident safety program staff work with other units such as human resources, information technology, and finance in deciding which data to collect.
The results of the analysis are used to refine the process and reported through the quality coordination mechanism to leaders.

group: Analysis and Validation of Measurement Data
statement: The long-term care organization uses an internal process to validate data. P
elements: The quality improvement and resident safety program uses data validation as part of the improvement process selected by team leaders.

Data are validated when any of the following conditions are met: • A new measure is implemented (in particular, those clinical measures intended to help a long- term care organization evaluate and improve an important clinical process or outcome). • Data will be made public on the organization’s website or in other ways. • An existing measure has changed, such as a change in data collection tools or in the data abstraction process or abstractor. • The data from an existing measure has changed in an unexplainable way. • The data source has changed, such as when part of the resident’s health record is in an electronic format; thus, the data source is now both electronic and paper. • The subject of data collection has changed, such as changes in average age of residents, comorbidities, research protocol alterations, new practice guidelines, or new technologies and treatment methodologies.
An evidence-based methodology for data validation is used.
Long-term care leaders assume accountability for the validity of the quality and outcome data made public.

group: Analysis and Validation of Measurement Data
statement: Data are always analyzed when undesirable trends and variation are evident from the data. P
elements: Defined data collection processes are developed and implemented to ensure accurate data collection, analysis, and reporting.
Data are intensely analyzed when adverse levels, patterns, or trends occur.
Data are collected and analyzed on the following: • All serious adverse drug events, if applicable and as defined by the organization (See also

statement: The long-term care organization achieves and sustains quality improvement.
elements: Improvements in quality and resident safety are planned, tested, and implemented; quality improvement projects as well as strategic and operational planning are prioritized based on information from data analysis. When appropriate, the long-term care organization tests improvement interventions before full implementation.
Data are available to demonstrate that improvements are effective and sustained.
Policy changes necessary to plan, carry out, and sustain the improvement are made.
Successful improvements are documented.

statement: An ongoing risk management program identifies and proactively reduces unanticipated adverse events and other safety risks to residents and staff. P
elements: The organization’s risk management program framework for all departments and services (clinical and nonclinical) includes the following: • Scope and objectives of the program as well as the individual responsible for the program • Risk identification • Risk prioritization (for example, through a risk register) • Risk reporting • Scope, objectives, and criteria for risk assessment • Risk management, including risk analysis (See also MMU.7.1, QRS.4, QRS.6, QRS.7, GLD.4,

statement: Leaders of long-term care departments and services define the desired education, skills, knowledge, and other requirements of all staff members.
elements: The long-term care organization’s mission, volume, and mix of residents, services, and medical equipment are used in planning.

The long-term care organization, through the department heads, defines the desired education, skills, and knowledge for staff and requests the resources required by the departments for a safe and quality service (for example, space, equipment, supplies, staffing, other resources).
The long-term care director ensures that competent, skilled staff are recruited and selected in compliance with applicable laws and regulations.

statement: Each staff member’s responsibilities are defined in a current job description.
elements: Each staff member not permitted to practice independently has a job description which is used when selecting employees for hire, evaluating performance, making internal promotions, and transferring employees. The job description specifies the reporting relationships.

The following individuals, when present in the organization, have job descriptions appropriate to their activities and responsibilities or have been privileged if noted as an alternative: • The individual serves in primarily a managerial role, such as a department manager, or in dual clinical and managerial roles, with the managerial responsibilities identified in a job description

statement: Leaders of long-term care departments and services develop and implement processes for recruiting, evaluating, and appointing staff as well as other related procedures identified by the organization.
elements: The long-term care organization establishes and implements a process to recruit staff.
The long-term care organization establishes and implements a process to evaluate the qualifications of new staff.
The long-term care organization establishes and implements a process to appoint individuals to the staff, including evaluation of verified credentials.
The long-term care organization establishes and implements a process that is uniform across the organization for similar types of staff.

statement: The long-term care organization uses a defined process to ensure that clinical staff knowledge and skills are consistent with resident needs.
elements: The long-term care organization uses a defined process to match clinical staff knowledge, skills, and competency with resident needs.

New clinical staff members are evaluated before or at the time they begin their work responsibilities. All new clinical staff go through a probationary period, during which they can work only under direct supervision for competency evaluation. Competency evaluation during probation is a structured process that aims to assess and review the employee’s knowledge, performance, capability, conduct, and suitability for the role.
The department or service to which the individual is assigned conducts the evaluation.
The long-term care organization defines the frequency of ongoing clinical staff evaluation.

There is at least one documented evaluation, designed to be a two-way process, of each clinical staff member working under a job description each year or more frequently as defined by the organization. The outcome of the performance evaluation is used to set objectives for performance improvement and professional development. The performance evaluation is signed by both the employee and the supervisor and documented in the personnel file.

statement: The long-term care organization uses a defined process to ensure that nonclinical staff knowledge and skills are consistent with organizational needs and the requirements of the position.
elements: The long-term care organization uses a defined process to match nonclinical staff knowledge and skills with the requirements of the position.

New nonclinical staff are evaluated before or at the time they begin their work responsibilities. All new nonclinical staff members go through a probationary period, during which nonclinical staff can work only under direct supervision for competency evaluation. Competency evaluation during probation is a structured process that aims to assess and review the employee’s knowledge, performance, capability, conduct, and suitability for the role.
The department or service to which the individual is assigned conducts the evaluation.
The long-term care organization defines the frequency of ongoing nonclinical staff evaluation.

There is at least one documented evaluation of nonclinical staff members each year or more frequently as defined by the organization. The outcome of the performance evaluation is used to set objectives for performance improvement and professional development. The performance evaluation is signed by both the employee and the supervisor and documented in the personnel file.

statement: There is documented personnel information for each staff member.
elements: Personnel records for each staff member are standardized, current, maintained, and kept confidential according to organization policy.
The long-term care organization has a policy guiding the initiation, management, content update, and retention time and disposal of personnel files.
Personnel records contain the staff member’s qualifications and work history.
Personnel records contain the staff member’s job description when applicable.
Personnel records contain a record of orientation to the organization and the staff member’s specific role and in-service education attended.
Personnel records contain the results of performance reviews.
Personnel records contain required health information.
Personnel records contain references.
Personnel records contain record of qualifications, including current licensure, certification, or registration, if applicable.
Personnel records contain record of leave and sickness.
Personnel records contain record of disciplinary actions, if any.
Personnel records contain any other documents as required by relevant laws and regulations.

statement: A staffing strategy for the long-term care organization, developed by the leaders of the organization’s departments and services, identifies the number, types, and desired qualifications of staff.
elements: The long-term care organization’s department/service leaders, in collaboration with the human resources department, develop a written strategy for staffing the organization in each department in a manner that complies with local laws and regulations and that supports its care, treatment, and services to fulfill its part of the long-term care organization’s mission.

The strategy identifies the number, types, and desired qualifications of staff, using a recognized staffing method. The staffing plan identifies an evidence-based estimation of the number of staff needed per shift, considering all relevant factors (for example, resident care hours, size of the long-term care organization, scope of services provided).
The strategy addresses staff assignment and reassignment.

statement: The staffing strategy is reviewed on an ongoing basis and updated as necessary.
elements: The effectiveness of the staffing strategy is monitored on an ongoing basis to identify any deficiencies and take improvement actions accordingly.
The strategy is revised and updated at least annually, consistent with the long-term care organization’s policy and when indicated.
The strategy is coordinated through a process that involves the department/service leaders.

statement: All clinical and nonclinical staff members are oriented to the long-term care organization, the department or unit to which they are assigned, and their specific job responsibilities at appointment to the staff.
elements: New clinical and nonclinical staff members are oriented to the long-term care organization, the department or unit to which they are assigned, and their job responsibilities and any specific assignments before staff provide care, treatment, and services independently. The long-term care organization provides all new employees with an employee manual or equivalent that summarizes the general orientation program as well as provides other relevant important information.

The long-term care organization orients staff on the following according to their job description as general orientation: • Infection prevention and control practices • The long-term care organization’s policies on telephone medication orders • Fire safety, disasters, hazardous materials, utilities, and equipment failures • The organization’s mission, vision, values, and organization chart • General information on the paging and telephone system • General information on staff evaluation process • Definition of adverse events and sentinel events along with the process of reporting • Policy on abuse and neglect of children and adults • Policy on credentialing and privileging • General information about staff health program • General information about important local cultural and social themes • General information about the organizationwide quality, resident safety, and risk management

statement: Each staff member receives ongoing in-service and other education and training to maintain or advance their skills and knowledge.
elements: The long-term care organization uses various sources of data and information, including the results of quality and safety measurement activities, to identify staff education needs. The training and educational needs are identified based on objective criteria that include, but are not limited to, the following: • The long-term care organization’s mission, vision, and scope of services • Individual staff member’s education and training history • Information from quality assessment and improvement activities • Needs generated by advancements made in the medical and health care management fields • Findings from department performance appraisals of individuals • Findings from peer review activities • Findings from the long-term care organization’s technology and safety management programs • Findings from infection control activities
Education programs are planned based on these data and information.
Long-term care staff are provided ongoing in-service education and training.

The education is provided as part of an educational program with an ongoing schedule of educational activities and is relevant to each staff member’s ability to meet resident needs and/or continuing education requirements.
The long-term care organization provides adequate time, facilities, and resources (for example, financial support) for all staff to participate in relevant education and training opportunities.

statement: Staff who provide resident care are trained and demonstrate competence in the resuscitative techniques specific to the level of training identified.
elements: Staff who provide resident care, including physicians, are trained in at least basic life support.
The long-term care organization identifies the level of training (basic or advanced life support), appropriate to their roles in the organization, for all staff who provide resident care.
There is evidence to show if a staff member passed the training.

The desired level of training for each individual is repeated based on the requirements and/or time frames established by a recognized training program, or every two years if a recognized training program is not used.

statement: Other staff identified by the long-term care organization are trained and can demonstrate appropriate competence in resuscitative techniques.
elements: If applicable, the long-term care organization identifies other staff who do not provide resident care to be trained in basic life support.
When other staff who do not provide resident care are trained in basic life support, there is evidence to show if a staff member passed the training.

When other staff are trained, training for each individual is repeated based on the requirements and/or time frames established by a recognized training program, or every two years if a recognized training program is not used.

statement: The long-term care organization provides a staff health and safety program that addresses staff physical and mental health and safe working conditions.
elements: The long-term care organization provides a staff health and safety program that is responsive to urgent and nonurgent staff needs through direct treatment and referral.

The staff health and safety program includes at least the following: • Initial employment health screening • Measures to control harmful occupational exposures, such as toxic drugs and harmful noise levels, including protective equipment and clothing, stress management, and ergonomics • Education, training, and interventions on safe resident handling • Education, training, and interventions on managing workplace violence • Education, training, and interventions for staff who may be second victims of adverse or sentinel

statement: The long-term care organization identifies staff at risk for exposure to and possible transmission of vaccine- preventable diseases and implements a staff vaccination and immunization program.
elements: The long-term care organization identifies epidemiologically significant infections, which includes hepatitis B and C, HIV, and tuberculosis, as well as staff at high risk for exposure to and transmission of infections. All employees have baseline screening for hepatitis B and C, HIV, and tuberculosis.

The long-term care organization develops and implements a staff vaccination and immunization program that includes the following: • Determination of the immune status of newly hired staff against hepatitis B, measles, mumps, rubella, and varicella by serological testing, and vaccinating those susceptible. Response to hepatitis B vaccination is monitored in vaccinated employees four weeks after completing vaccine series. Non-responders to hepatitis B vaccine are offered at least a second series of the vaccine. • Screening for tuberculosis of newly hired staff with a purified protein derivative (PPD) test. The test is repeated annually for those who are non-reactive. PPD conversion rates are calculated and monitored.

The long-term care organization evaluates the risks associated with unvaccinated staff and identifies strategies for reducing the residents’ risk of exposure to infectious diseases from unvaccinated staff.
The infection prevention and control program guides the evaluation, counseling, and follow-up of staff exposed to infectious diseases.

statement: The long-term care organization has a uniform process for collecting the credentials of those medical staff permitted to provide resident care without supervision.
elements: The long-term care organization has an ongoing, uniform process to manage medical staff credentials.

Medical staff members permitted by laws, regulations, and the organization to provide resident care without supervision are identified. All members of the medical staff must be registered with the Saudi Commission for Health Specialties before being allowed to work independently.

Education, licensure/registration, and other credentials required by laws or regulations are copied by the organization and maintained for each medical staff member in their personnel record or a separate credential file.
All credentials required by organization policy are copied by the organization and maintained for each medical staff member in their personnel record or a separate credential file.

statement: Medical staff’s education, licensure/registration, and other credentials required by laws or regulations and the long-term care organization are verified and kept current.
elements: Education, licensure/registration, and other credentials required by laws or regulations or issued by recognized education or professional entities as the basis for clinical privileges are verified from the original source that issued the credential. The process is defined in a policy and applies to full-time, part-time, visiting, and locum tenens medical staff members.
Additional credentials required by organization policy are verified from the source that issued the credential when required by organization policy.

When third-party verification is used, the organization verifies that the third party (for example, a government agency) implements the verification process as described in policy or regulations and that the process meets the the following expectations: • The long-term organization verifies that the third party implements the verification process as described in long-term care organization policy or regulations and that the process meets the expectations described in these standards. • The affiliated organization that has already conducted primary source verification of the medical staff applicant is acceptable if the affiliated organization has current Joint Commission International (JCI) accreditation with “full compliance” on its verification process found in MEs 1 and 2 of this standard. • The long-term organization that bases its decisions in part on information from a designated official governmental or nongovernmental agency must evaluate the agency providing the information initially and then periodically thereafter to ensure that JCI standards continue to be met. • The long-term organization receives confirmatory documentation.

statement: There is a uniform, transparent decision process for initial medical staff appointment.
elements: Medical staff appointments are made according to organization policy and consistent with the organization’s resident population, mission, and services to meet resident needs. The appointment, reappointment, and granting of privileges are based on the following: • Evaluation of verified credentials (license, education, training, and experience) • Evaluation of mental and physical health and capabilities • Competency, actual performance, and outcomes of care • Category of the medical staff as stated in the professional registration with the Saudi

group: Assignment of Medical Staff Clinical Privileges
statement: The long-term care organization has a standardized, objective, evidence-based procedure to authorize medical staff to admit and treat residents and/or provide other clinical services consistent with their qualifications.
elements: The long-term care organization’s privilege delineation procedure meets the following criteria: • Standardized, objective, and evidence-based • Documented in organization policies • Active and ongoing as medical staff members’ credentials change • Followed for all classes of medical staff membership • Can be demonstrated to show its effectiveness

The long-term care organization has a credentialing and privileging committee, chaired by the medical director or a designee, that oversees the credentialing and privileging processes to ensure that only qualified physicians and dentists are appointed and granted privileges.

The clinical privileges of all medical staff are made available by printed copy, electronic copy, or other means to the appropriate department/service leaders and to those locations (for example, technology- dependent or high-dependency units) in the organization where the medical staff member will provide services.
Each medical staff member provides only those services specifically granted by the long-term care organization.
The organization identifies the circumstances under which temporary or emergency privileges are granted. Temporary or emergency privileges are not granted for more than 90 days and are not renewable.

group: Ongoing Professional Practice Evaluation of Medical Staff
statement: The long-term care organization uses an ongoing, standardized process to evaluate the quality and safety of resident care provided by each medical staff member.
elements: All medical staff are included in an ongoing professional practice evaluation process as defined by organization policy and standardized evaluation at the department/service level.

The ongoing professional practice evaluation process identifies areas of achievement and potential improvement related to the medical staff member’s behaviors, professional growth, and clinical results, and the results are reviewed with objective, evidence-based information as available. These results are compared to other department/service medical staff members.

The data and information from the monitoring are reviewed at least every 12 months by the individual’s department or service head, senior medical manager, or medical staff body, and the results, conclusions, and any actions taken are documented in the medical staff member’s credential file and other relevant files. The data and information resulting from the medical staff performance review are used to do the following: • Provide feedback and counselling to medical staff regarding their performance • Recommend plans for improvement • Amend clinical privileges as necessary, by expansion or limitation, a period of counselling and

statement: At least every two years, the long-term care organization determines, from the ongoing professional practice evaluation of each medical staff member, if medical staff membership and clinical privileges are to continue with or without modification.
elements: The long-term care organization has a documented process for reappointing all medical staff categories.

Based on the ongoing professional practice evaluation of the medical staff member, the long-term care organization determines, at least every two years, if medical staff membership and clinical privileges are to continue with or without modification.
Each medical staff member’s record includes evidence that all credentials that require periodic renewal, payment of a registration fee, or other action by the medical staff member are current.

Credentials obtained subsequent to initial appointment are evident in the medical staff member’s record and have been verified from the primary source prior to use in modifying or adding to clinical privileges.
The renewal decision is documented in the medical staff member’s credential file and includes the reviewer and any special conditions identified during the review.

statement: The long-term care organization has a uniform process to collect, verify, and evaluate the nursing staff’s credentials (license, education, training, and experience).
elements: The long-term care organization has a standardized procedure, defined in a policy, to collect and document each nursing staff member’s education, certifications, and experience whether full or part time.
Education, training, and certifications are verified from the original source and documented.

Licensure is verified from the original source consistent with the following parameters and documented: • The long-term care organization must verify that the third party implements the verification process as described in the long-term care organization’s policy or regulations and that the process meets the expectations described in these standards. • The affiliated organization that has already conducted primary source verification of the nursing staff applicant is acceptable if the affiliated organization has current Joint Commission International (JCI) accreditation with “full compliance” on its verification process found in MEs 1 and 2 of this standard. • The long-term care organization that bases its decisions in part on information from a designated official governmental or nongovernmental agency must evaluate the agency providing the information initially and then periodically thereafter to ensure that JCI standards continue to be met. • The long-term care organization receives confirmatory documentation.
There is a record maintained of the credentials of every nursing staff member.
The long-term care organization has a process to ensure that contract nurses’ credentials are valid and complete prior to assignment.

The long-term care organization has a process to ensure that nurses who are not organization employees but accompany private physicians and provide services to the organization’s residents have valid credentials.

statement: The long-term care organization has a standardized process to identify job responsibilities and make clinical work assignments based on the nursing staff member’s credentials and any regulatory requirements.
elements: A nursing staff member’s licensure, education/training, and experience are used to make clinical work assignments.

The process considers relevant laws and regulations and ensures registration of all nursing staff with the Saudi Commission for Health Specialties and maintenance of a valid license to practice only within their profession.
The process supports nurse staffing plans developed by the nursing director that maintain an adequate staffing level in all nursing units.

statement: The long-term care organization has a standardized process for nursing staff participation in the organization’s quality improvement activities, including evaluating individual performance when indicated.
elements: Nursing staff participate in the long-term care organization’s quality improvement activities.
The performance of individual nursing staff members is reviewed when indicated by the findings of quality improvement activities.
Appropriate information from the review process is documented in the nurse’s personnel record or a separate credential file.

statement: The long-term care organization has a uniform process to collect, verify, and evaluate other health care practitioners’ credentials (license, education, training, and experience).
elements: The long-term care organization has a standardized process, defined in a policy, to collect and document the education, certifications, and experience of each health care practitioner whether full or part time.
Education, training, and certifications are verified from the original source and documented.

Licensure is verified from the original source consistent with the parameters below and is documented: • The long-term care organization must verify that the third party implements the verification process as described in the long-term care organization’s policy or regulations and that the process meets the expectations described in these standards. • The affiliated organization that has already conducted primary source verification of the other clinical staff applicant is acceptable if the affiliated organization has current Joint Commission International (JCI) accreditation with “full compliance” on its verification process found in MEs 1 and 2 of this standard. • The long-term care organization that bases its decisions in part on information from a designated, official, governmental, or nongovernmental agency must evaluate the agency providing the information initially and then periodically thereafter to ensure that JCI standards continue to be met. • The long-term care organization receives confirmatory documentation.
There is a record maintained on other health care practitioners that contains copies of any required license, certification, or registration.

The long-term care organization has a process to ensure that other staff who are not organization employees but accompany private physicians and provide services to the long-term care organization’s residents have valid credentials comparable to the organization’s requirement for credentials.

statement: The long-term care organization has a uniform process to identify job responsibilities and make clinical work assignments based on other clinical staff credentials and any regulatory requirements.
elements: Licensure, education, training, and experience of other clinical staff are used to make clinical work assignments and develop job responsibilities.

The process considers relevant laws and regulations and ensures registration of all other clinical staff with the Saudi Commission for Health Specialties and maintenance of a valid license to practice only within their profession.
The process supports the staffing process for other clinical staff.

statement: The long-term care organization has a uniform process for other clinical staff participation in the organization’s quality improvement activities.
elements: Other health care practitioners participate in the organization’s quality improvement activities.
The performance of other health care practitioners is reviewed when indicated by the findings of quality improvement activities.
Appropriate information from the review process is documented in the health care practitioner’s record.

statement: Hospital leaders ensure that environmental strategies are formally included and acted on as part of the organization’s operations and governance.
elements: Hospital leaders include environmental sustainability and low-carbon and resilient care on their board agenda to discuss at least once a year, with reporting of progress, declaration of resources allocated, and assessment of the implementation of the strategies. Minutes reflect actions taken and any follow-up on those actions.
Progress on environmental strategies is included in the organization’s annual report for wider public visibility and accountability to the community and other stakeholders.

Hospital leaders appoint or designate, and annually evaluate the performance of, a person in the lead role who reports to the board (for example, chief sustainability officer) to ensure that environmental strategies are part of the organization’s priorities and are effectively implemented in tracking and governance processes. (See also GLD.06.00, ME 1)
The person appointed or designated as having the lead role is responsible for the following: • Defining the hospital’s sustainability plan, strategies, and goals, in consultation with relevant

statement: Hospital leaders establish mechanisms to raise awareness and to engage and train employees on climate change and health across the organization.
elements: All medical and nonmedical staff across the hospital undergo specific yearly training sessions, aimed at providing basic knowledge about climate change, its impact on human health, and good practices they can implement for environmentally sustainable and resilient health care.
Hospital leaders communicate to employees about environmental sustainability and the organization’s low-carbon and resilient care goals and activities.
A process is implemented for collecting staff ideas, which are reviewed by the lead person for sustainability to identify potential new initiatives and priorities.
A module on climate change, environmental sustainability, and low-carbon and resilient care is included in new employee orientation/onboarding. (See also SQE.01.06, ME 1)

statement: Hospital leaders develop and start to implement a plan to measure and reduce the use of materials and environmental resources, including energy, water, and emissions.
elements: Hospital leaders and managers develop a written measurable plan including targets and the monitoring thereof to reduce waste, carbon emissions, and the use of environmental resources.
The percentage of renewable energy (bought or self-produced) compared to the total energy consumption is identified and reported to the board on a yearly basis.
Hospital leaders implement actions to optimize water conservation and report the amount of water conserved to the board on a yearly basis.

Hospital leaders and managers can demonstrate yearly progress regarding the reduction of carbon emissions or negative environmental impacts of operations in at least one of the following soft facilities management areas: • Waste management • Cleaning practices • Linen and laundry services

Hospital leaders and managers contribute to reducing the carbon intensity of food and catering supplies; for instance, by sourcing at least 50% of locally produced food whenever practicable and by providing vegetarian options daily.
Clinical practices are evaluated to reduce the environmental impact.

statement: Hospital leaders implement actions to reduce the environmental impact of the supply chain across all operations and identify areas to reduce the unnecessary use of supplies within the hospital.
elements: Climate and environmental sustainability criteria are included in the hospital procurement guidelines. (See also GLD.05.02, ME 3)

For any new contract with suppliers or vendors, department managers prioritize suppliers and vendors that have sustainability and carbon emission reduction objectives in place. (See also GLD.05.02, ME 3)

Hospital leaders and department managers identify opportunities to optimize processes within the hospital by identifying unnecessary and/or avoidable supplies in at least three of the following areas: • Pharmaceuticals and other chemicals used for treatments • Chemicals used for sterilizing, disinfecting, and cleaning purposes • Food and agricultural products • Medical devices • Hospital equipment and instruments
Hospital leaders and department managers implement actions to assess the benefits of reusable items instead of single-use materials in clinical and nonclinical areas. (See also PCI.03.01, ME 1)

statement: Hospital leaders assess the environmental risks and scenarios that may affect service delivery, hospital operations, and patient populations, with plans to comply with local emergency preparedness recommendations and rules, including those required by property insurance coverage.
elements: Climate change impacts are included in the hospital’s risk register or equivalent document.

Hospital leaders develop a written plan of adaptive actions to mitigate current and future climate- related hazards and risks based on recent (that is, within the last three years) information, and progresses toward the organization’s agreed targets. (See also FMS.09.00, MEs 1 and 2)

An assessment of the environmental risks, scenarios, and vulnerabilities within the communities is conducted every three years. The results are presented in a report and inform the plan of adaptive actions, which is updated accordingly. (See also FMS.09.00, ME 3)

Hospital leaders develop preparedness programs for adverse weather scenarios and disruptive events. The preparedness plan is tested and updated annually and includes measures taken to train the employees to respond to these scenarios. (See also FMS.02.00, ME 1; FMS.09.00, ME 1)
